And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant, and he became one of the disbelievers.

Then, after Satan had led them astray from obedience to Our command by enticing them toward that tree, and had removed them from the state they were in, We said, "Descend, all of you. You are enemies of one another, and you shall have a dwelling place on the earth and enjoyment for a time." Then Adam received words from his Lord and turned to Him in repentance, and his Lord accepted his repentance, for He is the Oft-Returning, the Most Merciful.

"Then, when We commanded the angels to bow before Adam, they all bowed. Now observe the exaltation of this corrupt and blood-shedding creature: it is being prostrated to by the angels of high rank and is raised above the angels. Why? Firstly, because the secret of recognizing God was bestowed upon it, and secondly, because it was created as a being endowed with will. Man may freely choose whatever path he wishes. In short, this dual nature of human disposition, his authority over his own will, his freedom to determine the path of his life through it, his responsibility for guiding humanity through his own particular efforts and struggle, and his capacity to bring this duty to completion are the things in which the secret of his great honour lies."

Thus, in this gathering, in obedience to the command of the Almighty, all the angels prostrated themselves before Adam, the earthly being. "But Iblis refused. He was consumed by the pride of his own greatness and became one of the disobedient." 

In this gathering, the wicked creature appears in embodied form. Disobedience to the Almighty takes place in the very presence of the Divine Majesty, and the favour and honour of the one who was given excellence is denied. This wicked creature persists in sin, and all the doors of understanding and discernment are closed to it.

From the context of the discourse it becomes clear that Iblis, although he lived among the angels, was not one of them. For had he been among the angels, he would not have had the capacity to disobey, since the attribute and characteristic of the angels is: "They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded" (لَا یَعۡصُوۡنَ مَا اَمَرَھُمۡ وَیَفۡعَلُوۡنَ مَا یُوۡمَرُوۡنَ). Although this exceptive clause, "all the angels prostrated except Iblis," apparently indicates that Iblis was one of the angels, it was introduced into the flow of speech because he used to associate with the angels. The Arabs say جَاءَ بَنُوا فُلَانٍ اِلَّا اَحۡمَدٌ, "the people of so-and-so came, except Ahmad," although Ahmad was not one of them but lived in their neighbourhood. Elsewhere the Qur'an explicitly states that Iblis was one of the jinn, and that the jinn were created by Allah from a flame of fire. From this it is definitively known that he was not among the angels.

The commentary, following this passage, moves to the field of battle in which the khalifah of evil, Iblis, and the khalifah of God, the human being, are in constant conflict. This struggle is in truth being fought within the conscience of the human being and in the arenas of his heart and mind, and in it those succeed who possess firm resolve. Those who prevail are those who firmly grasp the covenant they made with Allah. As a person becomes ever more a slave to the desires of his own self, he moves further away from Allah, and the forces of evil gain ground.

﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from it freely wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers.﴾ Then We said: O Adam, you and your wife dwell in the Garden and eat from it in ease wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree lest you be counted among the wrongdoers. Every fruit of the Garden was made lawful for Adam and Eve, with only one tree excepted.

Only one tree... Perhaps there is an indication in this that the human race on earth would be bound by the limits of lawful and unlawful, for how could free and self-determined will come into being without bounds and limits, and how could there be any distinction between a human being who moves by will and an animal that is compelled? Without this, there would be no possibility that the human being could be tested regarding adherence to the limits and bounds imposed by Allah. It is this power of will that distinguishes a true human being from a human-shaped animal that grazes about the world like cattle, and nothing more.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 36:

فَأَزَلَّهُمَا الشَّيْطَانُ عَنْهَا فَأَخْرَجَهُمَا مِمَّا كَانَا فِيهِ "At last Satan caused them both to slip away from it [the tree], and removed them from the state in which they had been." ........ Look at this masterpiece of expression. Satan made them slip. The very word "slip" paints the whole situation as a picture. It is as though we are seeing with our own eyes Satan pushing them again and again to drive them out of Paradise. It is as though he suddenly gives a shove to their firmness, and they fall and come down.

Here the first experience of the struggle between Adam and Iblis is completed. Adam (peace be upon him) forgets his covenant; he becomes weak before its seduction. The command of Allah comes forward as truth, and the decree of Divine Judgment is announced thus:

وَقُلْنَا اهْبِطُوا بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ وَلَكُمْ فِي الأرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَى حِينٍ "We said: Go down, some of you enemies to others, and for you on earth there is a place of settlement and provision for a time." This announcement was that now the battle between Adam and Iblis is to begin in its appointed place, that is, on this earth, and that this battle will continue thus until the Day of Resurrection.

After falling, Adam (peace be upon him) now recovers and rises, for falling and rising is the nature of man. Now the mercy of Allah takes him under the shade of its mercy and protection, and whoever takes refuge in the lap of Allah's mercy and comes to fall at His threshold, this boundless mercy always covers him.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 37:

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He turned to him in forgiveness. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ At that time Adam repented to his Lord by learning a few words, and his Lord accepted them, because He is the One who forgives greatly and shows mercy. This is a perpetual covenant of Allah with Adam and the offspring of Adam. The matter is complete. Adam was established on this earth as a vicegerent of Allah, empowered and endowed with will. His task is that he chooses either the path of success or the path of ruin and destruction.

This battle now shifts to its real arena, the earth, and from this point it continues without a moment's pause. Thus, from the dawn of humanity, man learns the secret of how to attain success and triumph in this world, if he seeks it, and what path leads to humiliation and disgrace, if he seeks that instead.

* * *

Pause for a moment and look back at some aspects of this fascinating account of early humanity. Allah addresses the angels saying: "Indeed, I am going to place a khalifah (vicegerent) upon the earth." It becomes clear that Adam was created from the outset for the earth. The question then arises: why was he first shown Paradise? Why was a tree made forbidden? Why was he put to trial, and thus brought down to the earth, even though, according to the predetermined plan, he was created precisely so that he might carry out the duty of khilafah on earth?

I believe that this first experience of the conflict between Adam and Iblis was arranged precisely so that, through it, Adam (peace be upon him) might be prepared to conduct the affairs of khilafah. In this way, Adam's hidden capacities were awakened. He was made to experience a lapse and was made to face its consequences. After that, he was taught remorse and regret, repentance, the recognition of the enemy, and the way to come under the secure refuge of Allah.

The story of the forbidden tree, Satan's whispering to make him taste it, the first man's forgetfulness of the covenant, his awakening after forgetting, remorse and seeking forgiveness: all these states are two realities of which every human being has an experience at every moment.

It was the requirement of Allah's mercy and compassion upon this human being that he should descend to his abode of khilafah equipped with all such experiences, the occurrence of which was an important part of his life, so that he might be prepared for this long and unending conflict (the conflict of Adam and Iblis), and that this experience might be for him a lesson and a cause of admonition.

You may ask again: then where did this experience take place? Which is the Paradise in which Adam and Eve dwelt for a time? What are the angels? What is the reality of Iblis? How did Allah address them, and how did they reply?

Brother! These and all other such matters mentioned in the Noble Qur'an are in fact among the secrets and mysteries of Allah, whose true reality is known to Allah alone. Allah, who is All-Knowing and All-Wise, knows that for man there is no benefit in attaining the true knowledge of these things and in discovering their essence. Therefore Allah has not given man the capacity to learn the reality of these things and to comprehend their true nature. He cannot encompass their essence, because the faculties Allah has given man were given only so that through them he might carry out the affairs of khilafah on this earth. These faculties cannot be used to acquire knowledge of the realities of the unseen. Moreover, it is not necessary for the duty of khilafah that we should also know the realities of the unseen. How far has man subjugated the laws of Allah's power? How much knowledge of the secrets of the universe has been given to man? How many hidden mysteries are there that are concealed from his sight? These are matters for whose knowledge and comprehension mankind has absolutely no need. The state of man is that, despite unveiling the countless secrets of this universe, he is still completely unaware of the events and occurrences that are about to emerge in the next moment. Despite all the instruments and means available to him, he knows nothing of what will happen in the next moment. He does not know whether the breath he is now taking is his last breath or whether he will be able to take another breath after it. Among the realities hidden behind the veil of the unseen, this is but one small example. In short, for the performance of the duty of khilafah, it is not necessary for him to know any of these unseen things. Rather, I would say that if some secrets were to be disclosed to man, they would have an adverse effect on his performance. Thus there are many kinds of such hidden secrets and mysteries which are concealed behind the veil of the unseen and of which no one besides Allah has knowledge.

Therefore it is not the work of the intellect of man to exert itself fruitlessly in this field, for it does not possess the means and instruments that are useful in this domain. Whoever strives in this field and exhausts his powers will find his striving wasted, utterly lost and fruitless.

When human reason does not possess the means by which it could perceive anything about the world of the unseen, it has no right to deny the unseen realities out of mere obstinacy. For before denying anything, it is necessary to have knowledge of its existence. The perception of the unseen is not the function of reason, nor do these things fall within its range of power and sphere of action. It has neither the means to perceive them, nor does reason need to perceive them, nor is it a religious duty of human reason to perceive them.

We acknowledge that accepting superstitions and myths is extremely dangerous and harmful, but it is far more harmful and dangerous for a person to deny something that lies beyond the reach of his knowledge, or to regard a reality as impossible merely because it is beyond the limits of human perception and the bounds of human power. If we set this as the standard of knowledge and certainty, it would be an animal standard. It would mean that humanity would regress and return to the level of animality, where nothing exists beyond the world of the perceptible, and where there is no possibility of going beyond the four walls of the sensible to reach absolute existence.

Therefore, it is better for us to entrust the world of the unseen to that Being who is the Master of this world, and for us, what suffices is what He informs us of. Only that much is needed by us in this world which will bring about our spiritual and material reformation, and nothing more!

Now we take up those aspects of this story which point to certain human and cosmic realities: the concept of the universe of existence, its mutual connection, human nature and its standard of good and evil, and so on, for it is in these aspects that there lies provision for human guidance and benefit.

Here, in keeping with the spirit of Zilal al-Qur'an, we wish to cast a brief glance, in brief, at these indications, concepts and realities.

1. What becomes clear from this story is the status and dignity which the Islamic conception of life grants to man himself: his importance in this universe, the importance of the values by which he is judged, and the importance of his role on earth, and so on. Furthermore, what is the nature of the relationship between man and the divine covenant according to the Islamic conception of life? And what is the reality of the covenant on the basis of which man is the khalifatullah fil-ardh (vicegerent of Allah on earth)?

Thus, the grand assembly held in the highest realm to honour humanity, and the magnificent proclamation that follows it, make clear what the worth of the human being is according to the Islamic conception of life: that is, he is a creature who has been granted the honour of being Allah's vicegerent on earth. This is most clearly manifested in the scene where, at Allah's command, all the angels bow in prostration before this creature of clay. In this gathering Iblis becomes arrogant and is cast out from the Divine presence, and all of this takes place from beginning to end under the direct supervision of the Supreme Majesty.

When this viewpoint about man is adopted, it has great and profound effects on his concept in both the theoretical and practical worlds.

The first concept that emerges is that man is the master of this earth; it has been created for him. All the things in this universe have also been created for this man. Therefore he is more honoured, more precious and more dear than any material thing; he is higher than all the material values of the world. Hence, it cannot be permitted that man be humiliated and debased for the sake of any great material interest or the greatest material progress. Accordingly, no kind of material research or conquest, no kind of material production, and no element of material substances can be disregarded, because all materials and all products have been created solely for the sake of man, so that his humanity may flourish and so that his life as a human being may be sustained here. Therefore, it cannot be permitted that, merely to preserve human life, one should abandon and destroy its lofty values and the constituent elements of its dignity and nobility.

2. The second aspect of this story is that on this earth man is the primary effective force. It is he who changes the face and form of the earth, and it is he who determines the nature of mutual connection and relationship in human social life. It is he who is the leader and commander of the caravan of life, and who determines the direction of its journey. No system of the means of production, or of the distribution of production, has been granted the station of leadership over man, such that the reins of man would be in their hands and he, humiliated and debased like an animal, would walk behind them in a state of helplessness, as some of today's materialistic philosophies depict him. Their concept of humanity is that in its life... he has no standing at all. In these systems, as the value of the machine increases, the humanity of man is trampled underfoot.

It is beyond doubt that the system of life which a person prescribes for mankind is either prescribed in accordance with this Islamic view, or it is formed in accordance with that materialistic outlook. As a result, lofty human values either attain ascendancy or are trampled. Man either becomes the most honoured of creatures, or becomes a contemptible machine and tool. In today's materialistic world, the trampling and destruction of every kind of human liberty, human nobility and the humanity of man for the sake of mere material progress and abundant production is the natural result of the viewpoint which these materialistic systems hold regarding the reality of man and his importance in the world.

But in contrast to this materialistic world, the concept which Islam gives regarding the reality of man and the purpose of his creation, in its balance and standard, elevates the values of human dignity, moral virtues gain importance, and qualities such as faith, goodness and sincerity acquire significance in human life, because according to the Islamic conception of life, these are the lofty values on which the responsibility of khilafah on earth depends.

"Then whenever guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve." (Qur'an 2:38)

In short, these values are more precious and superior to all material values. But it should also be kept in mind that the attainment of these material values is also included within the objectives of khilafah on earth. To that extent, these material values should be subordinate to the lofty moral and spiritual values, and should not themselves become the ultimate goals. That is why Islam inclines the human conscience towards purity and towards leading an exalted life, whereas all other materialistic doctrines look upon all spiritual values with contempt, and sacrifice even the dignity of humanity for the sake of materialism. And for what is all this sacrifice made? Merely for the sake of the necessities of life, the abundance of luxuries, and the gluttony of animals. (For details, see the book "Insan Islam aur Maddiyat" by Sayyid Muhammad Qutb.)

How lofty is the Islamic concept of man? Consider this aspect: according to it, man is a creature endowed with free will, possessing determination and resolve. For if he were not endowed with free will and firm resolve, what would be the significance of his covenant with Allah? For it is upon free will that man is held accountable and deserves reward and punishment. If he remains firm in his resolve and gains mastery over his carnal desires, then in this way he can attain a station even higher than the angels, and can protect himself from every deviation that confronts him. But if his desires overcome this resolve, if darkness prevails over guidance in his life, and he forgets the covenant of "Am I not your Lord?" which he made with his Creator, then he may fall from that lofty station and prepare for himself all the means of wretchedness and misfortune.

The Islamic system of life has indicated, through this story, only a glimpse of the principles of nobility and excellence which it has given to man in this universe. Man has been reminded that the paths of happiness and wretchedness, of exaltation and abasement, diverge from a point where there is a free, exalted human being on one side and a shackled, helpless animal that has fallen into the depths of degradation on the other.

In depicting the events narrated in this story, an effort has been made to remind us of the nature of the battle between Adam and Iblis: on one side is the covenant between the servant and God, and on the other side is the mischief of Satan. On one front is faith, and on the other is disbelief; on one front is truth, and on the other is falsehood. One quality belongs to the people of guidance, and the other to the people of misguidance. But where is the battlefield? It is man and his life. The victor is also man, and the vanquished is also man. This marketplace of profit and loss lies within his own conscience. Therefore Allah warns him to remain alert at all times, for he is always on the field of battle. There are only two outcomes: either he will be plundered, or he will return victorious with the spoils of war.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verses 38–39 (part 2 of 3)**

Through this story, the Islamic concepts of error and repentance are also clarified. Since sin is committed by an individual, repentance is also an individual act. This is a clear and straightforward view with no complexity. Unlike the People of the Church (Ahl al-Kanisa), there is no room in Islam for the idea that a person becomes a sinner before birth. In Islam there is no concept of a theological atonement for sins, such that Jesus (peace be upon him) was crucified to cleanse humanity of the sin of Adam (peace be upon him). That is a mistaken notion. The slip of Adam (peace be upon him) was an individual act, and the way to be freed from it was also an individual act: remorse and repentance. This is entirely clear, plain, and comprehensible. Every one of the children of Adam (peace be upon him) is responsible for their own deeds, and the door of repentance is open to all. Plain, simple, and easy:

*"Even if you have broken your repentance a hundred times, come back."*

Consider how clear and appealing this concept is. Every person should bear their own burden. This concept motivates every human being to strive for the attainment of good, and they do not fall victim to despair and hopelessness, because ﴿Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful﴾.

**Indications from the Story of Adam**

This is only one aspect of the story of Adam. In this place in Fi Zilal al-Quran, we will be content with this one aspect. Within this aspect alone lies a great treasure of priceless truths and wholesome concepts. This story contains an abundant store of valuable indications and guidance.

In it, the foundations of the Islamic concept of society and the manner of social life have been established, and these have been strengthened through goodness, morality, and other virtues. When we reflect on this aspect, we come to appreciate the importance and purposefulness of the Quranic stories, and how these stories strengthen the foundations of the Islamic worldview and clarify the lofty values that are built upon these foundations. The universe that Allah has created, which turns towards Allah and to which it must finally return, deserves that within it those values be exalted which are exalted in the sight of Allah.

**The Covenant of Human Vicegerency**

The human covenant of vicegerency (khilafah) is based on divine guidance. Its essential condition is that the human being will live in accordance with the Islamic system of life. After this covenant, the position becomes that the human being, as a creature endowed with will, stands at a crossroads. On one side, God is calling them, and they are listening. If they decide, they set out upon the Straight Path. On the other side, Satan is calling them. There is misguidance ........ or guidance, and falsehood ........ or truth, and success ........ or loss ........ This is the reality, and the Quran always presents it as the primary reality. All the ideas and concepts of humanity and all the ways of life rest solely upon this one reality.

**Lesson 4 at a Glance**

Here the discourse turns towards the Children of Israel. In Medina, they alone strongly opposed the Islamic call. They sought to end and resist the Islamic call through both open and secret stratagems. They continually plotted against the Islamic movement, and from the emergence of Islam up to this stage of the call, their intrigues never diminished for a moment. They had become certain that the keys of power were being transferred, one by one, into the hands of the Muslims. Since the wars between the Aws and the Khazraj ended, and the avenues closed through which the Jews had gained influence over the polytheists of Medina and affected them, and then when the formation of a new system of life began for the Muslims on the basis of this new Book, the Jews were acutely feeling that this new movement had expelled them from the important sectors of literature, culture, and both the economy and finance.

This, in short, is the struggle that the Jews began against Islam and the Muslims from the first day, and to this day it remains unchanged. Even today they are using the same crude weapons against Islam and the Muslims that they used at that time. The forms of the weapons are different, and their style is new, but their reality and their nature are exactly the same. It should be remembered that the Jews maintain this hostile attitude towards Islam and the Muslims despite the fact that, throughout human history, the whole world has always spurned this people. They were repeatedly driven from one place to another and from another back to the first. These people wandered through the dust. Centuries passed in this way, but ultimately they found rest and peaceful life in the world of Islam, which is open to all and in which, on the basis of faith and religion, no one is subjected to hatred. Where sectarian and religious riots have always been regarded with disapproval, and where every person who does not harm Islam or plot against the Muslims, and who lives peacefully, has always been granted open permission to come.

It was expected that the Jews of Medina would be the first to accept this new Messenger and this new call and believe. Whereas the Quran, in its general character, was confirming all the teachings that had been stated in the Torah. Furthermore, they were also awaiting the arrival of a new Messenger. They knew his attributes, and they possessed the good news about him in their heavenly scriptures. They would always supplicate to Allah, asking that, through the sake of the awaited Prophet, He grant them victory over the polytheists of Arabia.

This lesson is the first part of the extensive discourse of the Quran with the Children of Israel. This discourse with the Children of Israel is, in reality, a refutation of their position and a profound critical assault upon them, to expose their conspiracies. It was initiated as a matter of necessity and need at a time when the Islamic call, having come to Medina, had expended its full strength in calling them to Islam, had established the proof against them, and all means had been used to draw them towards this new movement.

This lesson begins with the sublime call of the Lord, in which He reminds them of His blessings and calls upon them to fulfil their covenant so that Allah may fulfil His covenant with them. As a preface, Allah first calls them to the fear of God, piety, and purity, and after this they are invited to accept this Book and this guidance, which confirms all the books and guidance that Allah Himself sent down to them. He condemns the attitude they adopted towards the Quran, and He counsels them not to be among those who were the first to reject this Book. Their behaviour of concealing the truth and mixing truth with falsehood in order to lead people astray from the right path is also condemned, especially the Muslims, and to stir up mischief within the ranks of the Islamic community and spread discord. Likewise, they were spreading doubts into the hearts of those who were newly embracing Islam. Allah advises them to abandon these acts of mischief and to join the Islamic community, to pray with the Muslims, to pay zakat, to establish the system of the congregation, and to seek help through patience and prayer in the difficult task of fully merging themselves into this new religion. Allah strongly criticises their conduct, in that they tell the polytheists to believe, but do not believe themselves, nor do they submit before Him.

After this, the Children of Israel are reminded of the blessings with which they had been favoured throughout their history. In the course of this discourse, the audience, the Children of Israel, are addressed as though those very people were present in the time of Moses (peace be upon him), the same people who are today in Medina. The reason is that the Children of Israel are one nation, and for centuries they have remained upon one nationality and the same disposition. Just as afterwards they remained the same in every age and continued to possess these same characteristics.

After this, they are warned of that day, the Day of Judgement, on which no soul will be able to repay on behalf of another. No intercession will avail, nor will any ransom or compensation be accepted from anyone, and on that day all people will be without helper or supporter, and there will be no one to save them from the punishment of the Hereafter.

Now there is presented to them the scene in which Allah delivered them from Pharaoh. This depiction is so vivid that it is as though the sight is before their eyes. Then there is mention of the favours that were bestowed upon them one after another. Shades of clouds were provided over their heads. They were sustained with manna and quails, and water was provided for them by splitting stones. After this, they are shamed by being reminded of the rebellions and the wickedness they committed, one after another, in return for these blessings. When Allah pardoned one of their errors, they fell into another. When He freed them from one calamity, they arranged for themselves another.

But the Children of Israel were, after all, the Children of Israel. The same corruption and malice, the same deviation and misguidance, and insistence upon it. They always violated the commands of Allah. They betrayed trusts. They broke covenants after firmly binding them. They discarded every pact made with Allah and with the Prophets. They advanced to the point of killing the Prophets without any justification. They began to deny the signs of their Lord. They worshipped the calf. Their insolence towards Allah reached such a level that they refused to believe until they should see Allah with their own eyes. Consider this carefully! After this, these people openly violated the command of Allah, and upon entering the town they did not utter the words that Allah had taught them and had commanded them to say. They continued to violate the laws of the Sabbath. They completely forgot the covenant of Mount Sinai. Regarding the cow that Allah had commanded them to slaughter, they began to procrastinate and started disputing and debating.

In short, they carried out all these actions while maintaining the claim that if there is any guided community at all, it is only the Jews and the Children of Israel. On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will be pleased only with the Children of Israel. All other religions are false, and all other nations are astray. The Quran, therefore, refutes this in this very first critical discourse, and says that whoever among the other nations believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, their reward is with their Lord. There shall be no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve.

This powerful assault on the Children of Israel, or the criticisms that come later in the course of the discussion of the surah, was an urgent need of the time. There was a pressing need to expose the hollow claims of the Children of Israel, to unveil all their conspiracies, and to make the Muslims aware of all the plots and deceits being carried out against their new society. The principles upon which the Children of Israel were carrying out these conspiracies were instilled into the minds and hearts of the Muslims. Moreover, the Muslims were encouraged to unite to confront this turmoil and mischief.

This criticism of the history of the Children of Israel was also necessary so that the Muslims themselves might become alert. They needed to know what difficulties lay before them in this new office of earthly vicegerency, where the dangers of slipping lay, and what slips had been made by the previous nations that had held this office, and because of which they were deprived of the office of vicegerency, and how they lost the honour of preserving and guarding the trust of Allah on this earth. And how and for what reasons the system of human leadership slipped from their hands. In short, throughout this entire critical discussion, the Muslims are warned, at some points openly and at others through hints, about what difficult situations they will face on this path and in this office, where there is a strong fear of slips and stumbling. As in the second part of this discussion, there will likewise be similar warnings.

In Medina, the Muslim community had an urgent need for these admonitions and guidance, just as the Muslim community has always, at every time and in every age, needed this guidance. Muslims should study the Quran with open eyes, with deep and enlightening awareness, and adopt the teachings and guidance that the Most Exalted and Supreme Leadership gave to the Muslims while they were fighting their ancient enemies. Muslims should always clearly know how to confront the conspiracies and deceits of these ancestral enemies, which they carry out through extremely secret means and deep, deceptive methods against the Islamic society. A person whose heart is not illuminated by the light of faith, and who, in the whole of his life, outwardly and inwardly, secretly and openly, does not take guidance from this Most Exalted and Supreme divine leadership, will never be able to discover those hidden paths, impure paths, and underground means through which these dangerous and impure conspiracies enter the Islamic society.

In this discussion, a particular aspect of the artistic and psychological harmony of the Quran's style deserves attention. The discourse on the history of the Children of Israel begins immediately after the conclusion of the story of the vicegerency of Adam. This discourse begins within the mental background to which we have pointed in the story of Adam and Iblis. Accordingly, the style of the Quranic expression takes into account that there must be complete correspondence and harmony between the story being presented and the environment within which the story is being presented.

Look back: during the discussion it was said that "Allah has created for you, human beings, all the creatures of this earth." After this, the account of Adam's khilafah (vicegerency) on earth begins, and a public covenant takes place between Adam and Allah. Adam is given precedence over the angels. After this come the themes of Adam being given instructions, his forgetfulness and error, his repentance and remorse, Divine guidance, and Divine forgiveness. And within Paradise itself, Adam (peace be upon him) is shown a glimpse of the long and unending struggle between the forces of evil and the forces of good, which was to continue in this world until the Day of Resurrection. The forces of goodness, reform and construction appear in the form of a human being who is a believer and holds fast to the rope of Allah, while the forces of evil, corruption and destruction stand embodied in the form of Iblis.

Having said all this, criticism of the Children of Israel now begins. It is described how they made a firm covenant with Allah and then broke it, what blessings were showered upon them and how they were ungrateful for them. Accordingly, Allah deprived them of the office of vicegerency on earth and imposed humiliation and wretchedness upon them. The believers are made aware of their deceptions, and it is told what lapses occurred from them in their history. Here a clear connection of meaning emerges between the making of a khalifah on earth and, after that, the making of the Children of Israel as khalifah, and the context of the discourse becomes clearly interconnected.

In view of the Qur'an, the purpose here is not to present the national history of the Children of Israel; rather, it refers to certain events of that history, with suitable brevity or suitable elaboration, presenting some scenes from that long history. Before Surah al-Baqarah, this story also recurs repeatedly in all the Meccan surahs of the Qur'an.

However, the purpose of narrating that story there was to give encouragement to the small community of Muslims in the turbulent period of Meccan life. At that time the aim was to present before the small community of believers the da'wah experiences of the caravan of the people of faith from the beginning of creation until today, and to give them guidance in accordance with the demands of the stage they were then facing in Makkah. But here (in Madinah) the aim was to make the Muslims aware of the intrigues and evil designs of the Jews, and to warn the Islamic community of what the Jews' intentions are and what resources they have to put those intentions into action. Furthermore, the Muslim ummah is being directed so that it does not itself fall into the same shortcomings and weaknesses into which the Jews had fallen before. Since the aims in Makkah and in Madinah were entirely different, the Qur'an presented the story of the Children of Israel here in a different style and from different aspects, although the realities presented were exactly the same in both places, namely the deviation of the Children of Israel and their departure from the straight path. (When the Meccan surahs, which were revealed before al-Baqarah in order of revelation, are discussed, we will explain this point further there.)

Wherever the story of the Children of Israel appears in the Qur'an, a careful study shows that the context in which it is presented is in harmony with it and completes the purposes, meanings and intellectual guidance and directions of that place. Here too, the story is fully in harmony with its context. Here, first, the theme of human dignity and honour was stated. After this came the themes of the covenant between man and Allah and man's forgetfulness, in which it is indicated in passing that humanity is a single unit, and that the messengers who came to it and the religion they presented all issue from one single source. In the course of the discourse, there are also repeated allusions to the human self and its constituent elements, and it is shown what the consequences will be of neglecting these constituent elements and deviating from them, upon which the human being's being Allah's khalifah on earth depends. Their importance is such that whoever denies them will become a denier of his own humanity; he will lose the very means by which he was given the office of vicegerency on earth, and as a result the human being will fall back into the lowest station of animality.

The story of the Children of Israel appears more than any other story in the Qur'an. Its various stations and its lessons are of great importance. From them is revealed the wise method of training which Allah adopted in order to prepare the ummah of Muslims for the office of the great vicegerency and for the purpose of its teaching and education.

After this general discussion, we now wish to cast a detailed look at the Qur'anic verses.

This battle now shifts to its real arena, the earth, and from this point it continues without a moment's pause. Thus, from the dawn of humanity, man learns the secret of how to attain success and triumph in this world, if he seeks it, and what path leads to humiliation and disgrace, if he seeks that instead.

Pause for a moment and look back at some aspects of this fascinating account of early humanity. Allah addresses the angels saying: "Indeed, I am going to place a khalifah (vicegerent) upon the earth." It becomes clear that Adam was created from the outset for the earth. The question then arises: why was he first shown Paradise? Why was a tree made forbidden? Why was he put to trial, and thus brought down to the earth, even though, according to the predetermined plan, he was created precisely so that he might carry out the duty of khilafah on earth?

I believe that this first experience of the conflict between Adam and Iblis was arranged precisely so that, through it, Adam (peace be upon him) might be prepared to conduct the affairs of khilafah. In this way, Adam's hidden capacities were awakened. He was made to experience a lapse and was made to face its consequences. After that, he was taught remorse and regret, repentance, the recognition of the enemy, and the way to come under the secure refuge of Allah.

The story of the forbidden tree, Satan's whispering to make him taste it, the first man's forgetfulness of the covenant, his awakening after forgetting, remorse and seeking forgiveness: all these states are two realities of which every human being has an experience at every moment.

It was the requirement of Allah's mercy and compassion upon this human being that he should descend to his abode of khilafah equipped with all such experiences, the occurrence of which was an important part of his life, so that he might be prepared for this long and unending conflict (the conflict of Adam and Iblis), and that this experience might be for him a lesson and a cause of admonition.

You may ask again: then where did this experience take place? Which is the Paradise in which Adam and Eve dwelt for a time? What are the angels? What is the reality of Iblis? How did Allah address them, and how did they reply?

Brother! These and all other such matters mentioned in the Noble Qur'an are in fact among the secrets and mysteries of Allah, whose true reality is known to Allah alone. Allah, who is All-Knowing and All-Wise, knows that for man there is no benefit in attaining the true knowledge of these things and in discovering their essence. Therefore Allah has not given man the capacity to learn the reality of these things and to comprehend their true nature. He cannot encompass their essence, because the faculties Allah has given man were given only so that through them he might carry out the affairs of khilafah on this earth. These faculties cannot be used to acquire knowledge of the realities of the unseen. Moreover, it is not necessary for the duty of khilafah that we should also know the realities of the unseen. How far has man subjugated the laws of Allah's power? How much knowledge of the secrets of the universe has been given to man? How many hidden mysteries are there that are concealed from his sight? These are matters for whose knowledge and comprehension mankind has absolutely no need. The state of man is that, despite unveiling the countless secrets of this universe, he is still completely unaware of the events and occurrences that are about to emerge in the next moment. Despite all the instruments and means available to him, he knows nothing of what will happen in the next moment. He does not know whether the breath he is now taking is his last breath or whether he will be able to take another breath after it. Among the realities hidden behind the veil of the unseen, this is but one small example. In short, for the performance of the duty of khilafah, it is not necessary for him to know any of these unseen things. Rather, I would say that if some secrets were to be disclosed to man, they would have an adverse effect on his performance. Thus there are many kinds of such hidden secrets and mysteries which are concealed behind the veil of the unseen and of which no one besides Allah has knowledge.

Therefore it is not the work of the intellect of man to exert itself fruitlessly in this field, for it does not possess the means and instruments that are useful in this domain. Whoever strives in this field and exhausts his powers will find his striving wasted, utterly lost and fruitless.

When human reason does not possess the means by which it could perceive anything about the world of the unseen, it has no right to deny the unseen realities out of mere obstinacy. For before denying anything, it is necessary to have knowledge of its existence. The perception of the unseen is not the function of reason, nor do these things fall within its range of power and sphere of action. It has neither the means to perceive them, nor does reason need to perceive them, nor is it a religious duty of human reason to perceive them.

We acknowledge that accepting superstitions and myths is extremely dangerous and harmful, but it is far more harmful and dangerous for a person to deny something that lies beyond the reach of his knowledge, or to regard a reality as impossible merely because it is beyond the limits of human perception and the bounds of human power. If we set this as the standard of knowledge and certainty, it would be an animal standard. It would mean that humanity would regress and return to the level of animality, where nothing exists beyond the world of the perceptible, and where there is no possibility of going beyond the four walls of the sensible to reach absolute existence.

Therefore, it is better for us to entrust the world of the unseen to that Being who is the Master of this world, and for us, what suffices is what He informs us of. Only that much is needed by us in this world which will bring about our spiritual and material reformation, and nothing more!
