Hence, it cannot be permitted that man be humiliated and debased for the sake of any great material interest or the greatest material progress. Accordingly, no kind of material research or conquest, no kind of material production, and no element of material substances can be disregarded, because all materials and all products have been created solely for the sake of man, so that his humanity may flourish and so that his life as a human being may be sustained here. Therefore, it cannot be permitted that, merely to preserve human life, one should abandon and destroy its lofty values and the constituent elements of its dignity and nobility.

2. The second aspect of this story is that on this earth man is the primary effective force. It is he who changes the face and form of the earth, and it is he who determines the nature of mutual connection and relationship in human social life. It is he who is the leader and commander of the caravan of life, and who determines the direction of its journey. No system of the means of production, or of the distribution of production, has been granted the station of leadership over man, such that the reins of man would be in their hands and he, humiliated and debased like an animal, would walk behind them in a state of helplessness, as some of today's materialistic philosophies depict him. Their concept of humanity is that in its life... he has no standing at all. In these systems, as the value of the machine increases, the humanity of man is trampled underfoot.

It is beyond doubt that the system of life which a person prescribes for mankind is either prescribed in accordance with this Islamic view, or it is formed in accordance with that materialistic outlook. As a result, lofty human values either attain ascendancy or are trampled. Man either becomes the most honoured of creatures, or becomes a contemptible machine and tool. In today's materialistic world, the trampling and destruction of every kind of human liberty, human nobility and the humanity of man for the sake of mere material progress and abundant production is the natural result of the viewpoint which these materialistic systems hold regarding the reality of man and his importance in the world.

But in contrast to this materialistic world, the concept which Islam gives regarding the reality of man and the purpose of his creation, in its balance and standard, elevates the values of human dignity, moral virtues gain importance, and qualities such as faith, goodness and sincerity acquire significance in human life, because according to the Islamic conception of life, these are the lofty values on which the responsibility of khilafah on earth depends.

"Then whenever guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve." (Qur'an 2:38)

In short, these values are more precious and superior to all material values. But it should also be kept in mind that the attainment of these material values is also included within the objectives of khilafah on earth. To that extent, these material values should be subordinate to the lofty moral and spiritual values, and should not themselves become the ultimate goals. That is why Islam inclines the human conscience towards purity and towards leading an exalted life, whereas all other materialistic doctrines look upon all spiritual values with contempt, and sacrifice even the dignity of humanity for the sake of materialism. And for what is all this sacrifice made? Merely for the sake of the necessities of life, the abundance of luxuries, and the gluttony of animals. (For details, see the book "Insan Islam aur Maddiyat" by Sayyid Muhammad Qutb.)

How lofty is the Islamic concept of man? Consider this aspect: according to it, man is a creature endowed with free will, possessing determination and resolve. For if he were not endowed with free will and firm resolve, what would be the significance of his covenant with Allah? For it is upon free will that man is held accountable and deserves reward and punishment. If he remains firm in his resolve and gains mastery over his carnal desires, then in this way he can attain a station even higher than the angels, and can protect himself from every deviation that confronts him. But if his desires overcome this resolve, if darkness prevails over guidance in his life, and he forgets the covenant of "Am I not your Lord?" which he made with his Creator, then he may fall from that lofty station and prepare for himself all the means of wretchedness and misfortune.

The Islamic system of life has indicated, through this story, only a glimpse of the principles of nobility and excellence which it has given to man in this universe. Man has been reminded that the paths of happiness and wretchedness, of exaltation and abasement, diverge from a point where there is a free, exalted human being on one side and a shackled, helpless animal that has fallen into the depths of degradation on the other.

In depicting the events narrated in this story, an effort has been made to remind us of the nature of the battle between Adam and Iblis: on one side is the covenant between the servant and God, and on the other side is the mischief of Satan. On one front is faith, and on the other is disbelief; on one front is truth, and on the other is falsehood. One quality belongs to the people of guidance, and the other to the people of misguidance. But where is the battlefield? It is man and his life. The victor is also man, and the vanquished is also man. This marketplace of profit and loss lies within his own conscience. Therefore Allah warns him to remain alert at all times, for he is always on the field of battle. There are only two outcomes: either he will be plundered, or he will return victorious with the spoils of war.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verses 38–39 (part 2 of 3)**

Through this story, the Islamic concepts of error and repentance are also clarified. Since sin is committed by an individual, repentance is also an individual act. This is a clear and straightforward view with no complexity. Unlike the People of the Church (Ahl al-Kanisa), there is no room in Islam for the idea that a person becomes a sinner before birth. In Islam there is no concept of a theological atonement for sins, such that Jesus (peace be upon him) was crucified to cleanse humanity of the sin of Adam (peace be upon him). That is a mistaken notion. The slip of Adam (peace be upon him) was an individual act, and the way to be freed from it was also an individual act: remorse and repentance. This is entirely clear, plain, and comprehensible. Every one of the children of Adam (peace be upon him) is responsible for their own deeds, and the door of repentance is open to all. Plain, simple, and easy:

*"Even if you have broken your repentance a hundred times, come back."*

Consider how clear and appealing this concept is. Every person should bear their own burden. This concept motivates every human being to strive for the attainment of good, and they do not fall victim to despair and hopelessness, because ﴿Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful﴾.

**Indications from the Story of Adam**

This is only one aspect of the story of Adam. In this place in Fi Zilal al-Quran, we will be content with this one aspect. Within this aspect alone lies a great treasure of priceless truths and wholesome concepts. This story contains an abundant store of valuable indications and guidance.

In it, the foundations of the Islamic concept of society and the manner of social life have been established, and these have been strengthened through goodness, morality, and other virtues. When we reflect on this aspect, we come to appreciate the importance and purposefulness of the Quranic stories, and how these stories strengthen the foundations of the Islamic worldview and clarify the lofty values that are built upon these foundations. The universe that Allah has created, which turns towards Allah and to which it must finally return, deserves that within it those values be exalted which are exalted in the sight of Allah.

**The Covenant of Human Vicegerency**

The human covenant of vicegerency (khilafah) is based on divine guidance. Its essential condition is that the human being will live in accordance with the Islamic system of life. After this covenant, the position becomes that the human being, as a creature endowed with will, stands at a crossroads. On one side, God is calling them, and they are listening. If they decide, they set out upon the Straight Path. On the other side, Satan is calling them. There is misguidance ........ or guidance, and falsehood ........ or truth, and success ........ or loss ........ This is the reality, and the Quran always presents it as the primary reality. All the ideas and concepts of humanity and all the ways of life rest solely upon this one reality.

**Lesson 4 at a Glance**

Here the discourse turns towards the Children of Israel. In Medina, they alone strongly opposed the Islamic call. They sought to end and resist the Islamic call through both open and secret stratagems. They continually plotted against the Islamic movement, and from the emergence of Islam up to this stage of the call, their intrigues never diminished for a moment. They had become certain that the keys of power were being transferred, one by one, into the hands of the Muslims. Since the wars between the Aws and the Khazraj ended, and the avenues closed through which the Jews had gained influence over the polytheists of Medina and affected them, and then when the formation of a new system of life began for the Muslims on the basis of this new Book, the Jews were acutely feeling that this new movement had expelled them from the important sectors of literature, culture, and both the economy and finance.

This, in short, is the struggle that the Jews began against Islam and the Muslims from the first day, and to this day it remains unchanged. Even today they are using the same crude weapons against Islam and the Muslims that they used at that time. The forms of the weapons are different, and their style is new, but their reality and their nature are exactly the same. It should be remembered that the Jews maintain this hostile attitude towards Islam and the Muslims despite the fact that, throughout human history, the whole world has always spurned this people. They were repeatedly driven from one place to another and from another back to the first. These people wandered through the dust. Centuries passed in this way, but ultimately they found rest and peaceful life in the world of Islam, which is open to all and in which, on the basis of faith and religion, no one is subjected to hatred. Where sectarian and religious riots have always been regarded with disapproval, and where every person who does not harm Islam or plot against the Muslims, and who lives peacefully, has always been granted open permission to come.

It was expected that the Jews of Medina would be the first to accept this new Messenger and this new call and believe. Whereas the Quran, in its general character, was confirming all the teachings that had been stated in the Torah. Furthermore, they were also awaiting the arrival of a new Messenger. They knew his attributes, and they possessed the good news about him in their heavenly scriptures. They would always supplicate to Allah, asking that, through the sake of the awaited Prophet, He grant them victory over the polytheists of Arabia.

This lesson is the first part of the extensive discourse of the Quran with the Children of Israel. This discourse with the Children of Israel is, in reality, a refutation of their position and a profound critical assault upon them, to expose their conspiracies. It was initiated as a matter of necessity and need at a time when the Islamic call, having come to Medina, had expended its full strength in calling them to Islam, had established the proof against them, and all means had been used to draw them towards this new movement.

This lesson begins with the sublime call of the Lord, in which He reminds them of His blessings and calls upon them to fulfil their covenant so that Allah may fulfil His covenant with them. As a preface, Allah first calls them to the fear of God, piety, and purity, and after this they are invited to accept this Book and this guidance, which confirms all the books and guidance that Allah Himself sent down to them. He condemns the attitude they adopted towards the Quran, and He counsels them not to be among those who were the first to reject this Book. Their behaviour of concealing the truth and mixing truth with falsehood in order to lead people astray from the right path is also condemned, especially the Muslims, and to stir up mischief within the ranks of the Islamic community and spread discord. Likewise, they were spreading doubts into the hearts of those who were newly embracing Islam. Allah advises them to abandon these acts of mischief and to join the Islamic community, to pray with the Muslims, to pay zakat, to establish the system of the congregation, and to seek help through patience and prayer in the difficult task of fully merging themselves into this new religion. Allah strongly criticises their conduct, in that they tell the polytheists to believe, but do not believe themselves, nor do they submit before Him.

After this, the Children of Israel are reminded of the blessings with which they had been favoured throughout their history. In the course of this discourse, the audience, the Children of Israel, are addressed as though those very people were present in the time of Moses (peace be upon him), the same people who are today in Medina. The reason is that the Children of Israel are one nation, and for centuries they have remained upon one nationality and the same disposition. Just as afterwards they remained the same in every age and continued to possess these same characteristics.

After this, they are warned of that day, the Day of Judgement, on which no soul will be able to repay on behalf of another. No intercession will avail, nor will any ransom or compensation be accepted from anyone, and on that day all people will be without helper or supporter, and there will be no one to save them from the punishment of the Hereafter.

Now there is presented to them the scene in which Allah delivered them from Pharaoh. This depiction is so vivid that it is as though the sight is before their eyes. Then there is mention of the favours that were bestowed upon them one after another. Shades of clouds were provided over their heads. They were sustained with manna and quails, and water was provided for them by splitting stones. After this, they are shamed by being reminded of the rebellions and the wickedness they committed, one after another, in return for these blessings. When Allah pardoned one of their errors, they fell into another. When He freed them from one calamity, they arranged for themselves another.

But the Children of Israel were, after all, the Children of Israel. The same corruption and malice, the same deviation and misguidance, and insistence upon it. They always violated the commands of Allah. They betrayed trusts. They broke covenants after firmly binding them. They discarded every pact made with Allah and with the Prophets. They advanced to the point of killing the Prophets without any justification. They began to deny the signs of their Lord. They worshipped the calf. Their insolence towards Allah reached such a level that they refused to believe until they should see Allah with their own eyes. Consider this carefully! After this, these people openly violated the command of Allah, and upon entering the town they did not utter the words that Allah had taught them and had commanded them to say. They continued to violate the laws of the Sabbath. They completely forgot the covenant of Mount Sinai. Regarding the cow that Allah had commanded them to slaughter, they began to procrastinate and started disputing and debating.

In short, they carried out all these actions while maintaining the claim that if there is any guided community at all, it is only the Jews and the Children of Israel. On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will be pleased only with the Children of Israel. All other religions are false, and all other nations are astray. The Quran, therefore, refutes this in this very first critical discourse, and says that whoever among the other nations believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, their reward is with their Lord. There shall be no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve.

This powerful assault on the Children of Israel, or the criticisms that come later in the course of the discussion of the surah, was an urgent need of the time. There was a pressing need to expose the hollow claims of the Children of Israel, to unveil all their conspiracies, and to make the Muslims aware of all the plots and deceits being carried out against their new society. The principles upon which the Children of Israel were carrying out these conspiracies were instilled into the minds and hearts of the Muslims. Moreover, the Muslims were encouraged to unite to confront this turmoil and mischief.

This criticism of the history of the Children of Israel was also necessary so that the Muslims themselves might become alert. They needed to know what difficulties lay before them in this new office of earthly vicegerency, where the dangers of slipping lay, and what slips had been made by the previous nations that had held this office, and because of which they were deprived of the office of vicegerency, and how they lost the honour of preserving and guarding the trust of Allah on this earth. And how and for what reasons the system of human leadership slipped from their hands. In short, throughout this entire critical discussion, the Muslims are warned, at some points openly and at others through hints, about what difficult situations they will face on this path and in this office, where there is a strong fear of slips and stumbling. As in the second part of this discussion, there will likewise be similar warnings.

In Medina, the Muslim community had an urgent need for these admonitions and guidance, just as the Muslim community has always, at every time and in every age, needed this guidance. Muslims should study the Quran with open eyes, with deep and enlightening awareness, and adopt the teachings and guidance that the Most Exalted and Supreme Leadership gave to the Muslims while they were fighting their ancient enemies. Muslims should always clearly know how to confront the conspiracies and deceits of these ancestral enemies, which they carry out through extremely secret means and deep, deceptive methods against the Islamic society. A person whose heart is not illuminated by the light of faith, and who, in the whole of his life, outwardly and inwardly, secretly and openly, does not take guidance from this Most Exalted and Supreme divine leadership, will never be able to discover those hidden paths, impure paths, and underground means through which these dangerous and impure conspiracies enter the Islamic society.

In this discussion, a particular aspect of the artistic and psychological harmony of the Quran's style deserves attention. The discourse on the history of the Children of Israel begins immediately after the conclusion of the story of the vicegerency of Adam. This discourse begins within the mental background to which we have pointed in the story of Adam and Iblis. Accordingly, the style of the Quranic expression takes into account that there must be complete correspondence and harmony between the story being presented and the environment within which the story is being presented.

Look back: during the discussion it was said that "Allah has created for you, human beings, all the creatures of this earth." After this, the account of Adam's khilafah (vicegerency) on earth begins, and a public covenant takes place between Adam and Allah. Adam is given precedence over the angels. After this come the themes of Adam being given instructions, his forgetfulness and error, his repentance and remorse, Divine guidance, and Divine forgiveness. And within Paradise itself, Adam (peace be upon him) is shown a glimpse of the long and unending struggle between the forces of evil and the forces of good, which was to continue in this world until the Day of Resurrection. The forces of goodness, reform and construction appear in the form of a human being who is a believer and holds fast to the rope of Allah, while the forces of evil, corruption and destruction stand embodied in the form of Iblis.

Having said all this, criticism of the Children of Israel now begins. It is described how they made a firm covenant with Allah and then broke it, what blessings were showered upon them and how they were ungrateful for them. Accordingly, Allah deprived them of the office of vicegerency on earth and imposed humiliation and wretchedness upon them. The believers are made aware of their deceptions, and it is told what lapses occurred from them in their history. Here a clear connection of meaning emerges between the making of a khalifah on earth and, after that, the making of the Children of Israel as khalifah, and the context of the discourse becomes clearly interconnected.

In view of the Qur'an, the purpose here is not to present the national history of the Children of Israel; rather, it refers to certain events of that history, with suitable brevity or suitable elaboration, presenting some scenes from that long history. Before Surah al-Baqarah, this story also recurs repeatedly in all the Meccan surahs of the Qur'an.

However, the purpose of narrating that story there was to give encouragement to the small community of Muslims in the turbulent period of Meccan life. At that time the aim was to present before the small community of believers the da'wah experiences of the caravan of the people of faith from the beginning of creation until today, and to give them guidance in accordance with the demands of the stage they were then facing in Makkah. But here (in Madinah) the aim was to make the Muslims aware of the intrigues and evil designs of the Jews, and to warn the Islamic community of what the Jews' intentions are and what resources they have to put those intentions into action. Furthermore, the Muslim ummah is being directed so that it does not itself fall into the same shortcomings and weaknesses into which the Jews had fallen before. Since the aims in Makkah and in Madinah were entirely different, the Qur'an presented the story of the Children of Israel here in a different style and from different aspects, although the realities presented were exactly the same in both places, namely the deviation of the Children of Israel and their departure from the straight path. (When the Meccan surahs, which were revealed before al-Baqarah in order of revelation, are discussed, we will explain this point further there.)

Wherever the story of the Children of Israel appears in the Qur'an, a careful study shows that the context in which it is presented is in harmony with it and completes the purposes, meanings and intellectual guidance and directions of that place. Here too, the story is fully in harmony with its context. Here, first, the theme of human dignity and honour was stated. After this came the themes of the covenant between man and Allah and man's forgetfulness, in which it is indicated in passing that humanity is a single unit, and that the messengers who came to it and the religion they presented all issue from one single source. In the course of the discourse, there are also repeated allusions to the human self and its constituent elements, and it is shown what the consequences will be of neglecting these constituent elements and deviating from them, upon which the human being's being Allah's khalifah on earth depends. Their importance is such that whoever denies them will become a denier of his own humanity; he will lose the very means by which he was given the office of vicegerency on earth, and as a result the human being will fall back into the lowest station of animality.

The story of the Children of Israel appears more than any other story in the Qur'an. Its various stations and its lessons are of great importance. From them is revealed the wise method of training which Allah adopted in order to prepare the ummah of Muslims for the office of the great vicegerency and for the purpose of its teaching and education.

After this general discussion, we now wish to cast a detailed look at the Qur'anic verses.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 2, verse 40:

Those who study the history of the Children of Israel are astonished at the blessings with which Allah favoured this people. And they are astonished at the contemptible manner in which, despite this continuous rain of blessings, they repeatedly denied the truth. Here, at the beginning, Allah mentions in summary the blessings He bestowed upon them. In the paragraphs that follow, these are mentioned in detail. These favours are recalled to them so that they may be invited to fulfil the covenant you made with Allah, so that Allah may continue His favours and bless them with His bounties.

﴿O Children of Israel! Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, I will fulfil your covenant.﴾ "O Children of Israel! Pay heed to My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil the covenant you had with Me, so that I fulfil My covenant with you."

Here, which covenant is being referred to? Is it the "first covenant", that is, the one settled between Allah and Hadrat Adam (ʿalayhi al-salam), in which Allah said: ﴿Then, if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve. (38) And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of the Fire, they will abide therein forever.﴾ "Then if guidance comes to you from Me, those who follow My guidance will have no fear and no grief. And those who reject it and deny Our signs, they are the people of the Fire, in which they will abide forever." Or is it the primordial natural covenant, which was concluded even before the covenant of Allah made with Hadrat Adam (ʿalayhi al-salam), between Allah and the human nature, in which it was made necessary for human nature to recognise Allah and to follow Allah alone, without partner? This natural covenant is such that it needs no explanation or proof, because human nature, by its very reality and innate inclinations, naturally turns towards the recognition of the Creator. It is only through misguidance and corruption of nature that a human becomes heedless of the knowledge of Allah. Or it is the covenant which Allah made with Ibrahim, the forefather of the Children of Israel, which will be mentioned soon in this same surah: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them, He said: "Indeed, I am making you an imam for the people." He said: "And from my descendants?" He said: "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers."﴾ (2:124) "Remember when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with certain words and he fulfilled them. He said, 'I am making you a leader for mankind.' Ibrahim said, 'And from my offspring too?' He said, 'My covenant does not extend to the wrongdoers.'" Or it is the particular covenant of the Children of Israel which Allah concluded with them at the time when Mount Sinai was suspended over their heads, and when Allah commanded them to act firmly upon the instructions given to them, and which is mentioned in the course of this lengthy criticism of the Children of Israel (2:93).

All these covenants are, from the perspective of the People of the House [Ahl al-Bayt], one and the same. Their purpose is that the servants of Allah turn to Him wholeheartedly, surrender their entire lives to Him. The religion of Allah is one, and the message which all the prophets brought is one, namely the religion of Islam, and from the beginning of creation until today the caravan of faith has continued to travel adopting this religion as its emblem.

In short, Allah invites the Children of Israel, by adhering to these covenants, to fear Him and to cultivate within themselves the awe of Him alone: ﴿And fear Me alone.﴾ "And it is Me alone that you should fear."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 2, verse 41:

The Children of Israel are invited to fulfil the demands of their covenants by believing in the Book that Allah has sent down, which confirms the Scripture that is already with them, and not to be hasty in denying and rejecting it, for it would have been fitting for them to be the first to believe in it.

﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it.﴾

The religion which Muhammad (ﷺ) has now brought in its final form is the same timeless religion that has always come from Allah. It is Allah's continuous message, and since the beginning of humanity it has been a covenant between Allah and mankind. Before this, He embraced all of humanity under His protection, and in the future too He will be the guide and leader of humanity. This religion joins the Old Testament and the New Testament together, and adds to them the good and benefit that Allah intended for the future of humanity. This religion now binds all of humanity into one thread, and declares them brothers who are acquainted with one another. It does not divide humanity into groups, communities, races and nations, but organises them as servants of Allah who hold firmly to the rope of Allah, a rope that has been unchanging from the dawn of humanity until today.

Allah forbids the Children of Israel from denying this Book merely for worldly interests, when it also confirms all the Books that are with you. They should not reject this truth for the sake of any worldly expediency or personal aims. Especially the rabbis and religious leaders, who hesitated to accept Islam merely because the position of leadership and authority they held in society would be taken away, and the material benefits they were obtaining would be cut off. Allah advises them to fear Him, and not to harbour such evil and base thoughts in their hearts: ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price, and fear Me alone.﴾

Servitude to money, wealth and worldly interests is an ancient trait of the Jews. It is possible that the material interests here refer to the benefits that the religious leaders of the Jews obtained through their religious services, false fatwas, and by distorting the signs of Allah in exchange for protecting the chiefs of the Jews from legal punishments, as the details of this appear in other places in the Holy Quran. To protect all these interests, these people would prevent their nation from entering Islam, because in that case there was a danger that leadership and chieftainship would slip from their hands. Moreover, as some Companions and Successors have stated in explaining this verse, this entire world is a small price, because compared with believing in the signs of Allah and the better outcome that awaits believers on the Day of Judgement before Allah, what is the reality of this whole world, or rather of this whole universe?

In the next clause, they are restrained from their second evil trait. It was their habit to present falsehood dressed in the colours of truth and to conceal the truth, even though they knew full well what they were doing. Their aim was to create intellectual confusion within the Islamic society and to raise a storm of doubts and suspicions in the hearts of the Muslims. ﴿And do not mix truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know it.﴾ "Do not make the truth doubtful by coating it with falsehood, nor try to hide the truth while knowing it."

The Jews concealed the truth on every occasion and in every context, mixed falsehood into it, and whenever they got the opportunity, they made every effort to deceive humanity. Therefore the Holy Qur'an repeatedly detailed this attribute and habit of theirs. They always kept creating mischief and disturbance within the Islamic society and the Islamic community, and remained busy in producing confusion and disorder. Several examples of this conduct are mentioned later in this same surah.

Then Allah addresses them, calling them to join the caravan of faith that is moving forward: "O wretched ones, join it, stand with the community, or you will be destroyed. Abandon your blameworthy prejudices, give up this exclusiveness, and join the Muslims in their collective worship and obligations. For separatism has been the constant habit of the Jews since ancient times."

﴿And establish prayer, and give zakah, and bow with those who bow﴾

"Establish prayer, give zakah, and bow down along with those who are bowing before Me."

Afterwards, the Jews in general, and their religious leaders in particular, are warned that among the idolaters of Arabia they call themselves proclaimers of faith, and as People of the Book they indeed are such, since in comparison with the polytheists they are the people of tawhid (monotheism). Yet despite this, you prevent your own people from accepting the religion of God, which confirms all earlier religions. ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book? Do you not then use your reason?﴾ You bid people to adopt the path of goodness, but you forget yourselves, although you recite the Book. Although in the beginning this verse reflects the weaknesses present among the Children of Israel at that time, it is nonetheless a collyrium of insight for the human soul and especially for the religious leaders of every faith and community. It is not restricted to one nation or country, nor confined to a particular act or era.

When religion becomes merely a profession and a business rather than a living and surging worldview, the condition of its leaders becomes such that what they say with their tongues is not in their hearts! They preach goodness while they themselves are immersed in evil. They call people to righteousness and piety, yet righteousness and piety, whatever that thing is, have not even touched them. They take a straightforward matter, give it a distorted meaning, and make a mountain out of a molehill. To fulfil their carnal desires, they resort to interpretations of decisive texts. They bring forward such beautiful interpretations and such well-argued verdicts which, apparently, are completely in accord with the outward meaning of the verses and texts, yet in their reality they are far removed from the truth and essence of religion. And all of this they do for their own interests and heart's desires, and for the sake of those people who are either wealthy or in positions of power. The religious leaders of the Jews used to do precisely this.

To call people towards goodness and then, in one's practical life, to act contrary to it is a disease and a plague which not only creates doubts and misgivings in the hearts of the callers themselves, but also makes the call itself suspect. Because of this contradiction between word and deed, confusion arises in the hearts and thoughts of people, for people hear the finest words with their ears, but see the most reprehensible deeds with their eyes. Seeing this contradiction between word and deed, those poor souls are left bewildered. The light that faith had kindled in their spiritual world through this call and preaching is extinguished, the light of faith vanishes from their hearts, and when no reverence remains for the religious leaders, as a consequence their trust in religion itself is also lost.

The word of a calling person without action is lifeless. It is a spark that is extinguished before it reaches others. The words of such callers are without effect, even if those words are rhymed and ornate, smooth and polished, full of fervour and zeal, because such words did not come from a heart that believes in them. Influence lies only in words that come from the heart. Words that issue from the heart have effect. A caller can become a true believer in his own words only when, by his conduct, he becomes the interpretation and translation of the message he is conveying, and the call itself is embodied in practice in his life. When a person reaches this standard, people place their trust in him and believe him, even if his words are not polished and his speech is not eloquent, for in such a case the influence comes not from his fluency of tongue but from his truthfulness and realism. At that time, the truthfulness of the speech itself becomes its beauty, and there is no need to create force of expression through smooth talk.

But the truth is that, despite all these considerations, the harmony of word and deed, and the concord between faith and action, is no easy task. It is not an easy path that can be adopted with ease. To attain it, severe discipline and striving are required. For this one needs a connection with God, and the help, enabling grace and guidance of God. Because the various circumstances of practical life, its needs and its compulsions, throw a person away from his inner convictions or from the things to which others are calling him. Such a person, however great a power he may possess, will remain weak and feeble unless he holds fast to the hem of the Master of the Kingdom and the Absolutely Powerful Being, because evil, corruption, and misguiding satanic forces spread their nets everywhere against man. Although a person can, at times and repeatedly, overcome them, yet the moment he shows weakness at any instant, he falls, becomes humiliated, and loses his past, present, and future. But when a person's trust is placed in that eternal and everlasting power, then his strength is beyond description; he overcomes everything. He subdues even his weaknesses and his carnal desires. He overcomes his needs and his compulsions. He prevails over all the forces that confront him.

Therefore the Holy Qur'an here first turns the Jews towards this, since the address is directed to them, and then, after them, turns the whole world towards it, so that they may seek help in patience, steadfastness, prayer, and supplication to master this difficult task and this arduous struggle. What was required of the Jews was that they regard their religious services, or the entire wealth and property of the world that they possessed, as a meagre provision, and prefer the truth over it. For, owing to their religious status and religious knowledge in Medina, they knew this truth and reality well. Therefore it was their duty to join the caravan of faith quickly, since they were already calling people to faith. Because such a decision required a great measure of strength and courage on the part of the Jews, they were commanded to seek help through patience, steadfastness, supplication, and prayer.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verses 45–46:

﴿Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is difficult, except for the humble (al-khashi'in), who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that to Him they will return.﴾

Pure Urdu translation of the Qur'anic verse as given: "Seek help through patience and prayer. Surely prayer is a hard task, but not for those obedient servants who understand that at last they have to meet their Lord and return to Him." ”

I understand that the pronoun in "innaha" refers to the situation (i.e., it does not point to a single individual but to the circumstance). That is, the situation is that calling the Children of Israel to acknowledge the truth, while such obstacles stand in its path, is a very difficult and arduous task. It is easy only for those elders who hold the fear of Allah in their hearts and are obedient to Him, who have a firm awareness of Allah's fear and His taqwa, and who have complete certainty that they will return to Him.

The truth is that the need to seek help through steadfastness and patience arises repeatedly for a person. It is the remedy for every calamity and hardship, and the solution to every difficulty. For a human being, the most difficult task is to step down from the position of leadership and politics, to sacrifice one's interests and earnings for the sake of truth and honesty, and, becoming indifferent to all things, to acknowledge the truth and submit to it.

The question is: how can a person seek help from prayer in this task?

Prayer is in reality a special meeting between the servant and his Lord. From it the heart draws nourishment and the soul feels a special connection. Within it lies for the human self a provision more precious than all the wealth and goods of the world. The condition of the Prophet ﷺ was that whenever any matter troubled him, he would hasten to prayer, and his state was such that he remained continually attached to his Lord; his soul was always connected with revelation and inspiration. The source of goodness and blessing is still within the reach of every believer: whoever seeks provision for the journey, who desires cool water in intense heat, who seeks help in a state where all help has been cut off, and who needs provisions at a time when his supply-bag is empty.

The certainty of returning to Allah (in the Qur'an, the word *zann* and its derivatives are often used in the sense of certainty; and in the Arabic language too, the general use of *zann* is in the sense of certainty) and the certainty of returning to Him in every matter is what creates steadfastness and perseverance in a person. Taqwa and the sense of goodness depend upon it. The correct balance between worldly values and otherworldly authority is dependent upon this certainty. When the balance of these values becomes correct, when the pointer of the scale becomes straight, then a person sees all this world as a brief enjoyment, a small and insignificant thing. Only then does the Hereafter appear clearly, and then no wise person hesitates even for a moment in preferring and choosing it.

When a person reflects upon the Qur'an in this manner, these guidances which were initially given to the Children of Israel become permanent guidance for all.

Thus, calling the Children of Israel again, reminding them again of His blessings, and, before the details that follow, warning them in summary of the coming hour, Allah addresses them in this manner.

Sayyid Qutb's commentary on Surah Al-Baqarah, verses 47–48 (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation)

The superiority of the Children of Israel over all of creation belongs to the time when they were, in the true sense, the vicegerents and successors of Allah on this earth. But when they turned away from the commands of their Lord and Master, began to disobey their prophets, were ungrateful for the blessings Allah had bestowed upon them, and fully broke the covenants they had made with Allah and the responsibilities they had taken on, then Allah also decreed that they would remain forever cursed, condemned, and humiliated. Their exile and their wandering from place to place was decided, and they became deserving of Allah's wrath.

Here they are reminded that there was a time when Allah's favour and grace were upon them, and they were the most excellent people of the world. This is related to them as an encouragement: that now too there are opportunities for them to regain the station they have lost. They can join this new caravan of faith, support the Islamic call, re-enter the covenant of Allah, give thanks for the superiority Allah bestowed upon their forefathers, and share in the station now being granted to the believers.

But alongside this encouragement, and alongside the reminder of favour, grace and the abundant blessing, there also comes a warning and a caution about the coming Day, in which "لَا تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَنْ نَفْسٍ شَيْئًا" (no soul will avail another soul in anything at all).

Because on the Day of Resurrection every person will receive the recompense of his deeds individually. There the reckoning will be personal, each will answer only for what he did, and no one will be able to be of use to another. It should be remembered that individual responsibility is, in this world and the Hereafter, a golden and great principle of Islam. This principle of individual responsibility rests upon man's free will and power of discernment, and in accordance with it Allah will carry out universal justice. This is the principle that creates in a person the sense of his own dignity, and through it a constant awakening of the spirit remains alive in his heart. Both of these are extremely beneficial for human refinement and training. Moreover, they increase those human values on the basis of which Islam has given man the station of the best of creation.

"وَلا يُقْبَلُ مِنْهَا شَفَاعَةٌ وَلا يُؤْخَذُ مِنْهَا عَدْلٌ وَلا هُمْ يُنْصَرُونَ" (nor will any intercession be accepted from it, nor will any ransom be taken from it, nor will they be helped). Intercession will not be accepted for anyone who does not come on that Day carrying the provision of faith and righteous deeds. No ransom will be taken for the forgiveness of disbelief and disobedience. "وَلا هُمْ يُنْصَرُونَ" (and they will not be helped): on that Day there will be no helper to rescue them from the punishment of Allah. There will be no one who could deliver them from His punishment. In this final phrase, the word in the plural gathers them all together: that is, all those people who will be unable to be of use to one another, whose intercession for one another will not be accepted, and from whom no ransom will be taken on behalf of one another. At the beginning of the verse the address was directed to the Children of Israel, but at the end the style of speech shifted from direct address to the third person, so that this principle becomes general, and so that those addressed and all other people are included in it.

After this, the Qur'an mentions one by one the blessings of Allah that were bestowed upon them, and shows what conduct they adopted in return for those blessings: how they denied, how they disbelieved, and how they strayed from the right path. Deliverance from the slavery of Pharaoh and his painful oppression was, among these favours, the greatest, and therefore it is mentioned first here.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 49:

Here, this painful situation is being highlighted again in their minds, the situation in which their forefathers were afflicted during the time of Pharaoh. For these people were the descendants of those Children of Israel who were afflicted with this punishment. After depicting the torment and oppression, Allah presents to them the scene from which they were delivered. They are told: Remember the time when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who kept you constantly under torment.

The meaning of "yasumunakum" (يَسُومُونَكُمْ) is "they kept you constantly in torment." These words come from "sama al-mashiyata" (سام الماشية), "he made the livestock graze (sa'imah) constantly." It is as if the Pharaohnites had made these oppressions a kind of food for the Children of Israel, which was fed to them continuously. After this, a specific form of this punishment is mentioned, namely that they would slaughter the men and keep the women alive so that the strength of the Children of Israel would be diminished.

Before the details of the account of the deliverance of the Children of Israel are presented, they are told that the calamity was a great trial for the Children of Israel. The purpose is that in their awareness and consciousness, and indeed in the awareness and consciousness of every Muslim who is afflicted with some calamity, it should be firmly established that the coming of hardships upon the servants of Allah is in reality a trial and test for them. They are put to tests and afflictions. The person who understands this reality of trial derives benefit from hardship and calamity; by virtue of this awareness, he gains something even from hardships and difficulties. If a person in grief and sorrow knows that he is being tested, and that some benefit will reach him after this hardship, then this grief and sorrow are not without benefit for him. When a person lives through a calamity with this conception, his difficulties become easier, especially when the steadfastness and knowledge and insight gained during these painful experiences are kept in view.

Moreover, while there is the awareness that the reward of this calamity is preserved with Allah, the submission and supplication before Allah continue, there is full hope of deliverance from Him, and there is no despair of His mercy and compassion. This is why, immediately after mentioning the calamity of the Children of Israel, Allah has said:

﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord.﴾

After this, the introduction to the account of the Children of Israel's deliverance begins.

The Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 50:

﴿And when We divided the sea for you, and saved you, and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on.﴾

The details of this deliverance had already been given at length in the Meccan surahs revealed before Surah al-Baqarah. Here it is mentioned as a reminder to those who were already familiar with its details. The addressees knew the details of this story, from the Qur'an, from their preserved narratives, or through their scriptures. Here the deliverance is painted again before them so that they bring it to mind and be moved by it. Observe the manner of expression: it is as though the addressees themselves are watching the sea splitting and the Children of Israel crossing it under the leadership of Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) before their very eyes. This style of expression, that is, making an impression on the addressee through vivid depiction, is the distinctive inimitable style that belongs to the Qur'an. Now the discourse continues alongside the Exodus of the Children of Israel. The Children of Israel have already been freed from slavery in Egypt.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 51–54:

The worship by the Children of Israel of the calf, and their making it a god in the absence of Moses (peace be upon him) when he had gone to Mount Sinai for forty days, has been described in detail in Surah Ta-Ha, which was revealed before Surah al-Baqarah. Here they are only being reminded of it, because they are thoroughly familiar with its details. Allah is reminding them that their condition was such that as soon as their prophet went out of sight, they fell upon the calf. Yet it was in Allah's name alone that the prophet had freed them from the painful punishment of the Pharaohs. Allah, commenting on their attitude, says: ﴿and you were wrongdoers﴾. Who could be a greater wrongdoer than one who abandons the worship of Allah, forgets the will of his prophet, and begins to worship a body like a calf, when it was Allah who freed them from the slavery of those people who regarded the calf of a cow as sacred?

Nevertheless, Allah forgives them. He gives their prophet the Book of guidance, the Tawrat (Torah), in which what was written was a Furqan (criterion) between truth and falsehood, in the hope that these people would abandon misguidance and accept the clear truth.

Even so, there was still a need to purify them with severity, because their corrupted nature could be set right only through the naked sword and the harshest punishment. Their nature demanded that their punishment be both severe and unusual. Accordingly the command came: ﴿And [recall] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf [as a deity], so repent to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator."﴾ "Kill yourselves" means that the guilty should be killed so that it purifies the one who is killed and also purifies the one who kills. From among them, the obedient and honourable should kill. The traditions indicate this to be the meaning of this harsh punishment and severe expiation. Indeed, it was a soul-crushing and heart-rending responsibility, for brother to kill brother, as though one were killing oneself. But this was necessary for the training of their corrupted temperament and cowardly disposition, because their nature inclined toward every evil, and they did not hesitate to commit any reprehensible act. Had they had the ability to refrain from reprehensible matters, they would not have fallen upon the worship of the calf the moment the prophet became absent. This was their remedy, for the ghosts of the kicks do not depart by means of words. It was appropriate for them to pay this heavy ransom so that they might gain some benefit and their corrupted temperament be trained.

But after this punishment, Allah's mercy covers them: ﴿Then He accepted your repentance; indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful.﴾ At that time your Creator accepted your repentance, for He is the One who forgives greatly and shows mercy.

But the Children of Israel were still the Children of Israel. They were thick-headed, worldly people, and the unseen world and the Hereafter were hidden from their sight. Therefore all they could think of was to demand to see Allah openly. Those who made this demand were not ordinary people; among them were seventy chosen and distinguished men whom Moses (peace be upon him) had selected from the whole nation at the time of meeting his Lord and had taken with him. The full details of this have already been described in the earlier Meccan verses. In short, before seeing Allah openly, the Children of Israel plainly refused to believe. The Qur'an, by recounting the impudence of the forefathers of the Children of Israel here, wants to show that from ancient times this people has been afflicted with obstinacy and stubbornness, and that their ancient obstinacy is exactly like the obstinacy they now display against the Final Prophet (ﷺ). Just as their forefathers did, these people themselves are demanding miracles, and they are also trying to persuade the simple-hearted believers to make such demands, so that they may test the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).
