However, within the meaning of this verse of the Qur'an, it includes people of every religion and community who conceal the truth despite knowing it. Whether for a few coins, for the worldly interests they obtain as a result of concealing the truth, or because they have certain interests in view which could be endangered if they stated the truth. Or, "thaman qalil" (a small price) may mean the entire world. By concealing the truth, these people are deprived of the reward of the Hereafter and of the pleasure of Allah, and this is a great loss. In comparison to this, indeed the entire world is a small price.

In the context of the explanation of lawful and unlawful food and drink, the proclamation is made: "Ma ya'kulna fi butunihim illa al-nar" ("They are only filling their bellies with fire"). This phrase was used here in relation to the explanation of lawful and unlawful. That is, by concealing the truth, the small wage they take and consume will in reality be fire in their bellies, and their food will also be nothing but fire.

They concealed the truth, and as a consequence, they will be punished. On the Day of Resurrection they will be left in a state of humiliation and disgrace. They will be deprived of the attention and gracious regard of Allah, and Allah describes this wretched condition, worthlessness and disgrace in these words:

﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them﴾. That is, no words will be addressed to them, there will be no care for them, they will not be purified, and there will be no forgiveness for them either. They will be completely disregarded. This is so that the punishment appears frightening in the eyes of the believers, and the situation comes close to the perception and understanding of ordinary people.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾.

And another living expression: "Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness." It is as though this is a transaction of buying and selling, in which these people turn away from guidance and buy error; they are deprived of forgiveness and purchase lasting punishment. How foolish are these people who make a bargain of such tremendous loss! The truth is that these people have bought a monstrous evil. Guidance was open to them, but they abandoned it and adopted error. The opportunities for forgiveness were available to them, but they squandered them and embraced punishment. "So how patient they are for the Fire!" How strange is their resolve, that they are ready to endure the torment of Hell; they are rushing towards it. Nature itself laughs at this foolish act of theirs.

They have committed a most abominable crime, and this is its full due punishment. Allah sent down the Book so that it would be conveyed to the people and enforced upon the earth, so that it would be their law and their system of life. But these wrongdoers concealed it, and by concealing it they removed it from the field of action, even though it was a truth sent down to be acted upon.

﴿That is because Allah sent down the Book with truth﴾ — "All this happened because Allah had sent down the Book in accordance with the exact truth." And those who believed in this Book were guided, became companions of the truth, and joined the company of those who were rightly guided to the truth. They sided with the nature of the universe and came upon the real principles of human nature.

﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning the Book are in far-off dissension﴾ — "But those who raised disputes over the Book went far away from the truth in their quarrels." Such people have already gone far from the truth.

They also clash with the principles of fitrah (innate human nature). They clash with one another, and indeed with their own selves. They were like this, and they will remain like this. This will be the fate of every ummah that creates disputes over the Book of Allah, that does not accept the Book of Allah in its entirety, but rather breaks it into pieces. In every age and every era, with every nation and every people, this has been Allah's way of dealing with them. In the world in which we are living, we can clearly see the fulfilment of this verse.

Finally, in one single verse, all the principles of the life-view of faith are placed together. The standard of conduct of faith is stated, and it is made clear what the qualities of righteous people are according to the Qur'an.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 177 (part 1 of 2):

The truth is that this verse is also connected with the rulings on the change of the qibla (tahwil al-qibla) and the lengthy objections and replies of the Jews concerning them. We have already discussed the wisdom behind the change of the qibla. Here, God Almighty, exposing the outward-looking mentality and the asceticism (taqashshuf) of the Jews regarding the outward form of worship and the symbols of religion, is stating a great standard of good and bad and the true reality of righteousness and wickedness. This is because the Jews were extremely sensitive about these outward matters and would quarrel over them.

The purpose of the change of the qibla, or of all acts of worship, is not that people should turn their faces towards the east or face the west while performing worship, or turn towards Bayt al-Maqdis or towards the Masjid al-Haram. Nor is it that the present outward form of worship is itself the essence of goodness and benefit. Rather, it is essential that there be an inwardly felt awareness in the heart and a living consciousness of the Islamic worldview. Alongside these mental matters, it is also necessary to adopt a particular pattern of conduct. Otherwise, the real aim of attaining righteousness and of bringing goodness into action will not be fulfilled. Righteousness is in fact a concept, a consciousness, a set of deeds, and a pattern of conduct. It is a conception of life. That which affects the conscience of an individual and a community, and that which produces desirable effects in the lives of individuals and communities, is an action. How can such a revolution in life come about merely by turning away from the east and the west? Whether one turns the face this way or that, what difference does it make? The real aim is the turning of the heart (rujū' al-qalb). Whoever obeys the commands of God attains his destination. The same applies to the outward form of all the religious symbols which people perform. Whoever obeys the commands of God attains his destination. The same applies to the outward form of all the religious symbols which people perform.

﴿But righteousness is this: that one believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets.﴾ "But righteousness is that a person believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book sent down by God, and His messengers, from the heart."

This is the standard of goodness which is the sum of all goodness. The values of righteousness established in this standard are very weighty. What is the worth and value of faith in God, faith in the Last Day, and faith in the angels, the Books and the prophets from the Islamic point of view?

Faith in God is a turning point in human life. Through it a person is freed from the servitude and slavery of various powers, various things, and various desirable conceptions, and accepts the servitude and slavery of only One. Thus a person, standing in one row with all other human beings, bowing before one Deity, attains the lofty station of brotherhood and equality. Faith is the station where, instead of the tawa'if al-muluk (the chaos of petty rival powers), an order is established; in place of dispersion, unity is established; in place of division, concord is established; and, along with the absence of misguidance, a lofty goal comes into view. If there is no faith in the one, unique God in a person's heart, then in this world he has no goal on which he can concentrate his powers with single-mindedness, and around which he can gather with equal standing. Just as the whole universe is centred around one point, with the parts of its existence mutually linked and with clear relations among them, so too, the various parts of the one whose mutual connections and aims are completely clear, known and coherent [are centred on faith].

The purpose of faith in the Last Day is that a person accepts with certainty the justice of God in reward and punishment. He understands that human beings have not been created on this earth without purpose, that he is not irresponsible, but that he will have to give an account. If he does some good, it cannot be destroyed, even if its reward is not received in this world. Faith in the angels is also a part of faith in the unseen. This is the difference between the understanding and perception of a human being and that of an animal. This is the difference between the human conception of life and the animal conception of life: a human believes in some things beyond the sensory, and can perceive them, whereas the awareness of an animal is limited to the sphere of the sensory. The purpose of faith in the Books and the prophets is that a person should believe in all the messengers without discrimination. That is, humanity is also one, and we believe in this. Its God is also one. Its religion and system of life are also one. In this way, the believer becomes the heir of the lofty ideas of the prophets and messengers. Therefore, faith in the Books and the messengers gives a believer a very precious consciousness.

Human beings have great love for wealth, but the sacrifice of wealth also has great importance. Spending wealth on poor relatives, orphans, the needy, travellers, and for freeing necks (from bondage) and for liberating people from slavery, all these acts raise a person to a high rank.

The effect of spending in the way of God is that a person is freed from the bonds of greed, selfishness and miserliness. The love of wealth draws the hands back from spending. A person falls from the lofty height of high-mindedness, ambition, generosity and magnanimity, and the spirit of man is no longer expansive. In the Islamic system, spending has a spiritual station. Therefore, Muslims are commanded that, despite their love of wealth, they should spend from the wealth that is most beloved and most desirable to them, with the readiness and openness of heart and soul. This has great spiritual importance, and by this method the believer will free himself from the worship of wealth and from slavery to wealth. Through the worship of wealth, a person is certainly humiliated: instead of exaltation, he is brought low. Through spending, he becomes free of the slavery of greed and covetousness. From the Islamic point of view, instead of being bowed down, he will raise his head high. But if he does not spend, he will be humiliated. The worth and value of spending wealth in the way of God is very great. This is because the aim of the Islamic system is that, first of all, it frees a person from psychological anxieties, moral weaknesses, and avarice and greed. This work is done before social freedom, and even before personal and political freedom. Why before? Because a person who is a slave to his own self easily becomes ready for the slavery of the tyrant (taghut). But the person who is freed from the prison and chains of carnal desires is also free in his society and community; he is not ready to become anyone's slave.

In human society, spending in the way of God also has a social value. Through maintaining kinship ties with relatives, a sense of compassion arises in the human soul, nobility of character spreads in the family, and the ties among relatives become stronger. The foundation of Islamic society rests upon the family, and therefore, through spending in the way of God, an effort has been made here to strengthen the family system. Then there is the command to give financial help to orphans. Its purpose is to establish a system of mutual support (kafalah) between the rich and the poor, and between the strong and the weak, within society. Orphans are deprived of maternal and paternal affection. Arrangements have been made for them so that the sense of their deprivation may be compensated. Then, as a result of this mutual solidarity (takaful), the whole society is protected from the multitude of those self-grown, unbridled and untrained individuals who create problems for society, become a burden upon it, and become the cause of mischief. Such people, in the long run, take full revenge for society's carelessness and lack of compassion. Spending on the needy, who have no means of livelihood but still sit quietly, who have self-respect and do not ask, is a protection of their dignity. It saves them from ruin. Through the system of spending, in an Islamic society, the sense of collective support and guarantee is created in the hearts of such people. An Islamic society is indeed one in which no individual is left without helpers, and in which no member of it is allowed to be lost. A wayfarer (ibn al-sabil) who is far from his family, who has no means, and who is suddenly caught in calamity, while his family members are far from him, is in such circumstances also afflicted. Spending for him is a kind of emergency aid. Through this aid he is given the awareness that all of humanity is his family. Every country is his country; everywhere there is his family; Muslims are his kinsfolk. Everywhere, in exchange for his own wealth, there is wealth for him. For him there is kinship (silat rahmi). And for him there can be provision for comfort. Spending on those who ask is necessary so that their need is fulfilled and they give up asking in the future. Islam dislikes begging. The teaching of Islam is that for one who has enough to sustain himself, it is not lawful to ask. For one who is able to work, asking is also not lawful. For such a person, the command of God is that he should work, not beg, or be content and not stretch out his hand in asking. Begging is permissible only when there is no work, no wealth, and no other means.

Spending is also one of the heads of expenditure for freeing people from slavery. The unfortunate one who became a slave because of his evil conduct, who raised the sword against Islam, and whose freedom ended as a result of war, has been temporarily deprived of his station of honour in society. Spending on him would be to buy him and set him free, or for the slave to make a contract of freedom with his master and be bound to pay the sum agreed upon. Islam established this law for slaves: whenever the slave wished, he would make a contract of freedom with his master and become free. According to that contract, he had to pay the amount that was agreed upon. (After such a contract, the slave) became entitled to receive wages for his work, which were deducted from the sum of the contract. Besides this, he became eligible for zakat. Likewise, he could be assisted from all the categories of spending in the way of God, so that he might quickly pay the sum of the contract and be blessed with the bounty of freedom.

Establishing the Prayer (Iqamat al-Salat)

In this standard of righteousness, prayer has very great importance. And establishing the prayer is not fulfilled merely by standing up facing the east and the west. This point has a broader meaning, which is that a person's outward and inward being, his intellect and his spirit, should all be fully turned towards God Almighty. Prayer is neither merely a name for physical exercise, nor merely a name for Sufi recitations and devotions. Prayer is in fact a reflection of the basic thought and outlook of Islam. Islam acknowledges the reality that a human being is a combination of three things in one existence: body, spirit and intellect. Islam also does not accept that there is any contradiction between the activities and the spheres of action of these three powers. It does not consider it lawful to free the spirit by destroying the body, because for spiritual freedom, physical annihilation or killing the body is not necessary. This is why Islam, in its most important and greatest act of worship, namely prayer, has harmonized the activities of these three powers. In prayer, all three powers turn towards their Creator with complete order. Standing, bowing and prostration are physical movements which draw the spirit towards returning to God. Recitation of the Qur'an, reflection upon it, and understanding its meaning is the work of the intellect, and during that whole period the human intellect is occupied in this task. Honouring God, complete submission and acceptance, and humility and self-abasement are the work of the spirit, and in this way these three powers are working simultaneously. In short, in this sense, establishing the prayer represents the whole Islamic way of thinking. And it reminds the seeing eye of this lesson: what is Islam's view of the whole of life? In every prayer and in every movement of the prayer, we repeat this lesson.

Payment of Zakat

This is an Islamic tax, imposed in the Islamic system upon the wealth of the wealthy and the affluent for the benefit of the poor and the needy. This tax has been imposed by God Almighty. In reality, God Almighty is the true owner of wealth; the servant has been made its owner only in a metaphorical sense. Therefore, from the Islamic point of view, certain conditions have been placed upon it, and among them the important and necessary condition is the payment of zakat. The mention of paying zakat comes after the general command to spend in the way of God, which has been mentioned above, namely that wealth is to be spent, despite the love of it, upon relatives and others. This means that zakat is a separate and independent category, apart from all the expenditures mentioned above and from spending in the way of God. This is a compulsory tax and an explicitly prescribed obligation, whereas general spending in the way of God is merely an encouragement. But this collective standard of righteousness which is mentioned in this verse will not be complete until both of these categories are acted upon according to their measure and according to one's capacity. These two categories are the basic constituent elements of Islam. But it is essential that both be found in every person's life. Acting upon one can never cancel the other.

Fulfilling Covenants (Wafa' al-'Ahd)

This is the sign of Islam, for whose protection Islam makes extraordinary efforts. It is repeatedly mentioned in the Holy Qur'an. It has been regarded as a sign of faith. It has been declared a sign of goodness and humanity, and thus it has very great importance. Fulfilling covenants is absolutely necessary to create trust and confidence in the relations between one person and another, between an individual and a community, and between one nation and another. The first fulfilment of covenants is fulfilling one's covenant with the Divine Being Himself. If a servant is not faithful to his Master, he will always remain troubled and dissatisfied and will be unable to fulfil any covenant. He will not be able to stand firm upon any compact, and will not place trust in any human being.

In the matter of fulfilling covenants, with friends and enemies alike, Islam has reached a lofty height of which no parallel is found anywhere else in the whole of human history. No nation, no community, has ever reached that lofty height. This station became known to humanity only under the shade of Islam and in the light of the Islamic worldview.

Patience in the Struggle between Truth and Falsehood

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 2, verse 177 (part 2 of 2):

Patience (sabr) is the quality that enables a person to bear hardships. The aim of Islam is that when a difficult stage comes, a person confronts it with great courage. At the time of calamity, one should not begin to sigh and lament. In hardships, one should not begin to wail and complain. Sabr, musabirah, and tahammul and thabat (steadfastness) are precisely this. Sabr is the name of firmly holding on to the truth. Its result is that the clouds of calamity disperse, the affliction is removed, and after difficulties, ease comes into being. It is accepting the will of Allah, being hopeful in Him, and placing trust in Him. The community to which the leadership and oversight of all humanity has been given, which has to establish justice in the world and discharge the duty of reforming all of humanity, must necessarily be richly endowed with the treasure of sabr. Difficulties may confront it, great obstacles may stand in its way. It may face straitness and calamities. When a struggle with falsehood is set in motion and the most severe conditions arise, then sabr and steadfastness alone should be its greatest weapon. Patience in calamity and poverty, patience in physical weakness and sickness, patience over the paucity and weakness of its members, patience in siege and struggle; in short, sabr in every condition and sabr at every moment. Only in this way can this community discharge its great responsibility, and only then can it fulfil its plan. Otherwise, it will not achieve success.

In this verse, Allah has addressed those who are patient in straitness and calamity, and in the struggle between truth and falsehood, with the word al-Sabirin in the accusative case (hal nasbi), which expresses the meaning of "especially." The qualities mentioned before this are in the nominative case (standalone sentences), but this quality has been mentioned in the accusative case (it is an object, and the verb is omitted). The meaning is: "I specifically mention the patient ones." In the context of mentioning qualities of righteousness and goodness, this is a special indication, and it has its own particular weight and a special importance: faith in Allah, faith in the angels, faith in the books, faith in the prophets, spending of wealth, establishing prayer, paying zakah. And among all the qualities of fulfilling covenants, the quality of sabr and those who possess it, the Sabirin, have greater importance; they hold the highest esteem with Allah. The station of the patient is the highest and loftiest. Seeing this lofty station of the patient, the gaze of all people is drawn toward it.

Look closely: in a single verse, the principles of ideology and belief, physical duties, financial responsibilities and the obligations of wealth have been stated. Theory and reality have been unified, in a form of unity that cannot be broken into pieces, whose parts can never be separated from one another, and the title of these diverse spheres of life is one: righteousness (birr). Some hadith call righteousness the very essence of faith. In short, this verse is a complete summary of the Islamic conception of life. The principles of the Islamic system of life have been gathered together in it. All these are essential principles, complementing one another, and without them the establishment of the Islamic system is absolutely impossible.

For those whose qualities are these, their station is also stated here at the end, as a result: "Those are the ones who are true (sadaqu), and those are the God-fearing (muttaqun)." (177)

These are the very people who, in Islam, were absolutely truthful with their Lord. They are truthful in faith and belief, and they are also truthful in giving practical form to their faith and belief in their lives. These indeed are the muttaqun, who attach themselves to their Lord and fear Him. They discharge their duties with a sense of responsibility and awareness.

If you glance from between these verses, you will see a lofty horizon; you will see a lofty station of honour. This is the station to which Allah, through the supreme system of life He has prescribed, wishes to elevate humanity. And when we look at the condition of people, they run away from this system, they evade it, they oppose it, indeed they become hostile to it, and they become mortal enemies of its adherents. When we see all this, we are left wringing our hands, and we must say what Allah has said: "Alas for the servants!" (ya hasrah 'ala al-'ibad).

Then we look again at that lofty horizon of the goal, and this state of despair and regret is immediately dispelled. A ray of hope appears; certainty in Allah becomes firm; unshakeable conviction in the strength and superiority of the Islamic system of life is created, and when we look at our future, we find on the horizon a ray of hope, which is brighter and clearer. It is necessary that this long fatigue and these calamities have once again firmed up their conviction in the Islamic system of life. It is hoped that humanity will once again advance toward this exalted and lofty system and will acknowledge that Allah alone is al-Musta'an (the One sought for help); He alone is the Helper and Supporter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 2, verse 178:

Lesson 11 at a Glance

This lesson systematically arranges some of the collective matters of the newly founded Islamic society of Madinah. Alongside them, some acts of worship, such as obligatory acts of worship, are also mentioned. Here both these things have been merged together in a single passage of this surah. The link between both kinds of teachings has been made taqwa (God-consciousness) and fear of God. Just as, at the end of the arrangement of collective matters, taqwa and fear of God are repeatedly mentioned, so too at the end of the prescribed acts of worship emphasis is placed on taqwa, gratitude and fear of God (khashyat Allah). Then this lesson has been placed after the verses of birr, which comprise the ideas of faith, the way of life of faith and the Islamic method of action, and in which the high standard of righteousness and taqwa is described.

In this lesson, the rulings on retaliation (qisas) for the slain are stated, and the necessary legislation in this regard is made. The rulings on bequest at the time of death, the rulings on the obligation of fasting, and the rulings on supplication and i'tikaf are stated, and at the end the rulings on the payment of financial obligations are stated.

After the rulings on qisas, the discourse concludes with taqwa: "وَلَكُم فِي القِصَاصِ حَيَاةٌ يَا أُولِي الأَلبَابِ لَعَلَّكُم تَتَّقُونَ" ("And there is life for you in retaliation, O people of understanding, that you may become righteous"). In the same way, when the rulings on bequest were stated, this matter again ends with taqwa: "كُتِبَ عَلَيكُم إِذَا حَضَرَ أَحَدَكُمُ المَوتُ إِن تَرَكَ خَيرًا الوَصِيَّةُ لِلوَالِدَينِ وَالأَقرَبِينَ بِالمَعرُوفِ حَقًّا عَلَى المُتَّقِينَ" ("It is prescribed for you that when death approaches any of you, and he leaves behind wealth, he should make a bequest to parents and relatives in a fair manner. This is a duty upon the righteous.").

Now let us study the ruling on the obligation of fasting. At its end too it is stated that it has been made obligatory so that you may become righteous. "O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may attain taqwa." "يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ"

After the rulings on fasting come the rulings on i'tikaf, and after them too the final outcome is taqwa. "These are the limits set by Allah, so do not approach them. Thus does Allah make clear His signs to people, that they may guard against wrong conduct." "تِلْكَ حُدُودُ اللَّهِ فَلَا تَقْرَبُوهَا كَذَلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ آيَاتِهِ لِلنَّاسِ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ"

Besides this, none of the comments made at the conclusion of the subject matter in this lesson is free from themes that create taqwa, fear of God, and awareness of God's majesty in hearts. For example, in one place it is said: "and that you should glorify Allah for having guided you, and that you may be grateful" "وَلِتُكْمِلُوا الْعِدَّةَ وَلِتُكَبِّرُوا اللَّهَ عَلَى مَا هَدَاكُمْ وَلَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ". In another place: "فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ" ("So let them respond to Me and believe in Me, that they may be rightly guided"). "إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ" ("Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing"). "إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ" ("Indeed Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful").

In short, taqwa is mentioned continuously throughout this entire text, through which the reality of religion is grasped at a glance, and it becomes clear that religion is a unity whose parts cannot be separated from one another. Its social system, its legal principles, and its forms of worship all spring from a single source of belief and a single ideology. All these branches emerge from a single worldview, and this worldview arises from the Islamic ideology. All these branches are bound in one thread, and their final point of convergence is Allah. The purpose and aim of all of them is one: servitude, exclusively to the One God, who created, who provided sustenance, and who appointed man as His successor on this earth. But this successorship is on the condition that he believes in the One God alone, worships the One God alone, and makes his worldview, his collective order, and his laws derive from Allah alone, Allah alone!

In short, from the study of this entire lesson, its subject matters, and the comments and conclusions stated at the end of those subject matters, it becomes clear that all parts of this religion are interconnected, and what is the connection? Taqwa, servitude, and faith in Allah!

This call is addressed only to the believers. The attribute of faith was used in the address; the demand of this attribute is that in the matter of retaliation, guidance should be sought from Allah alone, in whom you have believed. Allah announces that retaliation has been made obligatory for you regarding the slain. The first verse is within the context of legislation, and in the second the wisdom of this law is explained. The believers are invited to try to understand, and in this way a sense of God-fearing is created in the hearts of Muslims. In short, in the matter of killing and the punishment for killing, the Islamic system of qisas holds the position of a safety valve.

The law stated in the aforementioned verse is that in the matter of killing, retaliation will be such that if a free person has killed, then retaliation is taken against the free person; if a slave has killed, then retaliation is taken against the slave. But along with this, a concession has been mentioned that is necessary for the stability of human civilization. "فَمَنْ عُفِيَ لَهُ مِنْ أَخِيهِ شَيْءٌ فَاتِّبَاعٌ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَأَدَاءٌ إِلَيْهِ بِإِحْسَانٍ" ("But if the brother (heir) of the slain is inclined to show leniency to the killer, then the settlement of blood-money should be made according to what is fair, and the killer is obliged to pay the blood-money with goodness.").

The form of leniency and forgiveness is that the heirs of the slain agree to accept blood-money in place of the killer being put to death in retaliation. When they are willing to take blood-money, they should determine the amount of blood-money by mutual consent and according to recognized principles. And it is the duty of the killer and his guardians to pay the blood-money with uprightness and goodness, so that rancour is removed from their hearts, bitterness ends, and the surviving members of the slain person's family can re-establish brotherly relations.

By allowing for blood-money in this most important matter, Allah has shown Muslims lightness and mercy. For this reason they have been directed to regard it as a great favour of Allah. "ذَلِكَ تَخْفِيفٌ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ وَرَحْمَةٌ" ("That is a lightening and a mercy from your Lord."). This allowance was not in the law of retaliation in the Torah. It is a concession given to the Muslim community, granted solely so that if an agreement is reached between the parties and their hearts become clean towards one another, then in that case not only are grudges erased but also a human life is saved. "فَمَنِ اعْتَدَى بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ فَلَهُ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ" ("Whoever transgresses after this will have a painful punishment.")

As for the punishment in the Hereafter, that will certainly be, but the punishment in this world is that if the killing is proven, then execution is mandatory, and blood-money will not be accepted from him, because it would render mutual consent and reconciliation useless, and would create enmity after hearts have been cleansed. Likewise, if the heir has accepted blood-money, then there is no justification for him to take revenge again; that would be an unjustified act of aggression.

From the system of qisas and blood-money it is evident how broad the perspective of Islam is, and that at the time of legislation it keeps a full view of the motives of the human soul.

The Exalted Creator has placed in the nature of man certain inclinations, and these have been fully taken into account. Upon seeing blood, blood naturally boils. Islam fulfilled this demand through the law of qisas. True justice is that it cools hearts, removes the suffocation of vengeance found within hearts, and even corrects the thinking of the criminal. Despite all these measures, Islam prefers that a mistake be forgiven, and so it paves the way for pardon and forgiveness.

The purpose of inviting to pardon and forgiveness after the obligation of the law of qisas is that if anyone wishes to attain this high rank through forgiveness, it is better for him. But this pardon and forgiveness is not obligatory. This is so that the natural demands of a person are not suppressed, and so that no burden is placed upon him that he cannot bear.

Some narrations mention that this verse is abrogated (mansukh), and that it has been abrogated by the verse of Surah al-Ma'idah revealed after it: "وَكَتَبنَا عَلَيهِم فِيهَا أَنَّ النَّفسَ بِالنَّفسِ" ("And We prescribed for them in it that the life is for life...").

Allamah Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir, says: "Regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim is cited, transmitted through Abu Zur'ah, Yahya ibn Abdullah ibn Bukayr, Abdullah ibn Lahi'ah, Ata ibn Dinar, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Regarding the verse 'O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you in the case of the slain' (يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْقِصَاصُ فِي الْقَتْلَى), that is, if it is intentional killing, then a free person will be killed in retaliation for a free person. The occasion of its revelation is that shortly before Islam, in the period of ignorance, tribes fought among themselves. Many people were killed, countless were wounded, and even slaves and women were slain. They had not yet taken anything from one another when the Islamic system came, and they became Muslims. One tribe began to act unjustly against another in terms of wealth and numbers. They swore an oath that they would not be satisfied until our slave is paid back with a slave and our woman with a woman." But this verse is abrogated, and the verse "the life for life" (النفس بالنفس) has abrogated it. Thus it is narrated from Abu Malik that this verse was abrogated by the verse "the life for life."

But the truth is that the context and setting of this verse and the context and setting of the verses "life for life" in Surah al-Ma'idah are different. The expression "life for life" applies to individual killing, that is, a specific person kills a specific person or persons. If it is intentional killing, the criminal will be punished. But the context of the verse under discussion is different. It states the ruling for the case of collective killing, where a family raises its hand against another family, a tribe fights against a tribe, and one group attacks another group, as was the case with the aforementioned tribes, in which free persons, slaves and women were killed. In such occasions, when qisas is settled, a free person will be killed for a free person, a slave of one tribe will be killed for a slave of another tribe, and a woman of one side will be killed for a woman of the other. If this were not the context, then let it be explained: when in a dispute both sides consist of large groups fighting against each other, what would be the form of qisas in that case?

If this viewpoint is accepted, then this verse will not be considered abrogated, and there will be no contradiction among the verses of qisas.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 179:

Now the discussion of the law of retribution (qisas) is concluded by stating its profound wisdom and its far-reaching objectives: "And in retribution there is life for you, O men of understanding, that you may guard yourselves (against wrongdoing)."

"O people of intellect and understanding! In retribution there is life for you. It is hoped that you will refrain from violating this law."

It is not merely vengeance; rather, it has far loftier and more exalted objectives. It is a killing of the person who is an obstacle to life, in the path of establishing life. Indeed, the establishment of qisas is itself life. This is so that this obligatory truth may be understood, and that its wisdom may be pondered over. Hearts should be alive and the fear of God should surge within them.

A criminal begins a crime. He should reflect that this matter is not trivial, but that he will have to pay the price of his own life in return. Thus, through the system of qisas, two lives are saved.

When murder is committed, the murderer is punished: he is put to death in retribution. The heirs of the victim are satisfied, their hearts are relieved of rancour, and the feelings of vengeance cool down. Otherwise, that vengeance, which among the Arab tribes would not stop at any limit or point, continued for forty years, one killing following another in retaliation. For example, this happened in the War of al-Basus (Harb al-Basus). Even today, the Arabs, and others as well, bear witness to this, where life is sacrificed to family feuds and grudges, and this matter continues from generation to generation, and this chain never seems to end.

"In retribution there is life," in its general meaning: an attack on one individual's life is in fact an attack on life in its totality; it is an attack on the whole of life, an attack on every human being, on every person who is alive like the victim. If, because of the law of qisas, a criminal refrains from ending even a single life, he has saved the whole of humanity. Thus, refraining from committing this crime is itself life, and this life is not the life of one individual, nor of one family, nor of one group, but life absolutely.

Now, at the end, reflection upon the wisdom of the divine law is awakened and the fear of God is enjoined. (This is the important factor and the effective means through which human life can survive.) "It is hoped that you will refrain from violating the law" (tattaqun).

This is the real bond which restrains man from oppression and transgression: at the beginning it restrains him from the transgression of unjust killing, and at the end from the transgression of vengeance. What is it? The fear of God, taqwa, the awareness of the fear of God in the heart and an intense sense of it: the feeling of fearing the wrath and punishment of Allah and the attraction to seeking His pleasure.

Without this restraint no law can succeed, and no shariah succeeds. No person refrains from committing a crime. Without the concept of a power higher and superior to human power, without the spiritual sense of fear of the Hereafter and longing for it, no outward order and legal retribution can succeed.

In the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) and during the period of the Caliphate, crimes occurred rarely; and when crimes did occur, the criminal himself confessed. The secret of this lay in the strength of taqwa there. In the hearts and minds of the people, taqwa sat like a watchman in the form of a living conscience, which remained awake at all times. It kept them far even from the boundaries of crime. Alongside this, human nature, human emotions and inclinations were also being regulated. On the other hand, through Islamic worship, there was a flowing torrent of taqwa and fear of God. As a result of the mutual cooperation and harmony of both, there existed a harmonious, pure and clean law and shariah. On one side, from shariah, law and outward retribution, a pure, righteous conception of life and system of life was born, in which people's conduct was a pure and righteous mode of thinking. Why? Because this order first installed a judge in every person's heart and established a court. The situation was such that if at some time someone was overcome by bestiality and an error occurred, and this person even escaped the grip of the law, still his faith became for him a self-reproaching soul (nafs lawwamah). He felt a prick and a sting in his conscience. In his heart a crowd of frightening thoughts constantly arose. And the one who committed sin found peace only when he voluntarily confessed his crime before the law, presented himself for severe punishment, and bore that punishment with joy and contentment, solely to escape the wrath of Allah. This is taqwa, this is the fear of God.

Now the matters of the will at the time of death are explained. The connection between the atmosphere of the verses of qisas and the atmosphere of these verses (that is, the end of death and life) is quite evident.

Bequest (wasiyyah) is also one of the obligations. It is due to parents and relatives, provided the deceased is leaving wealth behind. "Good" here means wealth. What is the amount up to which a bequest is obligatory? On this there is a difference of opinion. The preferred view is that the exact amount may vary for different occasions according to custom. Some jurists said that if the sum is less than 60 dirhams, it is considered that there is no estate. Some people raised this limit to 80 dinars, some to 400 dinars, and some to 1000. But the reality is that the amount may vary across different eras and for different families according to circumstances and conditions.

After these verses on bequest, the verses of inheritance were revealed, in which the shares of the heirs were fixed. And in every case of inheritance, parents were declared to be entitled, so now there is no bequest for parents, because heirs are in any case deprived of bequest.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has given every rightful person his right, so now no bequest is valid for an heir." As for relatives, this ruling still remains in its general application. Therefore, whoever receives a share according to the law of inheritance cannot benefit from a bequest, and whoever is not an heir under the law of inheritance, the verse of bequest remains operative for him.

Some companions and some of the Tabi'un went in this direction in interpreting this verse. We also prefer this view.

According to the provisions of the law of inheritance, sometimes close relatives are deprived. The requirement of maintaining kinship is that such people too should be given at least something. In such circumstances, the wisdom of these rulings on bequest becomes understood on its own. The law of bequest is, in reality, a aspect of mutual support (takaful) within the family and of economic responsibilities outside the sphere of inheritance law. Therefore it was ordained that the right of bequest should be exercised according to recognized principles, and in this matter the fundamental principle of fear of God should be kept in view.

﴿بِالْمَعْرُوفِ حَقًّا عَلَى الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ "In a recognized manner; it is a duty upon the God-conscious."

The exercise of this right should be such that it does not wrong the heirs, that non-heirs are not left deprived, that it is done with moderation and justice, mindful of the fear of God, and for the sake of goodness and benevolence. This is why the noble hadith imposed a restriction on this right, fixing one-third as the limit, and it is preferable that the right be limited to one-quarter, so that the true heirs do not suffer greater loss because of this non-heir. The decision in this matter has been placed simultaneously in the hands of both law and piety, and this is the spirit of that social system which the Holy Qur'an seeks to establish.

Whoever hears the bequest must convey it faithfully and completely to the concerned parties. If he changes it, the sin will be grave upon him; and if the listeners change it on their own, the deceased will be free of blame. ﴿Then whoever alters it after having heard it, the sin of it is only upon those who alter it. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ Then those who heard the bequest and afterwards altered it, the sin will fall upon those who alter it. Allah hears and knows everything.

Allah is a witness to what this person heard and what he has knowledge of. Allah is also a witness for the testator. Therefore, the deceased will not be held accountable; and since Allah is also a witness against the one who alters it, he will be held accountable for any unlawful change or alteration.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 182:

There is a situation in which the executor (wasi) has the authority to make some alterations to the bequest of the one who made the will. But this will be the case only when it becomes known that the testator has shown unjust partiality to someone, or has unlawfully deprived an heir of his right. In such a case, the person who has the authority to execute the bequest is permitted to alter it to the extent that no unjust deprivation of rights remains, nor any partiality. The matter is brought into accordance with justice and equity. ﴿But whoever fears partiality or wrongdoing from the testator and then brings about reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

"But whoever has apprehension that the testator has, either unintentionally or deliberately, wronged someone, and then brings about reconciliation among those concerned in the matter, there is no sin upon him. Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

In all matters, the affair is entrusted to Allah's forgiveness and His special mercy. In every state, Allah's bounty and His protection are the thread that holds together the circumstances of our lives, and this is the final guarantee for the attainment of justice and equity. The law of retaliation (qisas) and the law of bequest have both been bound into a single cord. That is to say, the fear of God, indeed the entire system of Islamic life and every issue of the Islamic society, is bound up within it.

This Ummah has been made a witness over all of humanity; it is the supreme overseer of humanity. It is to establish the Islamic system of life on the surface of the earth, and in this regard, jihad in the way of Allah has become obligatory. Therefore, it is a natural matter that fasting also be made obligatory upon it. Fasting makes the will strong and the resolve firm. Through it, a person meets his Lord in obedience and submission, and through it a person strives to gain control over all the needs of the body, bearing their pressure and their burden, solely in the pursuit of the pleasure of Allah and in hope of the reward of the Hereafter.

All these measures are so that the human self may become prepared to endure the difficulties and hardships that lie in the path of the workers of the Islamic movement, and the obstacles on this path, and the thorns that have been strewn along it. This is a path which, besides its hardships, has desirable and pleasing things scattered on both sides. Thousands of such things lie along this path, ready to deceive a person at every step.

Now, the discoveries of the present age come to light. Physicians say that fasting has good effects on the body as well. Although I am not in favour of stating such worldly benefits of fasting or of other acts of worship, which relate to physical life and are confined to the senses and sight, because the real purpose and aim of acts of worship is that a person be prepared for the duty he has to perform on the earth, and on the other hand he has to strive for that success and perfection which he will attain in the Hereafter; yet, despite this, I am also not opposed to the idea that the benefits which science and experience establish regarding acts of worship be denied entirely. This is because the wisdom that is clearly apparent in the general measures which Allah has adopted in prescribing obligations and acts of worship for human existence must be relied upon. However, it should be kept in view that the wisdoms and benefits manifested through science and experiments should not be regarded as the real cause or the true reason behind the rulings and legal obligations of the Shariah. This is because the domain of science is very limited. The wisdom in how Allah wishes to train human beings by breaking their animality, and the wisdoms within it, is a level to which human knowledge cannot possibly advance. Likewise, as for the uncontrollable forces of this entire universe which Allah wishes to tame, when does science reach there?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 2, verse 183:

Allah knew that to carry out obligations and duties, a person's soul needs great strength. In this matter, a person is in need of Allah's special help. It was necessary that a spirit be instilled in these commandments so that the soul would be drawn towards them, become content, and be pleased to act upon them, even though the benefit of acting upon these commands lies in the person himself. Therefore, He called out in a very beloved voice: "O you who believe!" Consider this: this call reminds them of their true reality. Then fasting is made obligatory. It is said, and this was obligatory on earlier nations too; it is not a new matter.

Its purpose is to purify the hearts of the people of faith, to prepare them for the fear of Allah, and to awaken within them the awareness and consciousness of Allah's will.

﴿O you who believe! Fasting has been prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may become God-conscious (taqwa).﴾

In this verse, the real aim and purpose of fasting becomes evident, namely taqwa (God-consciousness). When a believer fasts in obedience to Allah's command and for the sake of Allah's pleasure, the awareness of taqwa is awakened in his heart. It is taqwa that is the guardian of hearts, and it is what protects a person from violating the rules of fasting. It also protects a person from a sin that is, to some extent, merely a whisper. The first addressees of the Qur'an, the Companions (sahabah) (may Allah be pleased with them), understood its meaning well. They knew how heavy taqwa is in the sight of Allah. Therefore, taqwa was their ultimate goal. They constantly advanced towards it, and since fasting is one of the means of attaining taqwa, it was made obligatory. In reality, fasting is the path whose final destination is taqwa. It seems that here the Qur'an, from an elevated position, places a bright sign of taqwa right in front, and the eyes of the people of faith become fixed upon that target, and they are seen striving to reach it through fasting and with the help of fasting.

﴿So that you may fear (Allah).﴾ (لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ)

The other side of the matter should be seen. It is said: these are only a few days; the fasts were not prescribed for a whole lifetime. They are not obligatory for all times. Alongside this, the sick are exempt until they recover, and travellers are not bound until they return home. This is a special concession granted by Allah as facilitation and relief.

أَيَّامًا مَعْدُودَاتٍ فَمَنْ كَانَ مِنْكُمْ مَرِيضًا أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ فَعِدَّةٌ مِنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ "Prescribed days. So whoever among you is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days."

With regard to travel and illness, the meaning of the verse is general. It should not be restricted. Whatever the nature of the illness, and whatever kind of journey one faces, it is permissible to make up the fast. However, after the journey has ended and the illness has gone, the fasts that were left must be kept. The verse does not make the severity of the illness or the difficulties of the journey the cause of this concession. Only "illness" and "journey" are mentioned in general terms, so that difficulties do not arise for people and ease remains. Now, what is the wisdom in Allah mentioning only illness and only journey, without attaching any condition? Only Allah knows. It is possible that there are things in illness and journey that Allah has in view which we do not know. It is possible that there are difficulties in illness and journey of which we are not aware. When Allah did not regard the outward sign of this command as the essential basis, then what need do we have for interpretations (ta'wilat) on this matter? In any case, whether or not we know their wisdom, we must certainly hold the belief that there is some wisdom and benefit behind them.

It may be said that this expression of concession for illness and travel will encourage those who are always seeking concessions and ease in religion. Should we abandon obligatory acts of worship for some trivial reason without cause? This is precisely why our jurists, with strictness, have imposed conditions and restrictions on benefiting from this concession. I consider this argument to be a weak argument. Merely for this reason, and solely on the basis of this argument, there is no justification for restricting an absolute verse. Binding people in chains and compelling them to acts of worship is not a permanent policy of Islam. Islam considers it appropriate to create attraction in acts of worship through taqwa (God-consciousness). Fasting is itself that act of worship whose purpose is only taqwa.

As for the person whose condition is that he seeks out concessions and runs away from acts of worship, he is already deprived of goodness. Even if he keeps the fast, the purpose that is the real demand of the obligation of fasting will not be achieved.

Then consider this: is this religion the property of people or of Allah? The religion belongs to Allah, and He knows well the places of concession, ease, and of resolution (azimah) and severity. Sometimes the goals that are intended through a concession cannot be achieved in any other way without the concession. This is why the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the Muslims that they should benefit from the concessions Allah has given them. Especially in an age when the moral and religious condition of Muslims has been ruined, in such circumstances severity in rulings is not useful for reform. What is needed is that people be given moral training with gentleness and ease, and that the fear of Allah be revived anew in their hearts and souls. If this is correct, then I would say that at a time of general corruption in the ummah, severity in rulings is an ineffective remedy. It closes the avenues of reform.

This must be understood: there is a very great difference between the obligations of worship and the rulings of dealings (mu'amalat). In acts of worship, the matter concerns only the servant and his Lord; there is no direct benefit or harm to the public in it. Whereas in dealings, the Shari'ah keeps its eye on the outward aspect of the matter. As for acts of worship, their outward form is not beneficial unless there is taqwa at their core. If there is taqwa in the heart, no person will even look here and there. And a God-conscious person will take advantage only of that concession about which his heart is satisfied that benefiting from the concession is itself obedience and pleasing Allah.

Being strict in the rulings of worship, or trying to create hardship, that is, adding restrictions to rulings which Allah has left general, sometimes creates severe difficulties for the common people, but as a result of that severity there is no reduction in deviant individuals. Therefore, in every situation the better approach is that we take matters in the way Allah has settled them in this religion. Allah knows better than us the wisdoms behind concessions and resolutions. I consider that what has been said on this point is sufficient and complete.

Now we wish to present all the numerous narrations that have been transmitted concerning the conditions of travel. Some of them incline toward breaking the fast; some do not prohibit breaking the fast. Reflecting on all these narrations fixes in the mind the picture upon which the practice of the Companions was based. Compared with the later jurists and their juristic discussions, the conduct of the early righteous predecessors and the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) in this matter was closer to the spirit and temperament of the religion of Islam. From studying the lives of the Companions and their conduct, a taste for the Islamic worldview and its characteristics is developed.

1. Hadrat Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out towards Makkah in the month of Ramadan in the year of the conquest of Makkah. He (ﷺ) fasted. When he reached Kura' al-Ghamim, the people also fasted. Upon this, he (ﷺ) called for a cup of water and raised it so that the people could see it. Then he drank it. It was said to him: "Some people are still fasting." He said: "They are disobedient, they are disobedient." (Muslim, Tirmidhi)

2. Hadrat Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey. Some of us were fasting and some had broken their fast. It was a very hot day. We stopped at a place. The one who had the most shade was the one who had a cloak. Some of us would shield themselves from the sun's heat with their hand. Those who were fasting collapsed, and those who had not fasted got up. They pitched tents and gave water to the animals. Upon this, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Today, those who broke their fast have taken away the reward.'" (Bukhari, Muslim, Nasa'i)

3. Hadrat Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: The Messenger (ﷺ) was on a journey. He saw that people had gathered around a man and shade had been cast over him. He (ﷺ) asked: "What has happened to him?" The people said: "He is a fasting person." Upon this, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Fasting on a journey is not righteousness." (Imam Malik, Imam Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Nasa'i)

4. Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: I came into the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a journey. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Abu Umayyah, wait for the food." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am fasting." He said: "Then listen concerning the traveller: Allah has remitted the fast for him and has remitted half of the prayer." (Nasa'i)

5. Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has remitted a part of the prayer for the traveller. On a journey there is a concession for him to break the fast. The same concession applies to a nursing woman and a pregnant woman, if there is fear of harm to the child." (Narrated in the Sunan)

6. Hadrat Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) narrated, she said: Hamzah ibn Amr al-Aslami asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about fasting on a journey. This man used to fast often. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If you wish, fast; if you wish, break your fast."

7. Hadrat Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated, he said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Some of us were fasting and some had broken their fast. The one who was fasting did not criticise the one who broke his fast, and the one who broke his fast did not regard the conduct of the one fasting as blameworthy." (Malik, Muslim, Bukhari, Abu Dawud)

8. Hadrat Abu al-Darda (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the month of Ramadan in intense heat. The heat was so severe that we would place our hands over our heads to protect ourselves from the scorching. Among all of us, only the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Hadrat Ibn Rawahah (may Allah be pleased with him) were fasting." (Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud)

9. Hadrat Muhammad ibn Ka'b narrated: "I came to Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) in Ramadan. He was about to set out on a journey. The mount was ready. He had put on travelling clothes. He called for food and ate. Everyone said: 'Is this the Sunnah?' He said: 'Yes.' After that he mounted." (Tirmidhi)

10. Ubayd ibn Habirah narrated: "I was in a boat with Abu Basrah al-Ghifari (may Allah be pleased with him), one of the Companions of the noble Messenger (ﷺ). In the month of Ramadan the boat was put into the water and food was brought near him. He said: 'Come close.' I said: 'Do you not see that the houses are still visible?' He said: 'Do you turn away from the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' So he ate, and I also ate." (Abu Dawud)

11. Mansur al-Makki narrated that Hadrat Dihyah ibn Khalifah (may Allah be pleased with him) set out in the month of Ramadan from a village in the vicinity of Damascus. The journey was as much as the distance from the village of Fisat to the village of Aqabah, and this distance is about three miles. He broke his fast. Many people broke their fast along with him, but some others disliked breaking the fast. When he returned to his village he said: "By Allah, today I have seen something that was never seen before. A group of people has turned away from the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. O Allah, take me to Yourself." (Abu Dawud)

All these narrations show that, even in a pleasant and comfortable journey, the concession of breaking the fast has been accepted, and indeed breaking the fast has been preferred. And hardship or difficulty of the journey has not been made an essential condition for acting upon the concession, as is especially evident from the last two narrations. From the eighth narration it appears that only the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abdullah ibn Rawahah (may Allah be pleased with him) were fasting. However, the narrations show that the Prophet (ﷺ) had certain specific features in acts of worship that were not for the ummah. For example, he forbade "continuous fasting" (sawm al-wisal), although he sometimes kept continuous fasts. ("Continuous" means that one day's fast is joined to the next without breaking the fast.) When the Companions raised this matter with him, he said: "I am not like you. My Lord feeds me and gives me drink at all times." (Bukhari, Muslim)

Then, from the first narration it appears that the Prophet (ﷺ) himself broke his fast, and about those who had not broken their fast he said: "They are disobedient, they are disobedient." Moreover, this narration is later than all the others, since it concerns the year of the conquest of Makkah. Therefore the ruling in it is the last one, and from it it appears what the preferred conduct is.

Keeping these circumstances in view, the picture that emerges clearly shows that at the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) there were certain specific events in which it was necessary to give a definite ruling. The Prophet (ﷺ) was training the Muslim nation. He was dealing with a living and dynamic situation, not merely with static and lifeless idols. For this reason, sometimes the narrations that come on a general subject contain variety in rulings and instructions, because rulings are given according to the occasion and circumstance.

Taking into account all the circumstances and narrations, the impression that is formed is that during travel, breaking the fast is more excellent than fasting, and there is no condition that hardship must actually be present or not.

As for illness, I have found nothing beyond the statements of the jurists on this matter. Apparently, what is meant by it is every condition to which the term illness and sickness can apply. There is no restriction on its nature, its extent, or its severity. There is only one condition: in the case of illness and travel, the fasts must be made up in place of the days, and as for making up, the preferred view is that the number of days must be completed. It is not necessary that the fasts be consecutive.

I have not mentioned these details in order to show that I have any particular interest in juristic differences. My purpose is only to clarify the basic principle according to which Islamic acts of worship should be viewed.

The question is: what is their real purpose? Is it that a certain state of conscious awareness should arise in a person's mind, which influences his conduct? It is this state that affects a person's conduct, and through it a person receives spiritual training. Khushu' in worship means that the heart becomes fully turned toward Allah and melted before Him, and good character and better conduct throughout life can arise only as a result of this conscious state. This is one aspect. The other aspect is that we accept this religion just as it is: with all its obligations and burdens, in submission and awe, acting upon its resolutions (aza'im) and benefiting from its concessions (rukhas), in full harmony, with peace of heart, believing in its wisdoms and fully sensing the fear of Allah.

After this discussion, now return to the context of the speech!

And for those who are able to fast (yutiqunahu), there is a redemption: feeding a poor person. Whoever volunteers good, it is better for him. And that you fast is better for you, if you know.

"And those who are able to fast only with great difficulty must give a ransom: the feeding of a needy person for each day. And whoever does good voluntarily, it is better for him. But if you understand, fasting is better for you."

Fasting was made obligatory in the second year after the Hijrah, shortly before the obligation of jihad. In the early period, the hardship of fasting was very heavy for the Muslims. Therefore Allah granted an open concession to those who could fast only with difficulty. (Yutiqunahu means those who can fast only with difficulty. Al-ittaqah in Arabic means bearing hardship.) The concession was that such people may break the fast, but they must feed one needy person for each day of fasting missed. After this, they were encouraged to do more good to the needy, for example by feeding more than the fixed number of needy persons without any ransom being required. For instance, if for one day of Ramadan a person feeds three, four, or even more people, then:

﴿فَمَنْ تَطَوَّعَ خَيْرًا فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَهُ﴾ "And whoever does good beyond what is required of his own accord, it is good for him."

﴿وَأَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ "But if you understand, it is better for you that you fast."

This is because in such circumstances, fasting is a very great good. Fasting in such conditions shows that the fasting person possesses firm resolve, has endurance within him, and is able to sacrifice his comfort for the worship of Allah. All these matters are the primary objectives of the training system of Islam. Moreover, it is also known from this that if people other than the sick fast with hardship and exertion, there is also physical benefit for them in it.

Anyway, this verse was a preface, and as mentioned in the other verse, the real purpose was that fasting be gradually made obligatory absolutely upon the healthy resident. Yes, however, this ruling still remains for an old man and an old woman for whom fasting is difficult and who have no hope of becoming healthy again and being able to fast. Imam Malik (rh) says that it has reached him that Hadrat Anas ibn Malik (ra) had become quite old and had no ability to fast. Therefore, a ransom (fidyah) was given on his behalf. (Hadrat Ibn Abbas (ra) says that this verse is not abrogated. It is for the old man and the old woman who do not have the strength to fast. It is obligatory upon them that they feed a poor person for each day's fast.) Narrated from Ibn Abi Layla, who says: I went to ʿAta during Ramadan and found him eating. When I asked the reason, he said: Ibn Abbas said, (Shahru Ramadan) this verse was revealed, and the earlier one was abrogated. However, for an extremely old person, this concession still remains: if he wishes, he may break his fast by feeding a poor person for each day. In short, from the following verse it is established that this concession has been removed from the healthy person who is resident at home. And the coming verse, "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it" (فَمَنْ شَهِدَ مِنْكُمُ الشَّهْرَ), has abrogated this verse.

The healthy resident is now again encouraged that he must fast. These are the fasts of the month of Ramadan. This is the month in which the Great Quran was revealed. Either the Quran began in Ramadan, or most of it was revealed in the blessed month of Ramadan. The Quran is an everlasting book for this ummah. It was the Quran that brought this ummah out of pitch-black darkness into light and raised it to that magnificent height. In place of fear, it received tranquility. It granted it establishment on this earth. It gave it foundations and elements on the basis of which it became a single ummah. Yet what was it before the Quran? Nothing. And even now, without this Quran, what standing would this ummah have on this earth? Without it, it would not even remain an ummah. It would have no place on earth and no mention in the heavens. Therefore, the least thanks for these blessings is that Muslims be in the blessed month of Ramadan, in which this Quran was revealed.

"The month of Ramadan is that in which the Quran was revealed, a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion (between truth and falsehood). So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it, and whoever is ill or on a journey, then (let him fast) a number of other days." (Al-Baqarah 2:185)

This verse absolutely makes fasting obligatory, and the concession to break the fast for the healthy resident is withdrawn. Now they cannot break their fast by paying a ransom, except for the old man and the old woman, as we mentioned earlier. "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it" (فَمَنْ شَهِدَ مِنْكُمُ الشَّهْرَ فَلْيَصُمْهُ): that is, from now on, whoever reaches this month must fast its entire duration. That is, whoever reaches the month and is not a traveler, whoever sees the moon of Ramadan. If anyone becomes certain that the month has begun, by whatever means, then fasting is obligatory upon him in the same way as it is obligatory upon the one who sees the moon.

Since this verse also carries generality, a further exceptional provision is prescribed here for the sick and the traveler: "And whoever is ill or on a journey, then (let him fast) a number of other days" (وَمَنْ كَانَ مَرِيضًا أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ فَعِدَّةٌ مِنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ).

Now, for the third time, encouragement is given to fulfil this important obligation. It is stated that the obligation of fasting is also a mercy, and the permission to break it is also a mercy: "Allah desires ease for you, and He does not desire hardship for you" (يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ بِكُمُ الْيُسْرَ وَلا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ الْعُسْرَ). In short, the fundamental principle of all worship and obligations in the Islamic worldview is that dealings be gentle and that there be no excessive harshness. These acts of worship are such that the heart in which right taste is produced receives the awareness that it should adopt a gentle attitude in the affairs of its whole life and not be harsh. As a result, simplicity arises in a Muslim and his life becomes pure. There is no pretension in it, there is no complexity in it. It appears that the whole life of a Muslim, in the performance of obligations and duties and in all the affairs of practical life, flows like a flowing stream. His life thus progresses imperceptibly, with contentment, certainty and submission, just as a tree keeps growing. And the awareness is always with the believer that he should not be deprived, through the mercy of Allah, of the reward of worship: "And that you complete the period and that you glorify Allah for having guided you, and that you may be grateful" (وَلِتُكْمِلُوا الْعِدَّةَ وَلِتُكَبِّرُوا اللَّهَ عَلَى مَا هَدَاكُمْ وَلَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ).

One of the purposes of this obligation is that a true awareness of the worth and value of this guidance, which Allah has provided to those who believe with great ease and abundance, be produced in their hearts; and that their condition become such that, compared to other days, their awareness of religion becomes more firm in the month of fasting. Their hearts should cease even to think about disobedience and sin. Their limbs should not be ready to commit disobedience. They should behave as though they are feeling, indeed touching, Allah's guidance. Their hearts should incline toward Allah with that obedience and servitude, as was said at the beginning of the discussion of Ramadan: "So that you may become righteous" (لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ).

Fasting, which at first sight appears hard and burdensome for the body, is in reality a great favour of Allah. Furthermore, it also becomes known what its educational purposes are, and that through this training a believer is being prepared for that great role for which this ummah was raised, so that he may fulfil this duty with the greatest fear of God, under Allah's watchfulness and with a living conscience.

Before the detailed rules of fasting are stated—namely, from what time to what time the fast is observed, and what is permitted in it and what is forbidden—we draw attention to the blessings of fasting and explain that in return for the hardships of fasting, Allah grants us full recompense. What is this recompense and reward? Nearness to Allah and the acceptance of supplications. Just look at the words of the Quran.

The Commentary of Sayyid Qutb, Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation), on Surah 2, verse 186:

"I am near." Whenever the supplicant calls upon Me, I hear his call. How gentle this is! Just look at the grace of it! Observe the clarity of its words and meanings! Observe the intimacy and love! What are the hardships of fasting, or indeed of all acts of worship, when set against this nearness and this love? Where does the sense of hardship remain in the cool shade of such intimacy and love?

Upon every word of this verse there is a fresh dew of intimacy and love. "My servant! If they ask you about Me, tell them that I am indeed near. When the supplicant calls upon Me, I hear his call and I respond." ﴿أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ﴾

This is a wondrous verse! It fills the heart of the believer with a sweet freshness, a pleasant love, tranquillity, contentment and firm certainty. The believer reaches the paradise of submission and contentment. He attains a tender union, and he arrives at a peaceful refuge and a restful resting place. In this atmosphere of intimacy and love, in this environment of eager acceptance and divine responsiveness, Allah the Exalted instructs His servants that they should answer My call and believe in Me. Perhaps this faith and this obedience will lead them to the path of guidance and the straight way. ﴿فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ﴾

"So let them answer My call and believe in Me, that perhaps they may be rightly guided."

The final benefit of submission and faith in Allah also belongs to the servants, namely guidance, direction and the rectification of their condition. What benefit does Allah gain from faith and servitude? He is free of need from both worlds.

In short, guidance is that which is founded upon faith in Allah and obedience to Allah.

Only the Islamic system can guide man to the right path, and the Islamic system alone is the correct way. All other systems are pure ignorance (jahiliyyah) and sheer folly. No seeker of truth can be content with them, nor can man find the path of guidance through those systems. Obedience and submission to Allah is possible only when the one who answers is upon the path of guidance. Seekers of the truth should call upon Allah, but they should not be hasty in the acceptance of their supplications, because Allah, in accordance with His wise purposes, responds to every call in His own time and in a suitable manner.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated, with their chain of transmission, the hadith of Ibn Maymun from Hadrat Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him). He said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, when a person raises his hands before Allah and seeks good from Him, Allah is very shy of returning those hands empty and disappointed."

al-Tirmidhi narrated, through Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman, the hadith of Ibn Thawban with his chain, and Abdullah ibn Imam Ahmad narrated the same hadith with his chain from Hadrat Ubadah ibn al-Samit. Both said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever on the face of this earth calls upon Allah and seeks some good, Allah either grants him that very thing, or, in accordance with what he seeks, removes some calamity that is coming upon him, provided that he does not seek something sinful or the severing of kinship ties."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Your supplication will not be answered provided that you are not hasty." For example, someone says: "I called upon Allah much, but my supplication was not answered."

In Sahih Muslim, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is reported to have said: "The supplication of a servant will certainly be answered, provided that it does not seek sin or the severing of kinship ties, and that he is not hasty." The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) asked: "O Messenger of Allah, how does haste occur?" He (ﷺ) said: "That he says: 'I have called upon Allah again and again, yet I do not see that my supplication is being answered,' and thus he abandons supplication and falls into loss."

The fasting person is indeed one whose supplications are readily accepted. Imam Abu Dawud (may Allah have mercy on him), in his Musnad, with his chain, narrates from Hadrat Abdullah ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). He said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "At the time of iftar, every fasting person has a right to the acceptance of one supplication." So Abdullah ibn Umar, whenever he broke his fast, would call his family and make supplication.

Ibn Majah, in his Sunan, with his chain, narrates from Abdullah ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For every fasting person, at the time of iftar, there is a right to the acceptance of one supplication."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from Hadrat Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three persons' supplications are not rejected: a just ruler, a fasting person until he breaks his fast, and the cry of the oppressed. On the Day of Judgment, Allah will raise him above the clouds, the gates of heaven will be opened for him, and Allah will say: 'By My might, I will surely help you, even though it be after some delay.'" This is the reason why supplication has been specifically mentioned in the discussion of fasting.

Now the necessary rulings for the believers are set out.
