The fasting person is permitted, during the month of Ramadan, from sunset until the break of dawn, to go to his wives, and likewise to eat during this period. The time of fasting is also stated: it is from the break of dawn until sunset. Similarly, during the period of i'tikaf, the command regarding going to one's wives is also given.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 187:

Initially the ruling was that if a fasting person went to sleep after iftar, eating, drinking and approaching one's wives became forbidden to him. If someone fell asleep and then woke up, even if he woke before the break of dawn (fajr), it was forbidden for him to approach his wife or to eat and drink. It often happened that a Companion was overcome by sleep at the time of iftar and fell asleep. Then there was no alternative for him but to keep the fast continuously into the next day. Such a thing happened to one man, who with great difficulty completed the fast the next day. The matter reached the Prophet (ﷺ). Similarly, there were incidents in which a man went to sleep after iftar, his wife also fell asleep, and when they awoke they had intercourse, and the matter reached the Messenger (ﷺ). From these events it becomes apparent that this ruling was becoming burdensome for the Muslims. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, abrogated this difficult ruling and the matter was made easy. Since they had already faced difficulties in these rulings of fasting, and the experience was fresh in their minds, they deeply appreciated the grace and kindness of Allah. The verse was revealed, and for them it was declared lawful to eat, drink and approach their wives between Maghrib and the break of dawn.

﴿It has been made lawful for you, on the nights of fasting, to go to your wives.﴾ The meaning of "ar-rafath" (الرفث) is either the beginning of intimacy or the act of intimacy itself. Here the permissibility of both is intended. Both are lawful, but in the course of explanation, a reader going over the Qur'an cannot help but feel a pleasant impression. In this relationship between husband and wife, a silk-like softness, freshness and a glass-like purity are created. Moreover, it is cleansed of animal harshness and animal defects.

﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them.﴾ A garment covers, protects from heat and cold; in the same way, the mutual relationship of husband and wife is a covering for both of them, and a protector of them. Islam looks at human beings according to their real nature, and according to that real nature it also fulfills their natural demands; and thus this system takes the hand of man and carries him to heights. This is Islam, and this is its view of life. It fulfills the natural demands of flesh and blood, and it fulfills them in a pleasant and gentle atmosphere, within the delicate veils of purity.

Allah is All-Knowing and All-Aware. He makes clear what your hidden feelings are, and then shows that He fulfills your needs in order to satisfy your natural impulses.

﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned to you and pardoned you.﴾ What was this betrayal? It was the desires hidden in their hearts, the secret feelings that were calling for the commission of a sin. Or the meaning is that you were secretly breaking this command, as some narrations mention that some people violated it, but Allah pardoned both kinds of people. Since their weakness and frailty had become apparent, and Allah knew it, their need was met: ﴿So now, have intercourse with them.﴾

But its permissibility was also linked to the pleasure of the Lord. It was commanded that in this too you should turn towards Allah: ﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you.﴾ That is, benefit from the enjoyment of women which Allah has made lawful for you, and also benefit from the children that result from it. Both things are included in the command of Allah; both are provisions which Allah has made lawful for you to seek and to enjoy. Yet behind this enjoyment lies deep wisdom. In the sight of Allah it is a purposeful duty. It is not merely physical desire and mere animal pleasure, whose connection is only with the act itself. In this way the relationship between husband and wife, linked to a lofty purpose, becomes a duty of nature. Instead of a brief moment of pleasure, it becomes purposeful on the horizon of humanity. On seeing these indications and commands within the Islamic system of life and the Islamic manner of living, it becomes known what revolution Islam wishes to bring into human life and along what lines it intends to develop it. It accomplishes all this within the limits of man, within his capacity to endure and in accordance with his innate temperament. This is the Islamic system of training, elevation and progress, whose source is Allah, who is thoroughly aware of the conditions of His creatures, who is subtle and all-aware.

Just as permission was given to approach one's wife during these hours, permission was also given to eat and drink during these hours: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn.﴾ That is, until light spreads over the horizon and the tops of the mountains. This does not mean the mere appearance of a white streak on the horizon; that is called the false dawn (fajr kadhib). After studying the narrations concerning the breaking of the fast, we can say that this time is a little before sunrise. The timings generally fixed in our area at present are those according to which we keep the fast. These timings are somewhat earlier than the legal time and have been fixed for additional caution.

Ibn Jarir (rahimahullah), with his chain, narrated from Samurah ibn Jundub (radiyallahu anhu) that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Let not the adhan of Bilal, or the 'long dawn' (mustatil), deceive you from taking suhur."

By this is meant the dawn that spreads across the horizon (al-mustatir), and before sunrise the dawn spreads a little. What used to happen was that Bilal would call the adhan very early to alert the sleeping people for suhur, and Ibn Umm Maktum would call the adhan at the end to close the fast. Therefore it was said that you should not be deceived by the adhan of Bilal.

After this, the ruling concerning intercourse during i'tikaf in the mosques is explained. I'tikaf means to seclude oneself in the mosque, turning towards Allah, and not to leave the mosque except for essential needs, such as eating, drinking, and relieving oneself. It is recommended and is performed in the last ten days of Ramadan. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) acted upon this in the last ten days of Ramadan. The period of i'tikaf is a time when one is separated from ordinary worldly routines and turns only towards Allah. Therefore, in order to complete this seclusion and detachment, it was commanded that during this period one should also abstain from approaching one's wives, so that the human self may be freed from all impurities and the heart may be purified from all preoccupations.

﴿And do not have intercourse with them while you are in seclusion in the mosques.﴾ Whether it is the time of fasting, that is the day, or the time of breaking the fast, that is the night.

At the very end, the whole matter is connected to the Divine Being, as is the constant style of the Qur'an in every disciplinary command and guidance: that is, in every matter, in every prohibition, in every movement and in every stillness.

﴿These are the limits set by Allah, so do not approach them.﴾

Here it is prohibited with such severity that one should not even come near, so that there is a necessary zone of safety between a person and what is forbidden. A grazing animal that roams around the pasture eventually enters it, and a person cannot always watch over his own self. Therefore it is not appropriate for him to keep roaming near forbidden things that are desirable, relying on the confidence that whenever he wishes he will control his self. No person should place himself in such a dangerous test. Thus this Ummah is involved in a matter that is pleasurable and among desirable things. Therefore it has been commanded: do not even approach. Yet the purpose is only that you should avoid falling into those forbidden things; approaching is not itself prohibited in the sense that... the intent is only that caution and fear of Allah should be exercised.

﴿Thus Allah makes His signs clear to mankind, that they may become righteous.﴾ It is stated that the ultimate purpose of the revelation of the Qur'an and the conveying of its verses is the attainment of God-consciousness. This is the precious and great purpose whose importance and value are recognized only by those who believe and who, in every age, seek the Qur'an.

In connection with the discussion of fasting, another kind of eating is also prohibited, namely the unlawful consumption of people's wealth, involving them in litigation, cunningly entrapping them, producing evidence and proofs against them before the authorities, and obtaining decrees against them through cunning and eloquent speech. This is strictly forbidden, because the judge decides according to the apparent circumstances of the case and the testimony and proofs. If false testimonies are presented, the decision will be against the proper circumstances. Therefore this prohibition has been made after the mention of Allah's help and after the continuous call to God-consciousness and fear of Allah, so that this important command of prohibition comes in an atmosphere of fear of Allah that restrains a person from committing forbidden acts.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 188:

Ibn Kathir, in his commentary on this verse, has written: 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah reports from Ibn 'Abbas: "This refers to a person who owes another person a debt, and there is no proof against him. He denies it and takes the matter to the rulers, knowing that the right is due from him, and knowing well that he is a sinner and one who consumes what is unlawful." Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Muqatil ibn Hayyan and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam also report it. All of them said: "If you know that you are doing wrong, then do not file a lawsuit."

In Bukhari and Muslim, it is reported from Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I am only a human being. You bring your disputes to me, and perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his plea than the other, and I rule in his favour. Know that whomever I rule in favour of, from the right of his brother, I have in fact given him a piece of the Fire. He may take it or leave it." Thus Allah leaves the matter of such people to themselves, who are aware of the reality of their claim.

A judge's verdict does not make the unlawful lawful, nor does it make the lawful unlawful. Its only effect is that the decision is apparently enforced. The sin rests upon the deceiver.

Just as the ruling on retribution (qisas), the ruling on bequest (wasiyyah), and the rules of fasting (siyam), so too in litigation and financial dealings the matter is entrusted to the fear of God and piety (taqwa). All these rulings are in fact parts of the collective body of the Islamic system, and the spirit of all of them is taqwa. All these parts are bound together with the strong cord of taqwa. This is why the Islamic system of life is a unity. It is an indivisible whole, a single entity whose parts cannot be separated. If we act upon some of its parts and abandon others, then this would be acting upon some of the Book and denying a part, which ultimately leads to disbelief. We seek refuge with Allah.

**Lesson 12: An Overview**

As in the previous lessons, this lesson teaches the community some of its obligations. It lays down legislation on certain national and some international matters of the Islamic system of life.

This lesson describes the waxing and waning phases of the moon. It mentions entering houses from the back, a custom that some people in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) observed. It contains the rules on fighting, on warfare near the Masjid al-Haram (the Sacred Mosque) in the sacred months, and the reformed rules of Hajj (pilgrimage) and Umrah (lesser pilgrimage), arranged in order and with appropriate amendments. From all these matters, the elements connected with the Age of Ignorance have been removed.

As in the previous lesson, some rulings here relate to belief and worldview, some to rites and worship, and some to war. All of them are strung together in a single thread: the remembrance of God and fear of Him, that is, taqwa (God-consciousness).

Where it is commanded that you should not enter houses from the back but come in through the front, the concept and meaning of righteousness is at the same time corrected. It is explained that the outward forms of movement and rest are not what righteousness is. Rather, righteousness is the name of fear of God.

﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: they are signs for people and for the Hajj. It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs; rather, righteousness is that one should be mindful of God. So enter houses through their doors, and fear God so that you may prosper.﴾

It is commanded that during war you should avoid oppression and transgression. But the motive for avoiding it should also be attachment to God and fear of Him. ﴿Indeed, God does not love the transgressors.﴾ In the ruling on fighting near the Masjid al-Haram it is also said: ﴿And fear God, and know that God is with those who are mindful of Him.﴾

Now the explanation of the rules of the Hajj stations (mawaqit) begins. During it, sexual acts, obscenity and quarrelling are forbidden, and the outcome is again taqwa. ﴿And take provisions, for the best provision is taqwa. So fear Me, O people of understanding.﴾

Spending in the way of God is commanded, and in it the final outcome is taqwa and ihsan (excellence). ﴿Do good, for God loves those who do good.﴾ ﴿Guard against violating the commands of God, and know that God is severe in punishment.﴾

After Hajj, people are guided to become absorbed in the remembrance of God. But the final advice is again taqwa: ﴿Fear God, and know that you will be gathered before Him.﴾

It is clearly evident that all these diverse rulings are bound firmly together in one strong rope. This rope and this connection arise from the overall temperament of this religion. The temperament of this religion is that in it, worship is not separated from consciousness, and general laws and worldly rules and regulations are not separated from worship. This religion cannot be established unless worldly affairs and the affairs of the Hereafter are brought together. Unless national and international matters are tied to a worldview and to the world of the heart and vision, and unless this religion is made to pervade and prevail throughout the whole of human life, and until the condition is reached where the whole of life runs completely in accordance with the concept of unity, with a single harmonious system dominating it, one complete system operating within it, a system founded on the Shariah of God, a single unity encompassing all the affairs of life within its bounds.

At the very beginning of this section of the surah, a scene comes before us. In this scene, Muslims look to the exemplary conduct of their beloved Prophet (ﷺ) regarding various forms of life. They ask about circumstances that arise in their lives day after day. They appear eager to know how they should behave in these matters according to their new worldview, so that it conforms to their new system of life. The first thing that draws their attention is the phenomena of nature. They reflect on the moon: what is its reality? It appears as a crescent, then gradually becomes full, then begins to wane, then becomes a crescent again, until it disappears, and then it rises again anew as a crescent. Then they try to understand: what should they spend? Which kind of wealth should they spend? How much should they spend? In what proportion should spending be made?

Then they consider: what is the ruling on fighting near the Masjid al-Haram? What is the ruling on fighting in the sacred months? Then they ask about gambling and games of chance: what is the ruling in the new system? Not long before, they were all wine-drinkers, and apart from gambling they had no other occupation.

Then suddenly they ask about women's menstrual periods: is marital relations permitted during those days? Then they ask about the special relations with their wives, and sometimes such questions were asked by the wives themselves. In short, not only does their thinking about the whole system of life change, but their conduct also changes. They appear at the pinnacle of perfection in purity and cleanliness.

These questions are of extreme importance, and countless realities are revealed through them. For example:

Firstly, this is evidence that the forms of collective life at that time, and the relationships among them, were alive, developing and expanding. The Islamic society was being reconstituted, its identity was being established, and new forms were being presented. The members of the society held firm conviction in their collective life. They were no longer scattered individuals and dispersed tribes. Now they had become one Ummah (community), which had a distinct existence, its own system, its own form, and all its members were firmly bound to this system. For every individual it was important to be fully aware of the pure lines of life and to be informed about the nature of mutual relations and connections. This new situation arose in fact as a result of a new worldview, a new system of life and new leadership. And their humanity, their consciousness and their thought, indeed the whole society, was progressing in every dimension.

This all-round inquiry also shows how keen the religious sense of the Muslims was, and how deeply the Islamic worldview had penetrated their hearts. This worldview had so overshadowed their lives that they would not do any daily task until, in the light of this new worldview, they were convinced that it was correct. This was because nothing of their former life remained in place. They had cast off the whole yoke of the customs and habits of the Age of Ignorance. They no longer had any trust in the old rituals, and at every turn of life and every task they awaited a new instruction. They were always awake and conscious, and this conscious state was due to their firm belief in the truth. Their souls had been purified of all jahili habits and ways. They examined carefully every aspect of jahiliyyah and abandoned it. They were always ready to take guidance from the new worldview. They had resolved to build their new life, purely and as quickly as possible, in accordance with this new worldview. This new worldview was reshaping their lives into new moulds. Even those matters of the old era which were retained out of necessity, they took with the new colour and training. It is not necessary that every new system abandon even the details of the old system. The real point is that the new system selects some beneficial details of the old and blends them into the new system; they become part of the new system. For example, most of the rites of Hajj are those which Islam has retained, and they have come to be as though they gushed forth from the fountainhead of the Islamic system of life.

The third point understood from the history of that period is that at that time the polytheists of Makkah and the Jews of Madinah repeatedly tried to create doubts in the hearts of the Muslims regarding Islamic values. Because of the amendments Islam had made to the ritual worship of the Age of Ignorance, or because of events that occurred in that period, these elements did not let any opportunity slip, and were constantly engaged in misleading propaganda against Islam. For example, the polytheists strongly objected to the expedition of Abdullah ibn Jahsh, in which he attacked the polytheists during a sacred month, and this gave rise to countless questions that needed answers. Internally, the Holy Quran was refuting jahili concepts, jahili rituals and the jahili system, while outwardly it had declared war against the enemies of Islam and the Muslims. This inner and outer struggle is still going on for the Muslims today. The reason is that there has been no change in the human soul or the human mind; the enemies of Islam are still armed to the teeth today, and the answer the Holy Quran was giving at that time, it still gives today. And this Ummah, even today, cannot achieve success unless it takes the Great Quran as its guide in this struggle between truth and falsehood. Surely the Holy Quran will still display today the remarkable feats it displayed hundreds of years ago. As long as Muslims do not believe in and accept this truth, and do not act upon it, there is no salvation for them, nor can they attain success in this world.

The least result of reflecting on this reality should be that a person accepts this Book with this understanding and perception. He should turn to it in such a way that its teachings appear in dynamic form, that it is in the field of action, giving the mind a new worldview, confronting the concepts of jahiliyyah, safeguarding this Ummah from slips and defending it, and not merely turning to it in the way we approach it today: as a good discourse, like a sweet melody being recited slowly, and nothing more.

The truth is that God revealed the Holy Quran not for the purpose of providing mental comfort but for a great objective. He revealed it so that it might create on this earth a pure and complete life. It was to set it in motion, and to guide humanity through the hardships, slips and thorns of the path to a peaceful destination.

In some narrations it is related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked, as we have mentioned earlier, about how the appearance of the moon and its waxing and waning come about. In other narrations it is related that the question was: why was the moon created? This manner of question corresponds more closely with the answer. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) was told: say, ﴿They are signs for people and for the Hajj.﴾ That is, the time for entering the state of ihram for Hajj, the time for leaving the state of Hajj, the time for breaking the fast, the time for ending the fast, the time of marriage, divorce and the waiting period (iddah), the times for commercial transactions and the payment of debts, and so on. In all religious affairs and in all worldly affairs, reckoning of time is necessary, and therefore keeping account of the lunar months became indispensable in all matters.

Whether this is the answer to the first question or to the second, its connection is in any case with a real problem of the Muslims' practical life. The solving of a purely scientific and academic problem is not intended here.

The Holy Quran also named for them the two benefits of the moon which were visible to them day and night in their practical lives. But the Quran did not tell them anything about the rotation of the earth or the rotation of the moon, although the meaning of the question also included the question of what its reality is. The question was: how does the crescent moon come about? Likewise, the Quran did not tell them what function the moon performs in the solar system, or what orbit the moon has in the motion of the heavenly bodies. This too was certainly included in the questioner's question. The question is: what is the secret of the practical answer that God gave? Why did the Holy Quran mention only practical benefits instead of scientific information?

In truth, the purpose of the revelation of the Holy Quran was to give humanity a particular worldview, to grant it a particular station in life, so that as a result a specific society would come into being. The formation of an Ummah on this earth was before the Holy Quran, an Ummah which was to discharge the important duty of leading all humanity on earth. Within the history of humanity it was to create a society which would be the most exalted of all previous human societies. It was to present a model of human life the like of which does not exist in the whole of human history. It was to lay down the fundamental principles of a way of life, and to invite people to them.

Does God answer this question in the language of the Qur'an with a scientific answer? Clearly the Qur'an is a collection of injunctions meant to purify human life and lead people to the worship of God. It is not a book of astronomy. So searching for a scientific answer in it would show ignorance of the Qur'an's character and subject. Moreover, these sciences do not follow a single fixed path. Theories keep changing. Bringing these theories within human understanding has always required countless pieces of information and theories. According to the sources of knowledge available to all of humanity at that time, such a scientific answer would have appeared as a riddle.

This is why the Qur'an left aside a scientific answer. The Qur'an gives priority to its purpose of revelation, and within that framework an answer in the style of astronomy would not have been suitable. Even if a scientific answer had been necessary, a book like the Qur'an, whose subject is not science, would not have been the right place for it, because the Qur'an was revealed for higher purposes. Some naive friends of the Qur'an search in it for modern sciences, which are not its subject at all. On the other hand, spiteful enemies think that the Qur'an opposes the natural sciences. This too is a baseless notion. Although the Qur'an's subject is not material sciences, its miraculous nature also lies in the fact that the springs of these sciences can be found in it.

These two opposite views have arisen because their proponents have not understood the temperament of this sacred book. These people have not even been able to determine its purposes and the scope of its work. The scope of the Qur'an is certainly the purification of the human soul and of human life. Its aim is to give a person a conception about this universe and its existences, through which people may be joined to their Creator. Then, on the basis of that conception, a complete system of life is to be built, in which a person uses all of his powers with freedom. Clearly, among human powers is the power of reason and perception, and this power can function properly only when a righteous system is established on this earth, and when the rational faculty is given the freedom to conduct scientific investigations, and to reach scientific and empirical conclusions to whatever level of progress and perfection it wishes. But whatever level a person reaches through this limited power of perception will not be the final level, as experience shows.

The subject of the Qur'an is "man." It concerns human conception and theory, human understanding and consciousness, human conduct and character, and human relations and mutual connections. As for the natural sciences and the various kinds of material inventions, they are not the subject of discussion in the Qur'an. Rather, they are the subject of discussion and the center of action for human reason. It is the task of human reason to form theories in this field and to make new discoveries. Because the understanding and perception of human reason is the distinction through which humanity has attained the status of khalifatullah fil-ard (vicegerent of God on earth), and this special quality has been given to humans from the time of their creation. As for the Qur'an, it is only the guide and guardian of human nature. It looks only to ensure that corruption does not occur in human nature, and that the order according to which a person lives, in order to use natural faculties, is not disturbed. The Qur'an gives humanity a comprehensive knowledge about this universe. It explains what the relationship of this universe is with its Creator, and what the relationship is among its various parts (one of which is man himself). After that, the Qur'an leaves the person free to understand the details himself, and to use in the performance of his vicegerency the abilities that God has given him. If the Qur'an does not provide the details of these matters, then this is among the duties of human beings in their role as vicegerents.

I am indeed amused by the simplicity of those so-called supporters who attribute to the Qur'an things that are not part of it and not included in its purposes. These people prove from the Qur'an details of medicine, chemistry, and astronomy. Do these people think that the only way to prove the greatness of the Qur'an is through this?

In terms of its subject, the Qur'an is certainly a great and perfect book, and compared to all these sciences, the subject of the Qur'an is a magnificent one, because its subject is man himself. The source of perception (of which these sciences are composed) is the human perceptive faculty, which makes discoveries, and the benefit that humans derive from them in the world. Research, experiments, and drawing conclusions from them are the properties of reason, and reason is itself a part of the human being. In contrast, the subject of the Qur'an is the formation and creation of the human being himself. It is the building of his personality, his conscience, his reason, and his thought. After that, the Qur'an deals with the building of a righteous human society in which people use the powers that God has placed in the human soul. When a person of sound nature attains a correct conception of life, correct thought, and mature consciousness, and when he is given an Islamic society in which he works freely, then the Qur'an leaves him free to conduct investigations and experiments in the fields of science and other disciplines. The Qur'an only establishes the standards of correct thought, correct consciousness, and correct conception of life, and nothing more.

Sometimes the Qur'an states certain final truths in order to give correct thought about the existence of this universe, the mutual connection of its bodies, and the connection between the universe and its Creator. These are the truths at which the science of physics ends. Therefore, we should not combine these truths with those hypotheses of human reason which are human theories, and which ordinary people call scientific facts. The truths to which humans arrive through these experiments, and which they consider definitive and final, are therefore not the same as the truths the Qur'an mentions, which are definitive and absolute. The truths that humans reach through reason and experiment are never final and definitive. They are obtained through human experiments and the instruments available, and the power of instruments also has a limit. Therefore these truths can only be within the limits of human understanding and the power of the instruments available to it. Even according to the accepted principles of human research and experimentation, we cannot claim that the truths discovered by humans can serve as a standard of correctness against the truths stated in the Qur'an, because those discoveries remain within the limits of human knowledge. (And the Qur'anic truths are beyond human knowledge.)

That was the matter of scientific experiments. As for the theories or hypotheses that are called scientific and academic, such as theories about astronomy, theories about the creation and development of humanity, theories about human psychology and conduct, and theories about human society and its progress, all of these theories are speculative and based on human conjecture and assumption. They cannot be called scientific facts in any sense. At most, it can be said that these theories are interpretations and explanations of the phenomena of this universe, human life, human psychology, and human society, and the reality of these theories is that one theory keeps being replaced by another. Their credibility lasts only until another theory takes their place.

This is why these hypotheses and theories are always subject to change and alteration, and their details keep increasing and decreasing. Sometimes they are suddenly overturned, because at times humans discover a new and more powerful instrument for experiment and observation. Or sometimes, when humans gather all these observations and reflect on them as a whole, they establish a new theory and hypothesis.

The effort and interpretation that links these general Qur'anic indications with the changing and shifting theories of science, or with scientific facts which are themselves not final and definitive, does not produce a result that can be called definitive. Such an effort is, first, against the methodology of inquiry and research of science itself. Second, the benefits and purposes of any such effort can only be three, and all three are contrary to the majesty and exalted status of the Qur'an.

1. This is a kind of inner and mental defeat. People who are caught in this mental subjugation think that perhaps science dominates the Qur'an and stands above it. They state scientific discoveries in the interpretation and explanation of the Qur'an. Yet the Qur'an is itself a complete book on its own subject, and the truths it has stated are final truths, whereas science is in such a state that it is deficient in every area of its subject. Today it proves a fact, and tomorrow it refutes that same fact. Wherever science's reach may extend, it cannot be called final and absolute. Every scientific discovery is restricted by the limits and conditions of human faculties, human rational perceptions, and their supporting instruments, and all these tools and instruments, by their nature and structure, cannot grasp any single final and absolute truth.

2. The second reason is that such people have not understood at all the temperament of the Qur'an and its purposes. The truth is that the Qur'an is a collection of final and absolute truths, and it wants to shape and train human beings in a manner that does not contradict the laws of nature and the temperament of this universe, and that is within the capacity of human nature. This is so that there is no conflict between humanity and the universe around it, but rather that humanity discovers the secrets of this universe, finds out the laws of nature, and uses them in carrying out the duties of its vicegerency on earth. These laws of nature should be those which humanity itself has obtained through complete thought and insight, research and application, and action and experiment. It should not be that someone provides humans with ready-made sciences and they accept them as they are.

3. The third flaw is that these people have to continually interpret the verses of the Qur'an with great contrivance and cunning. These people, carrying these verses, shamelessly run after those scientific theories and hypotheses which have no stability or permanence. In the cycle of these theories, every night becomes darker, and every day brings a new theory that nullifies the previous one. Should we also keep nullifying the earlier exegeses (tafsir)?

As we have said above, this way of thinking is not only against the majesty, greatness, and sublimity of the Noble Qur'an, but also against the methodology of scientific inquiry and experiment. But this does not mean that we should ignore the facts and theories about this universe, the human race, and life that science has presented or is continuously discovering, and not use them in understanding the Qur'an and completely disregard them. Certainly not. That is not our intention. God Himself says in the Qur'an:

﴿Soon We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves, until it becomes clear to them that it is the Truth. Is it not sufficient that your Lord is a witness over all things?﴾ (41:53)

The requirement of this verse is that we should continually reflect on the human soul and the horizons, on the fresh and up-to-date information provided by science, and within our limited capacity of perception and range of imagination, we should keep expanding the scope of Qur'anic meanings and concepts.

How is this done? And how can we do this without tying the absolute and final meanings of the Qur'an to scientific discoveries that are not final and not absolute, but relative? Here an example would be useful:

In the Qur'an it is said: ﴿He created everything and determined it with precise measure.﴾ (25:2)

When science progressed, it became known that on this earth there are very subtle provisions and extremely precise harmonies. This earth, with its particular shape, at its specific distance from the sun, at a defined distance from the moon, with a sensitive size relative to the sun and moon, moving so swiftly, tilted at a particular angle around its axis, with its present water and surface, and along with its thousands of other characteristics, is the only place where life and the other requirements of life can survive. None of these facts is a temporary arrangement, nor does this happen by chance without any plan. How much breadth does a scientific study of these facts add to the meaning of this verse of the Qur'an: ﴿He created everything and determined it with precise measure﴾?

Just consider how the discoveries of modern times have expanded the meaning of this verse. The whole of science has become the commentary on the verse. Therefore, seek to learn more of the creative workmanship of nature, and in this way keep widening the meaning of the verse more and more.

In the Qur'an it is said: ﴿He created man from an extract of clay.﴾ (32:7) Centuries later, Wallace and Darwin put forward the theory of evolution. They assume that life began with a single cell. That cell developed in water. Passing through the stages of evolution, that cell eventually resulted in present-day humanity. It was necessary to test this theory against scientific standards. But we rushed, taking up the Qur'an, and with great disrespect we welcomed this theory with open arms, and even made it into an interpretation of the Qur'an.

Science has discovered that the sun, in relation to the stars around it, travels at a speed of about 12 miles per second. But together with its galaxy, of which it is itself a star, it is moving along at 170 miles per second. Yet this information of science is also not the exact meaning of that verse of the Qur'an, because what science has discovered so far is relative. It is not the final knowledge or truth, and it can change. As for the verse, it expresses the final truth that the sun is moving along. We simply cannot tie this speed to any scientific speed, which is itself subject to change.

In another place the Qur'an says: ﴿Have not those who disbelieved considered that the heavens and the earth were a joined entity, and We separated them?﴾ Science presents a theory: "That the earth was a part of the sun which separated from it," and we ran, breathless, with tongues hanging out. We tried to take up this theory and bring it to the Qur'anic verse, and said: "This is exactly what the Qur'an has mentioned."

Never! This should never be our aim, because this is not a final scientific theory. Several scientific theories exist regarding the physical formation of the earth, and there may be several more. As for the Qur'an, it has said only this, which is the final truth: that the earth was separated from the heavens, and nothing more. How it was separated? From which part of the heavens was it separated? The verse does not mention these details. Therefore, whatever theory science presents on this subject, and whatever hypothesis it chooses to discuss, we cannot say that the meaning of the verse conforms to the present scientific theory and that this is the final word.

I think that for this verse, this much detail here is sufficient. Our only purpose here was: how can scientific discoveries be used to deepen and broaden the understanding of the verse and the meaning of the verses? Without the error of linking a verse to a scientific theory and treating the two as one, considering each to be the referent of the other. Our aim was only to distinguish between these two situations. Now we return to the original text of the Qur'an: ﴿And it is not righteousness to enter houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah. So enter houses from their doors and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:189)

The connection between the two parts of the verse is that the first part explained that the changing shapes of the moon are for determining the times and rites of Hajj, and the second part corrected the custom of the Days of Ignorance associated with the days of Hajj. (In Bukhari and Muslim, it is narrated from Hadrat Bara' ibn 'Azib (رضي الله عنه), who said: The custom of the Ansar was that when they went for Hajj, on their return they would not enter their houses through the doors. Once a man of theirs came and entered directly through the door. People blamed him, and then this verse was revealed: "It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah; so enter houses from their doors.")

Abu Dawud narrated through Shu'bah ibn Ishaq and Bara' ibn 'Azib (رضي الله عنه) that: "When the Ansar returned from any journey, they would not enter through the door, and then this verse was revealed."

Whether this custom was on every journey or only in Hajj (the context shows that it was in Hajj), in any case their belief was that this was a good deed, part of faith. The Holy Qur'an ended this false notion because it was a futile act. It had no legal standing, nor any worldly benefit. The Qur'an gave the correct concept of righteousness: that righteousness is the name of God-consciousness. Awareness of Allah's watchfulness over the outward and inward, and firm consciousness of His existence, is righteousness. It is not the name of an outward form that has no faith-consciousness behind it, but is merely a custom of ignorance.

The command was given to abandon the customs of the Age of Ignorance and enter houses through the doors, and then it indicated that taqwa (God-consciousness) is the path to salvation: ﴿So enter houses from their doors and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾

Thus hearts were connected to the true reality of faith, that is, taqwa was linked to the welfare and success of this world and the Hereafter, and that custom of ignorance, which had no faith-motivation behind it, was uprooted, and believers were directed to reflect on the blessing Allah has provided in the form of the moon, for determining their times and the rites of Hajj. Thus Allah, the Exalted, expressed such important themes in a single verse.

"Permission is given to those against whom war is being waged, because they have been wronged; and indeed Allah is able to give them victory. They are those who have been expelled from their homes without right, only because they said, 'Our Lord is Allah.' Had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques, in which the name of Allah is much mentioned, would surely have been demolished. Allah will certainly help those who help Him; indeed Allah is Strong, Mighty. They are those who, if We establish them in the land, will establish prayer, give zakah, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. And with Allah is the outcome of all affairs."

They understood the meaning of this permission themselves, because they were being oppressed, and so they could take retribution for the oppression. In Makkah their hands were tied and they could not even defend themselves against oppression. There they were commanded: كُفُّوا اَیدِیکُم وَاَقِیمُوا الصَّلٰوۃَ وَاٰتُوالزَّکٰوۃَ "Hold back your hands, establish prayer and give zakah."

The prohibition on raising hands in Makkah was also based on a particular wisdom. We mention some of its important aspects here:

1. The first reason for restraining them from war and self-defence was that the Arabs needed to be disciplined, so that they would become accustomed to obeying the leader, would be obedient to their leadership, and would await the command for defence and fighting. In the Jahiliyyah they were fierce warriors; at the first call they would lose control of themselves, and they had no capacity for patience at any pleasing matter. The role that the Muslim nation was to play in human history required that this community be trained and its character be built in such a way that these weaknesses would be transformed into discipline and order, and that they would become subject to a authoritative and far-sighted leadership. To such an extent that they would abandon all the tribal prejudices of the age of ignorance, the unjust partisanships and unlawful loyalties, in support of which they used to rise up at the first call of any caller for war and conflict.

This very character-building was the reason why men such as Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), a fiery man, and Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib (may Allah be pleased with him), and others like these fearless individuals, would see the Muslim nation in severe trials and hardships and yet not utter a word of complaint. Therefore they were commanded to keep themselves fully under control in accordance with the guidance of the Messenger (ﷺ), to obey their high command completely, since it was the command of the exalted leadership:

كُفُّوا اَیدِیکُم وَاَقِیمُوا الصَّلٰوۃَ وَاٰتُوالزَّکٰوۃَ "Hold back your hands, establish prayer and give zakah."

The result was that a balance was established between contrary qualities such as the hastiness to leap up, and thoughtfulness, impetuosity and deliberation, zeal and obedience to command, which existed in them; and then, among the Arabs, a people extremely passionate and warlike, the successful upbringing of such training and the emergence of discipline among them appears to be itself a miracle.

2. The second important reason why the Muslims were restrained from fighting in Makkah was that Arab society was a brave and noble society. People were self-respecting and proud. Among the Muslims there were some who could answer a brick with a stone, yet despite this, when they endured oppression, the honour and nobility of many noblemen would be stirred, and their hearts would incline towards Islam.

This became practically evident when the Quraysh boycotted the Banu Hashim and they were besieged in the Shi'b of Abu Talib. The demand of the Quraysh was that the Banu Hashim should withdraw their support for the Messenger of Allah. When the trials upon the Banu Hashim became unbearable, the bravery and zeal of some of the jealous and noble men were stirred. They tore up the document according to which they had agreed to the boycott, and purely because of this spirit of nobility, the siege ended. In the Makkan policy of restraining hands from war and defence, the Messenger of Truth (ﷺ) kept these sentiments of the Arabs in view. If the Prophet's biography is studied as the leader of a movement, these wisdoms are manifest everywhere.

The Messenger of Islam (ﷺ) did not intend that because of Islam bloodshed should begin in every house, since in every family there was some Muslim, and within the families themselves, the relatives were at the forefront in harming the Muslims and preventing them from the religion of Islam. There was no organised government that was oppressing the Muslims. If, at that stage, the Muslims had been given permission to fight in their own defence, the result would have been strife in every house, families would have clashed with families, and civil war would have broken out. Had such a situation arisen, it would inevitably have created the impression that Islam had kindled the flames of strife and discord in every home and family.

After the Hijrah the situation became entirely different. Now the Islamic community was a permanent and organised unity in Madinah Tayyibah, and it was confronting an organised community in Makkah Mukarramah in which an army was being organised, and that army was attacking the Islamic movement. This situation was entirely different from the situation in Makkah. Clearly the question of protection had now come to the fore, and this protection was of the whole nation rather than of individuals. These are the reasons that a human being, with his limited mind, can think of as to why the Muslims were prevented from answering violence and brutality in Makkah.

Beyond these reasons, it may also be said that at that time the Muslims were very few in number, and moreover they were besieged in Makkah. If they had begun resistance, immediate fighting would have started against them, and they would have been fighting people who were in every respect more powerful and influential than them. It was Allah's will that the number of Muslims should increase and that they should gather separately in their own permanent capital. When these things were accomplished, they were granted permission for jihad and fighting.

Thereafter, gradually, in the Arabian Peninsula and in regions outside Arabia, the Muslims were given commands for war as the need arose.

The verses under discussion are the initial verses of this sequence, and in them certain commands of fighting are given which were appropriate and necessary for the confrontation between the basic opposing camps of that time, the Islamic camp and the camp of the polytheists. Certain commands, however, are of a fundamental nature, and in every war such circumstances may generally arise. Minor modifications to these commands were made through the commands in Surah al-Bara'ah.

Here, before the exegesis of the verses of fighting, it seems appropriate to give a brief note on the subject of jihad, so that it may serve as a foundation for the exegesis of the verses of fighting and other verses.

The Islamic outlook on life appeared in its final form, namely in the form of the religion of Islam. The aim was that from now on it would become the principle of life for all humanity, that it would become the system of life for all of humanity, and that the Muslim nation would rise with this system and this methodology and lead all humanity on behalf of Allah. This system of life is one based on a broad conception of this universe, built upon the foundation of the true and real purposes of human existence, and its explanation and elucidation have been set out in a Book sent down by Allah, the Creator of the universe. Moreover, this nation has also been charged with guiding towards pure goodness and absolute virtue, which is not found in any other jahili system, and with raising humanity to a lofty station to which it cannot reach through any system other than the Islamic system of life. It has to bestow upon humanity a blessing against which no other blessing can compare. Islam is certainly that system of life that, if humanity is deprived of it, there is no salvation or deliverance for it. If humanity is deprived of that goodness, and it is prevented from reaching the heights, purity and felicity and perfection to which Allah wishes to raise it, then no greater wrong or more evil transgression against humanity can even be conceived.

Thus it becomes a right of humanity that the call to this complete Islamic system of life may reach all of humanity freely, and that there should be no obstacle in its path, that is, in the path of the Islamic call, and that no government should be able in any way to stand as a barrier.

Likewise, it was obligatory upon humanity that when the call of Islam reaches people, they should be completely free in accepting or rejecting it. There should be no obstacle in the way of accepting the religion. No government should remain as a barrier. If any person accepts the Islamic system, the government should not place obstacles in his way, and it should not have the authority to prevent the call of Islam from advancing to its destination. Moreover, it was also humanity's duty to guarantee peace and freedom to those who accept Islam, and to remove the difficulties faced by the Islamic movement in the propagation of religion. In this regard, no injustice should be done to the workers of the Islamic call.

If Allah guides someone and they accept the Islamic call, it is their fundamental right that no kind of oppression or injustice be done to them. They should not be subjected to violence, and no provocation should be directed against them. No obstacles of the kind should be placed in their way whose purpose is nothing other than to keep people away from the Islamic system.

It was among the duties of the workers of the Islamic movement to confront violence and provocation with force, so that fundamental rights such as freedom of opinion could be guaranteed in the world, and so that those people who are to adopt this religion could live in peace and security, so that the Islamic system might be implemented in life and humanity would not be deprived of that goodness and virtue. As a consequence of establishing these fundamental rights, another responsibility is imposed upon the Muslim community: that it must shatter every force that stands in the way of the Islamic call and its propagation, or that challenges the right of freedom of opinion, or that inflicts violence upon those who have freely adopted a belief in matters of religion and ideology. The duty of the Muslim nation remains in force as long as any oppression remains against those who accept the Islamic system, and as long as the system of life is not implemented exclusively for Allah. This does not mean that jihad will continue until people are compelled to adopt the Islamic system of life. The aim is only that the Islamic system should prevail on this globe, in such a way that whoever wishes to enter the religion of Islam should face no obstacle, and that there should be no power in the world that prevents anyone from accepting the religion of Islam, or from propagating it, or from remaining steadfast upon it. There should be no system in the world that conceals Allah's guidance and this light, or that obstructs the arrival of this guidance and light to those living under it, or that misleads the common people from this path of Allah, whatever the nature of that obstacle may be.

These were the fundamental aims for which Islam made jihad fi sabilillah obligatory. This jihad was only for these lofty aims; apart from them, Islam had nothing else in view. No other purpose and no other colour.

This jihad was for the Islamic outlook on life; it was to break the siege of the spread of the disbelieving ideology, it was against the ideology of violence, and it was for the preservation of the Islamic system in life and the establishment of the Islamic Shariah. Its aim was that the banners of Islam be raised high across the globe, in such a way that the opponents of the Islamic outlook on life are struck with awe, and every person who has an interest in the Islamic system of life may enter it, without any fear from any worldly power that they will be stopped or subjected to violence.

This is, and this alone is, the jihad that Islam commanded. It remains in force to this day, and the Islamic system is established upon it. Those who are slain in it are regarded as martyrs in the sight of Islam, and those who bear the hardships of jihad are called ghazis and awliya' Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 2, verse 190 (part 2 of 2):

This was the situation in which the Muslim community in Madinah found itself, and it was in regard to this that the verses of this lesson of Surah al-Baqarah were revealed. The polytheist Quraysh had unjustly expelled the Muslims from their homes. They were being subjected to persecution merely because they had embraced Islam. Their only objection was why they had freely accepted a way of life. In these circumstances, alongside specific guidance, these verses also state a general principle for the Islamic outlook, which is this: O Muslims, fight those who have fought you unjustly, and who remain at war with you; and for the future too, this is your guidance: fight whoever fights you, but do not transgress. The command was given: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾

This is the first of the verses on fighting, and in this very first verse a definitive decision has been made regarding the objectives of war, and it has been clearly stated what the banner is under which the Muslims are to conduct the struggle of jihad. ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾

This jihad, this fighting, is for Allah alone, and none of the well-known objectives for which humanity, throughout its long history, fought tremendous wars is desired by Islamic jihad. Not for the sake of family pride, nor for the sake of domination and superiority on earth, nor for wealth and spoils, nor for control of markets and raw materials, nor for establishing the supremacy of one class over another, nor for the rule of one race over another. Islamic jihad is only for those objectives whose limits Islam has defined: to raise the word of Islam in the world, for the establishment of the Islamic system of life, to save Muslims from oppression and violence, and to save Muslims from misguidance and error. These, in short, are the Islamic objectives. Wars fought for other objectives do not deserve to be called Islamic jihad, and whoever takes part in such wars, Allah the Exalted does not regard him as deserving any reward, nor does he have any station with Allah.

Along with the determination of the objectives of war, its extent and limit have also been fixed: ﴿But do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾

Transgression would be to inflict hardship upon peaceful citizens other than the soldiers who are fighting, who pose no threat to the Islamic call, nor do they pose any threat to the Islamic community. For example, women, children, the elderly, and those who have withdrawn themselves for the worship of Allah, regardless of which religion or community they belong to. It was commanded that the bounds and restrictions which Islam has set for war must not be violated in battle. Islam first placed a ban on those evils which were commonly prevalent in the age of ignorance, whether this ignorance is ancient or modern. These are evils with which the Islamic system is in conflict, and which the spirit of Islam abhors.

In this regard, study some of the hadiths of the Messenger ﷺ. Read the instructions of his Companions, and from them you will grasp the temperament of these etiquettes. These are the etiquettes of war, through which humanity first became acquainted with the system of war of Islam:

1. Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates, saying: "On one of the military expeditions of the Messenger ﷺ, a woman was found who had been killed, so the Messenger ﷺ forbade the killing of women and children." (Malik, the two Shaykhs [Bukhari and Muslim], Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi)

2. Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates, saying: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When you are fighting, avoid striking the face."

3. Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates, saying: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent us on a campaign. On that occasion he said: 'If you find so-and-so and so-and-so (two men of Quraysh), burn them with fire.' When we set out ready to depart, he said: 'I had commanded you to throw so-and-so and so-and-so into the fire! But punishing with fire is the right of Allah alone; therefore the command is that if you find them, kill both of them.'" (Bukhari, Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi)

4. Ibn Masud (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates that he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Among those in war, the most forgiving and forbearing are only the people of faith." (Abu Dawud)

5. Abd ibn Yazid al-Ansari narrates: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade theft from the spoils of war and mutilation in killing.

6. Abu Yala (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates: We took part in battle under the command of Abd al-Rahman ibn Khalid ibn al-Walid. Four of the enemy were brought in. It was ordered that they be killed with the flat part of the spear, and they were killed in that manner. When Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him) was informed of this, he said: "I heard the Messenger ﷺ forbidding killing by torture. By Allah, even if it were a hen, I would not kill it by torture." When this came to the knowledge of Abd al-Rahman (may Allah be pleased with him), he freed four slaves. (Abu Dawud)

7. Harith narrates from Muslim ibn Harith (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent us on a small expedition. When we reached the place of attack, I urged my mare on, and she outran my companions. I saw that the people of the settlement were crying out in fear. I said to them: "Quickly, declare the pure word, there is no god but Allah, and save yourselves." They recited the Kalimah. My companions severely reproached me and said: "You have deprived us of the spoils of war." When we returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, people informed the Messenger ﷺ of my action. He praised me, and then said to me: "Allah the Exalted has recorded for you such-and-such a reward for every single person of those people." (Abu Dawud)

8. Buraidah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates, saying: Whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ appointed someone as commander of a group of mujahideen or sent a small expedition, he would first counsel them to fear Allah. Then he would say: "Fight in the name of Allah, in the way of Allah, against those who have disbelieved. Fight, but do not betray. Do not mutilate the slain, and do not kill a child." (Muslim, Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi)

9. Malik narrates from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that, in advising his army, among other things he said: "You will find people who have, in their own estimation, devoted themselves to Allah; leave them in the state of seclusion they are in. Do not kill a woman. Do not kill a child or a very old man."

This is the war that Islam enjoins, and these are the etiquettes of war of Islam: the objectives for which Islam encourages the waging of battle. And the source of all of these is the command of the Qur'an: "And fight in the way of Allah against those who fight you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors."

The Muslims of the early generations well knew the reality that they could not achieve victory merely on the strength of their numbers. Their numbers were very small. They could not be victorious through their numbers and equipment, because their equipment was very meager in comparison with the enemy. They knew that victory can be obtained only as a result of faith, servitude, and the help of Allah. If they abandoned the guidance of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, they would be deprived of the victory and support which is their real stay. Therefore, in their battles they strictly observed these etiquettes of war, to the extent that they observed them even with those eternal enemies who had inflicted upon them the severest of torments, and who had mutilated the bodies of their martyrs. On one occasion the anger of the Messenger ﷺ was aroused, and he issued orders for some people to be burned, but after a short while he withdrew his orders and forbade burning, because punishment by fire is exclusively the prerogative of Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verses 191–192:

The Muslims are only commanded to fight against those who fought against them. They were subjected to persecution merely because of their religious beliefs, and they were expelled from their homes. The command is that the war against such people should continue until they are killed wherever they are and in whatever state they are found. The exception is the Masjid al-Haram. However, if the disbelievers initiate fighting within the Masjid al-Haram itself, then it becomes permissible for the Muslims to fight them there as well, except if they embrace Islam. In that case, even if they had killed Muslims, or oppressed them and committed violence against them, the Muslims are commanded to hold back their hands. ﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them, and expel them from wherever they expelled you, for persecution is worse than killing. And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you there. But if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers. But if they cease, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Subjecting people to violence merely because of a difference of religion, creed or ideology is, in reality, an assault on the sacred value of human life. For this reason Islam has declared it to be worse than killing. It has declared it a more heinous crime than taking a life and ending existence. What is this fitnah which is more severe than killing? Intimidation is included in it. Practical violence is also included in it. Creating circumstances in which people are led astray, and turning them away from the system of life that Allah has ordained, is also fitnah. For Muslims, making disbelief appealing and turning them away from Islam, and corrupting their morals, all fall within the definition of fitnah. The most apparent example of this fitnah is the communist system, where teaching religion is prohibited and teaching atheism is compulsory. Laws are made that declare prohibited things such as fornication and alcohol to be lawful, and through various means of propagation and dissemination these things are made appealing to human beings. Whereas they find fault with every aspect of the Islamic system, distort it, and the obedience to the system which such collective conditions produce becomes an absolute obligation for the common people there.

Regarding freedom of opinion: this viewpoint about the lofty status of freedom of opinion in human life is in exact conformity with that system. It is also in harmony with the purpose and objective of the existence of the universe that Islam has presented. According to Islam, the purpose and objective of the creation of the universe is worship. Worship is the name given to every good deed in which the doer's aim is the pleasure of Allah, and the worship of Allah is possible only when a person is free from all other forms of worship. This is why the highest value of a human being is his freedom, especially freedom of opinion. Now, whoever snatches away someone's freedom, and inflicts violence upon him merely because of his ideology, directly or indirectly, that person commits a greater oppression against him than killing him. This is why resistance against such persons is permissible in every way, even if it requires fighting. The Qur'an did not command (فاقتلوهم, fa-qatiluhum, "then fight them") but rather (واقتلوهم, waqtuluhum, "and kill them"), commanding that they be killed. ﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them﴾: wherever such people are found, whatever state they are in, and by whatever means you are able to kill such people. However, in this regard you must observe only the Islamic etiquette of war: do not mutilate anyone, do not burn anyone in fire.

The Masjid al-Haram is the abode of security. Therefore, do not fight near it. Allah accepted the supplication of His friend Ibrahim concerning it. It was made a centre for the people, and it was declared a sanctuary of safety. Therefore the command was given: do not fight anyone near the Masjid al-Haram, except if a group of disbelievers begins fighting with you here; but you should not initiate the fighting. If they initiate it and do not respect the sanctity of the Masjid al-Haram, then your hands are not tied either. These people persecute the masses because of their religion. There is no respect for the Masjid al-Haram; therefore this is the appropriate punishment for them. It was said:

﴿Then if they cease, indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Merely ceasing is not sufficient. They must cease persecuting the Muslims, cease fighting, and cease disbelief as well; only then will they become deserving of pardon and mercy. For merely ceasing from war, it may be done by the Muslims declaring a state of peace. But it is not possible that the disbelievers should become deserving of Allah's forgiveness and mercy merely by that. Yet the indication to forgiveness and mercy here means that the disbelievers are to be encouraged towards faith, so that after abandoning disbelief and oppression they may also become deserving of Allah's forgiveness and His mercy.

Behold the grandeur and generosity of Islam. Even to disbelievers and oppressors a signal is given: come, the rain of forgiveness and mercy is falling. Come, your past sins are forgiven, the retribution for your oppression and violence is forgiven, the blood money is forgiven; enter the ranks of Islam with the dignity of a believer, and everything is forgiven. You killed, you committed violence, you did whatever you did, but everything is forgiven, and the rain of forgiveness and mercy is falling.
