Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 193:

The entire purpose of war in Islam is that people should not be prevented from the religion of Islam through oppression. People should not be turned away from Islam through force, or through something even more effective than force, namely social conditions. Means that corrupt their morals, mislead them, and deceive them should not be employed. Furthermore, the Islamic system should gain standing and its scale should be heavy, so that its enemies are struck with awe. They should not have the audacity to persecute or harm the people of faith. And ordinary people should no longer feel any fear that if they accept Islam, they will be subjected to oppression or be made to suffer some harm.

It is a permanent duty of an Islamic community to remain at war until oppressive and tyrannical powers are eliminated, and until dignity and dominance belong to Islam alone, and no fitnah (tumult/persecution) remains. "And fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah. But if they cease, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers" (Qur'an 2:193). "Fight them until there is no fitnah and the religion is for Allah. Then if they cease, let there be no aggression except against the oppressors."

At the time this verse was revealed, its address was directed towards the polytheists of Makkah in the Arabian Peninsula, because at that time it was the polytheists of Makkah who were resorting to persecution. They did not accept that the source of the system of life is Allah alone. The meaning of the verse is general; it is in force at all times and is also a guidance for us, because jihad will remain a duty for the Muslim ummah until the Day of Resurrection, since in every age there are forces that prevent people from the religion. They block all means for the call of Islam to reach people's ears, and even if someone is somehow convinced by the call of Islam, these forces prevent people from accepting Islam and from practising Islam in a state of peace and security. Therefore, it is a permanent duty of the Islamic community at all times to crush such powers and to free people from their tyranny and oppression. People should be free to hear, and to accept or not accept.

After declaring oppression and fitnah to be worse than killing, the repetition of this matter is not devoid of wisdom. This repetition continues because this matter holds great importance in Islam. Here Islam is laying the foundation of a great principle: man is being transformed. This is, in truth, a new birth for man. This new life is being given to man through the Islamic system. Now the worth and value of man is not based on his animality or his physical life, but the determination of his worth is being made by his belief and ideology. On one side is human life, on the other side are a person's ideology and belief. The scale of belief is declared to be heavier. It is being stated that the enemies of humanity are only those who oppress other human beings merely because of differences of belief or ideology. Those who oppress a Muslim merely because he is a Muslim, and who want to turn him away from Islam through persecution, deprive humanity of a concept that is pure good. They do not allow people to come to the system of life given by Allah. Therefore, continuing to fight against them is the foremost duty of the Islamic community. It is its duty to eliminate such people wherever they are found, so that fitnah no longer remains and religion is for Allah.

This great principle, which Islam established in its early days, remains in its place even now. Today, various kinds of persecution are being carried out against the Islamic ideology and its adherents. The bearers of Islam, both individually and collectively, are being made the target of oppression and tyranny. And those people who are being subjected to oppression and tyranny merely because they have adopted an ideology of life or have embraced a system of life that is pleasing, whatever kind of persecution it may be, it is the duty of these people to rise up against such oppressors, to fight them, to be killed or to kill, and in every case to keep aloft that banner of freedom of opinion, which was first raised by Islam, through which an entirely new and free human being came into existence.

Whenever the oppressors give up their oppression and cease their interference between a human being and his God, then no aggression, that is, no defensive action against them, will remain. Because jihad is always only against oppression and the oppressor. It was said: "But if they cease, then know that there is no defence against anyone except the wrongdoers." "فَإِنِ انْتَهَوْا فَلا عُدْوَانَ إِلا عَلَى الظَّالِمِينَ"

Here, the defence against and confrontation with the oppressors is expressed through the word 'udwan (aggression), merely due to verbal difficulties; otherwise, the action against the oppressors is justice. It is fairness, and it is saving the oppressed from oppression, stopping oppression; it is not aggression.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 194:

After explaining the rulings concerning approaching the Masjid al-Haram, the rulings concerning fighting in the sacred months are now set out. ﴿The sacred month is for the sacred month, and violations of sanctity are subject to retaliation. So whoever attacks you, attack him in the same way as he attacked you. But fear Allah, and know that Allah is with those who are mindful of Him.﴾ The sacred month's penalty is the sacred month, and the observance of all sanctities will be upheld with equality. Therefore, whoever attacks you, you too attack him in the same manner that he attacked you. However, fear Allah, and know that Allah is with those who refrain from transgressing His limits.

Whoever has no regard for the sanctity of the month of Muharram is not entitled to disregard the restrictions imposed within these sacred months. Allah Almighty has declared only one place among all matters, the Masjid al-Haram, to be a place of security, and among the times, He has declared the sacred months to be a time of peace. In that place and in that time, no one's blood may be shed. Everyone's life and property will be protected. No living thing shall be harmed. Whoever wishes that he himself may enjoy comfort in this flourishing garden of peace while depriving the Muslims of it, the remedy for him is only that he too be deprived of it. Whoever violates the honour of others, his own honour will not be safe, because ﴿retaliation applies to violations of sanctity﴾, and the observance of all sanctities will be with equality. Yet, despite this, the Muslims were warned that in confronting oppression and taking retribution for oppression, they should not go beyond their limits, because it is only out of necessity that permission to fight is being granted to you within their sacred places and these sacred, inviolable months.

﴿So whoever attacks you, attack him in the same way as he attacked you﴾. "Therefore, whoever attacks you, you too attack him in the same manner." But in this matter, do not resort to excess and transgression. Allah Almighty has not fixed the measure of retribution in this regard; the measure has been left to their fear of God. As we have said above, the Muslims were well aware that their victory and support came from Allah alone. Therefore they are commanded to fear Allah. This is the limit at which they must stop. The truth is that fear of God is the greatest guarantee of peace.

In jihad, just as individuals are needed, wealth is also needed. Before jihad, a mujahid will need the means of war, such as a mount and other military equipment. In the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, salaries for soldiers and commanders were not fixed. Those people spent their wealth in the path of Allah just as they sacrificed their lives for Islam. When a collective order is founded upon a worldview, this is the natural result. If a government's foundation is a worldview, then there is no need at all to spend wealth to hire salaried employees for self-defence, for the defence of its people, or for any war against enemies; the army advances on its own, the leaders advance on their own, and they give both their lives and their wealth.

There was a need to consider that countless poor Muslims were filled with the spirit of jihad and were prepared to fight and die for the Islamic worldview and Islamic way of life, but their situation was that they had neither military equipment nor provisions for the journey. They had no means of transport to reach the battlefield. Such people would come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and plead that he carry them to distant battlefields, because sometimes the battlefield was so far that it was not possible to go there on foot. When the Messenger ﷺ expressed his inability, they would return disappointed. Concerning them, the Holy Qur'an says:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (*Fi Zilal al-Quran*, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 195:

They would turn back with their eyes overflowing with tears out of grief, because they had nothing to spend on that occasion. Countless verses of the Qur'an and countless hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) encourage *infaq fi sabil Allah* (spending in the way of Allah), especially for the provision of those who go out to fight. In many places in the Qur'an, the call to *da'wah* and *jihad* is accompanied by a call to *infaq*. Here, neglecting spending in the way of Allah is described as destruction and ruin, and the command is given to guard against it: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah, and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction. And do good, for indeed Allah loves those who do good.﴾ (195)

Those who do not spend in the way of Allah are stingy, and through stinginess the human soul becomes dead. A group whose member is stingy falls into sudden destruction because of its own weakness. This is especially so in a system of life that rests on voluntary sacrifice, as is evident in the early days of Islam.

By way of further emphasis, it is said: go beyond *infaq* and reach the level of *ihsan* (excellence in faith and action): ﴿And do good; indeed Allah loves those who do good.﴾

Among the levels of Islam, *ihsan* is the highest rank. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself defined *ihsan*: "Worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." A person who reaches this lofty station finds it easy to perform all other acts of worship, and all sins fall away of their own accord. Such a person fears Allah in matters great and small, and the fear of Allah remains before him everywhere, in solitude and in company.

This is the final result with which the verses on jihad conclude: in matters of jihad, the human self is entrusted to *ihsan*, which is the highest rank of faith.

From this point onward, the discussion turns to Hajj, Umrah and their rites (*manasik*). The flow of speech connects naturally. Earlier the discussion began with the crescent moons, and it was answered that they are for the benefit of people and for determining the times of Hajj. Then came the discussion of fighting in the sacred months and fighting near the Sacred Mosque. Now the rulings of Hajj and Umrah are stated, which are performed at the Masjid al-Haram.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 1 of 2):

We have no reliable knowledge of the date of revelation of the verses on Hajj. There is a narration concerning this in which it is said that the verse ﴿And if you are prevented, then [send] whatever offering is easy to obtain﴾ was revealed in 6 AH on the occasion of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. Therefore, the correct date of when Hajj became obligatory in Islam is also not known to us. There is a difference of opinion as to which verse made Hajj obligatory: is it this verse, namely ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾, meaning "when you intend Hajj and 'Umrah for the pleasure of Allah, then complete them," or the verse ﴿And due to Allah from the people is a pilgrimage to the House - for whoever is able to find thereto a way﴾, meaning "Hajj to the House of Allah is obligatory upon those who have the means for the journey from Allah." In any case, there is no narration transmitted that fixes the date of revelation of either of these two verses.

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim al-Jawziyyah writes in his book Zad al-Ma'ad that Hajj became obligatory in 9 AH or 10 AH. He fixed this year on the basis of the conjecture that the Messenger ﷺ performed Hajj in the tenth year of Hijrah. It is evident that he must have performed this obligation after it became obligatory, which could be in 9 AH or 10 AH; but this point alone cannot serve as a sound proof, because it is possible that Hajj was obligatory earlier, but due to certain compulsions and obstacles the Messenger ﷺ postponed it until 10 AH. Yet in 9 AH the Messenger ﷺ sent Hadrat Abu Bakr ؓ as the Amir of Hajj. It has already come in the narrations that when the Messenger ﷺ returned from the Battle of Tabuk, he had intended to perform Hajj. Then, when he considered that the polytheists, as is their custom, come to Makkah Mukarramah in the season of Hajj, and that some of them perform tawaf completely naked, he did not like to mix with those people. After this, Surah Bara'ah was revealed. The Messenger ﷺ sent Hadrat Ali ؓ so that he would recite the initial portion of Surah Bara'ah to the people, end the treaties that existed with certain polytheists, and, when people gathered at Mina at the time of sacrifice, announce: "Beware! No disbeliever will enter Paradise; after this year no polytheist may perform tawaf; no naked person may perform tawaf; and as for those who have a treaty with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it shall remain until its term." This was the reason why the Messenger ﷺ himself did not perform Hajj and waited until the House of Allah was made free of polytheists and of those who performed tawaf naked.

Here it seems fitting that Islam kept the obligation of Hajj and most of its rites intact. And there are narrations, though their chain is not strong, indicating that Hajj had already become obligatory in Makkah before the Hijrah, long before these dates. Surah al-Hajj, which according to the most correct opinion is a Makkan surah, mentions most of the rites of Hajj, in the form that Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had commanded these rites. Consider these verses of Surah Hajj:

(Remember when We assigned to Ibrahim the place of the House, [saying], "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who perform tawaf and those who stand [in prayer] and bow and prostrate. And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every distant pass, that they may witness benefits for them and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of.. livestock. So eat from them and feed the miserable needy. Then let them end their untidiness and fulfill their vows and circumambulate the ancient House." That is [the command]. And whoever honors the symbols of Allah - indeed, it is from the piety of hearts. For you therein are benefits until a specified term; then its place of sacrifice is at the ancient House.

And the camels We have made for you among the symbols of Allah; for you therein is good. So mention the name of Allah over them while standing [in sacrifice]; and when their sides fall [lifeless], eat from them and feed the contented and the beggar. Thus We have subjected them to you that you may be grateful. Their meat does not reach Allah, nor their blood, but what reaches Him is piety from you. Thus He has subjected them to you that you may glorify Allah for that to which He has guided you. And give good tidings, [O Muhammad], to the doers of good.)

Most of the rites are mentioned in these verses or alluded to, such as hadi (offering), nahr (sacrifice), tawaf, ihlal, ihram and tasmiyah (invoking the name of Allah). These very rites are the fundamental symbols of Hajj. The address, in the form of a historical account of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), is directed to the Muslims, and these verses clearly indicate that Hajj was obligatory in a fairly early period, because Hajj was the symbol of Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him), with whom the Muslims had a connection. Since the polytheists of Makkah were the custodians of the Ka'bah and its keys, and for a long period there was a severe conflict between the Muslims and the polytheists, it is possible that the performance of the obligation of Hajj was postponed to a suitable time. But that postponement is one matter. Thus, in the initial verses of this part, we have already preferred the view that some Muslims performed the obligation of Hajj long before, that is, in 2 AH after the change of the qiblah.

In any case, the discussion regarding the history of Hajj is sufficient. Now we shall explain the verses, the description of the symbols of Hajj, and the instructions given within them.

﴿And complete the Hajj and 'Umrah for Allah. And if you are prevented, then [send] what offering is easy to obtain, and do not shave your heads until the offering has reached its place of sacrifice. But whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head [requiring shaving] - then an expiation of fasting or charity or sacrifice. And when you are secure, whoever performs 'Umrah and then Hajj [i.e., enjoys the benefit of 'Umrah until Hajj] must make an offering of what is easy to obtain. And whoever does not find [an animal], then fasting three days during Hajj and seven when you return - that is ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Haram. And fear Allah and know that Allah is severe in penalty.﴾

In these verses, first of all, notable is the beauty of expression and the elegance of phrasing chosen for this legislation: the division of sentences, purposeful and excellent style, a separate statement in each sentence, words and clauses brief, in which no word is superfluous. Every command is accompanied by its conditions and limits, and all the rulings are linked continuously with the fear of Allah and taqwa.

In the first sentence it is said that once one has begun Hajj and 'Umrah, their completion is absolutely obligatory. When the pilgrim begins Hajj, and the one performing 'Umrah begins 'Umrah, and binds the intention, whether separately or both together, and the focus of their attention is purely the pleasure of Allah, then they are commanded: ﴿And complete the Hajj and 'Umrah for Allah, when you intend them﴾, that is, complete them.

Some exegetes are of the view that by the word "complete" the obligation of Hajj was first established. But others have understood from it that the meaning is: when you begin, then complete it, finish it. This meaning is more apparent, because here it cannot be taken to mean that Hajj became obligatory and 'Umrah also became obligatory, since some scholars do not consider 'Umrah obligatory. Therefore, the purpose here will be that Hajj and 'Umrah become obligatory once begun. Completion is mandatory; initially 'Umrah is not obligatory, but when one intends it and puts on ihram, then complete it. Now completion becomes obligatory, and 'Umrah in all its rites is like Hajj. The difference is only that in 'Umrah there is no standing at the plain of 'Arafat. Moreover, 'Umrah has no fixed time; it can be performed at any time of the year. Like Hajj, its performance within the known months is not mandatory.

From this general command to complete Hajj and 'Umrah, the state of ihsar (being prevented) is excluded. Ihsar may be due to an enemy who threatens life (on this all schools agree), or due to illness or some obstacle similar to illness that prevents the completion of Hajj and 'Umrah. Among the jurists there is a difference of opinion as to whether ihsar due to illness is valid. The preferred view is that ihsar due to illness is valid. ﴿And if you are prevented, then [send] whatever offering is easy to obtain﴾. In this state, the pilgrim or the one intending 'Umrah offers, according to his capacity and ease, whatever sacrifice he can, and releases himself from ihram, at the very place where the state of ihsar occurred, even if he could not reach al-Masjid al-Haram, and could not perform the rites of Hajj or the rites of 'Umrah apart from assuming ihram from the miqat. (The miqat is the place where the pilgrim and the one performing 'Umrah put on ihram; thereafter wearing stitched garments becomes forbidden, cutting or shaving hair and trimming nails becomes prohibited. Moreover, hunting land game and eating it becomes forbidden for him.)

In the sixth year of Hijrah too, this same thing occurred: when the Messenger ﷺ and his companions reached Hudaybiyyah, the polytheists prevented him from entering al-Masjid al-Haram. Negotiations took place and the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was concluded. According to it, it was agreed that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would perform 'Umrah the following year. It is reported in the narrations that this verse was revealed, and the Messenger ﷺ commanded the Muslims that they should stop where they had reached, sacrifice, end the intention of 'Umrah, and come out of ihram. The Muslims hesitated to comply with the command. It was difficult for them that they should sacrifice every offering before its place of sacrifice, when customarily they sacrifice at Mina. Seeing their hesitation, the Messenger ﷺ went forward, sacrificed his own offering, and came out of ihram. Then everyone complied.

By ﴿what offering is easy to obtain﴾ is meant whatever is available. The animals from which the offering may be made are these: camels, cows, buffaloes, and sheep and goats. Only in the case of camels, buffaloes and cows can up to seven persons share. As seven persons shared one camel at the occasion of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. This is tayseer (facility). Yes, a sheep or goat is an offering for only one person.

The state of ihsar, as occurred at Hudaybiyyah, or the circumstances of returning home due to illness, have been excluded from the original ruling so that there is no hardship upon the Muslims; the wisdom behind it is solely to provide scope for ease for Muslims. The purpose and goal of the rites of Hajj is precisely that a person draws near to Allah and fear of Allah arises in his heart. In this way he becomes prepared to carry out the duties imposed upon him by Allah. When he has made the intention, put on ihram, and the enemy has obstructed his way, or illness or some similar excuse has befallen him, why should the pilgrim or the one intending 'Umrah be deprived of the reward of Hajj or 'Umrah? The ruling in this state will be just as if Hajj had been completed and 'Umrah performed, so such a person will sacrifice right there and come out of ihram. This concession is one that fully accords with the spirit of Islam, the objectives of Islamic worship, and the very purpose and goal of the symbols of Hajj and 'Umrah.

After this exception to the first ruling, the address now turns to another ruling, a general ruling, for Hajj as well as for 'Umrah. ﴿And do not shave your heads until the offering has reached its place of sacrifice.﴾ This command is for the state in which Hajj and 'Umrah are being completed and there is no ihsar. In the case of intending Hajj, 'Umrah, or both, a person remains in the state of ihram, and is not permitted to shave his head until the offering reaches its place and is slaughtered. That is, after standing at 'Arafat, on arrival at Muzdalifah, at Mina on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah. After this sacrifice the pilgrim comes out of ihram. Before that, shaving the head, cutting hair, or committing other acts not permissible for the muhrim is forbidden. Now this general command also has an exception (proviso). ﴿But whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head [requiring shaving] - then an expiation of fasting or charity or sacrifice!﴾

If one is afflicted with an illness that makes shaving the head necessary, or lice develop in the hair because the head has not been combed for a long time, then it is permissible to shave the head before the sacrifice reaches its place (of slaughter). Because Islam is a religion of ease, one may shave even before completing the Hajj. However, in such a case the person must pay a fidyah: either fast for three days, or feed six needy persons, or sacrifice a goat and give it in charity. The limits of this fidyah have been set in the ahadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Imam al-Bukhari (rah) narrated with his chain of transmission from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, who said: I was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and my condition was such that lice were falling from my hair onto my face. He said: "I did not think that you had fallen into such hardship." He asked: "Do you have a goat?" I said: "No." He said: "Fast for three days, or feed six needy persons, and the amount of food should be that each needy person receives half a sa' of grain, and shave your head."

Now hear a second, general command concerning Hajj: ﴿Then, when you are secure, whoever benefits from the 'Umrah until the Hajj shall offer whatever sacrifice is feasible.﴾ The meaning is that when the situation of ihsar arises and you are performing the obligation of Hajj, then whoever wishes to perform 'Umrah before the days of Hajj arrive should offer whatever sacrifice is feasible. The implementation of this command is that a person sets out for 'Umrah, puts on ihram at the miqat, performs 'Umrah, that is, completes the tawaf and the sa'y between Safa and Marwah, and then intends Hajj and waits for the days of Hajj. This applies when a person performs this 'Umrah in the months of Hajj, which are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. This is one form of tamattu' (combining 'Umrah with Hajj). The second form is that one puts on ihram for both Hajj and 'Umrah from the miqat, and after performing 'Umrah waits for the days of Hajj. This is the second form of tamattu'. In both of these forms, the one performing tamattu' must offer a sacrifice. This sacrifice is to be made after the 'Umrah so that he may come out of ihram. This person remains permissible (halal) in the period between completing the 'Umrah and beginning Hajj. The feasible sacrifice may be a camel, a cow, or a sheep or goat.

And if a sacrifice is not available, then ﴿whoever does not find (the means), let him fast three days during Hajj and seven when you return; those are ten complete.﴾ In this regard, the preferable course is to fast the three days of Hajj in Dhu al-Hijjah before standing at 'Arafat, and to fast the remaining seven days after returning home, thus completing ten days. For added emphasis, it is said: the wisdom of the sacrifice and the fast is solely that the pilgrim's connection with Allah remain continuous, so that during the period between 'Umrah and Hajj, when he comes out of ihram, his awareness does not cease that he is in the atmosphere of the days of Hajj. He must especially guard himself against wrongdoing, and that Allah is continuously watching over him. This awareness and feeling is generally revived during the days of Hajj.

As for those whose residence is in Masjid al-Haram, 'Umrah is not permissible for them during the days of Hajj. They shall perform only Hajj. They cannot leave ihram by sacrificing between 'Umrah and Hajj. Therefore, fidyah, sacrifice, or fasting is not obligatory upon them. ﴿That concession is for those whose people are not present at al-Masjid al-Haram.﴾ After the rulings mentioned so far, the Qur'an now presents a forceful conclusion and summation, and an attempt is made to turn the hearts of the pilgrims toward Allah, the Exalted:

﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ Taqwa is itself the guarantee of obeying the command. The fear of Allah and the fear of His punishment is the guarantor of compliance with the commands. In ihram, restrictions are imposed only for a specific period.

The commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 197:

Legal restraint. But when the state of ihram ends, then taqwa (God-consciousness) and fear of Allah are the only vigilance that can have a good effect on a person and can serve as the guardian of a believer. Now the special rules of Hajj are explained. For example, what are the etiquettes of Hajj? What are its times? As in the preceding paragraphs, this concluding section also ends with the same admonition of fear of Allah and taqwa.

﴿The Hajj is in well-known months. Whoever undertakes the Hajj in them, let there be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no quarrelling during the Hajj. And whatever good you do, Allah knows it. And take provision, but the best provision is taqwa. So fear Me, O people of understanding.﴾

"The months of Hajj are known to all. Whoever, in these fixed months, intends the Hajj, should be warned that during the Hajj there should not occur from him any sexual act, any misconduct, or any quarrelling. And whatever good deeds you do, they will be in Allah's knowledge. Take provision for the journey of Hajj, and the best provision is piety. So, O people of understanding, refrain from disobeying Me."

From the apparent wording of this verse it is understood that the months of Hajj are known to all. The times are known: they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. Therefore, the intention for Hajj is valid only within these times. If someone forms the intention before them, it will not be valid. Although some schools of thought, on the basis of the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), have declared it permissible and explain the meaning of this verse as: the known times of Hajj are for performing the rites of Hajj, and an intention made earlier is also valid. This opinion has been adopted by Imam Malik (rh), Imam Abu Hanifah (rh), and Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (rh). Ibrahim al-Nakha'i (rh), al-Thawri (rh), and al-Layth ibn Sa'd also went in this direction. Whereas Imam al-Shafi'i (rh) adopted the first opinion. This is also narrated from Hadrat Ibn Abbas (ra), Jabir (ra), 'Ata' (rh), Tawus (rh), Mujahid (rh) and others. Therefore, this opinion appears more clear.

Now, if anyone during these known days imposes Hajj upon himself, that is, he firmly resolves that he will perform Hajj and puts on ihram, he should be warned that during the Hajj no rafath (sexual conduct), no misconduct, and no quarrelling or dispute should occur from him. Rafath here refers to sexual intercourse and the things that lead to it. Jidal (quarrelling) means a dispute that makes the other party angry, whether in the presence of women or in public gatherings. Fusuq (wickedness) means all misdeeds, minor or major. The mention of these acts means that during Hajj one should refrain from all those things that are contrary to caution and restraint and to the atmosphere of solitude and devotion to Allah, because during Hajj a person sets aside all worldly affairs, and this entire period is a time of spiritual exercises for establishing connection with Allah. The days of Hajj are a period in which a person even separates himself from his worldly clothing and goes into the House of Allah. Therefore, here he should observe the respect and courtesy befitting that House.

After forbidding evil acts, it is now said that you should do good deeds abundantly: "And whatever good you do, Allah knows it" (وَمَا تَفْعَلُوا مِنْ خَيْرٍ يَعْلَمْهُ اللَّهُ). Is it not sufficient for the believer that his Master sees every good deed of his at all times? Let the sense that Allah is watching be cherished; your Master sees you. Go forward, and gather as much goodness as you can. This is the awareness of a believer. Certainly, before the reward in the Hereafter, this is a great reward in itself.

After this, encouragement is given to arrange provision to the extent of one's capacity during the journey of Hajj, every kind of provision, for the soul as well as for the body. It is reported in the Hadith that some people from Yemen used to set out for Hajj in such a state that they had nothing with them. They would say, "We will go to visit the House of Allah, and He will not give us bread?" The temperament of Islam is that whatever a person does, he should do it with complete preparation, turn his heart toward Allah with full preparation, and then his reliance and trust should be entirely upon Him. That attitude of those people was not only contrary to the temperament of Islam, but also showed a kind of boldness in their dealings with Allah. It appears that these people considered performing Hajj a kind of favour upon the Divine Being. Since they perform Hajj for Allah, He is responsible for their provision. For this reason Allah commanded the arrangement of both kinds of provision: physical provision, and the provision of fear of Allah and taqwa. And He said that one should not show boldness in the presence of Allah. The expression is such that at all times, in every moment, taqwa should be your provision, your sustenance for life: "And take provision, but the best provision is taqwa, and fear Me, O people of understanding" (وَتَزَوَّدُوا فَإِنَّ خَيْرَ الزَّادِ التَّقْوَى وَاتَّقُونِ يَا أُولِي الألْبَابِ). Take provision for the journey of Hajj, and the best provision is piety and fear of Allah.

Taqwa is the nourishment of the spirit and the heart. Through it the soul gains strength. By taqwa and fear of Allah the soul becomes powerful, vibrant and flourishing. The soul is refined by it and becomes illuminated. Taqwa is indeed the means of salvation. Those are the people of understanding who adopt the path of taqwa and fear of Allah, and by applying it in every matter, attain goodness and blessing.

Further rulings of Hajj are explained. Is trade permissible? May a pilgrim work for wages during Hajj? Where should one stand (wuquf), and from where is it permissible to return? What is the method of remembrance (dhikr) and seeking forgiveness? Listen to these rulings!

﴿There is no blame on you if you seek bounty from your Lord.﴾ [2:198] ﴿Then when you depart from Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram (Muzdalifah), and remember Him as He has guided you, though before that you were certainly among those who went astray. Then depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Imam al-Bukhari (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated with his chain from Hadrat Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "Ukaz, Majannah and Dhu al-Majaz were famous trade fairs in the Days of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah). The Muslims thought that perhaps trading at these fairs was now no longer permissible in the Islamic era. Upon this, the command came during the season of Hajj: ﴿There is no blame on you if you seek bounty from your Lord.﴾"

Abu Dawud narrated, with his own chain through another route, from Hadrat Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Muslims used to refrain from buying and selling during the days of Hajj and in the trading season that followed. They used to say that these are the days of remembering Allah. Upon this, Allah the Exalted revealed this command: ﴿If you seek bounty from your Lord during Hajj, there is no blame on you.﴾"

In a narration of Abu Umamah al-Taymi, he says: I asked Hadrat Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "We are carriers of goods (porters). Will our Hajj be valid?" He said: "Do you not perform Tawaf, do good deeds, throw the pebbles at the Jamarat, and then shave your heads?" He said: "We replied, 'Yes.'" Ibn Umar said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him the same question that you are asking me. The Prophet (ﷺ) gave no answer until Jibril brought this verse: ﴿If you seek bounty from your Lord, there is no blame on you.﴾"

Ibn Jarir (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated from Abu Salih, the freed slave of Hadrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). He said: he asked, "O Commander of the Faithful, did you used to trade during Hajj?" He replied: "Brother, the livelihood of our people depended upon Hajj."

The caution of the Muslims regarding trade shown in the first two narrations, and the caution and abstention regarding carrying loads and wage labour mentioned in the second narration, is part of that same caution and piety which Islam had instilled in Muslims against every act and custom of the Days of Ignorance. The condition of the Muslims was that they would not commit any act or custom of the Days of Ignorance until Islam had issued its ruling concerning it. We have already discussed this at the beginning of this part (of the Qur'an), namely in the context of the explanation of Sa'y between Safa and Marwah. The Qur'an granted permission for buying and selling, and for carrying loads and labour, during the days of Hajj, but it expressed this by saying that it is the bounty of Allah.

﴿If you seek bounty from your Lord, there is no blame on you.﴾ Lawful earnings are described as the bounty of Allah, so that traders, labourers, and anyone else who engages in profit and work may understand that they are not merely acquiring wealth, but that it is also the bounty of Allah. This work is not merely the provision of material bodily needs; it has sanctity and is the bounty of Allah, and Allah bestows it with His bounty. Therefore, this nature of trade, namely the bounty of Allah, should always be kept in view. Obviously, this divine bounty can be attained only when a person conducts transactions and seeks it through the means which Allah has appointed for the system of provision. When this awareness settles in the heart of the believer and he then goes out in search of livelihood, he is in fact in a state of worship even in that effort, and this exertion does not contradict the state of Hajj, because Hajj too is for Allah, and this trade too is the bounty of Allah. Islam first instils such feelings and conceptions in the heart of the believer, and then puts them into action in the field, leaving him free to work in whatever manner he chooses. From this perspective, every act and every movement of his becomes worship of Allah.

This is why Allah placed the ruling on seeking livelihood and trade in the very midst of the rulings of Hajj, and alongside the seeking of bounty, the rulings on remembrance at al-Mash'ar al-Haram and on the return from Arafat were explained.

﴿Then when you depart from Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and remember Him as He has guided you, though before that you were certainly among those who went astray.﴾

Standing at Arafat (wuquf, standing) is the central pillar of the rites of Hajj. The compilers of the Sunan have narrated from al-Dayli, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Hajj is Arafat' (three times). Whoever reaches Arafat before the break of dawn has indeed attained Hajj. There are three days of stay in Mina, but if someone leaves after two days, there is no sin upon him, and if he delays, there is no sin upon him either."

The time for standing at the plain of Arafat begins from the decline of the sun on the day of Arafah, that is, the Zuhr of 8 Dhu al-Hijjah, and this time extends until the break of dawn on the second day, that is, Yawm al-Nahr, the day of sacrifice. Imam Ahmad's view is that the time of standing at Arafah begins from the start of the day itself. He relies upon a hadith which he narrated, and Imam al-Tirmidhi, besides the other compilers of the Sunan, narrated it and declared it authentic. Al-Sha'bi narrated from Urwah ibn Mudarris ibn Harithah al-Ta'i, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Muzdalifah, when he was standing for the prayer. I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, I have come from the mountain of Tayy. My mount has become exhausted and I am worn out. By Allah, I have stood on every mountain.' Has my Hajj been completed?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) replied: "Whoever joins our prayer here, and stays with us here until we depart, having previously stood at Arafat either by day or by night, his Hajj is complete and his hardship is removed."

According to the two statements above, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) extended the time of standing at Arafat somewhat, or extended it until the morning of Yawm al-Nahr, that is, until the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah. Why? So that the conduct of the Muslims would differ somewhat from the conduct of the polytheists. Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak narrated it. Both narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Mubarak, from Hadrat Miswar ibn Makhramah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered a sermon to us at Arafat. After praising and glorifying Allah, he said (amma ba'd): 'Today is the day of the greater Hajj. The polytheists and idolaters used to begin their departure before sunset, when the sun was still upon the mountaintops, and the mountains appeared before the sun like the turbans of men. We will depart, contrary to their conduct, after sunrise on the next day.'"

The Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) narration that he departed from Arafat after sunset on the day of Arafah is in the narration of Jabir ibn Abdullah in Sahih Muslim: "He remained standing at Arafat until the sun set and the yellow light had faded somewhat, and the disc of the sun had completely disappeared. Usamah sat behind him on his mount. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then moved forward, pulling the reins of his she-camel firmly, so that her head almost touched the front of the saddle. He kept gesturing with his right hand: 'O people, calmly, calmly!' Whenever a hill came in the way and the mount had to climb, he loosened the reins so that she could climb easily. When he reached Muzdalifah, he prayed the Maghrib and Isha prayers together with one adhan and two iqamahs. There was no tasbih between the two prayers. After that, he rested. When dawn broke and the light had spread well, he prayed the morning prayer with one adhan and one iqamah. Then he mounted his she-camel again and came to al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and facing the qiblah he made supplication there, and recited takbir and tahlil. He remained standing there until the yellow light spread, and he departed before sunrise." This is the obligation which he performed, and to which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pointed in this verse: ﴿Then when you depart from Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and remember Him as He has guided you, though before that you were certainly among those who went astray.﴾

Al-Mash'ar al-Haram means Muzdalifah. The command of the Qur'an is that on returning from Arafat one should come here and remember Allah; it is reminded that He has guided them to this remembrance as well. This remembrance is part of His guidance, and it is, as it were, their expression of gratitude for what they receive from Allah the Exalted, because it is He who guided them; otherwise, before that guidance, their condition was ﴿though before that you were certainly among those who went astray.﴾

The first generation of the Muslim community, the Companions, understood this reality well and felt its profound significance. The Arabs were immersed in misguidance, and they had seen it with their own eyes: corrupt beliefs, worshippers of idols, jinn, and angels, those who regarded the angels as the daughters of Allah, and those who considered the jinn to have a kinship with Allah. These and countless other ideological and practical deviations drowned these people. On the basis of these false conceptions and baseless beliefs, they had devised for themselves a system of worship and a system of life. Without any reasonable justification, they had declared the flesh of the backs of certain animals, or even the entire flesh, unlawful, arguing that these animals had a special relationship with Allah. They dedicated their children to Allah and associated the jinn with Him in this. Besides these, there were countless Jahili worships and customs for which there was no justification, and which were merely the outcome of these baseless and false beliefs. Moreover, because of these beliefs, their social order had become corrupt, and as a nation they had become morally degenerate. Class distinctions had taken root among them. For example, they would not go to Arafat, and this was rectified by this verse: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart.﴾ The Qur'an uprooted all these corruptions and customs. Besides this, continuous family rivalries and tribal wars persisted among them, so that they could never become a single nation collectively, which would have given them some standing in the community of nations. Their family system had been ruined, there was severe licentiousness in sexual relations, and they took pride in this sexual licentiousness. Their powerful people treated the weak with brutality, and in this matter, there was no standard of justice in their society except that might is right. In short, if one surveys the Arab society of that time, it was a supreme example of intellectual and practical misguidance and corruption in humanity.

It was Islam alone that elevated this society and rescued it from intellectual and practical error. When they heard this voice of the Qur'an: ﴿Remember Allah as He has guided you, though before that you were certainly among those who went astray,﴾ then upon the screen of their memory, in the chambers of their imagination, from the hidden recesses of their consciousness, suddenly there must have come before them the ugly pictures, the base images of their lives. Their history was full of those ugly scenes. Having looked at these images of themselves on the screen of thought and consciousness, when they then cast their gaze upon their present pure life and that lofty station which Islam had bestowed upon them, to the height to which Islam had raised them, they must have reached the depths of this truth. Without any discussion, they must have understood what the fundamental role of Islam in their lives was.

Non-Arabs too, among Muslims of every nation and every lineage, this is still a living reality. What would their standing have been without Islam? If this way of life were set aside, what weight would they carry? When people find the light of Islam, and when the Islamic system of life is implemented throughout their whole lives and becomes a reality, they find elevation in place of degradation, dignity in place of lowliness, guidance in place of error, and upright thought in place of confused imagination. This change does not take place in their lives until they truly become Muslims, and until they arrange their entire lives according to the Islamic system of life. The truth is that at this time all of humanity is wandering in a blind jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam), and it will remain so until it enters the enclosure of guidance of Islam. Only the person who has himself spent some days in that jahiliyyah, in which all of humanity today is afflicted, and which has filled the whole world with evil and is dominant everywhere, can fully grasp this secret: such a person then embraces the Islamic conception of life, lives according to it, tests it through experience, and learns how exalted and sublime the Islamic system of life is, while the other systems in his environment are nothing but heaps of impurity, filth and dirt.

When a person climbs to the highest peak of the Islamic conception of life and the Islamic system of life, and from there casts his gaze over all the conceptions of life of humanity, all the prevailing collective systems and all the ways and methods of life, over the conceptions of all the great philosophers, the thought of all modern and ancient thinkers, and all modern and ancient systems of life, then, when he looks down from that height and from the lofty peak of the Islamic system of life, he is astonished at what calamity and what misfortune humanity is afflicted with. These frivolities and these misfortunes have reduced it to such abjection and weakness. It is caught in such a confused intellectual and scholarly disarray that no wise person could fall into it. And yet this self-declared "wrong" humanity claims that it has no need even of the system of life sent down by Allah.

This is the reality of which Allah the Exalted is reminding here, and the favour of which He is recalling to the believers: that it is a great grace of Allah that He has blessed you with this supreme bounty. ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you, although before this you were certainly among those who had gone astray.﴾

Hajj is a great annual gathering of Muslims. Here they meet one another, and there is no support other than the support of Islam; all markers other than Islamic markers disappear. The body is clothed in two unstitched garments, stripped of everything else. Apart from the necessary covering of the private parts, the head and feet are bare. There is no separation between individual and individual, no distinction between tribe and tribe, no division between nation and nation. The Islamic way of life is the creed of all, the Islamic lineage is the lineage of all, and the Islamic colour is the colour of all. In the Age of Ignorance, the Quraysh called themselves "al-Hums" (the bold and the proud), and they had adopted for themselves distinctions that set them apart from all the Arabs. Among these distinctions was that, unlike the common Arabs, they did not "stand" (waqf) at Arafat during the standing at Arafat, and they did not return from the place of standing from which all the people return. For this reason a specific command was revealed concerning the rites of Hajj, and their distinction was abolished and they were brought within the circle of equality that Islam intended to establish. Thus, by abolishing all artificial distinctions, the Quraysh, the privileged tribe, were merged into the Muslim ummah. The command was given: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Imam al-Bukhari narrated, through Hisham, from his father, this hadith of Aisha. She said: "The Quraysh and those who followed their religion would not only stop there. They called themselves 'al-Hums', whereas all the Arab peoples would stand at Arafat. When Islam appeared, Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to go to Arafat, stand there, and then return from there. This is the meaning of the verse ﴿from where the people depart﴾."

Stay where other people stay, and depart from where other people depart. In the view of Islam, lineages and classes have no standing. All people are members of one ummah, perfectly equal like the teeth of a comb. No one has superiority over another except through taqwa (piety) and fear of Allah. Islam has commanded that they cast off the varied clothing that people commonly wear; they should come to the House of Allah with simple appearance and a common status, like brothers, and meet one another as equals. When even colourful garments were removed, what meaning is there in pride of nation and lineage? Leave, leave all the prejudices of the Age of Ignorance; they are impure. Be dyed in the colour of Islam. Become seekers of forgiveness from Allah. Whatever during Hajj has pricked your hearts, whatever sins you have committed, and whatever words came from your tongues in anger, even if they seem minor, seek forgiveness, because you were forbidden from them: you were commanded not even to think of any sexual act, not to commit any indecency, and not to speak angrily to anyone.

In this way, Islam sets right the conduct and behaviour of Muslims during Hajj, upon the concept of one ummah and one millah, in which there is no class distinction, no difference between nation and nation, no distinction among people on linguistic grounds, and in which a nation is not separated from another on the basis of homeland. In short, Muslims are commanded to seek forgiveness for everything that throws them far from this exalted and pure conception of life.

As mentioned above, after the conclusion of Hajj, the Arabs would proceed to the markets known as Suq Ukaz, Majanna and Dhu al-Majaz. These markets were not merely places of buying and selling. In them there was also a contest of speeches, poetry and the boasting of ancestral glories. In these markets every person would recite his genealogy. At that time the condition of the Arabs was such that, apart from the expression and display of these pride-filled boasts and feats, the Arabs had no programme at all. They had no human mission in whose path they would employ their great eloquence, rhetoric and great practical abilities.

It was Islam alone that gave the Arabs a lofty human mission. Before Islam, their condition was such that they had no programme on the earth, and no mention or station in the heavens. For this reason, after finishing Hajj, people would spend their precious time and their valuable energies in these fairs and markets on these futile and worthless matters. They would describe their lineage and noble descent, and recall the deeds of their forefathers and grandfathers, with pride and boasting ........ But when Islam came and gave them a great purpose, gave them a new concept of life, and indeed gave them a new birth, they became a purposeful and successful nation. The Qur'an gives them only that teaching in which lies their good.

Now that the rites of Hajj have been performed, Islamic teaching directs that, instead of recounting the deeds of forefathers, you should remember Allah. ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you used to remember your forefathers, or with even more remembrance.﴾ ".........." "As you used to remember your forefathers." From these words it is not understood that mentioning forefathers alongside the remembrance of Allah is still permissible. In this comparison there is a critical aspect, and the purpose is that you should spend your time on a better task than that: that is, just as you previously used to mention your forefathers, which was a futile act and not a permissible or commendable deed, change it. Now remember Allah, and remember Him even more, especially in the season of Hajj, when you have taken off your ordinary clothing and put on a special garment. Likewise, cast off the garment of arrogance and boastfulness about forefathers. Only through the remembrance of Allah is a person's rank elevated, not through the permissible or impermissible pride in ancestors. Now the balance and standard of the new values of life is piety (taqwa). It is the fear of Allah and attachment to Allah. Its remembrance and its awe-filled reverence (khashyah).

Now, human beings are weighed and assessed here according to the Islamic scale and the Islamic standard. Allah teaches the Muslims the values of human beings, and by these values He shows the different worth of different people:

﴿Among the people there is one who says, "Our Lord, grant us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter. And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, grant us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire." Those will have a share from what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ (2:200–202)

There are two viewpoints among people. One group has only this world in view. It has an intense desire to acquire worldly things and remains occupied with worldly affairs at all times. People with this outlook used to come for Hajj, and their supplications were of this kind: "O Allah, make this year a year of rain, a year of prosperity, a year of good children," and so on. These people did not even mention the Hereafter in their prayers.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (raḍiyallāhu 'anhu) that this verse was revealed concerning such people. However, the meaning of this verse is general and lasting, because such people are found in every generation and every region. They are people for whom there is only the world, and when they ask Allah for something, they ask only for the world, because their occupation is in the world. The world has taken over their minds and hearts, and the world has penetrated to the depths of their being. Sometimes Allah gives such people their full share in this world itself, if something has been decreed for them here, in their destiny; but as for the Hereafter, such people have no share at all.

The second group has a viewpoint broader than the previous one. Their souls are elevated and their nature is great. These people are those who are connected to Allah. They also seek a good world, but they also desire a share in the world to come, and they do not clearly forget it. This group says: ﴿Our Lord, grant us good in this world, and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾

These people seek from Allah the good of both worlds. They do not name the good or specify it; they leave it to Allah. Allah chooses for them whatever good He wills. He is the Chooser, and these people are content with His choice.

To people of this kind, Allah gives the assurance that their share will certainly reach them. There will be no delay in this, because Allah is very swift in reckoning.

In the light of these Qur'anic teachings, one looks at what a person's viewpoint is. Therefore, whoever turns toward Allah, entrusts all his affairs to Him, gives Allah the choice, and is pleased with whatever Allah chooses for him, such a person will receive worldly blessings, and in the Hereafter too, all good will be his share. And whoever keeps only the world in view has, in fact, already lost the Hereafter. The person with this viewpoint has also adopted the path of moderation in his supplication, and this is established upon a concept of life produced by Islam that is extremely appropriate and extremely pleasant.

Islam does not require its adherents to renounce the world, because they have been created for khilafah (vicegerency), and it is they who are to bear the office of khilafah on this earth. Islam's demand is only that Muslims remain turned toward Allah even in their worldly affairs. They should not restrict their outlook so much that they themselves become confined within the narrow circle of the world. Islam wants to free a human being from the four walls of his limited world, so that he works in this world and makes use of it, but does not get lost within it. He should remain free from its grip. He performs here all the duties of the office of khilafah, but his gaze is fixed on the lofty horizon. This is why, regarding all the arrangements and all the activities whose benefits are confined to this world, if a human being, a believing human being, casts a contemptuous glance at them from the lofty standpoint of the Islamic concept of life, then all of that will appear to him as lowly, base, and worthless, provided that he has reached the lofty peak of the Islamic concept of life.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 203:

وَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ فِي أَيَّامٍ مَعْدُودَاتٍ فَمَنْ تَعَجَّلَ فِي يَوْمَيْنِ فَلا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ وَمَنْ تَأَخَّرَ فَلا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ لِمَنِ اتَّقَى وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّكُمْ إِلَيْهِ تُحْشَرُونَ

"These are a few countable days, during which you should spend your time remembering Allah. Then whoever hastens off after two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever stays longer and departs, there is no sin upon him either, for those who fear Allah. Be mindful of Allah and know that you will be gathered before Him."

The preferred view is that the days of remembrance are the Day of Arafah, the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), and then the Days of Tashriq. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said that the "countable days" refer to the Days of Tashriq. Ikrimah (raḥimahullah) said that remembrance during the countable days means the takbirs recited after every obligatory prayer during the Days of Tashriq: Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. Earlier we cited the hadith of Abdur Rahman ibn Ma'mar al-Dayli, that "the days of Mina are three. Now if someone departs hastily after two days, there is no sin upon him, and if someone delays and comes after the full period, there is also no sin upon him." In short, it is appropriate that remembrance of Allah be as abundant as possible during Arafah, the Hajj, and the Days of Tashriq, whether one chooses the first two days or the latter two days, but in every matter the fear of Allah and piety should remain in view. "Provided they spend these days in taqwa." (li-man ittaqa)

Given the bustle of Hajj, the Day of Resurrection is now mentioned, the day on which all creation will be gathered for reckoning. There will be a frightening scene there, so prepare for that station and adopt the path of piety: "Wa-ttaqu Allah wa-'lam anna-kum ilayhi tuhsharun" — "Fear Allah's disobedience and know well that a day is coming when you will be presented before Him."

From a study of these verses it becomes clear how Islam made the Hajj, as commonly practiced by the Arabs, an Islamic obligation. Its connection to the jahili background was severed; it became a part of Islamic life, and it was purified of immoralities and impurities. Islam has adopted this same method in all matters of life: whatever custom or worship it has retained, it has kept purified of the blemishes of jahiliyyah. Its form has changed from what it was in the days of ignorance; it appears like a suitable piece in a modern garment. Now Hajj, in its well-known sense, is no longer merely a habitual and customary act of the Arabs; it has been declared an Islamic worship, because Islam is now the standard. It is Islam alone that has the right to retain a beneficial custom if it so wishes.

**Lesson 13: At a Glance**

In the Qur'an, Allah gives many kinds of guidance and lays down laws on various subjects. Taken together, these guidance and laws form a divine system of life that governs the whole of human life. Alongside this guidance and legislation, Allah has also given humanity a system of training. It is an excellent system of reform, because Allah has the most complete knowledge of the reality of the human soul and of its outward and inward dispositions and ways. Allah takes every aspect of the human self into account and draws a picture of different people with clearly defined features, in which all the intended qualities are plainly visible. When a person, holding this picture of words in the mirror of the mind, goes out into the crowd of humanity to look for those who possess these qualities, it seems as though those people are walking and moving through the streets and bazaars and across the earth, and a person can point with a finger and say: these are the people the Qur'an has described.

In this lesson, the clear features of two kinds of people are described. These kinds are commonly found among humanity. The first kind is that of the ostentatious, mischievous and foul-mouthed. Such a person makes his own self the centre of his whole life. Outwardly he seems very good, but when his inner self is revealed, there is nothing but filth. When he is called to reform his condition and to the fear of Allah, he does not come to the truth; he does not reform himself. Concern for his own dignity keeps him fixed in sin. Because of his arrogance, he turns away from truth and goodness. He ruins the fields and destroys the human race.

The second kind is that of the truthful believers who sell their whole existence in exchange for the pleasure of Allah. They sell their entire lives and do not keep any part of them back. In their striving and their deeds, in all their efforts, they keep no share for themselves. They annihilate themselves and turn wholeheartedly towards Allah.

After presenting these two standard examples of humanity, believers are now invited to enter fully into the religion of Islam, without hesitation, without doubt, and without demanding extraordinary signs and miracles. They should not be like the Children of Israel, who at every step demanded extraordinary signs and miracles, and who, abandoning Allah's blessing, namely the blessing of the Islamic system of life, took the path of disbelief. Allah said: "Enter into Islam completely." This points to the fact that Islam is a complete system of life, and that you must shape your entire life according to this system and act upon it. (Details come later.)

In contrast to the great blessing of faith and the shade of peace and tranquillity that it brings to Muslims, a glimpse is also shown of the wrong outlook of the disbelievers. Because of their defective conception of life, they mock the Muslims. But it is made clear what each person's worth is in the sight of Allah: "But on the Day of Resurrection, the God-fearing will be exalted above them."

After this, it is explained how differences of opinion arose among people, and that the only solution to them is for them to return to the criterion of truth and accept it as their judge. It is explained that this criterion of truth is the Book of Allah, which was revealed precisely so that it might judge between people in the differences of opinion about truth that have arisen among them.

In this connection, it is made clear that the bearers of the Book of Allah, who uphold this criterion of truth, face countless difficulties. The Muslim ummah (community) is told that on its path there are hardships and calamities, not only on your path, but in human history too, every community that has borne this trust has had the same experience. This is so that it may prepare itself to bear the burden of leadership of the ummah, which it must undoubtedly carry. And so that it may be ready, gladly and with tranquillity, to bear this burden. Whenever the atmosphere is polluted with dangers, and whenever it seems that dawn is far off, it should remain hopeful of Allah's help.

In this lesson, we see that alongside the legislation for the training of the Islamic community, the Islamic order and discipline of training is also being taught. The various aspects of this training are described in a manner that is extremely pleasant and impactful, and all of this takes place within the guidance and the laying down of laws from which the Islamic system is formed, a system that governs the whole of human life.

The strange features of the human soul are drawn by the pen of a master painter, and they are clear proof that this speech is not the speech of a human being. This picture was not painted by a human. The source of this speech and this psychological portrayal is certainly not the human mind. No person could reach so deep into the depths of human psychology, in such brief words and with such a concise portrayal. Nor could a person bring forward such deep features of the human soul that are at once so comprehensive and so clear.

Every word of this speech is a line of the picture, which expresses a feature or a quality of a human being. Soon these designs and figures appear in the form of living human beings who walk and move. The one whose portrait is drawn becomes a distinct personality, to whom one can point with the fingers. From among millions of people, that person can be singled out. You can say: this is the person whose portrait the Qur'an has painted. Depicting in words is also a kind of creation, just as living things are continually brought into being by the hand of divine power, as night and day are.

Now this is a living personality. He speaks and he walks about. His self is the essence of goodness and the image of sincerity. He is an example of devotion and single-mindedness and of high resolve. A longing for good, righteousness, purity and cleanliness is found within him.

And this second personality, whose words seem good, is very glib of tongue. His voice is thunderous. When he speaks, he speaks of goodness, righteousness and reform. He calls Allah to witness his good intention, so that his words may be more effective and clear, and so that there may be no doubt about his single-mindedness and sincerity. Through this he apparently displays goodness and fear of Allah, although in reality this person is the worst enemy of Allah. His soul is filled with malice and quarrelsomeness. There is not even a faint trace of love or nobility in him. He is completely deprived of love and goodness. Kindness and selflessness are not even to be found in him.

The outward appearance of this person is the opposite of his inner reality. His manifest is far from his apparent. He can give falsehood the colour of truth with great skill, but when the field of action comes, he is exposed there. The truth comes out from behind the veil, and his evil, corruption and mischief become fully visible before everyone. His enmity and spitefulness become evident.

﴿When he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and progeny. And Allah does not love corruption.﴾ When he is given authority, all his running about in the land is only for the purpose of spreading corruption, destroying crops, and ruining human progeny. Yet Allah certainly does not like corruption.

When he turns his attention to any practical matter, his inclination is towards evil, corruption, cruelty and oppression. In every matter he is a fierce quarrelsome person. He ruins the fields, snatches away the fruits, vegetables and growth and greenery of the crops, and also destroys the human race.

He is the enemy of every kind of goodness. He ruins the fields. Fruits, vegetables and grains are destroyed. In place of greenery and freshness there come dryness and desolation. His dominance becomes the cause of the destruction of the human race.

The destruction of life means that malice, evil, treachery and corruption which were being nurtured within the being of this ill-natured person. But this person keeps it hidden through his smooth tongue and sweet speech, through displays of goodness, and through the show of reform, nobility, goodness and piety. Yet Allah does not like corruption, and nor does He like those corrupters who become the cause of spreading mischief in this universe.

Such people can never remain hidden from Allah. Before Allah this greed and this polish are of no avail. Yes, among people such varnishing and greed may deceive them at times. Therefore the varnishing of this ill-natured and ill-disposed person cannot deceive Allah. Yes, the common people, before whom there are no secret mysteries, and for whom outward show can deceive, do indeed regard such people with some esteem in their eyes.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 2, verse 206:

The line of discourse now moves forward. The same picture stands before us: some further lines are drawn, and some marks become clearer as they come into view. ﴿وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُ اتَّقِ اللَّهَ أَخَذَتْهُ الْعِزَّةُ بِالإثْمِ فَحَسْبُهُ جَهَنَّمُ وَلَبِئْسَ الْمِهَادُ﴾ "When it is said to him, 'Fear Allah,' his self-regard takes hold of him to sin. For such a person, Hell is sufficient, and it is indeed a wretched resting-place." 

When he gains power, he spreads corruption on the earth, destroys the crops, destroys the human race, and devastation and ruin prevail. The lava of mischief and malice that was boiling in the breast of such a person bursts forth and comes out. When such a person begins to do all this, and to him, for the sake of advice, as a reminder of the fear of Allah, to protect him from the wrath of Allah, and to make him feel shame before that Benefactor, only this is said: "Fear Allah" (ittaqi Allah), then he becomes furiously angry that this boldness was shown toward him. Why was this said to him? This is a bad thing. Who are those who would turn him toward goodness? How did those who object to him dare to do so? Are these people guiding him? So his regard for his own dignity holds him, not to truth, not to justice, not to goodness, but fixes him in sin. He begins to regard crime as honour. He regards error as correctness. He considers sin to be virtue and becomes stiff-necked against the truth. He holds his neck high and, with great obstinacy, swaggers against Allah. Yet earlier, his own condition was that he would constantly call Allah to witness his good intentions, and would constantly display goodness, righteousness, single-mindedness and modesty.

This is a final touch, by which the features of this picture are completed. It becomes clearer, and its various types also come into view. This picture now takes the form of living, moving examples. Without any hesitation you can say: "There he is! There he is! There he is! The one whose picture the Qur'an has drawn in these words." In short, you will find such people in every age and every place, in the form of living persons.

Against all these qualities, namely persisting in disbelief, making sin a habit, taking up enmity against the truth, spreading corruption with callous cruelty, and spreading wickedness and immorality, Allah has only one whip: the whip of admonition! What is the one that is suitable for people of this kind and fits their circumstances? ﴿فَحَسْبُهُ جَهَنَّمُ وَلَبِئْسَ الْمِهَادُ﴾ "For such people, Hell is the cure, and it is indeed a wretched resting-place."

Sufficient for them is Hell, and it is what suffices: Hell, whose fuel will be men and stones; Hell into which such mischief-makers will be thrown head first, and into which the whole army of Satan will be thrown head first; Hell whose fire will burn the heart; Hell whose burning, like lightning, will tear cries from the heart; Hell which will annihilate and destroy everything, and reduce it to ashes by burning; Hell whose flames will be frightful and wrathful........ This Hell is their cure, and it is a wretched resting-place.

Reflect! How contemptuous is this picture of Hell, of this base abode! How wretched will be the state of the person whose abode this becomes. Just now in the world this person used to walk with arrogance, strutting about, and his state of pride and vanity was such that he would become fixed even in evil. But now where is he? In a place of humiliation!

This is the picture of one type of people. This is one side of the picture. Now look at the other side too. There are good people in this world as well. Let us cast a glance at those sacred souls too. In contrast to them: "And among mankind is he who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, and Allah is Kind to the servants" (2:207). "On the other hand, there is among mankind someone who spends his life seeking the pleasure of Allah, and Allah is very merciful to such servants."

The word yashri has a broad meaning: to sell off oneself, the whole self, completely. He hands over the whole of himself, leaving nothing for himself. But what does he receive as the price in this transaction? Only the hope of Allah's pleasure. Now his self is no longer his own. Nothing remains for him after his self is gone; without hesitation he has sold everything, given everything without fear, and taken nothing in return. He has sold his entire capital, his entire existence, and given it to Allah. No part of the self has been kept back for anyone other than Allah.

One interpretation can also be made: he has not sold his self but has bought it. His self was a slave to worldly aims; he bought it, and having bought it, he freed it, and having freed it, made it purely Allah's. Now no one has any right over this self; only Allah's right remains, the right of the Owner. This person sacrifices all worldly aims and all goals, and by subjecting his self, makes it dedicated to Allah.

Some narrations also mention the occasion of the revelation of these verses.

Ibn Kathir has written: Ibn Abbas (raa), Anas (raa), Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab (rh), Abu Uthman al-Nahdi (rh), Ikrimah (rh), and a whole group of Companions and Successors say: this verse was revealed concerning Suhayb ibn Sinan al-Rumi (raa). He embraced Islam in Makkah and began preparing to migrate. The people said: you cannot go with your wealth. If you must go, leave your wealth here. He secured his release on their conditions and handed over all his wealth. Then Allah revealed this verse concerning him. Umar (raa) and some other companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) met him around the outskirts of Harrah, and said to him: the transaction is profitable. He said: May Allah never let your trade suffer loss; what is the matter? They related the whole story to him and informed him that Allah had revealed this verse concerning him.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Suhayb has earned great profit in this transaction."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Suhayb (raa) through chains via Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, Muhammad ibn Abdullah, Sulayman ibn Dawud, Ja'far ibn Abi Sulayman al-Dabbi, Awf, and Abu Uthman al-Nahdi (rh). He said: "When I decided to migrate from Makkah to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the people of Quraysh said to me: Suhayb, when you came you had not a penny; now you are leaving with wealth. This cannot happen. I said to them: If I leave my wealth for you, will you let me go? They said: Gladly. I handed over my wealth to them, and they let me go. I set out and reached Madinah. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) learned of this matter, he said: 'Suhayb has profited well, Suhayb has profited well.'" He said it twice.

Whether the verse was revealed in this event, or the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Companions found it applicable to this event, its meaning is far broader than one incident concerning one individual. It is a depiction of the psychological state of a soul, and it describes the features of one type of people. Its examples are found everywhere and can be seen.

These are two features, two pictures. The first picture applies to every person who has duplicity, show, glib tongue, hardheartedness, nobility of spirit (in appearance), fierce quarrelsomeness, and whose nature has become corrupted... The second picture is of every person who is a believer: sincere in faith, single-minded for Allah, who has bidden farewell to worldly aims. These are two well-known examples of humankind. These are their wondrous, miraculous depictions through the creative pen. Before people these two pictures are being displayed. On one side, people reflect on the eloquent inimitability of the Qur'an, and on the other they are amazed at the miraculous way Allah has distinguished between people. It is one human being, yet a believer; and it is the same human being, yet a hypocrite. One face, but different tastes...

People are told: do not be deceived by sweet words; do not pass judgment on anyone merely because of glib tongue; behind sweet, flavorful words, seek the reality too. Also, behind words and artificial eloquence, behind pleasing hypocrisy, look for the meaning as well, and at the same time make clear what the values of faith are.

Two pictures, like oil paintings: two panels, one an example of corrupt hypocrisy and the other an example of pure faith. Placing them before us, and pausing under their shadow, the Islamic movement is called upon. It is addressed by the name of the believers, by the name by which they are known: O you who believe! Enter fully into Islam! Do not follow the footsteps of Satan! Be alert! Even after this clear address, let no thought slip away.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 2, verse 208 (part 1 of 3):
