Spending and charity begin only when a person has fulfilled his own needs to a sufficient degree. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The best charity is that which is given after meeting one's needs, and the upper hand is better than the lower hand, and begin with your own family."

Jabir (ra) narrates: a man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with gold the size of an egg. He said: "O Messenger of God, I found this in a mine. Take it; it is charity, and I have nothing besides it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned away from him. He came from the right side of the Messenger (ﷺ) and repeated the same words, and the Messenger (ﷺ) again turned away. Then he came from the left and repeated the same words, and the Messenger (ﷺ) again turned away. Then he came from behind and repeated the same words. At this the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took the gold and threw it at him, saying: "If it hits him, it will hurt. Know that one of you comes to me with everything he has and says, 'This is charity,' and then sits down to beg from people. The best charity is that which is given out of sufficiency."

It was known to God that man loves first his close family members, his children and his parents. Therefore God made these persons deserving of spending after the self, so that he would spend a portion of his wealth on them with joy and contentment. Here God has taken into account this natural inclination of man, which is harmless; rather, there is goodness and wisdom hidden in taking it into account. Along with this wisdom, the maintenance of certain persons is also secured, who are both close relatives of the giver and members of the Muslim community itself. If their close relative does not help them, they will be in need. For them it is better to obtain help from this close relative than to be compelled to seek help from a distant acquaintance or a stranger.

Furthermore, there is an additional benefit: through this, love and peace will increase within the first school of training of man, the family, and the bonds among family members will be strengthened, which holds the first brick in the building of a great humanity.

After his close relatives, a person naturally gives preference to all his relatives in gradation and according to the degree of their ties, and the Creator of nature knows this well. And this is not a bad thing at all, because these relatives too are, after all, a part of the Ummah and constituents of the Islamic society. Thus a wealthy Muslim steps one more pace beyond the circle of his close relatives. His progress continues in the direction of his natural inclinations and tendencies, and the needs of his more distant relatives are also being met, and bonds of love and kinship are being established with distant relatives. In this way the mutual relations of the basic unit of the Islamic community become bound together, and its ties become strong.

After spending on oneself and on close and distant kin, if something still remains, then Islam's command is to spend on the weak of society, those seeing whom alone a person is moved by nobility, a spirit of mercy and a spirit of sharing, and a noble person is ready to help such weak people. Among such people, orphans come first, for they are both young and weak. Then comes the rank of the needy, who have nothing for their expenses, but who, because of their dignity and self-respect, do not stretch out their hands before anyone. Then comes the wayfarer, who may have wealth but is far from home, and whose access to it is obstructed.

In the early period, there were many such people in the Islamic movement. These people had left their wealth behind in Makkah when they migrated, and now they were members of the Islamic society. Islam guides the affluent people of the Islamic movement to spend on such needy people. In this regard Islam awakens the pure natural inclinations of these people and purifies them, and very gently and gradually brings these people to the goal. First, the selves of these affluent people are purified; they spend what they spend with a contented soul, are pleased with the expenditure, and, without any constraint and without any compulsion, turn toward their God. Second, the weak and needy members of society receive their needs. Third, all members of society become bound together, becoming sureties and helpers of one another; yet in this collective support there is neither compulsion nor harm to anyone. This guidance of Islam is extremely subtle, extremely pleasant, and extremely far-reaching. There is nothing but goodness in it. This guidance is neither coercive, nor artificial, nor does it contain any kind of violence.

The thread of this system of support in spending in the way of God is also joined to the exalted horizon. Thus, by spending, a surge of attachment to God arises in the heart of the believer. In his giving and his generosity, in his speech and his action, in his conscience and intention, and in his understanding and perception, in short in every aspect of him, attachment to God comes into being. "Wa ma taf'alu min khayrin fa innallaha bihi 'alim" — "And whatever good you do, God is well aware of it." God is aware of this spending too; He is informed of its purpose, and He knows the intention behind it. Therefore this spending can never be lost. It is recorded in God's account, and nothing is lost in that account. He does not diminish people's rights, nor does He do any injustice to them; but riya' (showing off) has no effect on it, and deceit cannot succeed with Him.

Thus the guidance of the Quran takes hearts up by the hand to the lofty heights of the supreme horizon. These hearts become pure and clear, single-minded, and purified exclusively for Allah, Most High, yet with great gentleness, at a very gradual pace, without any artificial method and without any coercive means. This is the system of training that Allah has devised, who is All-Knowing (ʿAlīm) and All-Aware (Khabīr). And in accordance with the principles of this system of training, the Islamic way of life is shaped. This system takes the reins of human nature into its own hands and assumes the leadership of ordinary human beings. Wherever a person may be, it takes hold of their hand from that very place and leads them to that lofty station of ascent and perfection which humanity, throughout its entire history before Islam, could have reached. Indeed, if humanity has ever attained this lofty station, it has been only under the shade of the Islamic way of life, by walking upon the Straight Path of Islam.

After the spending in the way of Allah (infāq fī sabīl Allāh), the command of striving in the way of Allah (jihād fī sabīl Allāh) comes, and in this too Islam has adopted the same method of training that was adopted in the matter of spending.

Jihad in the way of Allah (fi sabilillah) is a very burdensome obligation. Despite this, it is such that its performance is obligatory, because in it there is great good for the individual Muslim, abundant good for the Islamic community, and indeed great benefit for all of humanity. This obligation is solely for the sake of truth, for goodness, and for the reform of conditions.

Since Islam is a natural religion (din-e-fitrat), it adopts its stance and viewpoint in every matter in complete accordance with human nature. Allah does not deny the hardships and difficulties involved in performing this obligation, nor is it regarded as easy and light. Nor is it denied that the human self (nafs), by its natural inclination, dislikes it and finds it heavy. Islam neither denies human nature nor conflicts with the system of nature in any matter. It does not declare forbidden for a person those natural feelings whose denial has no justification and which cannot be considered null and void. However, Islam treats these natural feelings by another method. Islam dispels the darknesses of human nature with a new kind of light. It says: the obligation imposed upon you is certainly hard and disliked, but behind it lies a great wisdom because of which it becomes very light, easy, and its burden is lessened, and the bitterness of its taste is reduced. Through it a hidden good comes into being, and this hidden good cannot be clearly seen by superficial human sight. Once a person attains this viewpoint, doors of recognition (ma'rifah) open upon the human soul, and through them a person can reach the reality of the matter. Now a person looks at the issue of jihad and qital from a new angle. Then, when a person encounters difficulties and is surrounded by calamities, a cool and pleasant breeze blows over his heart and vision from that angle of the soul and that new door of recognition, and he attains tranquility, because it is quite possible that after these difficulties there will be ease, and who knows that perhaps the outcome of a desired matter will not be this. Indeed, it is He who has knowledge of the farthest extremes, whereas all people are not aware even of a part of this knowledge.

When this pleasant breeze blows upon the human self, all the calamities, hardships, and difficulties that befall it become easy. Doors of hope and continuity open, and even in intense heat the heart feels coolness, and with certainty and hope it inclines towards obedience and the performance of duty.

Islam deals with human nature in such a way that it does not find fault with natural inclinations, nor does it compel a person to perform a difficult duty merely through orders and commands; rather, it trains the person and makes him ready for obedience. It widens the circle of hope. It teaches him that by spending something lowly you attain the highest, and it raises a person not in opposition to his personal desires but with joy and pleasure, so that human nature may feel that the mercy and compassion of Allah is upon it, because He is thoroughly aware of human weaknesses. He acknowledges that the obligation imposed upon man is a difficult task. He also knows his helplessness, values the human being, and by means of high resolve, supplication, and hope, continually gives him the strength to keep advancing.

Thus Islam trains human nature: it does not become dejected over obligations, does not lament and wail in the trial of calamities, and does not lose courage the moment troubles begin. If weakness appears in the face of difficulties, it does not simply become ashamed and fall away; rather, it strives to remain steadfast, and it believes that it will be regarded as excused before Allah. It has the hope that Allah will help it and grant it strength from Himself, and it firmly resolves to confront the trials, because perhaps some good lies hidden beneath these difficulties.

After difficulties, ease comes. After fatigue and weakness, great rest is attained. This nature does not become infatuated with beloved and desired things, because indulgence may result in regret, and something disliked may emerge from beneath what is beloved. Sometimes it may also happen that destruction and calamity are waiting behind brighter hopes.

This is a wondrous system of training: very profound and very simple. This system is acquainted with the springs of the human self, its hidden corners, and its various passages. This system of training deals in truth and sincerity. In it there are no false signals, no false impressions, and no deceptive trickery. Thus it is a reality that the imperfect and weak human mind may dislike something even though it is pure good. And it is also true that a person may like something and be devoted to it, yet there may be pure evil in it. And it is also true that Allah knows and humans do not know. What knowledge do people have of consequences and outcomes? How would they know, since the curtain is down and what lies behind it? In short, people cannot have knowledge of those realities which are not subject to our desires, ignorance, and the self.

This divine feeling within the human heart opens its doors. A new world emerges before it. This world is entirely different from the limited world that our eyes see. Before its gaze there also come other factors operating in the depths of this universe, which overturn the course of affairs and reverse the order of results in which a person has desires or expects them. When the believing heart, submitting to destiny, comes under the sway of this divine feeling, then it works with hope. It has hope and also fear of Allah, but it entrusts all outcomes willingly and with pleasure to the hand of power, which is All-Wise and All-Knowing, whose knowledge encompasses everything. This is in truth the entry through the open door of safety. The human self cannot attain true awareness of Islam until there arises within it the conviction that good lies in what Allah has declared to be good, and that goodness lies in adopting obedience and submission to one's Lord. There is no good in testing Allah or in demanding proofs from Allah. Firm certainty, tranquil hope, and continuous effort alone are the doors of safety, and Allah invites His servants to enter through these very doors, and commands that they enter fully through them, not halfway in and halfway out. Allah leads His servants towards this safety with a simple, wondrous, yet very profound method, with great gentleness, great ease, and a gradual pace. On this path to safety He leads them in such a way that eventually He also makes fighting obligatory upon them for the establishment of peace. What is safety? Safety means that in the battlefield the soul and conscience of a person remain content, at peace, and secure.

The indication made in this verse of the Qur'an concerning fighting is not limited to fighting alone. Fighting is a clear example of matters which the human self by nature does not like, yet in which, in terms of outcomes, there is good. This principle is in truth the philosophy of life of the believer throughout his whole life. Its shadow falls upon all the events of his life. Indeed, a person does not know in any matter where good lies and where evil lies.

On the day of Badr, the Muslims set out intending to plunder the caravan of Quraysh and seize its merchandise. Allah had also promised them booty, and they thought that this caravan and its merchandise were about to fall into their hands. It did not even occur to them that they would have to encounter the army of Quraysh. But Allah's doing was that the caravan escaped, and they came face to face with the army of Quraysh equipped with weapons and provisions, and as a result the Muslims attained that victory whose echo was heard throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Now look: in comparison with the victory of the Muslims, what value remains for the caravan and its trade goods? Now consider: what is the worth of what the Muslims chose for themselves, and what is the worth of what Allah chose for them? The reality is that Allah knows and people do not know.

The young companion of Musa (peace be upon him) forgot his food, namely the fish. When they reached the rock, the fish went into the river. Musa (peace be upon him) went on ahead and said to his servant: bring our breakfast, for we have become severely exhausted on this journey. The servant said: Did you see what happened? When we were resting by that rock, I did not remember the fish, and Satan made me so heedless that I forgot to mention it to you. The fish took its way into the river in a strange manner. Musa (peace be upon him) said: That is exactly what we were seeking. So the two of them returned upon their footsteps, and there they found one of Our servants. This was the very purpose for which Musa (peace be upon him) had undertaken the journey. Had the incident of the fish not occurred, Musa (peace be upon him) would not have turned back, and the whole purpose for which he had undertaken this exhausting journey would have been lost.

If a person reflects, he can discover this truth in certain specific experiences: that he has encountered many experiences in his life which were disliked by him, yet behind them lay great good; and some things were pleasant and delicious, yet at their core lay great evil. There are certain aims from which a person is deprived, and he suffers a great shock from this deprivation, but after a period, upon seeing the results, a person comes to know that by keeping him deprived, Allah had in truth saved him from a great calamity. Many trials and hardships are so painful that a person swallows their bitter draughts with great displeasure, and it is near that his very life may depart because of the severity of those trials; yet before long the results of those hardships turn out as good as the results that a long, comfortable life could not have produced.

This is the method of training by which Allah takes the human self, so that it may believe, enter Islam, and entrust the coming outcomes to Allah. Its only task is to exert its full strength, to the extent of its capacity, in the field of outward striving.

The Islamic movement was being led towards peace and safety so that it might enter entirely into the system of safety. One link in this same chain is also the ruling concerning fighting in the sacred months. Therefore, He says:

This passage is part 1 of 2 of the commentary, so I translate the text as given.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 217 (part 1 of 2):

Many narrations report that these verses were revealed concerning the expedition (sariyyah) of Abdullah ibn Jahsh. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave him a sealed letter and sent with him eight men, all of them Muhajirun; there was no one from the Ansar among them. The Prophet (ﷺ) instructed Abdullah not to open the letter until he had travelled for two days and nights. When he read the letter at the appointed time, its text was: "When you read my letter, proceed until you descend in the valley of Batn Nakhlah, which lies between Makkah and Ta'if. There keep watch on the affairs of the Quraysh and keep us informed of them. But do not compel any of your companions to go with you." This event took place before the Battle of Badr (al-Kubra). Abdullah ibn Jahsh read the letter and said, "I hear and obey." Then he said to his companions that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had ordered him to go to Batn Nakhlah, to keep watch on the Quraysh there and to inform the Messenger (ﷺ) of their situation. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had forbidden him to compel any of them to accompany him. "Whoever among you desires martyrdom and is eager for it, let him go; and whoever dislikes it, let him return. As for me, I will carry out the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." So he set off, and all his companions went with him; not one of them turned back. They took the route through Majaz, and while they were still on that road, the camel of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Utbah ibn Ghazwan was lost. They remained behind the caravan of Abdullah ibn Jahsh in order to search for the camel, while the other six pressed on. When they reached Batn Nakhlah, they saw a caravan of the Quraysh passing, whose camels were laden with trade goods. In that caravan were Amr al-Hadrami and three other persons. Amr was killed, two were taken captive, and one escaped. They seized the entire goods of the caravan. This detachment believed that the attack was on the last day of Jumada al-Akhirah, whereas in fact the attack had taken place on the first day of Rajab, and the sacred months had begun, which the Arabs also held in great honour and which Islam too had maintained in their sanctity. When this detachment came to Madinah with the caravan and the captives and presented the spoils before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said, "Did I ever command you to fight in the sacred months?" The caravan and the captives were held standing, and the Prophet (ﷺ) refused to accept them. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said this, the people became anxious and were certain that a great sin had been committed by them, and that they were doomed. Their Muslim brethren also rebuked them harshly, saying, "What have you done?" The Quraysh of Makkah said, "Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions have violated the sanctity of the sacred months; they have shed blood in them, seized property and taken people captive." The Jews drew an omen from this event against the Messenger (ﷺ). They said: "Amr al-Hadrami was killed by Waqid ibn Abdullah": "Amr" means the building of war has been erected; "Hadrami" means war has become green; "Waqid" means the flames of war have blazed up.

In short, after this event, a storm of misleading propaganda arose and it was spread among the Arabs through various cunning methods. In it, the Messenger (ﷺ) and his companions were presented in the guise of a person who rejects all the sacred things of the Arabs and tramples upon traditions established for centuries, and who breaks every bond whenever expediency requires. (God forbid.) In the midst of this storm of propaganda and impudence, Allah the Exalted revealed these verses, which cut the matter short and settled the issue with truth. The Messenger (ﷺ) accepted the spoils and the captives:

﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin).﴾ These verses were revealed. They declared fighting and quarrelling in the sacred months to be a grave and major sin, and said that this is correct, but:

﴿Hindering from the way of Allah, disbelieving in Him, and (hindering) from the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is greater with Allah; and oppression is worse than killing.﴾ 

The war was not begun by the Muslims; it was the polytheists who initiated hostility. It was these very people who barred others from the path of Allah, who disbelieved in Allah, and who barred the worshippers of Allah from the Sacred Mosque. It was these very people who committed every major sin in order to hinder people from the path of Allah. They themselves denied Allah and made others deniers of Him as well. They also denied the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque and violated it. They inflicted torment upon the Muslims, and for thirteen full years before the Hijrah they kept tormenting the Muslims and turning them away from their religion. Then they did not even stop there, but expelled the inhabitants of the Sacred Mosque from their homes, although it was a place worthy of respect and a place of security. They paid no regard to the sanctity of the Sanctuary and observed no principle of its reverence.

For Allah, expelling the people of the Sanctuary from their homes is worse than fighting in the sacred months; and subjecting people to afflictions and hardships merely for their religion and creed is worse than killing. Since the polytheists of Makkah had openly committed these two grave sins, their argument that the Muslims paid no regard to the honour of the sacred months, or to the sanctity of the Sacred House, is mere propaganda and carries no weight. Thus, through these verses, the position of the Muslims themselves became clear: the Muslims are in truth fighting against those who show no respect for the sacred Sanctuary. In reality, they have made the respect for the Haram and the sacred months a screen and a refuge for themselves, behind which they may, whenever they wish, proclaim their sanctity and purity, and whenever they wish, trample that sanctity underfoot. It was the duty of the Muslims to eliminate these people wherever they found them, for they are rebels and mischief-makers who show no regard for any reverence, and who should not be allowed to act arbitrarily behind a false screen, because there is no genuine reverence in their hearts.

The symbols and traditions of sanctity were in themselves a true matter, but these people made unlawful use of them. The propaganda of the Makkan disbelievers about the violation of the sacred months was merely outward show; behind that veil they really wished to prove that the Muslims were committing aggression and that their position was not correct. Yet it was they who began the injustice and aggression. It was they who paid no regard to the sanctity of the Sacred House.

Islam is a realistic system of life. It is not based merely on examples and ideal forms; it studies human life realistically. It keeps in view its difficulties, its inclinations and its actual conditions. It gives realistic guidance. It runs this life on earth as a concrete reality and gradually leads it in the direction of progress. It resolves its problems in such a way that the solution is a practical one, not merely wishful thinking or philosophical imagining, but a solution that can actually work in the practical world.

Now look at the condition of the Quraysh. These people were extremely oppressive and rebellious; they held no standing in regard to sacred places. They did not believe in the reverence of sanctities at all. They were crushing every good moral quality, every piety and every good principle. They had become arrogant against the truth and kept people from accepting it. They had put the believers into trials and inflicted severe torments upon them; they were expelling them from the Sacred Mosque. Yet according to the traditions of the Arabs, the Sacred Mosque and the Sacred House were places of refuge, and within them not only human beings but animals and insects enjoyed security. Despite all these facts, these people had raised the whole world on their heads under the cover of these sanctities and were proclaiming those sanctities loudly. They would cry out: "Behold, this is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions; they have trampled the sanctity of the sacred month."

Now see how Islam responds to them. Does Islam bring a theoretical, ideal and imaginary answer against them and offer a merely doctrinal analysis of the problem? If Islam had offered some imaginary solution in this matter, it would certainly have been an ideal, but the result would have been that the Muslims were disarmed, while they were confronting an evil and rebellious enemy who used every weapon and did not hesitate to employ any stratagem. Never! Islam would never adopt such an attitude, because it was confronting a real situation. It had to deal with that situation and remove it from its path. Islam wished to remove evil and corruption from its path. It wished to place the authority of this earth in the hands of a righteous power, to place leadership and authority in the hands of a righteous community. Therefore it could never allow these sanctities to become fortresses for mischief-makers and rebels, from behind which they might strike at pure, righteous and constructive people while remaining completely safe from retaliation.

Islam pays great regard to the sanctities in relation to those who themselves observe them, and it strictly adheres to the principles and rules of sanctity. But it by no means permits anyone who himself pays no heed to these sanctities, tramples them thoroughly, makes them a bulwark for himself, and from behind them persecutes the righteous servants, kills good people and commits every evil with ease, remaining safe and secure from retaliation behind these sanctities, while instructing others to observe these sanctities.

Islam has adopted this same policy in every matter. For example, in Islam backbiting (ghibah) is forbidden, but the backbiting of a wicked person is not backbiting at all. If he is known for his wickedness and debauchery, then those who bear wounds in their breasts as a result of his sin and debauchery are excused. Islam forbids abusive speech (al-jahr bi al-su'), but an exception is made for the one who has been wronged: if someone is oppressed, he may speak openly against the oppressor, because this is his right. If the voice is not raised against the oppressor, on the plea that it would be backbiting, then this means we are giving the oppressor the shelter of a good principle, although he does not deserve to benefit from that principle.

Yet, even in this matter of equal treatment, Islam does not allow its standard to fall. It does not descend from its lofty level to the level of these mischief-makers and oppressors. It does not use base weapons against its opponents, nor immoral means or hateful methods. It commands the Muslims only this: break the hands of the oppressors, fight them, kill them, and cleanse the environment of life from them, openly and in plain view.

The real issue is leadership. When leadership comes into the hands of pure people, who are believers and sound of nature, and when the earth is cleansed of the filth of those who pay no regard to any sanctity and trample all sacred things, only then will the sanctity of all sacred things be restored, and it will be restored in the manner that Allah wills.

This is Islam: clear, plain, strong, and one that breaks the head of falsehood, with nothing concealed and no trickery. It does not give any other power the opportunity to deceive it or to practise any deception upon it. And this is the Qur'an, which gives the Muslims a firm position, so firm that their feet will not slip. They will keep advancing in the path of Allah and will purify the earth of Allah from every kind of evil and corruption. The Qur'an gives their minds and hearts a clarity like polished glass; it leaves no kind of anguish or disquiet in their hearts, and doubts and whisperings are removed from their hearts. The Qur'an says plainly: behold, that is evil, corruption, disobedience and falsehood, and therefore it has no sanctity and no protection. Such falsehood cannot be permitted to use these sanctities as a shield and strike at their sanctities. The Qur'an clearly instructs: keep advancing toward your goal, with certainty, with tranquillity, with the peace of your conscience, and joined to your Lord.

After stating this truth and fixing it well in mind, and after giving the Muslims steadfastness and firmness, it is now told to them that the evil they face is no superficial evil; it is a very deep wickedness. The plan of the enemies is very deep, and they stand firmly upon it as a principle.

﴿And they will not cease to fight you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able.﴾

This is the sound report, from the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, which shows how stubbornly the Evil One (ash-sharr) holds to his impure position, how hard the disbelievers strive to turn the Muslims away from their religion, and that this is a constant aim of the enemies of Islam: they want, by some means, to keep them far from Islam. This aim of the enemies of Islam is so constant that it has never changed in any age or in any region. The very existence of Islam on earth is unbearable to them. The enemies of religion have always been fearful of it. In every age these people have feared the Islamic community and the Islamic movement. They have an innate aversion to Islam itself, and it causes them severe distress. They are always apprehensive of it. Every false-worshipper (batil-parast) is dismayed by the strength of the Islamic system and its seriousness. Every rebel against God is overawed by it. Every corrupter dislikes Islam. Islam, in its very self, is a battle against disbelief. The luminous truth of Islam, its enduring system of life and its enduring method of action, are themselves the challenge to falsehood. Because of these qualities, Islam in its very self is a declaration of war against disbelief and corruption. That is why false-worshippers, rebels and corrupters never tolerate Islam. They are always on the lookout for some way to put the people of Islam into trial, to bring them back to disbelief, whatever form of disbelief they may adopt, so long as they abandon Islam. As long as there exists on this earth any community whose aim is the Islamic system of life, which follows Islam and wishes to live within Islam, false-worshippers cannot remain peacefully on their falsehood and their corruption. Therefore they are always fearful of the Islamic movement.

The enemies of Islam wage many kinds of war against the Muslims and use many kinds of weapons, but their aim remains one and it is always before them: that, if they have the means, they will turn sincere Muslims away from their religion. When one of their weapons becomes useless, they immediately use another; when one of their weapons becomes blunt, they sharpen another. But this true report of the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, stands firm in its place, and it warns the Muslims against the schemes of these opponents, that they should not lay down their arms. The Muslims are called upon to remain steadfast against the plots of these disbelievers. If war with them comes upon them, they should act with patience and forbearance. And if they do not do so, they will suffer loss in this world and the Hereafter. They will be afflicted with a punishment that no excuse will excuse and that no justification will lessen:

﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

Habitat (ḥabaṭa) is derived from ḥubūṭ. The Arabs say ḥabaṭat al-nāqah, meaning the she-camel swelled up, when she eats something that makes her swell and eventually die (as certain grasses and some other plants cause animals to swell up). The Qur'an has used this word for the deeds of disbelievers, and this also shows a correspondence between the sensory and the figurative meanings. Just as the she-camel apparently grows large by swelling, yet her end is destruction, so the deeds of the disbelievers appear very great and inflated, but their end is nothing, rather they are destroyed.

The same is the condition of the person who, after understanding Islam and having tested it, turns away from it, merely out of fear of afflictions and calamities. If they go beyond bounds, their end will be just what God has mentioned: that their deeds will be rendered worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and in the Hereafter they will abide forever in the Fire of Hell.

For a heart that has come to savour faith, and has rightly understood Islam, there is no possibility that it will truly abandon Islam and take the path of apostasy, unless a person's heart and mind become so corrupt that there is no way left to reform them. But this ruling does not apply to those who adopt taqiyyah (outward concealment of faith) to save themselves from an intolerable punishment. God is Merciful and Generous; He has permitted Muslims that, when afflictions exceed their capacity to endure, they may adopt outward accommodation, provided their hearts remain steadfast in Islam and their inner faith is at peace. But God has granted no permission, in any circumstance, to adopt real disbelief and real apostasy, such that a person becomes a disbeliever; God forbid.

And this warning and admonition from God remains in its place until the Day of Resurrection. A Muslim has no excuse for abandoning his religion of faith out of distress from afflictions and hardships, and turning away from faith and Islam, and giving up the truth that he has tasted and known. Rather, it is the duty of a Muslim to strive as much as is possible, to persevere, to act with fortitude and steadfastness, until God's command comes. God does not leave such people, who believe in Him and then endure afflictions in His way, unrewarded; He grants them a good recompense for their sufferings, and this is one of two things that are certain: either His help arrives and the believer prevails, or he attains the exalted station of martyrdom.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 218:

Those people who are made to suffer for the sake of Allah hope for the special mercy of Allah, and the heart filled with faith never despairs.

﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the path of Allah – they are the ones who hope for the mercy of Allah, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ "Those who believed, and those who left their homes and strove in the way of Allah, are the rightful claimants to the mercy of Allah, and Allah is the One who forgives their slips and rewards them with His mercy."

When a believer hopes for the mercy of Allah, Allah never returns him empty-handed. The sincere believers among the Muhajirun and the Ansar, although they were few in number, had heard this promise of Allah with their own ears. They strove, and they bore patiently the hardships, and so Allah fulfilled His promise. Some were granted martyrdom, and some were granted the help of Allah. Both are good; both are the mercy of Allah. These people attained the ranks of Allah's forgiveness and Allah's mercy, because Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. This is the way of the believer.

Now the discourse turns to the prohibition of certain things. The rulings concerning wine and gambling are stated. These two are among those pleasures in which the Arabs were immersed up to their ears, because in that age they had no lofty goals with which to occupy themselves, so that their precious energies would have been spent in works of value.

This is the first part of the commentary. Translation follows.

The prohibition of wine and gambling had not yet been revealed at that time, but there is no verse in the Qur'an that proves their permissibility. However, Allah intended to lead the Muslims along a particular path, and His will was to bring them to it step by step, and to prepare this Ummah Himself under His own supervision for the role for which He had raised it up. This role was so great that intoxicants and gambling, which corrupt morals and waste time, could not coexist with it. Scattering one's life into pieces, bewildering one's understanding, and fragmenting one's struggle is not befitting of this role and this station. Its bearers cannot be like those whose only occupation is to chase after the pleasures of food, drink and flesh. Nor are they like those who have no ideology, and whose minds and consciousness are beset by a frightening void, and who wish to fill that void with the intoxication of wine and the distraction of gambling. Nor are they like psychological patients who flee from their own shadow and are compelled to seek refuge in wine and gambling. The bearers of jahiliyyah have always been afflicted with these corruptions. Even today they are afflicted with them, and in the future too this will remain the hallmark of jahiliyyah. Yet it is a fact that Islam, in accordance with its distinctive system of training, leads the human soul with great ease and trains it with great gradualness and progress.

This is the first link in the chain concerning the verse under discussion. This is the first step. It is not possible that any thing or any action is purely evil; it may be that evil contains some aspect of good, and it is also possible that good contains some aspect of evil. But the matter of what is permissible, lawful, unlawful, and of commanding and forbidding really depends on the predominance of good or the predominance of evil. Since the aspect of evil predominates in gambling and wine, these will become the cause for their prohibition, although the prohibition of these things is not explicitly stated here.

Here the Islamic system of training, the Qur'anic method of construction, and the divine style of teaching become clearly visible. This is an extremely wise method of training. In most of Islam's guidance, obligations and legislation, through examination and induction, it will be found that this very method has been adopted. Concerning the guidance on khamr and maysir, it seems necessary to point out here one principle of the Islamic system of training:

1. If a command or prohibition relates to a principle connected with Islam's beliefs and creeds, Islam immediately gives a definitive and unalterable decision.

2. If a command or prohibition relates to a matter that is practised as a habit or continues as a custom, Islam waits before taking a reformative step in that regard. It takes a step with gradualness, gentleness and ease, and before taking action it prepares such conditions in which the path for enforcing the law and the command becomes well paved.

For example, regarding the issue of tawhid and the issue of shirk, Islam made a decisive pronouncement at the first opportunity. It launched a decisive attack on shirkī beliefs, without any hesitation, without any reservation, without any compromise, without any bargaining, and without any policy of give-and-take. At the very first stage it struck such a blow that it tore apart the fabric of shirk. Because this issue was the foundational issue of the Islamic ideology of life, a matter of belief, faith could not be complete without it, and Islam could not remain standing in its place without its purification.

Wine and gambling were matters connected with custom. Bad habit is a disease that requires treatment. Therefore, for its cure, the Qur'an adopted the method of awakening religious consciousness against these things, and of establishing in the minds of Muslims the arguments by which these things could be declared unlawful. For instance, that the harms and evils in gambling and wine far outweigh the benefits they contain. This logical argument pointed to the fact that abstaining from these things is better and more appropriate. After this, the second step was taken through Surah al-Nisa: "O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying" (4:43). Now the five prayer times exist, and most of them are very close to one another. Between them there is not enough time for a person to drink wine, become intoxicated, and then recover. Thus the time available for it was effectively reduced. In this way the desire that arises in the self during the specific times of intoxication was broken. It is commonly known that addicts feel craving at the times when they usually indulge, and if that time is passed through with effort, the intensity of the craving subsides; and if this is done continually, it can be overcome. When these two stages were completed, the final and definitive command was revealed and wine and gambling were absolutely declared unlawful: "O you who believe, intoxicants, gambling, idols and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan; so avoid it, that you may be successful" (5:90).

The second example of this principle is slavery. Slavery was an essential part of the social and economic system of that time. It was an established international law of that era, and it was the custom of nations that prisoners of war would be enslaved and put to work. Before changing the outward form of these international social conditions, it is necessary to change the causes that gave rise to these conditions, and to alter the international relations from which the sources of slavery arise. Changes in international law and international customs require international treaties and agreements. As far as Islam is concerned, it did not issue any command for the establishment of slavery, nor was any verse of the Qur'an revealed stating that prisoners of war should be made slaves.

When the Islamic system of life began, a worldwide system of slavery was in force, and the matter was not only of slavery and prisoners of war, but slavery was also a part of international trade. Making prisoners of war slaves was a well-known international principle, and all parties participating in international and local wars acted upon it. Therefore it was necessary that Islam take concrete measures for the complete resolution of this global and social problem.

What Islam initially did was to abolish the oppression, violence and exploitation that were the hallmarks of slavery; it sought to end this very system of slavery. Islam did not take any extreme step to end slavery. Nor did it attempt, with a single jolt, to shatter the social order of that time in such a way that its consequences could not be controlled afterward or the leadership of that movement would become difficult. In short, alongside closing the springs of slavery, it increased the comforts of the lives of slaves. It guaranteed them a decent livelihood and permitted them to live honourable lives within broad limits.

Islam first closed all the sources of slavery except two. One is that a person becomes a prisoner of war and as a result becomes a slave. The other is that if a person's father is a slave, his son will also be a slave. This was so because in societies hostile to the Islamic system Muslim captives were enslaved, and this was the known practice of that time; and Islam was not at that time a dominant international power that could compel those hostile societies to renounce the system of slavery on which the social and economic order of the whole world rested. Had Islam unilaterally abolished the system of slavery, the result would have been that the application of Islamic law would have applied only to the captives in the hands of Muslims, while Muslim prisoners would have remained slaves according to the system of that time. Thus the enemies of Islam would have fought against Islam with great boldness, with the thought that if they were captured they would be released, while any Muslims who fell into their hands would become slaves. And before the economic system of the Islamic state had become stable, if the generation of slaves that actually existed at that time had been freed, those slaves would have had no source of income in the society of that time, no one to support them, and they would not have been regarded as members of any family, nor would they have had any kinship ties that could protect them from social and moral deviation. In such a condition, on the one hand, the economic circumstances of those people from whose slavery they were freed would have deteriorated, and on the other, these people themselves would have made the Islamic society, as a low and wretched class, corrupt and foul, while the Muslim masters' own circumstances were also not good and the Islamic society itself was entirely new. In short, this was the situation of that time, and in view of it, the Qur'an did only this: it did not place in the Islamic law any provision by which prisoners of war must necessarily be made slaves; rather, the Qur'an only issued this command: "So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, then secure bonds; and afterward either free them as a favour or ransom them until the war lays down its burdens" (47:4).

The Qur'an also did not say that prisoners of war should not be enslaved. Rather, it left this matter to the discretion of the Islamic state, so that it might adopt whatever position was appropriate according to the circumstances. Either there could be an exchange of prisoners on both sides, and those whom it was suitable to enslave could be enslaved. In that case the matter would be the same as the fighting power would deal with.

Similarly, with the closing of the other sources of slavery, the number of slaves gradually decreased, whereas at that time people had been enslaved through various means. The small number of slaves that remained was also being reduced by the Islamic system through various measures. For instance, when a slave entered the fold of Islam and then left the enemy camp and entered the Islamic camp, he was declared free. Furthermore, Islam gave every slave the right to contract with his master for his freedom, and he had full authority to enter into a written or oral agreement with his master regarding the payment of the compensation for that transaction. After this agreement, which was called mukatabah, the slave became free. He could conduct independent business; he might even remain in the employment of his own master; he was the owner of his own earnings; or he might work independently elsewhere and pay the fixed amount to his master.

Through mukatabah this slave became a regular member of that society. For such persons the Islamic system of zakat has fixed a share of one-seventh. Besides this, Muslims were also required to give financial assistance to such persons so that they could free their necks from the yoke of slavery. Furthermore, the Islamic system imposed expiations (kaffarat) on members of society in various matters, and one of the provisions of expiation is that a slave be freed; for example, in certain cases of accidental homicide, in the expiation for an oath, and in the expiation for zihar. The result of these measures was that, with the passage of time, the very existence of slavery came to an end, and this institution died a natural death. Had it been abolished all at once, great disorder would have arisen in the society of that time, and mischief and strife would have broken out in society.

The question is: why, after the age of the Prophet, did slavery increase in the Islamic society instead of ending? The answer is that the increase in slavery in later periods occurred solely because Muslims had deviated from the Islamic way of life; as Muslims moved further away from the Islamic system, the evils became greater. But the question is: was this the fault of the Muslims, or was there any fault in the Islamic system of life? After the age of the Prophet, if people deviated from the Islamic system of life, whether a little or a great deal, and did not properly implement the principles of the Islamic system of life, this does not mean that there is some defect in the Islamic system. Our view regarding Islamic history has been set out earlier. If, as a consequence of deviation from the Islamic system, some undesirable conditions arose at some period of Islamic history, these conditions cannot be imposed upon Islam. Such conditions would not be regarded as a link in Islamic history, because there has been no change in Islam. Nor have new principles been added to its principles. If a change has come, it is a change in people. People moved so far from Islam that they no longer had any connection with it, and their history ceased to be a part of Islamic history.

Now, if anyone wishes to establish the Islamic system afresh, he will by no means begin it from the point in Islamic history where Islamic history comes to an end; rather, the re-establishment of the Islamic way of life will now be carried out in the light of Islamic principles. In the light of purely Islamic principles!

This is an important truth, both from the standpoint of theory and outlook, and from the standpoint of the growth of the Islamic ideology and of the movement to establish the Islamic system. This point is being emphasized again here because a severe confusion has arisen in people's minds between the history of Islam and the Islamic way of life, whereas the Islamic way of life and the history of the Muslims are two different things.

For this reason, people fail to distinguish between the true Islamic movement and the true Islamic way of life. All the orientalists who have taken up the pen on Islamic history are caught in this delusion. Some people deliberately give Islamic history this colouring, and some are genuinely victims of misunderstanding.

Now, in the following verses, answers are given to some questions about the principles of Islamic life. These questions were asked by various people seeking to understand the matters.

Earlier they had also asked what they should spend. In response, the nature of spending and its recipients were explained. Here the question is the same, but the answer describes the quantity to be spent and its status. In Arabic, *al-'afw* (surplus, the excess beyond needs) means what is extra and in excess, that is, wealth beyond one's personal needs. Needs refers to requirements that are not luxury or ostentatious. Such surplus may be spent, and the order of recipients is the same as was stated before. The nearest have the greater right, and after them others follow in order of rank.

The command to spend is not fulfilled merely by paying zakat (obligatory almsgiving), because this verse has been neither abrogated (*mansukh*) nor restricted by zakat, as far as I understand. Paying zakat discharges one obligation, but its purpose is not that the giver is then free of all other social responsibilities. Even after zakat, the command to spend remains in force. Zakat is the right of the Muslims' public treasury (*bayt al-mal*), and it will be collected by the government that implements the Shari'ah of Allah. That government will spend it on its known and recognized purposes. Yet even after this, the responsibilities imposed by the Muslims and upon Muslim brothers toward one another remain in force. Moreover, zakat is prescribed at a fixed rate, and it is not possible that by paying zakat all surplus wealth would be removed from the hands of the wealthy. The verse under discussion, however, clearly indicates that *al-'afw* should be spent in full.

There is also a clear hadith on this matter. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, there is a right in wealth other than zakat."

This is a right which the wealthy person spends himself, seeking the pleasure of Allah, in suitable places. This is the highest and most complete form of spending. If he does not spend it himself, and the government that implements the Islamic system needs it, then the government has the authority to take this wealth from that wealthy person and spend it on those members of the Islamic community who deserve assistance. This prevents the wealthy person from using it for luxury, indulgence and pleasure, and also prevents him from hoarding it and thereby stopping its circulation, sitting upon it like a serpent. ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you the signs, so that you may reflect, concerning this world and the Hereafter.﴾

In this verse Allah says that He makes His commands clear so that you may reflect on both this world and the Hereafter. Reflecting only on the world does not allow human reason to make a correct analysis of the true nature of human existence, of human life, and of the real connection between human life and its duties.

Nor can a correct picture of the heart of Islam, its system of life, and its values be formed in that way. The world is only one part of life, and a very small and brief part. If a person bases his views and his system on this brief and superficial outlook, he will never reach a correct conception of life, nor adopt a correct way of conduct in life.

Furthermore, spending is connected both to this world and to the Hereafter. The decrease in wealth that results from spending brings, in this world, purity of heart and cleanliness of soul and vision. Then, the one who spends is reconciled with the society in which he lives, and relations among individuals become strong. However, not every member of society may be able to think of these things. Therefore, belief in the Hereafter, awareness of it, hope for its reward, and consideration of its ranks and values carry weight in everyone's mind, and through them the scale of spending is tipped in its favor. This brings contentment to the human self, and it attains peace and comfort. The scale comes into the hand of the human self, which remains balanced at all times, and worldly standards, which dazzle the eyes and have lost their values, cannot lighten its scale at any moment.

Social solidarity (social security) is the cornerstone of the Islamic society. It is the duty of the Islamic community to take care of its needy and weak, especially orphans who are minors and have been deprived of the shelter of their parents. Because they are weak, they deserve collective assistance and collective support. It is the duty of the Islamic society to raise them and to protect their wealth and their property.

Some guardians (*awliya'*) used to combine the food and drink of orphans with their own, and they had also combined the wealth of orphans with their own and invested it in trade. Sometimes this caused loss to the orphans. Then verses of the Holy Qur'an were revealed in which Muslims were severely warned against consuming the wealth of orphans. Upon this, some righteous people became so extremely cautious that they separated the food of orphans from their own. The situation then became that whoever had an orphan would prepare food for him from the orphan's wealth. If something remained, it would be kept aside and eaten at another time, or it would spoil and be thrown away. This was an excess of hardship which the nature of Islam did not accept.

Moreover, in some cases this was also harmful to the orphan. Therefore, these verses were revealed and Muslims were instructed to adopt the way of moderation and ease, in whatever way is in the interest of the orphan. In truth, the sincere goodwill toward them is better than isolating them. If living together and sharing food and drink is for the benefit of the orphan, then they should be kept together, because orphans, after all, are brothers of the guardians. All Muslims are brothers, and all of them are members of one great Islamic family. ﴿And Allah knows the one who causes corruption from the one who sets things right.﴾ Allah is aware of the condition of both the one who does good and the one who does evil. In the sight of Allah, judgments will not be made merely on outward appearance; intention and results will also be considered. Allah does not wish to put Muslims in difficulty, nor does He intend to impose any hardship on them in His commands and prohibitions, or to place them in trouble. ﴿Had Allah willed, He could have put you in difficulty.﴾ But this was not Allah's intention. He is Almighty and All-Wise. He does what He wills, but He is Wise. He desires nothing except ease, goodness and reform.

Thus the connection of all matters is established with the eternal God. All matters are tied to that fundamental axis around which the whole outlook on life revolves, around which the whole of life revolves. This is the state of a legal system that is based upon a worldview. The guarantee for implementing this law does not come from an external source separate from the human being, from outside the human self. Rather, from the depths of the human conscience arises the motive to act upon this law, and every person acts upon it of his own accord.

Lesson 15: A Survey

This lesson is, in effect, a code of family law. It systematises the structure of the family system. The family is the foundation of the organisation of the Islamic movement; it is the first brick. Islam has strengthened this foundation in every respect. It has given it immense attention, organised it in great detail, protected it in every way, and purified it of the anarchy of the age of ignorance (jahiliyyah). So much effort has been made in this regard that instructions are given in various surahs of the Holy Qur'an, and in them are provided all the foundations needed for the organisation and building of the first circle of the organisation of the Islamic movement.

The social system of Islam is a kind of family system. Its basis is the family, because it is the system prescribed by the Lord for mankind. In it, all the needs of human nature, all its characteristics, and all its fundamental matters have been fully taken into account.

The roots of the family system reach back to creation itself; its shoots sprout from the branch of human nature. The creation of human beings, and indeed of all animals, rests upon the family system. This is clearly apparent from the Qur'an:

﴿And of everything We have created pairs, that you may reflect.﴾

In another verse He says:

﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows, of themselves, and of what they do not know.﴾

Now mankind is examined from a further perspective, and reminded of the first human being through whom the settlement of human beings began. The first human population was a single pair. Then their offspring came into being, and from them humanity and the human population spread. 

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate, and dispersed from the two of them many men and women. And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you.﴾

Elsewhere: 

﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another.﴾

Then it is explained that there is a natural attraction between husband and wife. This is not so that men and women should be joined without any restriction, but so that from their affection and love there should arise the result that they lay the foundation of the family and that households are built:

﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.﴾

﴿They are clothing for you, and you are clothing for them.﴾

﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so approach your tilth however you wish, and send forth for yourselves, and fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾

﴿And Allah has made for you from your homes a place of rest.﴾

This is the nature which does its work. It is the family that answers the call of the profound purposes of nature in primal creation and then in the upbringing and formation of the human being. For this reason, in the Islamic system of life the family system is a natural and innate system, whose source has flowed from the beginning of human creation (from Adam and Eve). If one studies deeply, the beginning of the creation of all things in the universe also took place according to this system. Thus Islam has adopted the methodology of nature, just as the creation of the other things in this universe follows the pattern of the family system. Likewise, the family has been made the basis of the system, because man too, after all, is a part of this universe.

The family is, in truth, a natural nursery, where young children can be properly cared for and trained. Only in this nursery can they develop properly in spirit, intellect and body. Under the shelter of the family, a child develops love, compassion and a sense of reciprocal responsibility, and the colour that is imprinted upon him in this nursery remains throughout his life. The child opens his eyes to practical life in the light of the lesson he receives in the family nursery; in its light he interprets the realities of life, and in its light he acts in life.

Among all living creatures, the childhood of the offspring of Adam is the longest, longer than that of any other living thing. The reason is that the period of childhood of every living soul is in truth a time of preparation, training and education for the rest of its life. In it, the child is readied for the role he is to play in the rest of his life. Since the duties that man has to discharge in the world are great duties, and the role he has to play on earth is a great role, his childhood is also relatively lengthy, so that he may be prepared in the best manner for future responsibilities and be well trained. Therefore, compared with other animals, he is more in need of remaining with his parents. Hence a peaceful family environment and a stable family nursery are indispensable to the human system of life, closer to human nature, and more suitable for its formation, growth, and its role in life.

The experiments of the modern age have brought to certainty the fact that, in comparison with the family cradle, whatever arrangements people have made for the care of children have all proved deficient, and have not been able to serve as a substitute for the family. Indeed, none of these arrangements is free of elements harmful to the child's development, or in which his proper upbringing is possible. Especially the system of collective nurseries, which some artificial and oppressive systems of life of the modern age established for the sole reason that they could replace the firm, natural and righteous family system established by Allah. Merely because these people fell into enmity against religion, and by attacking religion blindly became opposed to everything in it, they forcibly abolished the family system and in its place set up nurseries for children. Although at times such nurseries were also established under governments, for example the savage wars which the Western countries, free of religious bounds, fought in the recent past are before everyone. In those wars the savages made no distinction between combatants and peaceful citizens, and as a result countless orphaned children were left without the shelter of a mother and father. The result was that some governments of Europe were compelled to establish collective nurseries for these children. Moreover, as a consequence of the jahili conception of life in the West, there came into being a deformed economic and social system in place of a suitable collective and economic system for the human being there, in which the mothers of newborn children were compelled to earn for themselves, and out of necessity collective nurseries for children came into existence. This was not a system but a curse. It deprived children of their mothers' tenderness and of their upbringing under the shelter of the family; infants were thrown into nurseries; the nursery system clashed with children's nature and their psychological make-up, so the result was that such children fell victim to mental confusions and were afflicted with countless psychological troubles.

It is astonishing that some of our contemporaries, despite these facts, insist that for a woman to take up employment is a sign of progress and freedom, and proof that society has been liberated from reactionary thinking. Behold! For these people, freedom and progress are the name of that curse by which the most precious treasure of humanity in this world, the psychological health of children and their moral development, has been ruined. Yet children are the capital of the future of humanity. The question is: what benefit does man gain by squandering this precious capital? Merely a trifling increase in the family's income, instead of its supporting its offspring. This situation arose because Western jahiliyyah and modern Eastern jahiliyyah and its corrupt social system refused to discourage the employment of the mother, for the sake of the support of the children. And the state of affairs became such that if a woman did not take up employment, no one would be ready to marry her. Yet whatever she earned by employment is nothing compared with the training and care of this great capital. Therefore children are the most precious and rare capital of humanity.

From the experiments of the nurseries, the first thing that has been proved is that in the first two years a child is, by nature and psychologically, in constant need of remaining in the lap of his parents. Especially in regard to the mother, his need is that the mother be exclusively devoted to his service, and that no other child share in this. After that, for a long period, he further needs that he have a mother and a father, and that he be associated with them. The first need cannot be met in a nursery, and the second cannot be attained except where the family system exists.

A child who is deprived of these two advantages will be deficient in vitality and psychologically. Such children inevitably fall victim to some psychological confusion.

If anyone suffers an accident and is deprived of one of these two provisions, this accident is destructive for that child. Yet we are astonished: where are we heading? Let us reflect upon that heedless and unaware jahiliyyah, whose endeavour is to make the nursery system universal and to subject as many children as possible to such destructive accidents, while certain spectators of jahiliyyah, who are deprived of the peace and security granted by Islam, think that this ruin, the ruin of little children, is progress and freedom, culture and civilisation.

These are the very reasons why the Islamic system of life has placed its social system upon the foundation of the "family". For Allah's pleasure was that Muslims should enter the sphere of peace and security, and live a life of safety and tranquillity under the shelter of Islam. That is why the Holy Qur'an has paid great attention to the stability of the family system, because in the social system of Islam the family was destined to be the basic unit. Accordingly, in various surahs of the Holy Qur'an, the various aspects of the family system have been organised for its stability, and basic material has been provided for it. Surah al-Baqarah is one of these surahs.

The verses revealed in this surah concerning the family system state the important matters of marriage (nikah), cohabitation (mu'ashrah), ila' (the oath of abstention from intercourse), divorce (talaq), maintenance (nafaqah), provision upon divorce (mut'ah), breastfeeding (rada'ah), and custody (hadanah). However, here these rulings are not presented as specific injunctions in the form in which readers of legal books usually find bare clauses and rulings in law books. Far from it! These rulings descend within an atmosphere in which the heart and mind of a person take them as a great principle: a great principle of the system of life that Allah has sent for human life, and a great principle of that conception of life from which the sprouts of the Islamic system of life emerge. And that this principle and this law are directly connected with Allah the Blessed and Exalted. This law is joined with His will, His wisdom, and His purpose, and this principle is an important part of the system of life which He has chosen for His servants. For this reason, Allah's pleasure and displeasure, reward and punishment, are bound up with it, and these rulings are connected with the Islamic conception of life. Whoever acts upon them will be called a Muslim; whoever does not act upon them will not be called a Muslim.

A person grasps at first sight the delicacy and importance of this matter. Likewise, it becomes clear to him that every part of this system, whether small or great, is of importance. Allah Himself is the overseer of this system, and His particular attention is directed to it. The smallest and greatest matter of this system is an end in itself, and has been placed by Allah for a great purpose. And that Allah Himself watches over the being of this person. Then the very Being of God Himself, in His own supervision, undertakes the building, upbringing and training of the movement; and the purpose of this building, growth and training is only that the Islamic movement be prepared for that great role which it is to play in this universe. Then a person perceives that neglecting any part of this system of life, weakening it, is an invitation to the wrath of Allah. Such individuals become deserving of severe wrath.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 2, verse 221 (part 2 of 3):

Then these rulings are explained in great detail: until one ruling is complete, all its implications and consequences are not set out, and the next ruling is not begun. After each ruling come concluding remarks, comments and results. Sometimes these follow-ups and admonitions come right in the midst of the rulings, the purpose being to show that the matter is of great importance. Especially those follow-ups whose connection is with the conscience, feeling and the taqwa (God-consciousness) of the heart, because this awakened taqwa, sense of obedience and vigilance of conscience cannot exist without which these rulings would be carried out through trickery and evasion.

The first ruling is that Muslims should not marry polytheist women, nor should they give their women in marriage to polytheists. The reasons given for this are: ﴿Those invite you to the Fire, while Allah invites to the Garden and forgiveness by His leave, and He makes clear His signs to mankind so that they may take heed.﴾

The second ruling concerns intercourse with women during menstruation. In the commentary on this, the act is elevated from merely a bodily pursuit of desire for a few moments of pleasure to the high station of lofty aims and a human duty. Indeed, it is explained that this is one of the important obligations within a person's private and personal duties, and that it is connected with the Creator's plan that His creation be purified through His worship and through fear of Him. ﴿So when they have purified themselves, go to them as Allah has commanded you. Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves. Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you wish, and send ahead for yourselves, and fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾

The third ruling concerns oaths. Since the rulings on ila' and divorce will be explained later, a general ruling about oaths is given here by way of introduction. The connection of swearing by Allah's name has also been established with firm belief in Allah and fear of Allah. In one place it is said: ﴿Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ and in another place: ﴿Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing.﴾

The fourth ruling is that of ila' (oath to abstain from wives), and at its end is this follow-up: ﴿If they return, then Allah is indeed All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. And if they resolve upon divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ "If they have returned, Allah is forgiving and merciful. And if they have resolved upon divorce, know that Allah hears and knows all."

The fifth ruling concerns the waiting period ('iddah) of a divorced woman, and several follow-ups are attached to this ruling as well. ﴿It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day.﴾ "It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs; they should not do so if they believe in Allah and the Last Day."

The sixth ruling concerns the number of divorces and the rules for taking back dowry and maintenance in the case of divorce. After these rulings, these follow-ups also appear. ﴿It is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame upon either of them for what she gives up to be released. These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ And: ﴿And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband. If the latter divorces her, there is no blame upon the two of them for returning to each other if they think they can keep within the limits of Allah. These are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear for a people who know.﴾

The seventh ruling is that if you divorce a woman, either you retain her in a proper manner or you release her in a proper, good manner. On this ruling, Allah's comment is: ﴿So either retain them in an acceptable manner or release them in an acceptable manner. And do not retain them to harm them, to transgress. Whoever does that has wronged himself. And do not take the signs of Allah in jest. And remember the favor of Allah upon you and what He has revealed to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He instructs you. And fear Allah and know that Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ "Either keep them in a good manner or release them in a good manner. Do not keep them merely to harm them and transgress, for whoever does so has indeed wronged himself. Do not make a mockery of Allah's signs. Remember Allah's blessing upon you and the Book and wisdom that He has sent down to you, by which He admonishes you. Fear Allah and know that Allah is aware of everything."

The second guidance is: ﴿This is admonished to whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day. That is more proper for you and purer. And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾ "This is advised to you, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day, that you refrain from such conduct. That is the more decent and purer course for you. Allah knows and you do not know."

The eighth ruling concerns breastfeeding and the wages for nursing, and after detailed rulings are explained, this advice follows: ﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ "Fear Allah and know that whatever you do is in Allah's sight."

The ninth ruling concerns the waiting period of a woman whose husband has died. The follow-up to it is a free permission: ﴿And when they have fulfilled their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in an acceptable manner. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ "When their term is complete, they have the right to decide for themselves in a reasonable manner, and there is no responsibility upon you for it. Allah is aware of all your deeds."

The tenth ruling concerns giving a woman in her waiting period an indirect proposal of marriage. On this, Allah's comment follows: ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them, but do not promise them secretly, except that you say a proper word. And do not determine upon the marriage contract until the decreed term has reached its end. And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ "Allah knows that the thought of them will come to your minds, but do not make secret pledges; if you have something to say, say it in a proper manner. Do not resolve upon the marriage contract until the waiting period is complete. Know well that Allah knows even the state of your hearts, so fear Him, and know that Allah is Forbearing and overlooks (minor matters)."

The eleventh ruling concerns a divorced woman with whom intercourse has not taken place, and for whom no dowry has been fixed, or whose dowry has been paid. Observe this intuitive comment upon it: ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to righteousness. And do not forget graciousness among yourselves. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ "And if you (men) act with gentleness, that is closer to taqwa. Do not forget generosity among yourselves. Allah sees your deeds."

The twelfth ruling concerns divorced women and the widow, that provision for maintenance be given for one year. At the end of this ruling comes the ruling: ﴿And for divorced women is a provision in an acceptable manner, a duty upon the righteous.﴾ "And divorced women have the right to be released with some fitting provision. This is a duty upon the God-fearing."

Now, after explaining all these rulings, a comprehensive comment is made upon all of them: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, that you may understand.﴾ "In this way Allah makes His rulings clear to you; it is hoped that you will act with understanding."

All these rulings are acts of worship. In marriage there is servitude to Allah. In intercourse and the propagation of offspring there is servitude to Allah. Divorce and separation too are servitude and bondage to Allah. The waiting period and the return from divorce during the waiting period are also servitude. Maintenance and the provisions for departure are also servitude to Allah. Keeping a woman in a proper manner and making her a wife is servitude.
