Otherwise, releasing her in a good manner forever is also servitude to Allah; paying ransom is also servitude; giving compensation is servitude; breastfeeding is servitude, and weaning is also the worship and obedience of Allah. In short, in every movement and every event that befalls him, if a Muslim's conduct accords with divine guidance, it is servitude. This is why, right in the midst of these rulings, the command to prayer suddenly comes too: that prayer is to be performed in fear and in safety. ﴿Guard strictly the prayers and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devotion.﴾ ﴿And if you fear, then on foot or riding; and when you are secure, remember Allah as He taught you what you did not know.﴾ "Maintain your prayers, especially the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devotion as obedient servants stand. If you are in danger, pray on foot or mounted, in whatever way is possible; and when you are secure, remember Allah in the manner He has taught you, which you did not know before."

Observe that this command about prayer occurs in the midst of the family rulings. The family rulings had not yet ended when mention of prayer came in between, so that the command to worship through prayer blends with the other acts of worship of life. This blending occurs because it accords exactly with the temperament of Islam, and according to the Islamic view of life, complete servitude and worship in every action is the fundamental purpose and goal of human existence. The style of this whole lesson points very subtly toward this: that all these things are acts of worship, just as in the matter of prayer obedience to the commands of Allah is worship, so too in these other family matters obedience to the commands of Allah is worship. Life is a unity, and all acts of worship are of one kind. The commands come from Allah, and all these commands are the system of life that Allah has prescribed.

In all these rulings, just as the atmosphere of Allah's worship and servitude, the hue of obedience and worship of Allah, and the tranquil shade of slavery to Allah are present, so too the realities of actual life's environment have not been ignored. Human natural constitution and its innate desires have not been disregarded, and the human needs of people on this earth have been well fulfilled.

The law that Islam makes is being made for a group of human beings; it is certainly not being made for angels, nor for some imaginary creature in the realm of soaring fancies. Therefore, when Islam, through general guidance and legislation or shari'ah rulings, tries to raise them to the atmosphere of Allah's servitude, this reality is clearly before it: that it is doing all this for a human being. That servitude is to be rendered by a human, and human beings have human emotions and inclinations. They have weakness and many kinds of frailties. They are subject to needs, they are influenced by their environment, they have feelings and they are conscious creatures. On one side they have spiritual illumination, while on the other side there are also human impurities, and the Islamic system of life is a system that takes account of all these matters, and despite them it sets a person on the path of pure servitude. It shows them a bright lamp, the bright lamp of guidance. But without any compulsion, without any artificial means, it bases its entire system of life on this: that this human being is, after all, a human being!

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 2, verse 221 (part 3 of 3):

That is why Islam has permitted "ila" (a vow of abstention from marital relations). That is, a man is permitted to swear that he will not have intercourse with his wife for a set period of time. However, the condition is that this oath shall not exceed four months. Then Islam makes provision for divorce, and enacts systematic legislation for it. It also binds its rulings and consequences to a regulated legal code. In such circumstances, divorce has been provided for by law, while on the other hand the policy adopted is to fully strengthen the foundations of the family system. Efforts have been made to further strengthen family ties, and the mutual bond of the family members has been elevated above mere social benefits, giving it the lofty concept of obedience to God and the worship of the Lord. This is the balance which truly makes the practical aspects of the Islamic way of life very lofty and a genuinely ideal system, one that, while being ideal, also remains within the bounds of human capacity and scope. And it appears that this is indeed the system made for ordinary human beings.

What is the system? It is nothing but the facilities of human nature. There are wise facilities for both men and women. If a family that has been formed, founded on the marriage of a man and a woman, does not succeed, and peace and tranquility cannot be established in this initial human cell, then Allah is the One who is All-Knowing and All-Aware; He knows about people what they themselves do not know. Therefore, the Divine Being did not wish to make the marital bond between man and woman inseparable, thereby turning the first human couple from a cradle of affection and love into a prison. Spouses may wish to see each other, yet separation is impossible; all doubts and suspicions in their hearts have taken the form of a flood, yet there is no way of escape. The relationship between husband and wife may be buried in the pitch-dark gloom of doubt, yet there is no way to emerge toward the light. Whereas Allah created the union of husband and wife and this small family so that it would be a abode of tranquility and an abode of security. If this purpose is not being fulfilled, and is not being fulfilled because of differences in the nature and temperaments of the two parties, then in such a case it is better that the spouses separate and this sick family be brought to an end, and they may then try again to reunite. But the decision of separation is also not made merely on the basis of trivial disagreements; rather, all means are employed to save this family. This is because, in the Islamic way of life, the family is the most sacred gathering within human society. Yet even in the case of separation, such rulings have been given that neither the husband is harmed, nor the wife, nor the child, nor the unborn child.

This is that divine way of life which Allah has ordained for humankind.

When a person reflects on the foundations of this system which Allah has prescribed for humankind, and then on the pure society that results from this system, in which peace and security prevail, and then studies in comparison the system of life that actually existed and was practiced in human life at that time, he sees that the difference between the two is that of earth and heaven. The Islamic society is an ideal society. And if the Islamic society is compared with the modern jahili societies of East and West today, this ideal society still appears at a lofty station, although the supporters of those modern jahili societies consider themselves a very advanced society. As a result of this comparative study, one clearly realizes that Islam has established a high standard of nobility, purity, peace and tranquility. How Allah made law to carry human beings to that lofty station. Especially, women have been given special concessions in this system. A great deal of dignity and nobility has been bestowed upon her. I am confident that any woman of upright nature who reflects on the special concessions which Allah has given to women in the Islamic system will involuntarily begin to love Allah with immense love, provided she reflects with steadfast thought.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 222:

This is another look at the relationship between husband and wife. It is a glance in passing. This natural relationship is raised a little towards Allah. The most intense physical and animal pleasure of the vital organs of the human body, that is, intercourse (mubashirat), is also given a lofty purpose, and a certain colour of sanctity comes into it as well.

In the relationship between husband and wife, intercourse is also a means and a vehicle; it is not an end in itself. It is the means to a profound secret of human life and a lofty purpose: the propagation of the species, the continuity of life, and this perspective ultimately leads us to Allah. Although intercourse during menstruation certainly causes harm to both man and woman, yet the mere animal pleasure is still present. Why then has it been prohibited? Because in that case the lofty purpose cannot be fulfilled. Also, there is this reason: during that time a sound nature (tab' salim) also recoils from intercourse. For just as Islamic law from outside forbids intercourse during this period, so too the sound human nature from within forbids it. This is because it is not a suitable season for sowing. In this season no crop can grow, nor can any plant be added to the field of life through such sowing. By contrast, in the days of purity, intercourse brings full pleasure, and those natural purposes for which this system has been established are also fulfilled.

That is why the answer to the question about the days of menstruation was given: ﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: It is a harm, so keep away from women during menstruation, and do not approach them until they are purified.﴾ "They ask what the rule is about menstruation?" It is a state of filth; so keep away from women during it and do not go near them until they have become pure.

But even after this, you are not completely free to do whatever you wish according to your desires. Even after the days of menstruation, you are bound by commands and prohibitions. Thus intercourse too is a religious duty of life, and in it too you are bound by the limits and restrictions revealed by Him. ﴿So when they have purified themselves, go to them as Allah has commanded you.﴾ That is, from the place which Allah has commanded, not from another place, because the purpose is not merely sexual gratification, but also to continue the chain of life on earth. Through intercourse one attains the wealth of offspring, whose coming Allah has decreed. Allah prescribes what is lawful and permissible and makes it obligatory. The Muslim seeks that lawful portion which his Lord has written for him; he does not devise his own plans. All the obligations that Allah prescribes for His servants are so that these servants may become pure and clean. Allah loves those who refrain from evil. If any mistake occurs from them, they should turn to Him, seek His forgiveness, and return to Him.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who turn back in repentance, and He loves those who purify themselves.﴾

This is one of the pleasant shades of the Qur'an, a shade in which one of the many colours of the relationship between husband and wife is given the form of an image. It is suited to the teachings of the Qur'an and fully in harmony with the life the Qur'an envisages.

﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you wish.﴾ (2:223)

Here, in this verse, attention is drawn to the nature of the relationship between husband and wife and to one particular aspect of it, namely what the purposes of this relationship are and what its true orientation should be. Not all of its aspects are mentioned here. In other places, according to the context of those places, other aspects have also been highlighted. For example, in one place it is said: ﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them.﴾ (2:187) In another place it is said: ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you, from your own kind, spouses, that you may find tranquillity in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾ (30:21)

Thus each of these expressions reveals some aspect of this profound and great relationship, each aspect being used where it is appropriate. Here, the context is one for which the expression "tilth" is more suitable, because here the atmosphere is one of freshness, creation and growth. Therefore this relationship is expressed through the word "tilth", and it is commanded that one may go to one's wives as one wishes, but only through the place of the womb, from where the process of production takes place. ﴿Go to your tilth as you wish.﴾

But at the same time, do not forget the real purpose of this union. Regard it as worship and as an expression of fear of Allah. If you observe the limits and bounds set by Allah even in this, it will be a provision for you for the Hereafter. And be certain that one day you will have to stand before Allah, and there you will receive the reward for all your deeds. ﴿But send ahead for your souls, and fear Allah, and know that you are going to meet Him.﴾ (2:223) And, O Prophet, give good news to those who accept your guidance.

The verse ends here, and the believers are given the good news that Allah has prepared a great good for them, and that this good includes the good they have sown in their own tilth, because whatever the believer does is good, and Allah gives reward for it. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers.﴾ (2:223)

From this it is apparent that Islam is a natural and simple system of life. It takes man as man. It recognises his inclinations and tendencies. It does not wage war against nature in the name of loftiness and purity. It does not declare as filth those human needs over which people have no control. Rather, it declares that these are essential duties and natural obligations for the growth, development and continuity of life. Islam's effort is that human humanity should remain intact, that it should be advanced within the bounds of that humanity, that it should be connected to Allah, that its physical inclinations should also be fulfilled, that a harmony should first be created between physical demands and human consciousness, and then that the colour of religious consciousness should dominate it. Thus, while fulfilling temporary physical demands, this pleasure is linked to lasting human obligations, and all this takes place within an atmosphere of religious feeling and religious consciousness. In short, in one moment, at one time and in one direction, religious consciousness and physical pleasure come together in this small being of man. He is the vicegerent of Allah on earth, and this is because Allah has placed in his being powers of many different kinds: religious consciousness and physical demands. This is the Islamic system, and this is the nature of man. Since Allah is both the Creator of nature and the Islamic system of life has come from Him, all natural demands have been fulfilled in this system. All other systems of life that are not from Allah are in conflict with nature, and in some this conflict is less, and in some it is very great. Therefore their end is destruction and ruin. In those systems there is misfortune for individuals and destruction for communities, because Allah knows and man does not know.

After the rulings on intercourse during the days of menstruation (hayd), the ruling on ila' is now explained. Ila' means that a husband swears that he will not have intercourse with his wife. Before the oath of ila' is explained, instructions are given concerning the nature of oaths in general. Thus, the oath is a preface to ila'.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 224:

وَلا تَجْعَلُوا اللَّهَ عُرْضَةً (And do not make Allah the target [of your oaths]...)

In the tafsir of this verse, Hazrat Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه) narrates that it means: do not use your oaths as a pretext to abstain from doing good deeds, rather fulfil the expiation for your oath and continue doing good. The same interpretation has been reported from Masruq, Sha'bi, Ibrahim Nakhai, Mujahid, Tawus, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ata', Ikrimah, Makhul, Zuhri, Hasan, Qatadah, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, Rabi' ibn Anas, Dahhak, Ata' Khurasani and al-Suddi. For details, see Ibn Kathir.

In support of this, Imam Muslim (رحمه الله) narrates from Abu Hurairah (رضي الله عنه) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath and then finds that the opposite is better, let him make expiation for his oath and do the thing that is good."

Similarly, Imam Bukhari has reported from Hazrat Abu Hurairah (رضي الله عنه) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, if any one of you keeps his oath concerning his family, he is more sinful in the sight of Allah than if he gives the expiation which Allah has made obligatory."

In the light of these hadiths, the meaning will be that making Allah's name the subject of an oath should not prevent you from acts of righteousness, piety and reconciliation between people. If you have sworn such an oath, break it, continue doing good deeds, and pay the expiation for breaking the oath, because acting upon righteousness, piety and good works is better than fulfilling one's oath.

An incident of this kind occurred to Hazrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه). His relative was named Mistah, and he used to help and support him. In the matter of the slander (ifk) against Hazrat Aisha (رضي الله عنها), this man unintentionally became a participant, and Hazrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) swore that he would not give him any assistance. Upon this, the following verse of Surah al-Nur was revealed: "And let not those of you who are endowed with grace and abundance swear against giving to the near of kin, the needy, and those who migrate in the way of Allah. Let them pardon and overlook. Do you not wish that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful." (24:22). Upon this, Hazrat Abu Bakr (رضي الله عنه) broke his oath and paid the expiation.

Allah is Ra'uf and Rahim (Most Kind and Most Merciful), so He has placed expiation (kaffarah) upon the oath that is made deliberately, in which the one swearing swears with intention, and his intention is that he will not commit the thing he has sworn about. But as for the oaths that people commonly take without intention and without purpose, no expiation has been imposed on them.

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned. And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ The oaths that you take without intention, meaning meaningless oaths, Allah does not seize you for; but for the oaths that you swear with a sincere heart, He will surely call you to account. Allah is very forgiving.

Abu Dawud related with his chain from Hadrat 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Laghw (vain) oath in an oath is that a man says in the house, 'No, by Allah,' or says, 'Yes, by Allah.'" Ibn Jarir transmitted this narration from 'Urwah through 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) as a statement of hers (mawquf), saying: the meaningless oaths for which Allah does not seize people are these: that someone says, "No, by Allah," or says, "Yes, by Allah."

In a mursal hadith from Hasan ibn Hasan, it is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by a group who were shooting arrows, and a Companion was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). One man from among them stood up and cried out, "By Allah, my arrow hit the target and your aim was not correct, by Allah!" The Companion who was going with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O Messenger of Allah, this man has broken his oath." Upon this the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "No. The oaths of those who compete in archery are laghw (vain); they are meaningless. There is neither expiation for them nor any punishment."

From Hadrat Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) it is related that he said: laghw oath is when a person swears in a state of anger. Also, it is narrated from him that the oath of laghw is that you declare unlawful the things that Allah has made lawful; in this there is no expiation upon you.

From Hadrat Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib it is related that he said: there was a dispute over inheritance between two Ansari brothers. One said to the other that he should give him his share. Upon this, the other swore that if you ever again demand your share from me, all my wealth is dedicated to the Ka'bah. Hadrat 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The Ka'bah is not in need; the Ka'bah does not require your wealth. Make expiation for your oath and speak with your brother. I heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that any oath you swear in disobedience to Allah is not an oath, nor is it a vow; and no oath to sever ties of kinship is binding, nor an oath concerning something you do not own.

From these narrations what becomes known is that if there is no intention of doing or abstaining from the thing sworn upon, then such an oath is meaningless and there is no expiation for it. That alone will be called an oath in which the one swearing firmly intends to do something or to refrain from some action upon which he swears. If such an oath is broken, expiation becomes obligatory. And if an oath is taken to refrain from a good deed, or to commit an evil deed or wrong act, then breaking such an oath is obligatory. As for the person who swears on a matter about which he is certain that he is lying, some scholars hold that there is no expiation for such an oath, and this sin cannot be atoned for by any expiation.

Imam Malik (rahimahullah) said in the Muwatta: The best thing I have heard on this matter is that laghw oath is when a person swears on a matter while knowing that he is lying, that he is sinful; by doing so he is pleasing someone, or wants to usurp someone's right. This is a grave sin, and it cannot be atoned for by expiation.

For the oath whose breaking contains good and benefit, at the end of its ruling it is said: ﴿And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ This points to the fact that He hears what you say, but He also knows well where the good lies, and therefore He gives this command.

And at the end of the laghw (vain) oath and the true oath, Allah says that He is "Ghafur Rahim" — Forgiving and Merciful — that He does not hold His servants accountable for every action. When something slips from their mouths by mistake, He does not hold them accountable for it. He forgives small mistakes, provided that the servant returns to Him. Through these two comments and conclusions, all these matters of oaths become connected to Allah, and the heart of a Muslim turns toward the Being of Allah in every word and every action.

Following the explanation of the general rule regarding oaths, the discussion now turns to the matter of ila', which is itself a kind of oath. A husband swears that he will not go to his wife, either permanently or for a limited period; in the technical terminology of the Shariah, such an oath is called ila' (a vow of abstention from marital relations). ﴿For those who swear off their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. Then if they return, indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. And if they resolve on divorce, indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ (226–227) Those who take an oath to abstain from their wives are given a period of four months. If they return, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. And if they have firmly resolved upon divorce, then know that Allah is All-Hearing and All-Knowing.

In the life of husband and wife there is a long companionship, in which various kinds of circumstances arise. Different psychological states affect the spouses, and they have countless causes. When these circumstances reach a point of intensity, the spouses sever even intimate relations. This temporary separation and cessation of relations is extremely difficult for the wife, as a result of which psychological and nervous effects are produced upon her being. As a woman, her self-respect is wounded. In short, all the bonds of marital relations come to an end, and all the ties of good companionship are broken; and if this condition should continue for an indefinite period, the whole family would be ruined.

Islam did not declare ila' unlawful from the very beginning. Therefore, it is possible that in certain circumstances it may serve as a beneficial remedy for a sharp-tempered wife, especially the remedy for a wife who is very proud of her femininity, who is afflicted with arrogance and pride, and who wishes to humiliate the man through her haughtiness or coquetry, or who thinks she can subdue the man however she likes. Moreover, at times this period provides an opportunity to relieve mental distress and fatigue, just as at times a person comes under a state of anger, after which the heart's resentment is released, and the cart of life starts off anew with great strength and joy.

However, Islam has not left the man completely free in this matter either. It is possible that at times he may go beyond limits, begin to commit oppression and cruelty against the woman, and reduce her to humiliation. Her condition would then be like something suspended in the air: she can neither live as a wife nor is she free to establish a home elsewhere.

Therefore, bearing in mind the various forms, the different kinds of circumstances, and the practical realities of life, Islam decided that the ultimate period for ila' and for the boycott of marital relations is four months. No husband is permitted to maintain the boycott beyond this. The period of four months has also been fixed by the Creator of nature, and in it the natural desires and endurance of the woman have also been taken into account, lest she turn towards some other unlawful means to fulfil her natural needs instead of her husband. It is related in the narrations that once Hadrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) went out secretly one night to learn the conditions of the people and to know their needs. From one house he heard a voice: a woman was singing this verse:

The night is long, and all its sides have grown dark!
I am awake. Why?
By Allah! By Allah, the Watcher who is observing!
Had it not been for Allah, the four corners of my bed would be shaking.

Hadrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) asked his daughter Hafsah (may Allah be pleased with her) how long a woman can remain without her husband. Hadrat Hafsah (may Allah be pleased with her) replied, "Six months or four months." Upon this, Hadrat Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "I will not keep any of my soldiers away for more than six months." Following this, he issued orders that soldiers should not be kept away from their homes for more than six months.

In any case, people differ in temperament in these matters. Yet four months is sufficient for a man to test his self and his emotions. During these four months either he returns, and a healthy conjugal life begins anew between husband and wife, and he embraces his wife and returns to his bed; or, even after four months, he finds himself unable to renew the relationship and the severance continues out of necessity. If the circumstances are of the second kind, then the Qur'an's command is that the marriage bond should be dissolved. The wife should be released by divorce. Or she herself should pronounce divorce, and if she does not, the judge should pronounce divorce on her behalf, so that both husband and wife are free to begin a new, healthy conjugal life with another partner. This is the dignified and pure path for the wife, and it is also the pleasant and joyful path for the man. This is what is appropriate. This is the path that is serious, the path that is just. It is the path upon which the course of life can continue; otherwise, in the case of strained relations, life, the life of both parties, becomes frozen. The matters of oath and ila' ultimately led to divorce. In this connection, the detailed rulings on divorce are given here, along with related matters such as the waiting period ('iddah), compensation (fidyah), maintenance (nafaqah), the provisions for departure, and other consequences. First, the matters of the waiting period and return (ruj'ah).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 2, verse 228:

Restrain yourselves; keep your emotions under control. Restrain yourselves until three menstrual periods have passed, or until three periods of purity from menstruation. I have reflected deeply on this expression and style of the Quran; it is a remarkable depiction of a subtle psychological state. The meaning and purpose is that they should refrain from remarrying until three menstrual periods have come or they have become pure from them. But beyond this rational and legal meaning, the Quran's manner of expression indicates something more. The style of expression, "restrain, pull the reins tight, keep control despite the urge to leap and bound," points to the psychological state found in such circumstances. In such situations, a divorced woman generally has an intense desire to begin a new life as soon as possible under a new husband. This state is natural. In such circumstances the woman is under intense nervous pressure. She wants to prove that she was not at fault in the previous marital experience, that there is no physical defect in her, and that she can at any time become attractive to another husband and begin a new marital life. Whereas this urge and feeling is not found in the man; therefore the right of divorce is in his hand, he has delivered the blow of divorce, and the woman has borne that blow. For this reason the woman is told to hold her self back a little, to keep the rein pulled tight for at least three months. Thus the Quran, through a single word and a single style of expression, reveals the atmosphere of the psychological state, and it gives instructions and codifies rules while keeping this psychological state in view.

They should restrain themselves for this period so that their wombs become free of traces of the former marriage, and then they can begin a new marital life afresh, if they wish. "لا يحل لهن أن يكتمن ما خلق الله في أرحامهن إن كن يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر" ["It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day."]

It is not lawful for them to conceal whether there is pregnancy or menstruation in their wombs. What is in the womb has been linked to Allah's act of creation, so that fear of Allah may arise in their hearts. By stirring in them a sense of honour regarding faith and certainty in Allah and the Last Day, it is said that if you are believers, you must never conceal anything. The Last Day is mentioned here because the Last Day is the Day of Recompense. Whatever is lost in this world while carrying out the commands of Allah is given to a believer there as a reward. Here, since a command is given to women that, despite their feelings having been wounded, they should restrain their selves, it is said that a reward is coming. But if they conceal and do not clearly declare what is in their wombs, there is also punishment for that. Nothing is hidden from Him; can anything be hidden from Allah? Therefore do not conceal. Do not let yourselves be influenced by anything, for any purpose, or overcome by any desire, and do not conceal the creation of Allah.

This is one aspect. The second aspect is that before the definitive separation, a period of interval is needed, a reasonable interval. In this interval both parties can thoroughly test their feelings after separation. It may be that a spark of love still remains in their hearts and then love flares up again. It may be that a tumult arises in the feelings of love and they come back together. It may be that their thinking has been buried under emotions, shortcomings, or pride, and in the interval they regain clear thought. When anger subsides, when fury passes, when the self becomes calm and the factors that caused the separation are overshadowed, some words of reason come to the fore and new paths of thought open up. The causes that had been regarded as great when the decision of separation was made appear insignificant in this interval, and in both parties the desire to begin life afresh arises. Or in this period, through some other good deed and wise measure, the course of affairs may change. Therefore it was very necessary that after one divorce, the woman wait for the three menstrual periods or their purity. Divorce is permitted in Islam, but it is also greatly disliked by Allah and His Messenger. It is an act of cutting, and it should be adopted only when no method of cure and no means of reconciliation can succeed. (The Quran mentions in detail elsewhere that before a divorce takes effect, there should be a serious effort for reconciliation and settlement. It is also guided that divorce should be given in a state where the woman has become pure from menstruation and the man has not yet had intercourse with her, so that the man has sufficient time for reflection, merely for the purpose of giving divorce or at the final shaping of the divorce. If she is in menstruation, the man will wait for purity before divorcing.)

As for the first divorce, it is a trial. Through this trial, husband and wife both learn what direction their feelings and perceptions take. If during the waiting period they perceive that they can begin life anew in companionship with each other, the way is open: "وبعولتهن أحق بردهن في ذلك إن أرادوا إصلاحا" ["And their husbands have more right to take them back in that period, if they desire reconciliation."] Their husbands are entitled to take them back into marriage during that waiting period, if they are inclined to set matters right.

"في ذلك" means: in that, that is, during the waiting and period of expectancy. Provided the intention is to take up marital relations afresh, and the aim is not merely to cause the woman distress, nor to return her, merely for revenge, to a life full of thorns, nor is the return merely out of pride, nor merely because, if he does not return, another husband will take her into marriage, which he regards as shameful. "ولهن مثل الذي عليهن بالمعروف" ["And they have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable."] That is, women in this state have rights just as they have obligations: they are bound to restrain themselves during the waiting period and not to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs. It is the husband's duty that if he takes her back, he does so with sincere intention, not to cause women hardship, nor to harm them. Moreover, during the waiting period they are entitled to maintenance and support, as will be explained shortly, because they are in that state by law. "وللرجال عليهن درجة" ["But men have a degree over them."] This degree means that men have the right, during the waiting period, if they wish, to take the divorced woman back into their marriage. Allah has given this right to the man because the right of divorce belongs to the man. Some people have taken from this phrase the meaning that men generally have superiority over women. These scholars do not mean by it that only the man has the right of return; rather they give the right of return to the woman as well, so that the woman too has the choice to come back and take the man into her marriage. But their argument is extremely weak, out of place, and inappropriate. This right is tied to the right of divorce and belongs to the man alone.

Now the final comment and conclusion: "والله عزيز حكيم" ["And Allah is Mighty, Wise."] That is, Allah possesses power and supreme authority; therefore He is entitled to enforce every kind of command. And further, He is Wise; His commands are also wise. The effect of this final comment is that you should not, influenced by various reasons and various circumstances, deviate from Allah's commands or cast them behind your backs.

Now the command that follows concerns the limitation of the number of divorces. That the divorced woman has the right to receive her full dower. It is forbidden for the man to take anything from her at the time of divorce. Yet there is one case in which the man has the right, if he wishes, to take something back. If the situation is that the woman has intense hatred for the man, and she is unable to live with him while observing the limits of Allah, fearing that she may fall into sin, that is the state of khul', in which the woman, in exchange for a ransom, wishes to purchase her freedom. In this case the man has the right to take something.

The divorces after which the spouses may begin married life again are two. If the husband goes beyond these two, then marital relations between them can be established only on the condition explained in the following verses, namely that she first marries another husband and is separated from him. Only then is it lawful for the former husband, who had used up the right of three divorces, to remarry her, provided that she herself agrees to a fresh marriage with him.

Regarding the reason for this restriction, some narrations state that in the early Islamic period too (as in the time of ignorance) the number of divorces was not limited, and a man also had the right to take his wife back (ruju') during each waiting period (iddah). Thus some people would divorce, then take their wives back, and this cycle would continue. In the Islamic period, a man from the Ansar had a falling-out with his wife. He said to her, "By Allah, I will neither keep you near me nor let you go from me." She asked, "How will that be?" He said, "I will divorce you, but when the waiting period is about to end, I will take you back." She was distressed and complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Then this revelation came from Allah: "Divorce is twice" (al-Talaq marratan).

In the wisdom of its legislation, Allah followed a wise policy in revealing the rules of the Islamic system: whenever a ruling was needed, it was revealed. In this way, the complete rulings were gradually revealed, and the principles of Islamic life were completed. What remained was the application of these principled rulings to particular and new circumstances, so that solutions to particulars could be found in the light of the principles.

As a result of this restriction, the number of divorces became limited. The previous situation, in which a husband would keep divorcing and make her a plaything, no longer remained. Now the procedure became that when a man divorces his wife once, he can take her back during the waiting period without any legal complication. And if the waiting period passes in this way, the woman will be separated, which in jurisprudence is called "ba'inah." Even now, after the waiting period has passed, he cannot take her back merely by ruju'; rather, he must bring her back into marriage through a new contract, with a new dower fixed, with her consent. Both options are lawful: that the husband takes back his wife within the waiting period through ruju', or after the waiting period has passed, renews the contract and returns her with a new dower.

After this, if the husband divorces her a second time, he will have the same right: ruju' within the waiting period and a new contract after it. But if he divorces her a third time, then she will be separated from him forever. In the technical terminology of jurisprudence, this is called the "great separation" (bayunat kubra). Upon the third divorce, the woman becomes "ba'in," that is, considered separated. Now this husband cannot exercise the right of ruju' during the waiting period, nor can he remarry her by a new contract. Unless her marriage to another man takes place and this second husband divorces her during his married life and does not take her back, or this second husband also uses the right of three divorces and she is separated forever, then it is lawful for the first husband to take her into his marriage again. But all of this must happen in its natural course.

The first divorce is a touchstone and a criterion, as we mentioned above. The second divorce is a renewed test and a final experiment. If after the second divorce the cart of life moves on, well and good; otherwise, the third divorce provides clear proof that the difference in temperaments and natures between the spouses is of a very fundamental kind and cannot be reformed.

Nevertheless, divorce is also a final remedy. If after efforts there remains no possibility of reconciliation between the parties, then it is better that a permanent separation takes place. If two divorces have occurred, then the wife must either be kept in a reasonable manner, beginning anew with gentleness and love, or else be released in a good manner, with grace, with kindness, with decency, that is, by giving a third divorce, after which the woman must take up a new path in life. This is realistic legislation, made with regard to the true and moral life of human beings, and it offers the best and practical solution to the complex problems of family life. In this legislation there is no severity that is not beneficial; it does not attempt to mold a person into a moral system that clashes with his nature, nor does this legislation insist on leaving a person and his powers unused, as if they would yield no benefit if left so.

During married life, the dower that the husband has given to the wife, or the various expenses he has incurred on her, it is not lawful for the husband, after the third divorce, to take back anything from her, unless... [the text continues here]

Just as we have stated above, a third divorce is evidence that there is a fundamental discord between the husband and wife, so deep that no path to reconciliation remains. In such a case, the appropriate course is that the husband and wife be separated forever, and each be set free to seek a new life companion and begin a family life afresh. And if the husband is pronouncing these divorces merely out of idle talk, hastiness, and arrogance and pride, even then the third divorce has been made to take effect. This is because, in such a delicate matter, there must be a limit even to idle talk. The permission for divorce has not been given so that it be turned into a joke. It has been prescribed so that it be used in those cases that are curable and beyond reform. Thus, a couple in whose hearts there is no respect for this sacred contract and no sanctity for it should also be separated. And the husband keeps using divorce again and again and takes no precaution in this matter.

Here a question may be raised: why is the peace and tranquility of an innocent woman destroyed as a result of the word "divorce" from an irresponsible husband? Why is her life being put at risk? The answer is that in human society, indeed, such events occur that require treatment, such disputes arise that require a decision, and legislation is necessary. If we do not apply this remedy which the Holy Qur'an has taught, and do not decide according to the law that Allah has given, then tell us, what should we do? Should we force this woman upon this man, saying: "She is your wife; whether you want it or not, she is your wife. Even if you divorce her a hundred times, we do not accept your divorce; your divorce is ineffective," although the man has no regard in his heart for his wife and no love whatsoever for her? In truth, what greater humiliation can there be for a woman than this? What greater degradation of the marital relationship could there be? In Islam, respect for women is essential. Islam regards the relationship between men and women as a sacred bond. It does not consider this bond merely a bond of pleasure, but grants it the status of a life duty and of worship and servitude to Allah.

As for the husband who turns divorce into a joke: if he has pronounced one divorce or a second divorce, and before taking back (raj'ah) the woman has become ba'in and separated, then his punishment is that if he wishes to remarry her, he must win her consent again. The marriage will take place and he must pay the mahr. And if he pronounces the third divorce, then his punishment is that the woman becomes completely unlawful (haram) for him, even if he later repents. He cannot marry her again until after she marries another husband and that marriage ends in divorce or failure. Moreover, he must pay her mahr and he will be deprived of recovering what he has given her. In every case, he must also pay maintenance (nafaqah) during the period of 'iddah. Most importantly, we must examine human psychology realistically and consider the practical aspects of human life. We should not dwell in an imaginary world, even if its practical existence is not on this earth, such that that ideal is not workable in the practical life of man.

Now, if after the third divorce this woman, as naturally happens, marries another husband, and this second husband also divorces her by chance, then this wife and her former husband may, if they wish, enter into a new marriage contract again, and there is no prohibition for them now. The only condition (not legal, but a moral and faith-based condition) is:

"In ana zanna an yuqeema hudooda Allah" — ﴿if they both think that they will be able to keep within the limits of Allah﴾. And the situation will not be as it was before. For in Islam, the marriage bond is not merely the name of following one's desires; it is not merely an agreement for satisfying the urge of lust. And in the Islamic society, the husband and wife have not been left free to simply indulge in unrestrained lust, to marry whenever they wish and separate from each other whenever they wish. They must observe the limits of Allah. The Islamic system of marriage is the binding together of human life, a frame for life. If life steps outside this frame, then that life is not desired by Allah; it is not pleasing to Him.

"Wa tilka hudoodu Allah yubayyinuha liqawmin ya'lamoon" — ﴿These are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear for a people who know﴾ (i.e., who know the consequences of transgressing His limits).

It is a great mercy of Allah upon His servants that He has explained His limits openly. No doubt and no complexity has been left in them. All of them have been made clear, but for those who know, who value them. Those who truly know these limits stop at these limits. If they cross these limits, ahead lies the condemnable jahili world, and blind ignorance.

Now instructions are being given to the men who exercise the right of divorce. It is said that you should treat divorced women with kindness, adopt a gracious attitude, and even in the bitter period immediately following divorce, maintain a behavior of kindness in accordance with what is known and customary.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 231 (part 1 of 2):

In every situation, whether family ties are being severed or being joined, Islam gives the guidance that goodness, kindness and conduct recognized as fair and commendable should prevail over the atmosphere. If ties are breaking, the intention should not be to cause the opposing party distress, nor should they be made to suffer as a matter of policy. In an atmosphere of separation and divorce, souls and temperaments pull away from one another. In such circumstances, this exalted standard of good treatment can be established only if its foundation rests upon a principle that is higher than the conditions of this worldly life. It is a principle that removes envy, hatred and rancour from hearts, widens the horizons of life, and expands life from the present and the visible to the unseen and to the other world. This foundation can be nothing other than faith in Allah. It can be the foundation of faith in the Hereafter. It can be the foundation that a person reflects upon the blessings of Allah, the greatest of which is the blessing of faith. Then he reflects upon the abundance of provision that He has given each person according to their measure. Then he reflects upon the health and vigour that He has given every person; and the level of a person's thinking can thereby be raised. Then the fear of Allah should be present in the heart, along with the hope that Allah can grant a better replacement for what has been lost: the marital life that has failed, and the losses and expenses that have been wasted. In short, this is the foundation which those verses present, the purpose of which is simply that, whether a relationship is breaking or being joined, in every case the conduct of sacrifice, goodness and kindness should be adopted.

In the age of jahiliyyah, whatever oppression against women was possible used to occur. In childhood she would suffer oppression; she would be buried alive, and if she escaped being buried alive, she would live a life of humiliation, hardship and severe disgrace. Then, when she entered married life, she was regarded merely as a possession, like the ordinary goods and property of a man. Even as property, she was of such a kind that in comparison a horse would be valued more highly.

Very often, if as a result of discord the husband divorced her, she would remain bound like a useless limb, and until the husband who had divorced her, out of mercy, gave her permission, she could not marry another husband, or her relatives, in their honour, would shut her in. And if the one who had divorced her wished to return in repentance, these people would prevent her from going back to him.

Generally, women were looked upon with contemptuous eyes. In society she was considered a lowly thing. In short, the status of women in Arab society was the same as the status of women in the other ignorant societies of that era.

It was in such circumstances that the Islamic system was revealed. Now, instead of the stormy and hot winds of the Arabian desert, the afflicted woman feels the pleasant breezes of a gentle wind, some examples of which can be seen in these verses. Now the view is given regarding women that man and woman have both been created from a single soul; the Creator of both is one. Marital relations were given the status of worship and kindness, not merely as a means of pleasure. They were given the status of a duty of life. This was given at a time and in circumstances when no women's association had made any demand, nor was the woman then aware of the importance of these rights. Nor had the male guardians of women then made any demand for women's rights, nor did any such demand even enter their minds. This was a general rain of Allah's mercy and grace, from which both men and women benefited at once, and which watered the whole of humanity and human life.

"And when you divorce women and they reach their term, then either retain them in a fair manner or release them in a fair manner. And do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress. And whoever does that has wronged himself." [Qur'an 2:231 translated as it appears in the passage: "And when you divorce women and they reach their term, then keep them in a good manner or release them in a good manner, and do not keep them to harm them so that you transgress."]

The meaning of "fa-balaghna ajalahunna" is that the period fixed in the previous verse comes to its end. When the 'iddah is about to finish, there are two options: either, with good conduct, take them back with the intention of reconciliation, that is, return to them from the divorce. This is the meaning of imsak bi-ma'ruf. If the intention of reconciliation is not desired, then do not take them back, and let the 'iddah complete, so that the woman's divorce becomes irrevocable (ba'in). This is the meaning of tasrih bi-ihsan: that is, without any kind of harassment, without demanding a ransom, and without any kind of ignorant restriction, such as that she shall not marry in such-and-such a place or within such-and-such bounds. "And do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress": do not keep them merely to cause them trouble.

As we have already quoted above, an Ansari's narration in which he told his wife that he would neither take her in marriage nor divorce her. This is retaining in a wrong way, retaining merely to cause harm. Islam does not permit such retention. The repeated emphasis in these verses on this matter is because this oppression was widespread in the Arab society of that time. Indeed, this oppression can become widespread in any society that Islam has not civilized and that faith has not elevated.

Here the Holy Qur'an stirs the understanding and consciousness of man, awakens the feelings of modesty and shame in man, and at the same time warns him of his evil end. All these means are being used for the sole purpose that the traces of jahiliyyah be erased from human life one by one, and that man be brought to that high station of nobility and honour to which the Islamic system of life wishes to lead him by the hand.

"And whoever does that has certainly wronged himself. And do not take the signs of Allah in jest, and remember the favour of Allah upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He admonishes you. And fear Allah and know that Allah is Knowing of all things." [Qur'an 2:231]

Whoever keeps a woman whose 'iddah is ending merely to annoy her or to harm her wrongs himself. After all, this helpless woman is also a daughter of Adam, and thus she is his sister; she is of his kind. If he oppresses her, he is in effect oppressing his own self. Then he also wrongs his own soul, because by committing disobedience he makes it deserving of punishment and turns it away from the path of obedience. This is the first sense that these verses bring.

The verses that Allah has stated concerning social life and divorce are clear, evident and perfectly straightforward. Their purpose is that the organization of collective life should rest upon truthfulness and seriousness. No one should make these verses a plaything; they should not be used to cause a woman mere distress or to harm her. These concessions were given by Allah so that social life might become a place of peace and tranquillity. Allah gave the husband the right to take back his wife so that the discord between husband and wife may end and marital life may begin anew between them; not so that a man may misuse this right to harm this woman or to subject her to violence. If anyone uses this right for that purpose, he is making a plaything of the signs of Allah and mocking them. This condition is very common in our present jahili society. People use jurisprudential concessions and jurisprudential issues as a cover, and through them they carry out deception, harm and mischief. Moreover, they make a very wrong use of the right of divorce and of return given to the man. Woe to those who make the signs of Allah a plaything and use them for their stratagems, and who feel no shame in all this.

Here Allah awakens in man the sense of modesty and the recognition of blessings. He is reminded to reflect upon the favours and bounties that Allah has bestowed upon him. He sent down to them His Book and gifted them from the treasures of wisdom and understanding. The reminder of Allah's blessing to the believers of that time was in fact intended to turn their attention to the great revolution that had taken place in their whole life through the Islamic movement. For those Muslims, the reminder of the favours of Allah carried a deep meaning. Perhaps people today cannot even properly imagine it.

The believers felt that the first of the favours of Allah upon them was that they were now a nation present on this earth. Let them consider what the Arabs and the A'rab were before Islam came. What was their reality? They had no noteworthy standing.

The world did not know them, nor did the world regard the Arabs as anything. They were scattered in pieces in the form of tribes. They had no weight and no value. They had no message that they could give to humanity, so that they would thereby be recognized. Rather, they had nothing that they themselves used and by which they could at least have been independent of other nations. In short, they were empty-handed; they had nothing at all. They had no material thing, no spiritual thing, neither manufactures nor ideas. They lived a life of poverty like the poor. A small number of them could be called prosperous, but even their prosperity was like the nomadic life of the Bedouin: for example, a Bedouin pitching his tent in a place where much game is found. That is to say, even this prosperity was very simple and primitive, which in today's world could not even be called prosperity.

In terms of intellect, soul and conscience they were completely empty-handed. Their beliefs were utterly baseless, absurd and very simple. The concept of life in their minds was entirely simple, primitive and tribal. The only occupation of their lives was limited to plunder and robbery. If there was anything beyond that, it was that the people were extremely vengeful by temperament. They were addicted to frivolity, wine and kebab, gambling and games of chance. In short, in every aspect of life these people were in a completely primitive state.

This was the abyss of degradation into which the Arabs had fallen, and this was Islam, which rescued them from it, and indeed re-created them. It gave them new life, brought them into being and bestowed upon them a great existence, one by which they were recognized by the whole of humanity. Islam gave them a message which they gave to the whole of humanity. Thus the Arabs too became renowned through this message.

Islam gave them a great outlook on life, a complete outlook on life. This outlook on life gave a heartfelt interpretation of this universe, such as no outlook on life before it had given. This outlook on life gave them a position of leadership, and they led all of humanity in human history, with a very exalted and lofty leadership. Among the community of nations they had no standing before; through this outlook on life and this message they attained a lofty station and an elevated rank among the nations of the world, and indeed their personality became a distinguished personality in world affairs. Then this outlook on life brought them forth in the form of such a great power that the whole world came to fear that power and began to give it highly valued importance, whereas before this they had been regarded as servants of the empires surrounding Arabia, or as a lowly people and Bedouin tribes to whom nobody at all paid attention. And then, most distinctively, in place of this poverty, Islam bestowed upon these people great wealth and affluence. The doors of wealth opened on every side, and the riches of the whole world gathered with them. And most importantly, Islam gave them peace and security: the peace of the self, the security of the home, and the tranquillity of society, in which they began to live a life of ease and comfort. Their hearts became content, their consciousness and conscience were gladdened, and they settled firmly upon the system of life that they had found. And He gave them that exaltation and that high station from which they look upon the misguided of all humanity, and see that these people have lost the way of life in the dense darkness of jahiliyyah and are groping blindly, and that this is the condition of the whole world. From that lofty station they realize that in truth it is they who are the superior ones, the exalted ones, and that Allah has given them a wealth of which the whole inhabited world is deprived.

These circumstances, when the Quran reminds the believing Arabs of His favours, do not require them to think long over a list of those favours or over this call to remembrance. Their whole life was itself a model of the bounties of God. They were the very people who for a long time had been crushed in the age of jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance), and they are the very people who are now enjoying the blessings of the Islamic system of life. With their own eyes they were witnessing that great revolution which man could not even have imagined, and which was a living miracle of Islam and the Quran. In the form of the Book of God and the wise philosophy of life explained in it, they had this supreme blessing; they were seeing it and were living examples of it. The Quran was addressing them directly, saying: وَمَا أَنْزَلَ عَلَيْكُمْ ("and what was revealed to you"), addressing them and saying "upon you," so that they might develop an awareness of the greatness of this favour, reach its depth, and see that this divine favour is for them, overshadows them, and clings to them. God is sending down these verses of wisdom upon those for whom they explain and complete the Islamic system of life, and the family code of the Muslims is also a part of this divine system.

Now look at the final sentiment. For the last time a pinch is given: be alert, think, know that God is 'Alim bi-dhat al-sudur (the All-Knowing of what is within the hearts). Know that He is the Knower; be wary: وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ اللَّهَ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ ("Fear Allah, and know that Allah has knowledge of everything"). After modesty and gratitude, here the feelings of fear and vigilance are being awakened. Thus, by surrounding the human self from every side, it is being compelled to adopt good conduct, a compassionate manner of behaviour, and an attitude of truthfulness.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 232:

Furthermore, if you have divorced a woman, a helpless one, and you no longer consider her fit for your companionship, then do not hold her in bondage. When she completes her waiting period (iddah), then set her completely free, free in every way and from every direction. If she wishes to remarry her former husband and both of them agree to it, then do not make it a matter of your honour and allow her to do so. ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands when they have agreed among themselves in a reasonable manner.﴾ ﴿And when you have divorced women and they have fulfilled their term, do not prevent them from marrying their (former) husbands, when they have agreed between themselves in a reasonable manner.﴾ (Urdu rendering: "And when you divorce women and they complete their waiting period, then do not obstruct them from marrying those husbands of theirs, when they are mutually agreed upon in a proper manner.")

In the Tirmidhi, it is narrated from Ma'qil ibn Yasar that he had given his sister in marriage to a Muslim man. She stayed with him for some time, then he divorced her with one divorce, but did not take her back, and her waiting period ended. After that, he began to desire her, and she began to desire him. Then he proposed to her again along with other suitors. Ma'qil said to him: "O you lowly son of a lowly one! I honoured you by giving you my sister in marriage, and I gave her to you in nikah, but you divorced her without right. By Allah, she will never return to you." And, Ma'qil says, Allah knew that the two of them loved each other, so these verses were revealed: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term...﴾ up to ﴿...and you do not know.﴾ When Ma'qil heard that these verses had been revealed, he said: "My Lord hears; I am obedient to His command." Then he called that man and said: "I give you my sister in marriage and I honour you."

Allah knew that the husband and wife both sincerely wished to begin married life and were inclined towards each other. Therefore Allah, with compassion and in a gracious manner, immediately accepted their wish. This shows how great Allah's kindness and mercy towards His servants is. This verse shows with what gentleness Allah desires to deal with His servants. See how much the Muslim community is being trained: under the shade of the Islamic system of life they are becoming refined human beings, and under the shade of the Islamic system the rain of divine favours is pouring upon them. At every turn of life, their best guidance is being provided.

After this prohibition and warning, the conscience and inner sense of the Muslims are now being awakened: ﴿This is an admonition for whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day. That is more virtuous for you and purer. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾ (Urdu rendering: "You are being admonished with this, whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day. That is more proper and purer for you. Allah knows and you do not know.")

Faith in Allah and His Messenger is the operative force by which this admonition reaches to the depths of hearts, and this happens when those hearts are attached to the wider world beyond this one, namely the Hereafter. When the likes and dislikes of hearts come under the pleasure of Allah, when there arises in hearts the awareness that the conduct which Allah directs is itself the highest, the most refined and the purest, then it becomes the duty of the believers to adopt it and to pursue purity and refinement, both for themselves and for their whole society. At the end, the impression is given that the One who selects a course of action for you is the One who knows everything; therefore it is your duty to respond to every word of His in a state of submission and contentment.

Thus Allah raises these small matters of family life to the level of worship. These matters become connected with the rope of Allah. They are cleansed of earthly impurities and cleared of the filth of life, and these matters are no longer mere worldly tug-of-war or mere family and social conflict, which generally create an atmosphere at the time of divorce, but rather, having been purified, they are linked with divine instruction.

The next command, concerning child-rearing and breastfeeding after divorce, is as follows. The reality is that often the mere completion of divorce does not end the mutual dealings of husband and wife. Often children remain, in whose upbringing both have had a share, and who themselves remain a means of mutual contact for both. If the parents cannot get along, what is the fault of the little ones? For them there should be a proper and detailed guarantee, so that they may be able to step into practical life, a guarantee which is beneficial for them in all circumstances:

Divorced mother: she is not relieved of responsibility toward her children, especially nursing infants. Obligations are imposed on her in this matter. These obligations come from Allah Most High. Allah has not left the woman entirely free, because in such circumstances, if the woman were left free to act according to her own nature, she could make a wrong decision due to strained relations, and as a result of that wrong decision the child could be lost or harmed. Therefore Allah prescribes a rule for the children here and imposes on the mother the obligation that, in such circumstances, she should not adopt any attitude that would harm the child. Allah is more loving to us than we are to ourselves. He is the Most Merciful, and indeed He is more compassionate and generous than parents are. The mother's duty is to nurse the child for two full years, because Allah Most High knows best that, according to the principles of health, two years of breastfeeding are necessary for the child. This is so both according to the principles of health and according to the principles of psychology: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing period﴾. The findings of modern principles of health and modern psychology show that, both in terms of health and psychology, the child needs to be in the lap of its mother so that it may develop properly in both respects. But the mercy of Allah and His blessing did not wait for the time when Muslims would on their own reach the secrets of the principles of nature and then act upon them, because Allah could not for centuries leave the precious generation of children to human ignorance. Allah is boundlessly merciful to His servants, and particularly to these small and helpless children He is very merciful, because they are more in need of His mercy and compassion.

Against the obligation imposed upon the mother, a right has also been given to her, and this right is the responsibility of the father: that he provide the mother with maintenance and clothing in a reasonable manner, and treat her with kindness, because both are partners in the matter of the children. Regarding this small child who is nursing, both are responsible: she will nurse and look after the child, and the father will provide maintenance and clothing for the mother. Both will discharge their duties within the limits of their own capacity: ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾.

It is also not appropriate that either parent use the child as a means of harm and revenge: ﴿Let no mother be harmed because of her child, nor a father because of his child﴾. Neither should the mother be put to hardship on account of the child being hers, nor should the father be troubled on account of the child being his.

A mother has very deep love for her child; she cannot live without the child. It is not appropriate for the father to take unfair advantage of the mother's love and force her into conditions that are not reasonable. Nor is it appropriate for the mother to take unfair advantage of the father's compulsion and his affection, and place upon him a burden beyond her endurance, or in stubbornness refuse altogether.

If the father dies, the same obligations fall upon his heirs that fall upon the child's father. ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾: the heir has the same duty toward the nursing mother as the father would have had, namely to provide her maintenance and clothing in a reasonable manner and with kind treatment. This is so that the collective responsibilities of society may be fulfilled. On one hand the inheritance of the deceased goes to the heirs, and on the other hand the obligations that were imposed on the deceased fall upon the heirs as well. Thus, if the child's father dies, the child is not lost. In this way, in the Islamic system, the rights of such a child and of its mother are preserved forever.

After all these precautionary measures, the Qur'an now turns to another situation of nursing: ﴿And if the two of them desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them﴾. If the father and mother, or the heirs and the mother, decide by mutual consultation to wean the child before the two-year period is completed, because in this there is benefit for the child, for example from the standpoint of the principles of health or for some other reason, then there is no harm in it, provided that this decision is made by the mutual consent and consultation of both parties, and there is a benefit for the child in it, the upbringing of which, through these two, is a duty imposed by Allah upon both of them.

The same ruling applies when the mother wishes to nurse another person's child for a fixed wage. This is permissible provided it is in the child's interest, provided the one who hires pays the agreed wage, and that kind treatment is also shown to her. ﴿And if you wish to seek a wet-nurse for your children, there is no blame upon you, provided you pay what you agreed upon in a reasonable manner﴾. This payment is a guarantee that the wet-nurse will treat the child well, will serve it, and will fulfil all its needs. Finally, the whole matter is linked again with Allah, linked with taqwa (God-consciousness), linked with this deep and subtle awareness, which can accomplish what other means cannot accomplish or cannot cause to be accomplished: ﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾. This is the final guarantee, a firm guarantee, and it is this final guarantee alone which is worthy of trust.

After explaining the rulings concerning divorced women and legislating regarding the matters arising from divorce, now the ruling concerning the woman whose husband has died is stated: the rule regarding her waiting period ('iddah), concerning offering her a second marriage proposal after the end of the 'iddah, and the rulings regarding expressing the desire to marry through allusions during the 'iddah:

In the Age of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah), when a woman's husband died, she would fall into severe hardship. Her own family, the family of the man, and the entire society would oppress her. The custom among the Arabs was that when her husband died, she would go and live in a dilapidated dwelling and wear the most worthless clothes. For one full year she could not apply perfume, nor could she do anything of adornment. After this, that age of ignorance would end with the performance of a few ignorant rituals, all of which were demeaning and degrading, just as the other rituals of ignorance used to be. For example, she would take camel dung and throw it away, and ride on some conveyance such as a donkey or a goat, and so on and so forth. But when Islam came, it freed this poor woman from all these hardships. It lifted all these burdens from her shoulders. After this, she would not be caught in two calamities at the same time: that her husband dies, and then her family treats her badly. They would close all the doors of dignified life upon her and not allow her to be free to live a settled married life. Islam prescribed her waiting period (iddah) as four months and ten days, provided she is not pregnant; otherwise her waiting period is until she gives birth. This waiting period is somewhat longer than the waiting period of a divorced woman. In it, on the one hand, her womb is cleared, so there remains no doubt that traces of the former husband are in it. And in the waiting of four months and ten days there is also this benefit: the feelings of the husband's family will not be hurt, because if the husband dies here and the woman goes out in search of another husband there, the husband's family will necessarily feel it. During this waiting period, it is permitted to wear good clothes, but she should not wear such clothes as would cause people to propose to her for remarriage. And when the waiting period ends, she is now completely free; no one has any authority over her, neither from her own family nor from her husband's family. She may freely adopt for herself, in accordance with the Qur'an and Sunnah, whatever dignified conduct she wishes to adopt in a recognised manner. Adornment is lawful for Muslim women; she may adopt it, she may seek proposals of marriage. She may marry whomever she wishes. Now no Jahili custom stands as an obstacle in her path, and no base arrogance or pride can restrain her. Now there is no guardian or watcher over her except Allah Ta'ala. ﴿وَاللَّهُ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرٌ﴾ "And Allah is Aware of what you do."

That was the woman's side. Now Allah gives instructions to the men as well, who wish to bring such a woman into marriage while she is observing her waiting period ('iddah). The instruction given to them takes into account personal courtesy, social courtesy, the feelings and inclinations of both parties, and the interests and requirements of such a stage, all together:

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you imply of your intention to propose to women or for what you conceal within yourselves.﴾ "During the 'iddah, whether you make your intention to become engaged to these widowed women known through allusion and hints, or whether you keep it hidden in your hearts, in both cases there is no harm."

During the 'iddah, the family of the deceased still holds certain memories tied to the woman, which remain alive. Moreover, there is still the possibility that signs of pregnancy may become apparent in her womb, or that a pregnancy is clear and the 'iddah extends until delivery. All these circumstances are such that no decent woman considers it appropriate to speak openly about a new marital life, because in such circumstances such talk is not fitting. In this way the woman's feelings are wounded, and the memories are still fresh.

Keeping these courtesies in view, speaking through hints and allusions has been permitted, but concluding any matter openly has been forbidden. A hint should be such that the woman understands from it that this man is interested in taking her as a life companion, but in allusions. Hadrat Ibn 'Abbas (raḍiyallāhu 'anhu) has been reported to have given this example of allusive speech: "I am in need of a life companion. I am interested in women. I wish that some righteous life companion may be found."

Similarly, the Qur'an has not prohibited inner desire and wish either, provided it is not expressed explicitly nor shown through allusion or hint, because a person cannot exercise control over the desire of the heart. How can one control the heart?

﴿Allah knows that you will certainly think of them.﴾

Allah has permitted this because it is a natural inclination. And marriage itself is permissible; there is no prohibition of any kind in it. Here, for certain external reasons, it is prohibited to convey an explicit marriage proposal during the 'iddah, and no practical step should be taken. Islam does not intend to uproot natural inclinations; rather, it brings them within the sphere of refinement and reforms them. It does not suppress the natural emotions of a human being but regulates them. In this matter it imposes only those restrictions that are contrary to the purity of consciousness and inconsistent with the cleanliness of conscience: ﴿But do not make promises with them in secret.﴾ "There is no blame upon you if you draw the woman's attention through hints and allusions toward a proposal, or if you harbour the desire for marriage within your hearts. What is forbidden is that you secretly make a binding agreement for marriage before the 'iddah is completed. This act is against the norms of sensibility and wounds the memories of the former husband. Allah has placed the period of 'iddah as a dividing boundary between two phases of married life; we should feel shame at doing such a thing, and should refrain from it until the 'iddah is over." ﴿Except that you say a fair word.﴾ "If you have something to say, say it in a proper manner."

That is, a manner in which there is nothing disapproved, nothing obscene, and nothing by which the limits of Allah that He has set in this matter are violated. ﴿And do not determine upon the tie of marriage until the prescribed term reaches its end.﴾ "Here the words of the Qur'an are worthy of reflection. It does not say: 'Do not marry,' or 'Do not contract the marriage tie,' but rather it says: 'Do not resolve to contract the marriage tie.' The meaning is: avoid strictly the contracting of the marriage tie during the 'iddah, to the extent that you should not even decide upon it, because the decision is what produces the contract, and Allah has prohibited that."

We have already explained above, in the verse ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them,﴾ this subtle style of expression of the Qur'an. That is, the Qur'an merely through the choice of a single word points toward a meaning that is extremely subtle and fine. ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him.﴾ Here the Qur'an, in perfect accordance with its method, connects legislation with the fear of Allah, showing that the One who is legislating knows the secrets of your hearts. The relationship between men and women is deeply tied to profound inclinations and hidden emotions. In this relationship, heart is connected to heart, and mutual love reaches the depths of the heart. Therefore, here the impression is given to them that Allah is aware of every secret of yours, knowing your inner hidden matters. Beware, and fear Him!
