In the matter of Allah's limits and Allah's law, your cunning or any matter kept secret and hidden will not remain hidden before Him. Beware!

Until now, the human conscience has been awakened, alerted and shaken by fear, and within it caution and the fear of Allah have been produced. Then the Merciful, Kind and Generous God, without delay, Himself gives it consolation and provides the means of tranquility of the heart. It is assured that He is the Forgiving and Merciful. He is most forbearing and does not hasten to punish: ﴿And know that Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing.﴾ He forgives the lapse of a heart in which there is consciousness of Allah, which is cautious about its hidden and concealed secrets. He is Forbearing and Patient; He does not hasten to punish, awaiting that the poor, helpless servant may perhaps refrain and repent.

The discussion of family laws continues. Now come the rulings concerning the woman who is divorced before consummation. This case differs from those in which the divorced women have already been cohabited with, about which the explanation has been fully given. This is a case that frequently arises, and in this situation the rights of the spouses are as follows:

This passage has two situations. The first is that the divorced woman is given some provision according to the means of the husband. Through this, first, the woman's heart is consoled, and psychologically a pleasantness is created between the two families; and second, she gains some financial benefit. In such a separation, a woman feels anguish and pain; it becomes for her a lifelong taunt and enmity. In such circumstances, if he gives her something as a gift, then psychologically the bad feelings in that woman may diminish, and the conflict and strained relations between the two families may be dispelled like clouds, and this gift can be an expression of love of this kind, and at the same time an acknowledgment of fault and an apology. Through this, the man himself also shows that he too regrets this divorce and separation and is apologetic. That this was an unsuccessful attempt at the relationship, but this is not something by which the door of good conduct between them should be closed forever. Therefore, here it is enjoined that in this case the woman should definitely be given something, according to what is customary (ma'ruf), so that love and affection may remain on human grounds between the two parties, and the good memories of the broken relationship may remain. But the Holy Qur'an, along with this, also gives the guidance that a burden beyond the husband's capacity should not be placed upon him. The wealthy should give according to his means, and the poor man according to his capacity: ﴿عَلَى الْمُوسِعِ قَدَرُهُ وَعَلَى الْمُقْتِرِ قَدَرُهُ﴾ "The affluent according to his means, and the straitened according to his means."

It is indicated that this gift, given according to what is customary, comes with kindness, so that dry hearts may be refreshed and the deep clouds that hang over the atmosphere of mutual relations may disperse. ﴿مَتَاعًا بِالْمَعْرُوفِ حَقًّا عَلَى الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾ "A provision according to what is customary, a duty upon the good-doers."

The second case is that divorce is pronounced before consummation, but a dower (mahr) has been fixed along with the marriage. In this case, half of the dower becomes obligatory. This is the law; but the Qur'an, rather than leaving the matter to law, leaves it to kindness, good conduct and facilitation. It is more appropriate for the woman, or, if she is an adult, for her guardian (wali) at the time of the marriage, that she pardon and waive her legal right. In such strained circumstances, the party who waives its right is in truth a person of great nobility of character, good manners, forbearance and forgiveness. He allows the property of a person with whom he no longer has any other relationship to remain with that person. Yet the Qur'an, until the very end, is intent that the bitterness between them be cleared, that no rancour remain between them, and that hearts be lightened: ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to righteousness. And do not forget graciousness between yourselves. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

At the very end, the sense of taqwa (God-consciousness) is sharpened. Mutual good conduct and the attitude of benevolence are encouraged, and it is said: create in your hearts the awareness that Allah is Seeing and Watchful, so that in your mutual relations kindness, gentleness and benevolence remain dominant, whether family relations succeed or have already failed. Hearts should be kept clean and free, and in every state the connection with Allah should remain established and firm.

In all the above rulings, an effort has been made to strengthen the hearts' connection and bond with Allah, and an endeavour has been made that goodness and benevolence in social life be regarded as worship. In the midst of such an atmosphere, mention is made of prayer (salah), which is the greatest and most important worship in Islam. Although the discussion of family rulings was still continuing and had not concluded, one ruling remained: that for a woman whose husband has died, a bequest be made in her favour that she not be turned out of the house for one year and that she be provided maintenance. Second, that divorced women be generally given something by way of a gift. The purpose of this is to show that just as prayer is an act of worship, so too acting upon these rulings is worship. Both these matters fall within servitude to Allah. This is a very subtle allusion, and this allusion concerns the creation of man, and is in exact accordance with the Islamic outlook. Allah says: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they may worship Me.﴾ (Worship and servitude are not confined only to those things which are the symbols of worship, but every act in which a person turns towards Allah, and whose purpose in that act is solely that Allah be obeyed, is worship.)

Here the command is given: guard the prayer (ḥifẓ al-ṣalāh). That is, perform it at its appointed time, performing all its pillars correctly and fulfilling all its conditions.

The preferred view is that the "middle prayer" (ṣalāt al-wusṭā) refers to the ʿAṣr prayer. On the occasion of the Battle of the Confederates (Yawm al-Aḥzāb), the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They distracted us from the middle prayer, the ʿAṣr prayer; may Allah fill their houses and their hearts with fire." The ʿAṣr prayer is mentioned specifically because the prayer often comes after the midday rest (qaylūlah), and there is a risk that it will be missed or delayed.

The preferred view is that qunūt means humility and submissiveness (khushūʿ). Within prayer it also includes being wholly focused on the remembrance of Allah. For a time, when there was great need, Muslims would converse with one another during prayer. After the revelation of this verse, Muslims understood that during prayer no occupation is permitted other than the remembrance of Allah, humility and focus.

If a person is in a state of fear and danger, and it is not possible to pray facing the qiblah, the prayer is still valid and is not to be suspended. If someone is riding on a mount, or is in a dangerous situation and engaged in defence, he should pray in whatever manner is possible, facing in that direction as best he can. He should pray by gesture, making a slight gesture for bowing and prostration. This prayer differs from what is called ṣalāt al-khawf (the prayer of fear), whose details are described in Surat al-Nisāʾ. That prayer is performed in circumstances where the Muslims can stand in rows: the imam stands, one row comes and prays one rak‘ah with him, then the second row comes and prays one rak‘ah with him, while the other row remains standing in protection of them. The prayer mentioned here refers to the prayer performed in circumstances where fighting is actually underway, swords are clashing, gunfire is taking place, and it is not possible to form rows.

This is a remarkable matter. It shows how great the importance of prayer is in the sight of Allah. The Muslims are indirectly told that prayer must be performed even in the most extreme conditions of fear and the severity of war. For this reason, even in such fear, at the very moment of battle, with the sword in hand, or rather with the enemy's sword over one's head, the prayer is still performed. The truth is that prayer is the weapon of the believing man, his equipment for war. It is a defensive measure for the believer. In such circumstances, when the believer stands in prayer, he reaches Allah, and this is precisely the time when the need to reach Allah is most acute. In an environment in which a person is surrounded by dangers from every side, he draws very close to Allah.

How excellent is our religion! It is a system of worship, consisting of various forms and under various headings, in which prayer is a prominent title. Through this worship, this religion raises a person to a lofty station. Through this worship, Allah makes the believer steadfast at times of severe trial. Through this worship, Allah refines the believer in times of peace and security. Through this very worship, a believer enters entirely into a world of peace and tranquillity, where tranquillity and safety rain down upon him. For this reason, this worship is emphasized most strongly precisely in circumstances in which swords are cutting down heads and severing necks.

And if there is complete security and peace, then prayer is as it has been taught, and in addition they should remember Allah at all times. This is because Allah taught them things they did not know: ﴿So when you are secure, remember Allah as He has taught you what you did not know﴾ — "And when security is attained, remember Allah in the manner that He has taught you, which you did not know before." What would people have known had Allah not taught them, had Allah not guided them moment by moment at every turn of life?

Amid the rules of married life and the rules of divorce, this brief discussion of prayer is of great importance. Its purpose is to establish in the hearts of Muslims that comprehensive concept of worship and servitude which is the fundamental principle of the Islamic system of life, namely that compliance with the command is itself worship. Thus the original subject, the family laws, is now completed here:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 240:

The first verse commands that a woman whose husband dies must, before his death, certainly leave a bequest that she not be expelled from the house for at least one year, and that she be permitted for one year to spend from his wealth. She should not leave the house. And if she deems that her circumstances are not yet suitable for a second marriage, or that her feelings are still wounded, she may remain in the house for one year. However, this is the woman's right, and after completing the waiting period of four months and ten days she is in any case free. If she wishes to leave the house, she may leave, because the 'iddah (waiting period) is an obligation upon her, while remaining in the house is not an obligation upon her; rather it is her right, the use of which is not compulsory for her. Some exegetes have said that this verse has been abrogated (naskh) by the verse of 'iddah. But my view is that there is no need for abrogation, because the two verses differ in their subject-matter (mahall). As we have said, the 'iddah is a duty upon her that she must fulfil, and the one-year period is her right, the use of which is not binding upon her.

Fa-in kharajna fa-la junaha 'alaykum fi ma fa'alna fi anfusihinna min ma'ruf (﴿But if they leave [of their own accord], there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves, in an acceptable manner﴾). The words 'alaykum (upon you) refer to the collective system of the Muslims, which is responsible for every act that occurs within the Islamic society. In the Islamic system of life, the matter of every idea, the matter of every individual, and the responsibility for every event rest upon the society. If good or evil occurs in an Islamic society, its reward and accountability will also fall upon the Islamic society. The reality of the Islamic community and the nature of its obligations are also well understood from this indication. It shows that the establishment of an Islamic movement is necessary so that the Islamic system of life can be established in practice; and after its establishment, that this system may be preserved, and that oversight may continue, so that no member of the Islamic society commits a violation of or rebellion against this system. This is because the ultimate responsibility for every small and great act of the members of the community has been placed upon the Islamic community itself. By using the word "upon you," an effort has been made to impress this reality upon the Islamic community, so that this truth takes firm root in the perception and consciousness of the Islamic community and of each of its members.

The final comment: Wallahu 'Azizun Hakim (﴿And Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾). He is the supreme authority, and so He has the right to make law; but whoever makes law will do so wisely. He is Mighty, possessing power, and He can punish you for disobedience.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 241:

In the second verse, while calling people to Allah's fear (taqwa), a command is given that every divorced woman must be provided with some provision at the time of her release: "And for divorced women is a provision according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the Muttaqun (the God-conscious)." That is, those women who have been divorced should also be sent off with something suitable, some provision. This is a right upon the God-conscious.

Some scholars are of the view that since detailed rulings regarding divorced women have already come in the preceding verses, this verse is to be considered abrogated (mansukh) by those verses. However, there is no need to consider it abrogated here, because mata' (giving something as provision) is a thing separate from the obligatory maintenance (nafaqat wajibah). If we reflect on the reality of the rulings the Qur'an has given so far, then keeping room for giving every divorced woman something by way of a gift is in complete accordance with Islamic teachings, whether or not intimacy took place with her, and whether or not her mahr was fixed or could not be fixed. Because divorce creates dryness in the relations of both parties, and a feeling of estrangement and hatred against one another arises in their hearts; at such a moment, this kind of good treatment can bring freshness into relations and remove the mutual estrangement of hearts. This is the sole guarantee, which has been strongly emphasized, and through which the relations of the Muslim community can be set right.

Now the third verse. Here there is a comment on all the family laws that have been stated throughout this section. "Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses, so that you may understand." ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses, that you may use your reason.﴾

In the same way as this explanation that has passed before your eyes in the course of this section regarding the rulings, which is a firm, precise, divinely inspired and impactful exposition, Allah clarifies His commands, in the hope that you will act with understanding, that you will come to your senses, and that you will reflect on these rulings, think deeply, and strive to grasp the wisdom that lies beneath them. Within them you will be able to see the glimpse of Allah's mercy, and you will come to know the blessings hidden in them for you: the blessing of ease and facilitation, the blessing of simplicity and clarity, the blessing of firmness and definitiveness, and then, through them, the blessing of a torrential downpour of peace and security over the whole of life.

Alas! If only people understood the Islamic system. If only they reflected upon it. Had they understood it properly, their relationship with the Islamic system would not be what it is today; rather, they would submit to the Islamic system, bow before each of its commands, their hearts would always be ready to accept it, their hearts would be content with each of its guidance, and their hearts and souls would be filled with peace, security and certain tranquility. If only they would reflect; if only they would understand.

Lesson 16 at a Glance

The importance of this lesson, and the true value of the accounts of earlier nations it contains, can only be fully grasped once we first understand clearly that the Qur'an is a living book for the Muslim ummah. It is a guiding and sincere mentor for it, its murshid, its school where it learns the lesson of life in peace. Allah made this Book the constitution (dastur tarteeb) for the first Islamic community, which in its own time established the Islamic system in the light of this Book and presented it to the world. That community was appointed to this station only when it had been properly prepared according to this Book. Allah has also determined for this Book the status of a living leader of the Islamic movement, and after the Messenger ﷺ, this Book will serve as a living leader for the coming generations of this movement. It will train those generations and prepare them for the leadership role for which this Book has made a firm promise to every generation of this movement: whenever the Islamic movement accepts this Book as its guide and guardian, adopts its guidance, fulfils its pledge to be obedient to its command, takes its way of life from it, regards this Book with honour, and makes it dominant over all systems, then the Islamic movement will attain a high station in the world and will be supreme. This is Allah's promise, and it is this Book's promise.

Remember! The Qur'an is not merely a book to be recited; it is a complete constitution of life. It is a constitution of order, a constitution of action, and a path of action for the whole of life. This is why the Book also relates the experiences and events of earlier nations, so that the Muslim community may take a lesson from them. For this reason the Book was revealed, so that through it this community may be formed. In this Book, from Adam (peace be upon him) down to the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the experiences of all the faith-based calls upon the entire earth have been related. All these experiences of calling to faith are provisions for the journey of the Muslim ummah until the Day of Resurrection. The experiences of the human soul and the various historical experiences of human life are preserved in this Book, so that the Muslim ummah may be informed of its path and manner, prepare the equipment of provisions for itself, and so that the store of these varied experiences on that path may be a torch for it.

These are the very purposes for which many narratives are mentioned in the Qur'an. These stories are of different kinds, and in every story there are clear indications for the ummah. The Qur'an has related, in greater number than those of other nations, the stories of the Children of Israel, for which there are several reasons. Some of these reasons we have explained in our commentary of Fi Zilal al-Qur'an, Part One, at the beginning of the mention of the Children of Israel. Some reasons we have stated at various other places. Some reasons are presented here as appropriate to the context. It was within Allah's knowledge that some coming generations of the Muslim ummah would pass through the same circumstances through which the Children of Israel passed. Muslims would adopt, in matters of their religion and their ideology of life, the same stance that the Children of Israel adopted. Therefore the Qur'an, in reality, has presented in the form of the stories of the Children of Israel a mirror, so that the coming generations of Muslims may take advice and take warning from them. It is as if Allah has placed in the hands of the coming generations a clear mirror, so that they may always see their own form in it, and so that they may have advance guidance regarding the ups and downs that keep coming along the roads of life.

It is the duty of all generations of the Muslim ummah to read this Book of Allah with deep understanding and reflection, considering its guidance as though it were being revealed by Allah today, so that today's problems may be solved in its light, and that it may illuminate the darkness of humanity's future in today's journey. Do not sit back having merely read this Book as beautiful speech and recited it with excellent recitation, nor read it with the thought that it is merely an account of a past and bygone reality, which is never repeated on this earth again.

We cannot benefit from this Qur'an unless we seek in it guidance concerning the realities of our daily, lived life: the solution to today's problems and the planning for tomorrow's problems, exactly in the way the first Islamic community took it. That community sought the solution to all its present problems in this Book. Whenever we read the Qur'an with this understanding and reflection, we will find in it what we seek. Indeed, we will find in it wondrous guidance to which the mind of a person who reads this Book heedlessly cannot reach. Every word of it, every term, every expression and every guidance will appear to us as living and everlasting. It will appear moving, living and dynamic, and it will clearly point out: this is your path! This is the signpost! This Book will say: do this and avoid that. It will say: this is your friend and this is your enemy. It will say: take precaution and make preparation. In short, this Book will converse with us at length and in detail about every condition of our lives. If we study the Qur'an in this manner, we will surely find in it life, and we will find the provisions for life. Then we will be able to understand correctly the command of Allah:

﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when He calls you to that which gives you life.﴾ The Qur'an is in truth an invitation to life: an invitation to eternal life and to fresh, renewed life. It does not invite you to a life that has passed and has become a page of the pages of history.

Now, in the light of this preface, let us cast a glance over this entire lesson. In this lesson, two experiences from the earlier nations are presented. The practical experiences through which the Muslim ummah passed: these two experiences are also being included in this store. By placing these experiences before the ummah, it is being prepared for the circumstances that are to come in its life, because it is the inheritor of the ideology of faith, and this green field of the experiences of earlier nations has now come into the hands of this ummah, and it has an important role to play on the field.

The first experience is of people whose name the Qur'an has not mentioned. This event the Qur'an has related with complete brevity, yet the purpose for which it has been brought is fully achieved. It is the experience of those who, ﴿Have you not seen those who went out from their homes, being thousands, fearing death?﴾ They went out from their homes in fear of death and were in the thousands. But that departure, flight and that fear and panic gave them no benefit, and the end they were fleeing from, which Allah had decreed for them, overtook them. Allah said to them: "Die!" Then ﴿He gave them life﴾. Neither their striving could save them from death, nor did they have to strive to obtain life again. In both conditions it was the will of Allah that decided.

In the light of this experience, Allah addresses the Muslims and urges them to fight in the way of Allah and to spend in the way of Allah, because the giver of life is He, and the giver of wealth is also He. He is capable of taking life and of taking back wealth.

The second experience is taken from the history of the Children of Israel after Musa (peace be upon him). In that period their kingdom had been destroyed. Their sacred objects had been plundered. They had been humiliated before their enemies. They had put aside the teachings of their Prophet and the guidance of their Lord, and because of this they had fallen into disgrace and humiliation. But after this decline they rose again. They shook off their garments, prepared afresh, the ideology of life was revived in their hearts, the zeal for jihad for their ideology of life was born again in their hearts, and they said to their Prophet: ﴿Appoint for us a king, so that we may fight in the way of Allah.﴾

The manner of the divine address with which the Qur'an relates this experience reveals all the realities clearly, and in it the clear indications for the Islamic movement of the first age, as well as clear guidance for the Islamic community of every age, are present.

The general lesson drawn from this story is that a handful of believers showed steadfastness, and as a result the Children of Israel attained a great victory. Although throughout this whole event the army of Islam faced difficulties again and again, and in this campaign there were several defects that came to light, many weaknesses appeared repeatedly. At various stages of the military expedition, groups separated and kept disobeying. Yet despite all these weaknesses, the rising of the Children of Israel, rising after shaking off their impurities and rising with their ideology of life, succeeded because of a handful of steadfast believers. As a result of this success, the Children of Israel attained victory, honour and stability, although before this they had suffered a crushing defeat, were living a life of extreme humiliation, had been in exile for a long period, and other nations had been imposed upon them. As a result of this victory, the government of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and Dawud (peace be upon him) was established among the Children of Israel, in whose time the government of the Children of Israel reached its height, and their period came to be regarded as the golden age of their history, about which the Children of Israel speak with pride, and to that station the Children of Israel did not even reach in the time of their great prophethood. All this success is the result of that ideological stand, when they took the ideology of life out from under the heaps of jahiliyyah, and a small community rose with this ideology in such steadfastness, and clashed with the great army of Goliath and prevailed.

During this experience, certain partial matters have also been given guidance, which the Islamic community of that time greatly needed and which were very important for it. For example, that collective enthusiasm sometimes deceives the leader, if he relies merely on outward appearances and does not strive to reach the reality. Therefore it is the duty of leaders to test their workers before placing them in a difficult battle. In this event, the leaders of opinion among the Children of Israel went to the Prophet of their time and made a demand that he appoint a king under whose leadership they might fight against the enemies of their religion, because those enemies had taken away their rule, taken possession of their wealth, and they had also been deprived of the sacred objects that had been preserved with them in the time of the family of Musa and Harun. When the Prophet of their time sought assurance from them regarding this intention and said: ﴿Is it possible that if fighting is prescribed for you, you will not fight?﴾ they did not regard this question and request for assurance as good. This was disagreeable to them, their enthusiasm reached its peak, and they said: ﴿And what is wrong with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah, when we have been driven out from our homes and from our children?﴾ But the fire of that enthusiasm soon went out. The storm of emotions subsided, and in the various stages of that path they kept sitting back, as the details of this event show, or as the context of the discourse makes clear: ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a small number of them.﴾ It is a distinctive feature of the Children of Israel that they break promises, go back on their covenant, and abandon their companion halfway. Yet such events are found in human communities in any case, and especially in those communities which, in their faith and conviction and in their high training, have not yet reached a high standard. Therefore this scene of communal life also had to be presented before the Muslim community of every age, so that the Muslim community of every age might benefit from the experience of the Children of Israel.

From this event it is also known that trials of this kind of outward enthusiasm, emotional and hasty action, should not be applied only once, but workers should be tested again and again. When fighting became obligatory on the Children of Israel at their own demand, the majority of them turned their backs. Only the small number remained who kept the covenant they had made with their Prophet. These were the same people who, at first, kept fighting under the leadership of Talut, saying that he was not even fit for kingship. But when the sign of his kingship became manifest, and the Children of Israel regained under his leadership those sacred objects that had gone into the hands of the enemies, and which were brought back by angels, then the Children of Israel were content with the leadership, but their majority, already at the first stage, backed out of jihad. And in the very first trial, which their leader had established, they failed.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 2, verse 243 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Then when Talut set out with the troops, he said: "Indeed, Allah is going to test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who takes a single handful with his hand." But they drank from it, except for a few of them.﴾ Then when Talut set out with the army, he said: "A test from Allah awaits you at a river: whoever drinks from it is not my companion. My companion is only the one who does not quench his thirst from it, except one who takes a handful with his hand." Yet, all of them drank from the river except a small group. But even this small number could not remain steadfast to the end. This small number came face to face with a living danger, and when they saw the multitude of the enemy and their strength, their resolve weakened and their hearts wavered. ﴿Then when he and those who believed with him crossed it, they said: "Today we have no strength against Goliath and his troops."﴾ Then when Talut and his Muslim companions crossed the river and advanced, they told Talut that today they had no power to confront Goliath and his armies. In opposition to this shameful stance, only a handful of chosen people stood firm. They placed their trust in Allah and believed in Him, and they said: ﴿"How often has a small company overcome a large company by the permission of Allah! And Allah is with the steadfast."﴾ "How often has it happened that a small group, by the permission of Allah, has prevailed over a large group. Allah is with those who are patient." This was the small group that tipped the balance. Allah's help came, and the Children of Israel became masters of honour and stability.

From this incident we learn what the qualities of a righteous, wise and faithful leadership are. All these qualities are present in the leadership of Talut. From this we learn that Talut knew people's psychology well. He was not deceived by the outward enthusiasm of the Children of Israel. Then he did not rely on just one test. He tested the resolve and obedience to command of his soldiers even before entering the actual battle. Those who were found immature in these trials were separated and left behind. Most importantly, they did not lose courage even in the most difficult circumstances. After each trial their army kept shrinking, yet they kept advancing and did not lose heart. In the end only a handful remained with him, but they were chosen, elect fighters. Now, relying on pure strength of faith and trust in Allah, they plunged into the battle, and Allah's promise is certainly true for the believers.

The final lesson in this battle is that when a person attaches himself to Allah, his values change and the measures of his concepts change, because his view does not remain confined to the narrow circle of this world, but he thinks far beyond this world, in a wide sphere, which is the fundamental principle of all matters. This handful of believers who remained steadfast, who plunged into the battle, and who obtained Allah's help, also saw their own scarcity, that their number was small and their enemies were very numerous. Seeing them, their other brothers had already cried out: ﴿"We have no strength today against Goliath and his troops."﴾ "We have no power to fight Goliath and his armies." But this handful of believing community did not make that decision about this situation. It made a very different decision. They said: ﴿"How often has a small company overcome a large company by the permission of Allah!"﴾ "How often it happens that a small group, by the permission of Allah, has prevailed over a large group." After this, this group, the handful of believers, turns toward Allah: ﴿"Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make our feet firm, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people."﴾ This community felt that the balance of powers is not in the hands of the disbelievers; it is in the hands of Allah alone. Therefore this group sought help from Allah, and He received them the help from the hand that was the owner of that hand, and which it could bestow. When believers reach Allah, their measures change, their values change, and when true faith is born in the heart. From this it also follows that dealing with Allah in the inner world of the heart is better than our conducting ourselves according to the standards of this outward and false world.

In these lines we have not encompassed all the indications contained in this story, because the inspiration of Qur'anic indications and wisdoms comes to each person according to his circumstances and also according to the measure in which he needs it. Nevertheless, each person takes his share, and still a large part of the indications and wisdom remains preserved, and according to different circumstances, these indications continue to be revealed according to each one's portion.

So, after this general commentary, it is now appropriate to discuss the verses in detail.

Who were these people who were in thousands and who left their homes in fear of death? In which land did these people live? In which period of history did they set out? We do not want to lose ourselves in the heap of interpretations and conjectures about them. If Allah had intended to tell us about them, He would surely have told us, as has been done in the case of some other specific narratives of the Qur'an. Here the purpose is only the acquisition of a lesson and admonishing the Muslims. The aim is not that the story is itself the object, so that details of its persons, place of occurrence and time of occurrence be given. Even if the place and time are determined here, this would neither add to nor subtract from the meaning and purpose, that is, taking a lesson from the event.

Here the only aim is to correct the outlook of Muslims regarding the outward causes of life and death, and beyond those causes, their true reality, and to make clear that the decision of life and death is not made in this world. These decisions are made by the Almighty and the Governor of the universe, and that in this matter one should be fully reassured regarding Allah's decree and His writ, and that in this world a person should carry out his duties without any fear or danger and without any anxiety or lamentation. The writer of destinies exists, and the final decision of life and death is in His hand alone.

Here the aim is to say that death is not averted by fear of death, and by lamentation and wailing, by crying and calling out, life is not increased, nor can the decree of Allah be averted by them. Nor can the appointed term be postponed by a moment because of them. It is Allah who gives life; He is the one who grants life, and He is the one who takes back life. In both circumstances His grace accompanies a person: if He takes, it is His grace, and if He gives, it is grace. In the context of giving life and in the context of not giving life, in both circumstances His great wisdom is at work. In both circumstances there is benefit for people. In both cases, in taking and giving, Allah's grace accompanies us: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks.﴾ (243)

The gathering of these people, then their gathering in thousands, then their leaving their homes and setting out for fear of death, necessarily means that in such circumstances there would be a state of lamentation and wailing. Whether their flight was from a warlike enemy or because a severe epidemic had broken out, whatever the cause, it cannot be a remedy against death: ﴿So Allah said to them: "Die."﴾ "Allah said to them: Die."

How did Allah speak to them? How did they die? Did they die from the same calamity from which they had set out, or did they die from some other cause of which they had no suspicion or imagination? The Qur'an has not given any detail of this, because such details were not needed for this purpose, namely the lesson. What is to be conveyed is that through lamentation and fear and dread they could not escape that from which they were fleeing. They could not escape death, and there was no way to reject Allah's decision. If they had returned to Allah and adopted patience, steadfastness and a sober attitude, it would have been much better.

﴿Then He gave them life again.﴾ "Then He gave them life again." How did He bring those people back to life? Was it that after the death of these very people they were raised miraculously, or were such people produced from their descendants who were strong and brave and not given to wailing like their forefathers? The Qur'an has not presented details of these matters either. Therefore we too have no need to begin all sorts of conjectures in explaining it and to lose ourselves needlessly in the heaps of baseless narrations, as has been mentioned in some commentaries. What is understood from this verse is that Allah, without any struggle or hardship, gave them life again, although the lamentation and wailing they had made to avoid death did not prevent their death.

The summary is that wailing cannot stop Allah's decision; lamentation does not preserve life. Life is in Allah's hand, and it is granted to a person even without his own struggle. If this is the reality, then, O cowards, may your eyes long for sleep and may you never find peace:

The commentary continues here with another aspect of this event, and its core purpose comes into view. It also becomes clear why this account was related to the first generation of Muslims. The purpose was: lest, out of love of life, you sit down in your homes; lest, out of fear of death, you draw back; lest, for these reasons, you abandon jihad fi sabilillah (struggle in the way of Allah). Life and death are in the hand of Allah, so fight only in His way, and do not fight for any other aim. Gather only under the banner of Allah and abandon all other banners. Fight in His path, and remember: ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ "And know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing." He hears the matter and also knows its background. He hears, and He answers supplication, and He also knows what is beneficial and what is not for human life and for the heart and vision of man. Your task is only this: that you continue your striving in the way of Allah. None of your deeds will be lost. And it is He who gives life, and it is He who takes life back.

Jihad fi sabilillah is another name for sacrifice and spending. In many places of the Qur'an, mention of fighting and jihad is accompanied by mention of spending wealth and infaq fi sabilillah (spending in the way of Allah). Particularly in the era of the Messenger ﷺ, the importance of infaq fi sabilillah was even greater, because in the time of the Messenger ﷺ people took part in jihad fi sabilillah voluntarily, and the mujahideen bore their own expenses. Sometimes it happened that they were filled with the spirit of jihad but were deprived of wealth, and did not have weapons or mounts. Therefore, for the facilitation of needy mujahideen, it was necessary that people be repeatedly directed toward infaq fi sabilillah. For this reason, the Qur'an calls to spending in a very effective manner:

The commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 245:

Just as life and death are in the hand of Allah, and if Allah has written life, death cannot come, so too wealth is not lost through spending in the way of Allah. It is in fact a good loan (qard hasan) to Allah. Allah is its guarantor, and He will increase that loan manifold and multiply it many times over. In this world too, the wealth of such a person will grow, and he will be granted felicity and blessing, and in the Hereafter too he will be granted peace and comfort. And in the Hereafter, such a person will have countless provisions and rewards and honours. He will be granted nearness to Allah, and Allah will be pleased with him.

A person does not become rich through greed and miserliness. Richness and poverty are in the hand of Allah. They have no connection with spending and expenditure: ﴿وَاللَّهُ يَقْبِضُ وَيَبْسُطُ﴾ "It is Allah who withholds and grants abundance."

And in the end, all of you will have to return to Allah. When you proceed to Allah against your will and depart from this world, what benefit will wealth and riches be to you at that time? ﴿وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ "And to Him you will be returned." And if you must surely go back to Him, then why fear death? What is gained by lamentation and wailing? Neither should there be fear of death, because one has to go to Allah, nor fear of poverty and destitution, because in any case one has to leave this world. Therefore, the believers should begin striving in the way of Allah with full vigour and force. They should offer both their lives and their wealth. They should be convinced that their breaths in this world are counted, that life is limited, and that their sustenance is determined. Their well-being lies in living a life of courage and bravery, living a dignified and free life. In the end, they will have to go before Allah alone.

After explaining these verses, presenting the guidance of faith and expressing the instructions of training, it is appropriate that we also devote some time to the literary beauty of expression and the artistic excellences of the Qur'an's discourse. It is not appropriate that these passages simply pass by: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى الَّذِينَ خَرَجُوا مِنْ دِيَارِهِمْ وَهُمْ أُلُوفٌ حَذَرَ الْمَوْتِ﴾ "Have you not seen those who went out of their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death?" The manner of expression is such that it is as if these people are standing in rows, thousands in number, and they are being inspected (just as a guard of honour is inspected). With only two words, the Qur'an has drawn the complete picture of these people: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾ "Have you not seen?" No other mode of expression could have drawn the picture that these two words imprinted upon the screen of imagination. It appears as though these people are standing in lines and we are looking at them.

Their condition is that they are thousands in number. They have come out of their homes, frightened and terrified, looking about with wide, startled eyes. Now the Qur'an uses only one word, and all these people, instead of the field of inspection, now arrive at the field of execution. As if the commanding ruler, who is inspecting the guard of honour, gives a command: ﴿مُوتُوا﴾ "Die!" and the picture changes. This word makes one feel that no barriers can be set up before death. Your conduct is wrong. This word shows that the decrees of Allah are implemented like a command: as soon as the word is uttered, it is carried out, just as happens on the parade ground.

﴿ثُمَّ أَحْيَاهُمْ﴾ "Then He brought them to life." How? No details are given here. Allah is capable and sovereign; the reins of life and death are in His hand. He alone disposes of every matter of His servants. None of His wills can be rejected; whatever Allah wills, that alone happens. This mode of expression itself shows how the decisions of life and death are made with Allah and what the scene of the execution of the command of Allah is like: like a parade ground and command upon command.

Above, the scene of life and death was before our imagination: scenes of seizing the soul in the grip, of withholding it, and then of suddenly releasing it. Immediately after this, when the matter of sustenance comes, the Qur'an uses the words of withholding and extending for it: ﴿وَاللَّهُ يَقْبِضُ وَيَبْسُطُ﴾ "Allah withholds and extends." This expression for restriction and abundance of sustenance was chosen so that words harmonious with the preceding themes of seizing and restoring the soul would come. The brevity of words and the retention of meanings in both places is a magnificent miracle of the Qur'an.

On one side there is a wondrous depiction; on the other side there is a wondrous coherence and harmony in the use of words. Meanings appear to walk about, and there is no limit to the beauty of expression.

Now the Qur'an presents a second experience before the Muslim Ummah. Its characters are the Children of Israel. The incident belongs to the period after the time of Musa (peace be upon him):

Have you not considered? It is as though this event has just happened and is a scene witnessed before one's eyes. The chiefs of the Children of Israel have gathered; there is a great assembly of their elders and men of judgment. They come to the prophet of their time. Within the context of the discourse, the prophet's name is not mentioned, because the purpose is not storytelling. Mentioning the prophet's name would add nothing to the purposefulness of the account. There was a multitude of prophets among the Children of Israel; countless prophets were sent during their long history. In short, these leaders and nobles are assembled, and they are demanding of the prophet of their time that he appoint a king over them, under whose command they may fight in the way of Allah (fi sabilillah, "in the cause of Allah"). In this matter they use the words "in the way of Allah," because they also wish to express the nature of the war. This shows that faith has stirred in their hearts. Faith has come alive and risen up, shaken itself off, and become ready for action. Their awareness has been revived that they are bearers of faith and a way of life; they are standard-bearers of truth and righteousness, while their enemies are standard-bearers of misguidance, disbelief and falsehood. Before them now is a goal: the goal of jihad in the way of Allah.

Thus, with this clarity of purpose, this definition of purpose, and this certainty of purpose, half the journey to success and victory is covered. Therefore, the believer's mind must first be firmly settled on the conviction that he is upon the truth and his enemy is upon falsehood. In his awareness, the purpose must be defined, purely for Allah, without any admixture of other things, and without any ambiguity by which he would not know where he is heading.

The prophet wished to be assured of the steadfastness of their intention and the sincerity of their resolve, to ascertain whether they possessed the strength to bear so great a responsibility or not. He wanted to know that they were serious in this matter and were demanding it after careful thought: ﴿Said he: "Is it possible that, if fighting is prescribed for you, you will not fight?"﴾ "The prophet asked: Might it be that if fighting is ordained for you, you would not fight?" Is it possible that jihad is made obligatory upon you and you turn away from it? Now you are free; you need not fight. But if Allah accepts this demand of yours and you are commanded to fight, then it will become obligatory upon you, and then you will not be able to refuse. The truth is that a prophet should indeed ask such a question, so as to confirm and affirm the matter. The words and utterances of the prophets are not jest; their commands admit no hesitation, nor can they suffer even the slightest delay.

Upon this inquiry of the prophet of their time, their enthusiasm reached its peak. The chief said that war had become unavoidable; there was no other course left. The rectification of circumstances now depends solely on jihad and jihad in the way of Allah. The war is determined, and there is no room for hesitation in it. ﴿They said: "How could we not fight in the way of Allah, when we have been driven out of our homes and from our children?"﴾ They said: "How could it be that we would not fight in the way of Allah, when we have been expelled from our homes and our children have been separated from us?" It appears that the matter was clear in their hearts. They had resolved that war was necessary. Their enemies are the enemies of Allah, enemies of Allah's religion. They have been driven out of their homes; their women and children have been made captives. Therefore, fighting these enemies is obligatory. Indeed, for them the only path before them is to fight these enemies of truth. Hence there is no need to question them repeatedly or to argue about this matter. This is a firm resolve, and we hold this resolve.

But this momentary courage, and this boldness of conduct in times of peace, does not last long. The Qur'an soon presents the other side of the picture: ﴿But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them.﴾ "But when fighting was ordained for them, they all turned back, except a small number of them."

Here one learns an important characteristic of the Children of Israel. In their history they have been notorious for breaking covenants: they make a pledge and then immediately go back on it. When commanded, they hold back from obedience. They lag behind in discharging obligations, turn away from truth, and disunity is their hallmark. But these qualities are found in every community whose faith has not been fully trained, which has not been subjected to long, deep and high-standard training. This is a weakness against which the leadership of any movement must remain vigilant and must take care of; it must be watched for on the path of difficulties, lest weaknesses appear in times of hardship and matters become difficult. Such circumstances arise for all human communities whose ranks still contain weak people, who have not been refined by the fire and cleansed of their dross.

Upon this turning away, Allah makes only this comment: ﴿And Allah knows the wrongdoers well.﴾ "And Allah knows every wrongdoer." This is a severe reproof to the Children of Israel. These people first demanded jihad; jihad was prescribed, and before they went out to the field of jihad, they refused. Although they are numerous, they are very base people. Along with their baseness they are also wrongdoers: wrongdoers toward their own selves, wrongdoers toward the prophet, wrongdoers toward the truth. They recognized the truth and then allowed it to be humiliated at the hands of the people of falsehood.

Whoever recognizes truth and certainty, and believes that he is upon the truth, and knows that his enemy is upon falsehood, just as the chiefs of the Children of Israel knew and asked their prophet to appoint a king for them, so that under his leadership they might fight their enemies for the sake of Allah, and then this person turns his back, does not raise the banner of jihad against the enemy, and does not bear hardships, despite knowing everything, then this person is a wrongdoer, and he will be punished for this wrongdoing. ﴿And Allah knows the wrongdoers well.﴾ "And Allah knows every wrongdoer."

The Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 247:

Through this debate, dispute, and question-and-answer, another characteristic of the Children of Israel is revealed, one that has been mentioned repeatedly in this surah. Their demand was that a king be appointed for them, under whose leadership they would fight in the way of Allah. Yet as soon as the appointment of the king was announced, they lowered their heads, turned their necks away, and became engaged in argument and dispute over this matter, both regarding the appointment of the king by Allah and its announcement by the Prophet. They began to frown upon the kingship of Talut (Saul). Why? Because they considered themselves, by hereditary right, more deserving than Talut. Talut was, firstly, not from a royal family, and secondly, he was not a wealthy man, so that the claim of inheritance could be set aside on the basis of wealth. In short, this narrow-mindedness and this obstinacy is a constant characteristic of the Children of Israel.

The Prophet of the time told them that he was more deserving because of his personal qualities, and that there was wisdom at work in his selection: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him abundantly in knowledge and physique. And Allah grants His kingship to whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing.﴾ Allah has chosen him over you and has granted him abundant capacities, both of mind and of body, and Allah has the authority to give His kingdom to whomever He wills; Allah is vast in His bounty and everything is within His knowledge.

He is a person whom Allah has chosen. This is his attribute. He has been given mental and physical capabilities. This is his second merit. Then Allah grants His kingdom to whomever He wills. It is His kingdom; the world belongs to Him; He is the disposer and the one with full authority. He chooses whom He wills from among His servants. He is of vast reach and great knowledge. There is no treasurer appointed over His grace and generosity; there is no limit or restriction on His giving. He alone knows where good lies, and He alone knows what decision is best at each moment.

These are matters regarding which a Muslim's outlook ought to be correct, and his mind ought to be free from rancor. But what can be done, the matter has fallen upon the Children of Israel. Their Prophet is well aware of this. The Prophet of the time knows that the temperament of the Children of Israel cannot bear these lofty truths. The circumstances are such that there is no time for admonition; the battle between truth and falsehood is upon them. Therefore, the most appropriate course is that, given the shortage of time, a miracle be displayed before them that would soften their hearts. They would be deeply impressed, they would be reassured about this leadership, and they would believe:

The period in question follows the wandering in the wilderness (Tih) and the death of Musa (Moses) (peace be upon him). It was the time when Hushaʿ (Joshua) was a prophet. In this era the enemies of the Children of Israel attacked them. They seized their territory from them, and also took the sacred relics that had been preserved for them in a chest (box), handed down from the families of Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both). Some narrations state that this chest also preserved the copy of the Torah that had been given by Musa (peace be upon him) at Mount Sinai (Tur).

The Prophet of that time made this event a sign from Allah: that this miracle would manifest before them, and the chest would return to them. Angels would be carrying it so that a rain of tranquility would descend upon their hearts. The Prophet of that time said that this miracle would be a true witness that Allah had appointed Talut (Saul) as king for them, on condition that faith was present in their hearts.

From the context it appears that this miracle did occur, and only then did those people become certain that Talut had been appointed by Allah.

Now Talut organized those who had not refused to take part in the jihad, and who remained steadfast upon the firm covenant they had made with the Prophet of that time. The Qur'an, in strict accordance with its narrative style, omitted all these matters. The Qur'anic style is that it presents one scene of a story immediately after another, and leaves out the unnecessary links in between (see my book At-Tasvir al-Fanni fil-Quran). Thus, here too, the scene that is presented is this: Hadrat Talut is leading the army of Islam on a march towards the enemy:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 2, verse 249:

Right at the first step it becomes clear why Allah chose Hadrat Talut (Talut). He was setting out to undertake a severe battle, but the army with him was made up of defeated people. These people had repeatedly suffered defeat in their long history, and they had become accustomed to repeated humiliation. And the fighting was against the army of a victorious and dominant nation. Therefore there was a need that, to face that outwardly splendid and mighty army, he should take an army whose hearts were filled with a hidden strength, and this hidden strength can only be the strength of will: a resolve so firm that it can restrain every desire and every inclination, that can stand like a rock against deprivation and hardship, that rises above even essential needs and necessary wants, that prefers obedience to command and welcomes difficulties and pains in this cause, and that passes from one trial to another. Therefore, it was the duty of this chosen commander, chosen and loved by Allah, to test the willpower of his army, to examine their steadfastness and patience, and to see to what extent they could hold firm against the desires of the self and the things they crave, and to what extent they could bear deprivation of the necessities of life and hardships. It is related in the narrations that the commander gave this order to the army at a time when they were extremely thirsty and were exhausted by thirst, so that it might be known who would be patient and who would turn away, go back on their heels, and sit in the corner of comfort. Thus the far-sighted judgement of this chosen commander proved correct.

﴿فَشَرِبُوا مِنْهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِّنْهُمْ﴾ "Then they drank from it, except a small number of them." Yet they drank and drank their fill, although they had been permitted only to take a handful or a single scoop with the hand, enough to end the sharpness of their thirst, without giving the impression that they intended to turn back. Most of these people, as it were, laid down their arms before thirst, and turned their backs on the enemy, and so they separated. They were not fit to be included in the mission that Talut and his companions had to accomplish. The better course lay in this, and wisdom lay in this: that they should separate from the army that was to fight the actual battle. In reality, they were the seeds of weakness, defeat and failure. The truth is that the success of an army does not come from its great numbers, but from firm resolve, strong faith, a steadfast heart and perseverance.

From this experience it became clear that a hidden intention alone is not enough, and that practical testing is also necessary. Before stepping onto the battlefield, familiarity with the ups and downs of this path is essential. This experience also shows how high-minded was the leader whom Allah had chosen for these people. Look at the loftiness of his resolve: most people refused at the very declaration of jihad, yet his determination did not waver. Then, in the very first test, the majority of his army failed and turned their backs, but he remained steadfast and continued on his path.

Here, although the first test sifted the army of Talut and the weak ones separated, the testing process still continues:

Now, at this point, they were truly left in a small number. They knew that the enemy possessed a great power, led by a commander like Jalut. They are believers, and they still abide by what they had pledged to their Prophet. But now they see the situation with their own eyes, and they feel sincerely that they are not in a position to confront that great power. Now this is the final and decisive test: the test of who relies on the outward power of the world, and who relies, against outward power, on the great power of Allah. In such matters only those can remain steadfast whose faith is complete, whose hearts have reached Allah, whose values have changed, and who determine good and evil by the light of their faith, not by the outward circumstances in which common people are entangled.

Here, now, that handful of chosen believers stands out openly. They are people for whom the certainty of their number is governed by the light of faith, and whose measure differs from the measures of the superficial observer:

This is the principle of those who are certain that one day they will stand before Allah: that it has repeatedly happened that few have overcome many, because they, having passed through various stages of trials and hardships, having been confronted with difficult circumstances, have attained the station of election and the lofty station. And they prevail because the fountainhead of power is in their hands. They have already reached that great power which is the source of all powers and which prevails over all powers, whose commands are enforced, which is the Mighty (al-Jabbar) over its creation, which shatters the tyrants of the world, which humbles the oppressors and overcomes the great and haughty ones.

This success comes by the permission of Allah; there is no perfection in them themselves. Its true cause is the exalted Being of Allah. ﴿وَاللَّهُ مَعَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾ "And Allah is with those who are patient." Because Allah is the companion of those who are patient, they succeed because the permission of Allah is such. By saying all these things, this handful of people proves that they are the ones who have been chosen for the battle between truth and falsehood.

Now let us move the story further forward. We see a group made up of very few individuals who are certain that one day they will stand before Allah. They have full certainty of that meeting, and this very certainty is the source of their steadfastness. This group seeks its strength in the command of Allah and the permission of Allah. They have complete reliance on Allah, and therefore they have full certainty of their success, and this group stands shoulder to shoulder with those who are called the patient (al-Sabirin) in the sight of Allah. In short, this group that is patient is steadfast and unwavering, and despite its weakness and fewness it is not fearful. This group suddenly plunges into the battlefield against a great power and plays a decisive role. It renews its covenant; its hearts reach Allah, they seek help from Allah alone, and they plunge into that terrible battle.

"This is the correct way: 'Our Lord, pour out upon us patience.' This is an expression through which the whole scene of the outpouring of patience comes before the eyes. The outpouring from Allah happens in the way that a vessel is filled and poured over them, and their cup-like heart becomes overflowing with it. As a result, tranquility and serenity descend upon them, and they become ready for that terrifying battle. 'And make our feet firm.' Because feet are in the power of His dominion. It is He who keeps them steady in their place, so that they do not waver, do not slip, and do not leave their position. 'And grant us victory over the disbelieving people.' The stance is clear: faith is confronting disbelief, and truth is arrayed against falsehood. That is why Allah is called upon: 'O Allah, help Your friends who are arrayed against Your disbelieving enemies.' There is no doubt in the consciences of these people, no uncertainty, no flaw in their thinking, and no doubt about the soundness of their goal or the determination of their method."

The outcome was what they had been waiting for, what they were fully certain of: فَهَزَمُوهُمْ بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ — "So they routed them by the permission of Allah." In the words "by the permission of Allah" it is shown that victory and succour lie in the hand of Allah. Muslims should clear their minds on this point: whatever happens in this universe happens by the permission of Allah, and in accordance with the will of the Power that runs this universe. The believers are in reality a hand of divine power. Through them Allah does what He wills, and through them He enforces what He wills. They are not independent, nor do they hold any power in their hands, nor do they possess any strength of their own. Allah enforces His will through them, so whatever He wills is brought about through them. This is the truth that fills the heart of the believing man with faith, tranquillity, certainty and peace. The believer is a slave of Allah. Allah has employed him to perform an important role, and it is the grace and bounty of Allah that He has chosen the believers for this important role, so that they may perform it, that is, that they may make real the decree of Allah. Having chosen them for this important role, Allah further manifests His grace by bestowing on them reward for it, along with the honour of performing this important role. Were it not for Allah's grace, He would certainly not have done so; and were it not for His bountiful favour, He would not have granted reward for it. Then the believing man is certain that he will surely reach his destination. His purpose is pure and his method is pure, because his jihad in the way of Allah has no personal interest attached to it. He is the enforcer of the will of Allah, subject to His command, and he deserves this position because his intention is sincere. He has firmly resolved to obey, and he turns to Allah with sincerity.

The Qur'an mentions the name of Dawud: وَقَتَلَ دَاوُدُ جَالُوتَ — "And Dawud killed Jalut." Dawud was a small boy among the Children of Israel, while Jalut was an emperor and a fearsome commander. But it was the will of Allah that He should teach the Muslims, at that very moment, the lesson that affairs do not always proceed in the manner that they appear outwardly, but that matters are decided in accordance with realities, and knowledge of realities belongs to Allah alone. The measures of events lie in the hand of Allah. The duty of the believers is to discharge their assigned responsibility, to fulfil the covenant they have made with Allah, and then to leave the outcome to Allah; what He wills will come to pass. See how Allah willed that the task of that tyrannical and powerful king should be completed by the hand of that small youth. Thus it happened, so that people might see that those tyrants and oppressors whom the weak fear, when Allah wills their end, meet their fate at the hands of such small children. Another hidden wisdom was that it was decreed in the will of Allah that after Talut, Dawud would take up the system of government, and that after Dawud this system would pass to his son Sulayman, so that the era of Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salam) and Dawud (ʿalayhi al-salam) would become the golden age of the Children of Israel. This is because the Children of Israel, merely carrying the Islamic outlook on life, rose up; for a long time they wandered in a state of misguidance, repeatedly breaking covenants and disobeying, but whenever they brought about a revolution in accordance with the Islamic outlook on life, Allah, as recompense, raised them to the summit of glory: وَآتَاهُ اللَّهُ الْمُلْكَ وَالْحِكْمَةَ وَعَلَّمَهُ مِمَّا يَشَاءُ — "And Allah gave him kingship and wisdom, and taught him of what He willed."

Dawud was simultaneously a prophet and a king. Allah had given him the skill of making armour and other war equipment, the details of which the Qur'an has given elsewhere. Since the purpose of bringing this story here is different, the details have been omitted here.

When the matter had reached this point and it had been announced that victory would belong to the outlook on life and to firm beliefs, that materialism would be defeated, that high resolve, not numerical multitude, would attain success, then the lofty wisdom here is stated. The philosophy that lies behind this clash between truth and falsehood is explained. Allah did not enjoin jihad and fighting so that spoils of war might be obtained, plunder might be carried out, or honour and superiority might be gained in the world; rather, the philosophy of war in Islam is that this struggle is in reality a clash between good and evil, so that truth, righteousness and goodness may gain dominance on the earth and evil may be overcome. It is so that power may be used for the reform of the earth.

Now individuals fade into the background, events come to their conclusion, and Allah, in a brief sentence of the Qur'an, sets forth the great philosophy of the clash of various powers on this earth, the rivalry of various forces, and the striving and struggle to advance in the field of life. Now on the screen is the vast and wide field of the earth; in this field there is a surging sea of people; the jostling has begun, the pulling and hauling has begun, different people have different aims, and in pursuit of their aims each is pressing ahead of the other. Every person strives to take the ball away, but the thread of all of them is in the hand of Allah, the Glorified. He pushes forward whomever He wills, and pulls back the thread of whomever He wills. In this throng, those who strive for goodness, reform and progress, in the end their outcome is that they move ahead, and the hand of power seizes the reins of all the people of falsehood.

If people were not arrayed against one another, and their temperament, upon which they were created, were not different from one another, and their outward inclinations and immediate aims were not in conflict with each other, then life would become stale and rot. But Allah has made their temperaments different so that they may employ all their powers and resist one another, strive to outdo one another and endeavour to overcome one another; they should cast off sloth and stagnation, awaken their hidden powers, remain ever alert, search for the hidden treasures of the earth, discover the hidden forces and secret mysteries of the earth, and at last the age of reform, goodness and progress should prevail.

But how does Allah accomplish all this work? Through the establishment of a righteous, guided and sincere community, which is aware of the truth that Allah has declared to be truth, and which is also aware of the method that Allah has prescribed. It must be certain that it has been commissioned from Allah to make truth dominant on this earth and to confront falsehood. It must be certain that its salvation lies in performing a lofty role. It can attain salvation only if it endures hardships to achieve this goal. And all this it should do while obeying Allah and seeking the pleasure of Allah.

When such a community is established and strives, then command and prohibition take effect, and the decree of Allah becomes manifest. The word of truth, goodness and reform is raised high. The outcome of this struggle, mutual rivalry and mutual defence falls into the hand of the power which is the standard-bearer of goodness and construction on this earth; as a result of this struggle they advance, and they are carried to the heights of perfection that were fixed and decreed for them. At the very end, there is a concluding remark on this whole story:

These verses are exalted and carry far-reaching purposes, and Allah Himself recites them to His Prophet: نَتْلُوهَا عَلَيْكَ (We recite them to you).

"We recite them to you." We Ourselves are reciting them. How great a matter this is, and how awe-inspiring a reality. Consider it: the Lord of Majesty Himself recites these verses, and recites them with truth (بالحق). The Divine Being Himself recites these verses, the One who has the right to recite them, the One by whose command these verses are being revealed, and by whose command they have become the constitution of human beings. This station belongs to no one except Allah. Therefore, whoever on his own devises a system for mankind is a fabricator (muftari). He fabricates a lie against the Truth-Exalted (Haqq Ta'ala). He wrongs himself and also wrongs the servants of Allah. He makes a claim to which he has no right. He is a follower of falsehood (batil-parast) and does not deserve to be obeyed. Obedience is reserved for the command of Allah (amr-i-Ilahi). Then obedience is to be rendered to the one who takes guidance from Allah. Apart from Him, no one deserves obedience.

وَإِنَّكَ لَمِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ ("Indeed, you are certainly among the messengers"). This is the reason why the Lord Himself recites verses upon you and informs you of all the experiences of the entire history of mankind. The experiences of the caravan of the believers, and the ups and downs of all its stages, are being related to you, and the inheritance of all the messengers (mursalin) is being handed over to you.

Here this lesson concludes, which is filled with the store of the experiences of the movement (tahrik). With this lesson, this second part of Fi Zilal al-Quran also concludes, in which the Islamic movement was taken in various directions and turned across various fields, and it was trained for the great role it was to perform on the earth, the role to which Allah appointed it as guardian (nigran) and designated it as the middle nation (ummat-i-wasat), so that it might embody this divine system of life for people until the end of time.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 253 (part 1 of 3):

Juz' Three at a Glance
(The Latter Part of Surah al-Baqarah)

This third juz' consists of two parts. The first comprises the remainder of Surah al-Baqarah (it should be remembered that the first two juz' have consisted entirely of Surah al-Baqarah), and the second comprises the opening portion of Surah Al 'Imran.

Here we shall discuss only the latter part of al-Baqarah in outline. The discussion of the portion of Al 'Imran will take place when we begin the study of Surah Al 'Imran.

In this portion of Surah al-Baqarah too, the same fundamental theme has been taken up, which we described at the beginning of the first part, and which we continually study in every surah. That theme is: preparing the Muslim community for the goal for which it has been raised up, so that it advances carrying these objectives, in circumstances where it has the Islamic conception of life before it, and where it feels that this great community and movement has been raised up for these very objectives. The experiences of earlier nations have also been laid open before it. It has been informed of the resources it must employ for this path, what the difficulties of this path are, and what plots the enemies of the movement can devise against it. This is because they are enemies of God, enemies of truth and enemies of faith, and this is so that this community may advance on this difficult path with wakefulness and pass through all its stages.

The training and preparation of the Muslim community, all its equipment, its comprehensive training, its ideal and its aims and objectives, are the subjects through which the Qur'an, after the first generation, keeps the community of Muslims fresh in every age. This is because in every age the path of guidance and leadership of the Islamic movement is this same firm way. Therefore the Qur'an is a living, active and motivating means of training, and at every time and in every age it is a living, active and complete constitution. Indeed the Qur'an is, at every stage, every step and every era, a leader, a guide and a director, but only for the person who seeks admonition, guidance and direction from the Qur'an.

The second juz' ended with this verse: "These are the signs of God, which We recite to you with truth, and you are certainly among the messengers" (2:252). This came after the account of some of the Children of Israel, which occurred after Moses, when the chiefs of the Children of Israel said to their prophet: "Appoint for us a king so that we may fight in the way of God" (2:246). At the end of that account it was said: "And David killed Goliath, and God gave him the kingdom and wisdom and taught him of what He willed" (2:251). Thus the second juz' ended with a matter concerning the people of Moses (peace be upon him), in which the details of the account of Prophet David were given. In it there was also an allusion to the messengership of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it was made clear that he (ﷺ) was being equipped with the experiences that all the messengers have encountered throughout human history.

For this reason the third juz' begins in a way that connects it to the speech that preceded it. That is, the discussion about the earlier prophets proceeds in such a way that some of them were more exalted than others, and some had higher ranks than others. It also says that the followers of those messengers, in later times, created mutual differences, even though they knew well who was upon the truth. Despite this, they maintained their differences. Some of them remained upon faith and some took the path of disbelief. Some of them killed others: "Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others. Among them was one to whom God spoke directly, and some He raised in rank by other distinctions. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear signs and supported him with the Holy Spirit. Had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after clear signs had come to them, but they differed; some of them believed and some of them disbelieved. Yet had God willed, they would not have fought, but God does what He intends" (2:253).

The connection of the speech is perfectly clear: at the end of the second juz' too the subject was the messengers, and at the beginning of the third juz' it is the same subject. Indeed the speech is connected throughout this entire surah. Throughout this surah there is an intellectual debate between the Islamic community organized in Medina and the Children of Israel. In the first two juz' of the Qur'an these are generally the subjects under discussion. In this connection, the sectarian differences and mutual killing among the messengers and then among their nations is taken up here in detail. That is, some of these nations remained upon faith, some took the path of disbelief, and then they fell into unjust mutual strife. Therefore the connection of the speech is clear. (The late Sayyid Qutb wrote his tafsir with the juz' divisions in view, although the Qur'an was not arranged with regard to juz' divisions. The division into juz' was made merely to facilitate recitation of the Qur'an in one month. Therefore it is evident that the speech which begins with "Those messengers" is connected with the preceding verses. — Translator.)
