The reason this matter is raised here is so that before the Islamic movement, the Muslims of that time, the followers of the prophets, the Children of Israel and others, may spend their wealth, which is genuinely better, and this is merely provision for the Hereafter, a day on which "there will be no trade, no friendship, and no intercession" (2:254). Therefore spending in the way of God is a financial obligation that is a necessary consequence of the obligation of jihad in the way of God, especially in the circumstances that the Islamic movement faced at that time, in which the warriors of God were being prepared for war with their own wealth and with the wealth that was gathered through spending in the way of God.

After this, some aspects of the intellectual foundation upon which the Islamic community was established are discussed: the existence of God and His oneness, that God alone is the manager of everything and everything subsists by Him, that He is the absolute owner of this universe, that He has knowledge and awareness of everything in this universe, that He has power over this entire universe, that it is wholly in His control and under His protection, that on the Day of Judgment no intercession will be effective with Him unless He permits it, and that in this world man has only the knowledge that He bestows, so that a Muslim may proceed on his path with a clear conception of the ideas upon which he intends to establish the system of life. Thus God, exalted is He, says:

"God — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass not a thing of His knowledge except for what He wills. His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation does not tire Him. And He is the Most High, the Most Great" (2:255).

According to this conception of life, a Muslim advances and begins fighting in the way of God, not so that he may force his way of life and his beliefs upon people by force, but so that a distinction may be made between guidance and misguidance, the root causes of strife, corruption and error may be eliminated, and after that people will have complete freedom to adopt whatever attitude they choose.

"There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clearly distinct from error. So whoever disbelieves in Taghut and believes in God has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which will never break. And God is Hearing and Knowing" (2:256).

Thus a Muslim proceeds on his path of life with complete tranquility. He considers himself under the protection of God, and God's help is with him. He is certain that God's guidance and God's support are with him:

"God is the ally of those who believe. He brings them out from darknesses into light. And those who disbelieve — their allies are taghut, who take them out of light into darknesses. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally" (2:257).

In short, at the end of this juz' too, this passage continues steadily toward the same goal toward which the opening of this juz' was directed, namely the statement of the aims and objectives of the Islamic movement and the nurturing of these objectives within the Islamic community.

After this, a look is cast upon the reality of death and life from the Islamic standpoint. In this connection two experiences from the theoretical life of Prophet Abraham (peace be upon him) are related, along with one observation concerning another person whose name is not disclosed. In these experiences the reality is described that the matter of death and life is connected only with God's knowledge and will, and that human limited perception is unable to encompass the true reality of death and life, because the true reality lies beyond perception and its reality is known only to God, exalted is He.

Here death and life are clarified so that, first, the human conception and thinking about human life may be corrected, and second, that those who take part in jihad and fighting must also have a correct conception of death and life before them.

After these intellectual guidances, there is a rather lengthy discussion concerning the collective affairs of the Islamic society. It is explained that social security is the foundation of the Islamic society, and that the concept of riba cannot even be imagined in this society; it would be regarded as a deserving-of-curse act. In contrast, in the Islamic society there is encouragement to spend greater wealth through charity and spending in the way of God, and this is discussed at some length. The description of spending in the way of God contains excellent portrayal, excellent impressions and indications, and high artistic qualities. We shall, God willing, speak on this artistic and literary aspect when these beautiful verses are before us during explanation. Here it is sufficient to point out that jihad and fighting and spending in the way of God go hand in hand. Moreover, spending in the way of God and charity and almsgiving are an important aspect of the collective life of Islam, and in this surah this aspect of economic life has been organized through various methods of exhortation and legislation.

Opposite to benevolence and charity stands the foul system of usury. The Qur'an has waged a lengthy war against this foul system, and it seems as though the Qur'an, by bombarding it, has also demolished the foundations of this reprehensible institution from the economic system of collective life. The Qur'an wishes to establish in place of the usurious system a firm and healthy economic system, through which the economic system of society can progress.

After this, legislation is made concerning mutual transactions, and such a law is enacted that no legal system in the world had this law (the written form of contracts). This legislation is made in two verses. One verse is among the longest verses of the Qur'an. From this it becomes known what method of procedure the Qur'an adopts in legislation, and in what manner it does so. The Qur'anic law is a living, unique and miraculous law, and suitable for every age and every era.

The conclusion of this surah is also made upon the same words and themes with which it began, namely the Islamic concept and view concerning God's essence, the angels, God's books and messengers: "We make no distinction between any of His messengers" (2:285). This is the principle that has been repeatedly expressed in this surah. Finally, believers are taught the manner of supplication, and it is shown what the relationship of a believer with his Lord should be. In this supplication too there is an allusion to the history of the Children of Israel, namely that they did not join their relationship with their God. The surah concludes with this supplication, which is a fitting conclusion to a lengthy surah comprising various themes:

"Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistake. Our Lord, and lay not upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, and burden us not with that which we have no ability to bear. And pardon us; and forgive us; and have mercy upon us. You are our protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people" (2:286).

Lesson 17 at a Glance

At the very beginning of this lesson we find the Qur'an's distinctive mode of expression regarding the messengers: "Tilka al-Rusul" ("Those messengers") and not "Haa'ulaa' al-Rusul" ("These messengers"). Why was this particular mode of expression adopted at the beginning of the speech regarding the messengers? There are clear indications in it. It is appropriate that before explaining the verses, something be said about this style of discourse.

The passage is the second part of the commentary on surah 2, verse 253. Below is the translation.

"Those messengers..." This group of Messengers (rusul) is a special community. This community has a particular temperament and a particular nature. Although they are human beings, then who are they? What is the reality of prophethood? What is the temperament of prophethood? How is this duty discharged? Then why were these particular individuals alone raised to the rank of prophethood, and how was it done? These are questions upon which I have been reflecting for a long time, and I have been in search of a satisfactory answer. Certain meanings and concepts rise upon the surface of my awareness which I cannot transfer in the form of words and expressions. Nevertheless, it is necessary that I bring this intuition and consciousness of mine, and these ideas and concepts, closer to words and understanding.

This universe in which we live, and of which we are an important part, runs upon certain principles and rules. These principles are the cosmic (takwini) laws and regulations which Allah, the Exalted, has laid down for this universe, and He has commanded the universe to continue in accordance with them, to move in accordance with them, and to proceed in accordance with the purpose of these principles. And in this universe, whenever man takes a step forward in the field of knowledge and discovers some new findings, or Allah provides man with opportunities to acquire some further information, this perception and discovery lies within the limits of his limited power of perception, and it is only to the extent that is necessary for him to live in this world, so that he may be able to perform the duties of human vicegerency (khilafah) well during his limited life here.

And in this universe, in order to discover these natural laws and regulations, man, from the standpoint of his personality, makes use of two things: one is observation (mushahadah) and the other is experiment (tajribah). Observation and experiment, by their very nature, are both partial sources of knowledge. In terms of their results, they are neither absolute, final nor conclusive. Nevertheless, through these two sources, certain universal rules and regulations of this universe are discovered, which are regarded as universal laws for a long time, but eventually this discovery too becomes a partial discovery, which is neither ultimate nor absolute. This is because the harmony and coherence among the laws of this universe is linked to that universal order (namus) which binds all these universals together. And this supreme order (namus-i-akbar) has always remained hidden, and it lies beyond the scope of partial observation and experiment, even though a long period of debate and research may pass, because time is not a significant factor in this matter. In this universe, in its importance and in its formation, this is a limit for the field of human self and power. And even this status is a partial and relative status. Then, the time granted to the whole of humankind is also partial and limited. Therefore, our means of knowledge and all the results that come from these means remain partial, because they come to light through partial and relative means.

Here it becomes clear what the importance of prophethood is in this universe. Prophethood has a special temperament, and this special temperament and this capacity is granted to it by Allah, so that it may receive that supreme order and reach its depth, upon which the existence of this universe is established. We have not yet been able to grasp the reality of the nature of the relationship a Messenger has with this supreme order; we can only understand the traces of that relationship and connection.

It is the special natural capacity of the Messenger which receives revelation from this supreme order, and it has the ability to do so, because the temperament of the Messenger is prepared to receive that message. And this message is the same message which this whole universe also continually receives from this supreme order. Therefore this whole universe is directly connected with that supreme order and is under its control and command. Now, how does the Messenger receive this signal, through what means or from whom does he receive this signal? We can give the answer to this question only at the time when Allah grants us also that capacity which He grants to those chosen and selected individuals among His servants who are called Messengers. And "Allah knows best where to place His message" ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾. This is a magnificent matter, and it is that magnificent secret of this universe which lies beyond the perceptive power of man.

All the Messengers had attained the reality of tawhid, and the doctrine of all the Messengers has been the doctrine of tawhid. This is because the capacity to connect with the supreme order was deposited in the very being of those Messengers, since the source of guidance of all those prophets was one and the same. If this source and origin of guidance had not been one, the teachings of those prophets would have been different and their methods of work would have been varied. This realization of the Messengers took place at a time when humanity was in its early stage, and the means of understanding, perception, observation and experiment which exist today were not available to humanity, nor had universal laws of humanity been revealed in that period which point to the doctrine of tawhid.

From the beginning of humanity until today, all the Messengers have called only to the worship of Allah. All these prophets have been calling to this one reality, and through their special temperament and distinctive nature they have received this same message. Therefore, when that universal order was communicated upon their prophetic temperament, a natural thought arose in their hearts which was fully connected with that universal order. Then the propagation and dissemination of this message was also a natural result of their thought and conviction. They had a firm faith that this is the truth, and that the thought had been communicated to them by Allah alone, and that because of their firm and strong connection with the higher world and their special prophetic nature, they were fully certain that that order is the one Allah, without partner, and that multiplicity is not possible in His Being.

The belief in tawhid is the necessary consciousness of the prophetic nature of the Messengers. The Holy Qur'an, in the narratives of the prophets (peace be upon them) that it relates, contains certain words which point to this prophetic nature. Sometimes the prophets are described with this nature. For example, in the story of Prophet Nuh (peace be upon him) it is mentioned:

﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I were upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He had given me mercy from Himself, but it was hidden from you, shall we compel you to accept it while you are averse to it? And O my people, I do not ask you for wealth in return for it; my reward is only with Allah. And I will not drive away those who have believed; indeed, they are going to meet their Lord, but I see you as a people who are ignorant. And O my people, who would protect me from Allah if I drove them away? Will you not then pay heed?"﴾ (11:28-30)

And through Prophet Salih (peace be upon him) it was said:

﴿He said: "O my people, have you considered: if I were upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He had given me mercy from Himself, then who would protect me from Allah if I disobeyed Him? You would only add to my loss."﴾

And in the conduct of Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him) too, the same is seen:

﴿And his people argued with him. He said: "Do you argue with me concerning Allah while He has already guided me? And I do not fear those you associate with Him, unless my Lord should will something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not then be mindful? And how should I fear what you associate, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has sent down to you no authority? So which of the two parties has more right to security, if you should know?"﴾ (6:80-81)

And in the account of Prophet Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) the same matter has been told:

﴿He said: "O my people, have you considered: if I were upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He had provided me from Himself with good provision, and I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from. I intend only reform as far as I am able, and my success is only through Allah. upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back."﴾ (11:88)

And this matter was stated by Prophet Ya'qub (peace be upon him) in these words:

﴿He said: "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know."﴾ (12:86)

Thus, and in this manner, in the sayings and attributes of all the Messengers, the effects of this profound harmony and connection are found, which form part of their nature and are embedded in the depths of their conscience, and because of which the speech of these Messengers is varied and adorned.

With the passage of time, human knowledge and understanding have discovered certain signs and findings which show that there is a law of unity in this universe. Among human beings, people of knowledge have reached the conclusion that in this vast and extensive universe there exists the unity of existence and the unity of motion. And man, while remaining within his limited knowledge, has attained the understanding that the construction of this universe begins from the atom, and that the atom is in reality (Power). Thus both matter and energy are combined in this atom, and the scientists of physics, who for a long period held the theory that this universe is composed of two separate things, matter and energy, have now abandoned it. The correct position now is that the universe is composed of the atom, and if the atom is broken, it is a tremendous force. And man, to the extent of his limited knowledge, has found that this atom is active within its internal system, and that it is composed of electrons, protons and neutrons. And electrons constantly move around the two, which is the centre (nucleus) of the atom. This motion is perpetual and is present in every atom. And just as Farid al-Din al-Attar said, every atom is like a sun around which stars revolve, just as the stars revolve around our sun, and which are revolving continuously.

The unity of this universe and the unity of its motion are characteristics of this universe which man has discovered, and these two characteristics from a distance indicate that this universe is encompassed by a broader comprehensive order. Human knowledge has reached this truth only to the extent that the power of observation and experiment of man made it possible to reach. But the innate faculties of the elect are so powerful that they grasp all these realities in a single moment, because these realities are communicated to them directly, and the power to perceive these realities exists only with those elect.

These elect have not perceived these observations and characteristics through scientific experiments; they have been granted a perceptive faculty which directly attains this reality of unity. These elect directly attain this single order, and this is an inner process within their own being. They find that this uniform communication must necessarily have been emitted from one single source and origin. The special perceptive faculty or special perceptive instruments which are placed within the being of these elect, attain with certainty the reality that Allah, glorified is His Majesty, His Unique Being alone is the true controller of this universe. The mechanism of their perception is extremely perfect and extremely intricate, because they attain this reality in an instant, the source from which guidance comes to them, which is one, and the will under which they act, which proceeds from that same source. Therefore this special perceptive faculty of theirs, or these special perceptive instruments, with the certainty of conviction, attain the reality that Allah, glorified is His Majesty, is the sole Being who is the true disposer of this universe.

I am not saying this on the basis that modern science has claimed to have discovered one or two facts about this unity of the universe. This is because scientific facts are sometimes considered established and sometimes they are refuted, and the facts that science reaches are partial and relative facts, since it is not possible for science to reach any absolute and immutable reality. This is because scientific theories keep changing. Some theories refute other theories, and some modify one another.

What I have said about the unity of the universe and the unity of motion is not because there is any resemblance between it and that law of unity which is revealed by Allah to these special messengers. That is not my intention at all. My purpose is another matter, namely that the reliable source and fountain of guidance and direction lies only with the prophets, and it is only the prophets who can give a unified, complete, comprehensive view of this universe that is based on truth.

It is possible that modern scientific discoveries have found some aspects and some characteristics of the supreme reality of this universe, and they have come to know that the supreme reality is only one. But it is that very reality which the messengers have attained directly through their special power of perception, and have fully encompassed, and that reality is directly and fully present in the natural perceptive faculty of those messengers. And this perception of the messengers is based on truth in its own place, whether or not modern science has correctly grasped some of its characteristics. This is because scientific theories are subject to debate and to review. At first they are not established; they are based on conjecture and estimation, and then, even if they appear established, this proof is not immutable. Therefore the reality of prophethood cannot be measured against these theories, because the standard and criterion must always be something that is established and immutable. Therefore we necessarily arrive at the conclusion that prophethood itself is that standard and criterion by which we shall examine modern scientific theories.

The appeal in this verse is a loving one, addressed to the hearts of the believers. It is a spiritual bond between the believers and the One who makes the appeal, because they have faith in the Divine Being: ﴿O you who believe!﴾

The appeal is that you give Us a part of what We have bestowed upon you. After all, it is We who are the Giver and the Bestower, and it is We who are asking for something from what We Ourselves have given: ﴿Spend out of what We have provided for you﴾.

Consider that such opportunities do not come again and again. If you do not benefit from this, such opportunities will not be granted to you again: ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾.

This is the last opportunity. If it passes you by, you will not get it back. At this moment, wealth is being invested in a profitable enterprise. After this, no friendship and no intercession will be available to compensate for that loss and deficit.

Here, attention is also drawn to the purpose for which the Creator of the universe Himself is calling for donations, namely, the demand for jihad fi sabilillah (striving in the way of God). Jihad is for the purpose of repelling disbelief and removing from the world the oppressive system that exists in the form of disbelief: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers﴾.

Those who reject the truth have committed oppression. They have oppressed their own souls, which they are casting into the pit of everlasting destruction. They are also oppressing the common people, in that they prevent them from coming onto the path of guidance, mislead them, and do not allow them to reach that goodness than which there is no other goodness: namely, the goodness of peace and security, the goodness of tranquility and love, and the goodness of reform and certainty.

Those who are enemies of the reality of faith taking root in the hearts and minds of people, those who are enemies of the faith-based way of life becoming pervasive in our lives, and those who strive so that the Islamic law (Shariah) is not implemented in our collective system, they are the worst enemies of humanity. They are oppressors of the highest order. If humanity has attained the right path, then it is its duty to pursue such people until they desist from this oppression, which they continually inflict upon humanity. The first duty of humanity is to sacrifice its life and wealth to confront such people. This is also the duty of every Islamic community that God Almighty has raised for this task, and that has been invited to carry out this obligation, and that its Lord is calling out to in such profound, inspired words.

After the explanation of ideological differences among the communities of the Messengers and of the historical wars and conflicts, and after making clear that despite clear evidence of faith, they adopted unjust disbelieving notions, it was deemed appropriate here to reveal a comprehensive verse containing the principles and foundations of the concepts of faith. This is Ayat al-Kursi (the Verse of the Throne), which presents the doctrine of tawhid (the oneness of God) in its full depth and with clear signs. It is a verse of great rank, containing profound meanings, and its scope of application is very wide. (It states the minimum beliefs that define the boundary between disbelief and faith.)

The qualities mentioned in this verse each rest on one of the foundational principles of the Islamic worldview. Although the Meccan revelations discuss the fundamental beliefs of the Islamic way of life at length, the Madinan revelations also sometimes address this important and foundational subject. This is because the Islamic system of life is built upon these beliefs and concepts, and until the foundation is sound, the whole wall cannot be upright. Without it, this system cannot be explained, cannot harmonize with the established realities of the human soul, and cannot be given a reasonable and comprehensive interpretation.

In the first part of this book, in the commentary on Surah al-Fatihah, I explained this misguidance in detail. I stated that there is a great need to purify the human conscience and belief concerning the Divine Being. The human conscience lay buried beneath layers of ignorant (jahiliyyah) thought merely because the concept of the Deity did not exist in people's minds in its clear, pure and evident form. This belief was buried under superstitions and mythological beliefs. Even the great philosophers did not have a clear and pure concept of God. Then the Islamic way of life came, presented the Divine Being with its correct concept, removed the human conscience from the burden of these unbelievable prevailing notions, and delivered humanity from the darkness in which it was groping.

In short, all the qualities mentioned in this verse are a general foundation for the Islamic worldview, and in this way these qualities are in turn the source for the detailed Islamic system of life.

﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him﴾: This is a decisive oneness (tawhid, the affirmation of God's absolute unity), in which there is no room for any deviation, and it contains none of the polytheistic (shirk) taints that had overshadowed the concept of the Deity in earlier religions. For example, the invented doctrine of the Trinity (tathlith) which the people of the Church adopted after Prophet Isa (peace be upon him)... or the beliefs held by the ancient Egyptian peoples, who at one time believed in one God but in later ages that one God was represented in the form of the disc of the sun, and afterwards many lesser deities were fashioned under that great sun-deity.

This decisive oneness is the foundation of Islamic beliefs and concepts, from which the Islamic system of life takes its detailed form. This is the concept of Allah, as a result of which in our worship and obedience we turn only towards Allah. According to this, no person can be obedient to or the slave of anyone other than Allah. He can worship only Allah, and obedience to Allah alone is obligatory upon him, in the matters in which Allah has clearly commanded obedience. From this very concept of God springs the principle that sovereignty belongs exclusively to Allah. Therefore, only He can legislate, and human beings may formulate their rules and regulations only in the light of the Shariah. From this same concept of the Deity it follows that a person may derive his values of life only from Allah. If a value of life carries no weight in the scale of Allah, then it shall have no weight at all. Any law, custom or organization that opposes the system of Allah is entirely null and void. In short, as a result of the belief in tawhid, a consciousness arises in the human conscience, and then as a result of that a detailed blueprint of life takes shape.

﴿The Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all﴾: The life which is attributed here to the Divine Being is an essential attribute. It is not a life that a created being borrows from its Creator. In this sense, only Allah is the Ever-Living. He is eternally and everlastingly alive. He has neither a starting point nor an endpoint. The life of God is free from the concept of time and space which is a necessary feature of the life of creatures, whose life begins at a point and ends at a certain limit. For this reason it is said here, ﴿He is the Ever-Living﴾, meaning that He alone is living; no one else is alive in this sense. Furthermore, the life of God is free from those conceptual attributes with which a human being may conceive of life, because ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. Therefore, the characteristics associated with the general meaning of life have not even the slightest trace in the life of Allah. The life of Allah is an absolute and unconditioned life, free from the qualities that are necessary to human life. Consequently, all the imaginary and mythological notions which people have attributed to Allah are negated by this.

The meaning of al-Qayyum is that Allah is the Guardian of all creation, and all existence exists because of Him. All beings are dependent upon Him for their existence and continuance, and they are under His management. It is not the case that Allah, after creation, has no concern for His creatures, as was the view of Aristotle. Aristotle held that God cannot be concerned with anything other than His own essence. He believed that in this concept of divine sustenance there is complete purity and greatness. Yet as a result of this view, the connection of Allah, glorified is He, with His creation is severed, and Allah abandons creation. In contrast, the Islamic concept of Allah is a positive concept; it contains no negativity. It rests on the foundation that Allah is the guardian of everything, and every being in the world, in its existence, depends upon the existence and management of Allah. Thus the conscience and awareness of a Muslim believer, his whole life and his entire existence, and the existence of the universe around him, become connected and related to the existence of Allah, glorified is He. It is Allah who exercises control over the life of this believing Muslim, and then the same Being exercises control over the universe around him, and this governance of the Divine Being is extremely wise and well-ordered. In this manner he derives his values of life and his standards of good and evil. In this whole life and in this whole process, Allah remains the guardian of the human being.

﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: This is an all-encompassing and unrestricted ownership. It is not conditioned by any condition, nor limited by any boundary. It has no partner, and this ownership never ends. This is one of the meanings of ﴿Alone, with no partner﴾ and the ﴿One God﴾. He alone is Allah. He alone is the Ever-Living. He alone is the Guardian. He alone is the Owner. By this, all the polytheistic beliefs that could enter human reason are negated. The concept of ownership and sovereignty in this world would also be clarified: when Allah is the Sovereign and Owner, then in this world no one shall have a right of ownership. Man is not the sovereign, but rather he is the vicegerent (khalifah) of that same sovereign who has no partner. And in the system of vicegerency, he shall be bound by all those limits and restrictions which the One who appointed him as vicegerent has imposed upon him in His Shariah. Therefore no vicegerent can be free of the limits and restrictions of the Shariah. And if any vicegerent does not observe those restrictions which are imposed upon him by virtue of the office of vicegerency, then his vicegerency itself becomes null and void. And it shall be the duty of the believers to reject any measures taken by such a vicegerent that contravene the Shariah. This is the Islamic concept that operates in the Islamic Shariah, and the practical life that is formed upon that Shariah also rests on this concept. When Allah says in the Holy Qur'an ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, He does not mean merely a belief, a theory, or a mere idea. This statement is in fact a constitutional provision for the entire life of a human being. Furthermore, the connections formed among people in worldly life are also based on the foundation that whatever is in this world belongs to Allah.

When this truth settles in the human conscience, when a person truly comprehends that his Owner, in reality, is the Owner of the heavens and the earth, and when he removes from his heart and mind the false notion that what he considers his property is not truly his property, and when he consciously regards all his possessions as belonging to the true Owner, and when the feeling arises in his mind that what is in his hands is only temporarily loaned to him, and has been given to him by the true Owner for a specified period, then the mere realization and feeling of these truths reduces in his heart the intensity of his greed, avarice, covetousness, stinginess, and the constant anxiety of accumulating wealth day and night. Through this outlook on life and these feelings, qualities of patience, contentment, satisfaction and acceptance of Allah's decree (ridha bi al-qadar) develop within the person. He becomes generous and liberal. Peace and tranquillity arise in his heart. Whether he is rich or poor, a kind of calm, serenity and stability comes into his bearing. If he does not receive something, he feels no regret, and if he does not obtain what he desires, he does not find jealousy or constriction in his heart.

﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾: This is another attribute of the Divine Being. Through it the station of divinity (uluhiyyah) and the station of servanthood (ubudiyyah) are well clarified. All servants stand in the court of Allah in the station of servitude. They can neither advance beyond that station nor transgress it. They stand in the station of a servant, in a state of humility and submission. They can neither move forward towards the Lord, nor dare to intercede with Him, unless they have been given prior permission; in that case, they may intercede within the limits of that permission. Yes, these servants and slaves do indeed have differences of rank among themselves, and in the sight of Allah too their degrees and stations certainly vary. But in the presence of the Lord, they have a limit of servanthood, beyond which they are neither permitted nor able to go.

Here a hint is given to the majesty of Allah, His grandeur and His awe-inspiring dignity, and by using the interrogative form of denial, this hint is made even more powerful. This shows how this could be possible? And if it were to happen, it would be disapproved of. Therefore, who is there who could dare to do such a thing in the presence of the Lord? Yes, if He grants permission, then........

In the light of this truth, all those false concepts become clear which arose among people who came after the prophets and messengers, whose adherents created confusion between the reality of divinity and the reality of servanthood. These people adopted the belief that Allah has a son, who by virtue of the relationship of sonship is in some form a partner and a mixed-in element with Him. Then they made partners with Allah those who intercede with Him, and they assumed that He necessarily accepts their intercession. Or they appointed some human beings as successors of Allah, who had acquired authority by virtue of their kinship with Allah. But after this truth is made manifest, there is no intercessor with Allah. All these notions are false and disapproved of, and the human mind does not accept them. The human conscience rejects them, and they do not even occur to the mind of a believer.

This is one of the splendours of the Islamic concept of life: there is no illusion or deception in it. In Islamic thought there is no flexibility. Divinity is divinity, and servanthood is servanthood. Between these two realities there is no possibility of any essential meeting. Lord is Lord, and servant is servant. Their natures and temperaments cannot be shared, nor can they be merged or united.

Yes, the servant does have a relationship with his Lord. From the Lord there descends mercy upon the servant. There is nearness, love and assistance. Islam acknowledges this relationship, and it saturates the human soul with a relationship with Allah. Through this the heart of the believer is filled, and the outpouring of mercy and love falls upon it, and the believer lives his life in the pleasant shade of the Lord's mercy. This is without any mixing of the divine essence and the human essence, and without presenting a concept in which truth and falsehood are blended, or in which a heap of false ideas is piled up to create an intellectual confusion and turmoil in which truth and reality do not appear in any clear, pure and transparent form.

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾: Two opposite aspects of this truth are present here. On one hand, it reveals what the concept of the Deity is for a Muslim; on the other hand, it reveals what the station of the Muslim servant is before that Deity. The station of Allah is that He has complete knowledge of every apparent and hidden thing, the present and the absent. He is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. His knowledge is complete, encompassing all particulars and comprising all existence. He encompasses the present existence of a human being, and He also encompasses the past and the future which are hidden from them. He encompasses the matters which human beings know, and also those about which they have no knowledge. In short, in these words there is an indication of the inclusion and comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge. As for human beings, they know only as much as Allah permits them to know.

The first aspect of this truth is that Allah is the Knower of the apparent and the hidden. This truth shakes a person's soul to its core: the human being and his conscience stand completely naked before the Lord. The Exalted Creator is the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing of the apparent and the hidden. Whatever knowledge a person has and whatever he expresses is before Him, and whatever he does not know is also before Him. He knows the past, the present and the future, and that which is concealed, of which the human soul is ignorant. When a person gains true awareness of this reality, a trembling overtakes his body, because he is certain that he stands completely naked before the Lord. Moreover, this conception produces in the human soul the feelings of submission, contentment and fear of God, because He is the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing.

The second aspect of this truth is that human knowledge extends only to the extent that Allah wills. Human beings should reflect on this truth with a calm heart, especially in this age, when they have acquired some information about the natural and creative domains of this universe.

﴿And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾. Only Allah possesses complete knowledge of everything, which is comprehensive and all-inclusive, and His knowledge is unrestricted. By Allah's permission alone certain sciences are unveiled to human beings, and Allah causes these unveilings for the reason that He has promised them, and His promise is always true. He says: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves, until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾. Yet human beings forget this, and the knowledge and truths that Allah unveils to them become a trial for them, whether the unveiling concerns the laws of nature in the universe or concerns those hidden matters which they grasp for a few moments within a set limit. Through these two kinds of truths and the information bestowed upon them, a person falls into trial and misguidance, and he forgets the reality that the true Giver of these unveilings is Allah. Because of this trial and misguidance, they neither give thanks to Allah nor is the remembrance of Allah in their hearts; rather, they become arrogant and conceited, and at times they reach the point of disbelief.

When Allah wished to make the human being His khalifah (vicegerent) on this earth, He favoured him with His recognition. Allah made a promise to the human being that He would soon show him some signs within his own self and in the horizons. Allah's promise is always true, and Allah has fulfilled it in such a way that new secrets are unveiled to the human being day after day. Across generations, the graph of these discoveries keeps rising. These discoveries include natural energies and the physical principles of this universe, which are necessary for the human being to perform the duty of earthly vicegerency, so that through the discovery of these principles he may reach those high ranks which Allah has destined for him.

In this field, Allah has given the human being as much knowledge as He deemed appropriate and has permitted him to work within it. There are also some areas about which Allah has not given the human being knowledge, because he did not need those areas for the office of vicegerency on earth. For example, the secret of life has been kept hidden from the human being, and it remains hidden to this day, and in the future too it does not appear to fall within the grasp of the human mind. Thus the present position is that to debate this subject is like groping in the dark, since there is no clear proof for anything. Likewise, the events of the very next moment have been kept safe and hidden from the human being, because those events are the unseen, and there is no means of access to them. A heavy wall has been erected before them such that the human being cannot remove it. Yet at times Allah lets His special servants glimpse something from behind that hidden veil; then the curtain falls again, silence descends, and the human being's progress halts at a certain point and he cannot advance beyond it.

Many mysteries and secrets have been kept hidden from the human being, the knowledge of which he had no real need of. He could perform the duties of vicegerency on earth without them. And what is the reality of this earth? It is but a speck floating in the expanse of this vast universe created by Allah.

Despite this limitation of his knowledge, and despite the fact that what he has been given is from Allah and by His permission, the human being falls into trial. He begins to regard himself as a god on this earth. Adopting the path of disbelief, he refuses to acknowledge any other deity for this universe. Yet today the scientists of the twentieth century are humbly beginning to admit that their knowledge is limited. They acknowledge that the parts of this universe which they have been able to comprehend are very few. As for some ignorant people who consider themselves scientists, they are deluded into thinking that they know a great deal.

﴿His Throne encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preserving of them does not tire Him﴾.

This position would have called for the sovereignty of Allah to be stated in the abstract, but it is a particular style of the Qur'an that it presents even abstract realities in the form of tangible things. Through this concrete style of depiction, the human mind comes close to the true reality, and thus the truth settles in the human heart and mind. The Kursi is generally understood to mean supreme authority, and when it is said that His Kursi extends beyond the heavens and the earth, it is as if His supreme authority is established over the heavens and the earth. This is a matter from the conceptual aspect, but the picture that settles in the mind through a tangible and solid mode of expression is lasting and firm. The same point lies in ﴿and the preserving of them does not tire Him﴾. In it, by way of metonymy, the perfect power of Allah is declared. Yet this expression too is presented in a tangible manner: Allah does not have to exert any effort in this great act of preservation, nor does any fatigue overtake Him. The Qur'an adopts this mode of expression so that meanings are depicted in such a way that they penetrate the senses, and in this manner these meanings settle well in the human mind and appear as clearly as tangible things do.

Whoever understands this manner of the Qur'an's expression will have no interest in those debates and objections which arose, under the influence of Greek philosophy, concerning this tangible mode of expression in the Qur'an, and over which lengthy disputes continued for a long time. For those debates needlessly tried to make the simple and natural expression of the Qur'an into a riddle, and destroyed its simple beauty. (For details, see my book Al-Tasweer al-Fanni fil-Quran, the chapter on Al-Tasweer al-Fanni and Tariqat al-Quran.)

It suffices here to say that I have not found any authentic hadith in which the Kursi and the Arsh are explained and elucidated. Therefore I consider it appropriate not to say anything further about them.

﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾. Among the attributes mentioned in this verse, these are the last ones, which state a truth and are intended to instil that truth in the human soul. That is, He alone is exalted, and He alone is great. The meaning is that there is none great other than Him and none sublime other than Him. It is not said "He is exalted and great" but rather "He is the Most High and the Most Great." The first expression establishes the attribute of highness and greatness; the second restricts highness and greatness to the Divine Being, and it indicates that none shares with Him in this matter.

He alone is the Most High. He is unique in greatness. And whoever among the servants claims highness and greatness, Allah humiliates and abases him, and in the Hereafter he deserves a humiliating punishment. Allah says: ﴿That is the Last Abode; We assign it to those who do not desire haughtiness upon the earth or corruption﴾ (28:83). And when Pharaoh was destroyed, this comment was made upon him: ﴿Indeed, he was of the haughty﴾.

A human being can rise very high; he can reach the lofty stations of greatness and elevation. But he cannot step outside the bounds and limits of servitude to Allah. When this belief firmly settles in the heart of a believer, it brings him to the station of servitude, and he is protected from arrogance and pride. A humility arises in his disposition, and the fear of Allah and His awe settle in his heart. A consciousness of Allah's majesty and the dignity of His greatness arises in his heart. His conduct becomes extremely respectful, and he does not adopt an attitude of pride or arrogance even towards the servants of Allah. In short, this consciousness is on one side a creed and a conception, and on the other side a manner of conduct and a way of behaving.

After this explanation and elucidation of these subtle aspects of the Islamic conception of life, and after the explanation of what the relationship of this universe and its creatures is with their Creator, and after the clarification of the attributes of the Creator of the universe, the discussion now turns to this topic: once the believers have made this faith-based conception of life their goal, what will their method of action be? How will they call others to this ideology? And what approach will they adopt for the guidance of this misguided humanity?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 256:

A doctrine is something that, once it has been stated and understood, is to be grasped and conveyed through understanding. Doctrines cannot be spread through coercion, oppression and aggression, and this is the very policy Islam has adopted regarding the Islamic way of life. The religion of Islam addresses the human faculty of perception with its full strength and power. It addresses minds that reflect and reason, and it gives a clear line of thought. And it addresses the receptive intuition. Islam addresses the sound human nature, and indeed it influences the whole human personality, and it tests every aspect of human understanding and perception, in which it does not employ coercion and oppression. Indeed, in giving its way of life it does not make much use even of extraordinary means. This is because, as a result of extraordinary events, the human mind is compelled to believe, but despite that belief the human mind remains unable to comprehend the reality. The matter does not enter the human intellect, because by reason of extraordinary spectacles it lies outside the sphere of reason and perception.

If the religion of Islam does not consider it appropriate to use extraordinary spectacles and miracles to implant the Islamic way of life in people's hearts, because this too amounts to compelling the addressee in a certain manner to accept it, then the question of force and compulsion does not arise at all in spreading the Islamic doctrine. It is not Islam's policy to bring people into the fold of Islam through pressure and intimidation; in this matter Islam uses only preaching, exhortation, and mutual understanding and explanation. And it satisfies the hearts and minds of people.

Before Islam, Christianity was the last true religion. Its followers used weapons to spread it. People were burned alive. And as soon as Constantine, the ruler of the Roman Empire, accepted Christianity, the state employed all the means of coercion and oppression and compelled people to accept Christianity. Yet earlier this same government had employed all the means of coercion and oppression against those Christians who had accepted Christianity willingly. The oppression of the Roman Empire was not only against those who were not accepting Christianity, but this oppression also continued ruthlessly against those orthodox Christians who were not prepared to accept the false Trinitarian beliefs of the Roman government concerning the person of Hazrat Masih (peace be upon him).

When Islam came, its very first proclamation was this golden principle: no one should be compelled to accept Islam. Guidance has become clearly distinct from error. Now it is the task of people themselves to accept guidance willingly.

By establishing this principle, Allah honoured the human being with dignity and nobility. His will, his thought and his consciousness were respected, and he was left free to choose either guidance or error in matters of belief. It was told to him that he is a responsible being, and that his deeds and actions will be called to account. This freedom is the most important of the human freedoms that Islam granted to man. It is the freedom of which man is deprived even in this twentieth century. Bigoted ideologies and oppressive systems of life still do not grant man this freedom today. The human being, whom Allah has made honoured, has today been made helpless and subjugated in matters of his beliefs. He is being compelled either to adopt those doctrines which the ruling government spreads with all its resources and through the media, and which are based on conceptions denying God, or else to prepare himself for death.

The truth is that freedom of belief is the first right that a human being should have as a human being. Whoever or whatever system deprives a person of intellectual freedom, in reality strips him of his humanity. The natural demand of freedom of belief is that a person be permitted to propagate his faith, and that he be safe and secure in doing so. If freedom of belief is not accompanied by freedom of expression, then freedom of opinion becomes meaningless and loses all reality.

Islam is an excellent conception of life and existence, and without doubt it is an excellent and firm system of life. It is Islam alone that proclaims openly that in the religion that is chosen there is no compulsion or coercion. It first enjoins upon its adherents that they cannot compel people to accept the religion of Islam. When a religion of nature like Islam cannot compel people to become Muslims, how can its other prevailing false religions be permitted to make life narrow for those who do not accept those religions merely on the strength of state power?

Here the absolute negation of compulsion and coercion is made. That is, in religion there is no compulsion at all. That is, the very genus of compulsion will not exist in religion. That is, the existence of compulsion itself will not be there; it will not even occur. It is not said here, "Do not commit compulsion," which would imply that compulsion would exist but you should not commit it. The negation of the genus of compulsion and of the existence of compulsion means that Allah is emphatically insisting that in Islam the question of compulsion simply does not arise, and this manner of expression is extremely effective.

Here the context of the discourse touches the human conscience and awakens it, encourages it to adopt the path of guidance, turns it towards the straight path, and it is made clear that the reality of faith which has been proclaimed has become clear and distinct. It says: "The right course has become clearly distinct from the wrong..." (qad tabayyana al-rushdu mina al-ghayy). The path of faith is the path of guidance. A person should seize it and hasten towards it. And disbelief is misguidance. A person should hate it and should not provide for himself occasions to be associated with it.

The practical situation is such that people are not trying to attain the reality of the treasure of faith. Faith gives humanity a clean and pure conception of life. It grants humanity tranquillity of heart and safety. It produces in the minds and hearts of people lofty values and pure priorities. It gives human society a healthy system of life and a progressive policy, by which life becomes developed and diversified. If a person were to reflect upon the reality of faith along these lines, then none but a fool would fail to adopt the path of faith. He would abandon guidance for error, and leave the straight path for a crooked one. In place of tranquillity, safety, elevation and loftiness, he would adopt restlessness, anxiety, decline and misguidance.

Then, further clarifying and explaining the reality of faith, it is said: "Whoever disbelieves in the Taghut and believes in Allah has indeed grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which will never break..." (faman yakfur bil-taghuti wa yu'min billahi faqadi istamsaka bil-'urwati al-wuthqa la infisama laha).

Al-Taghut derives from tughyan (transgression). The meaning is every person who goes beyond sound thought, who rebels against the truth, who moves beyond the limits that Allah has set for His servants. One who has no organised belief about Allah, who is not bound by the Shariah of Allah. Likewise, every system that is not derived from the Divine Being is a taghutish system. Likewise, every belief and all customs and traditions that are not derived from the Divine Being are taghut. Thus, the one who is upon the right path is the one who rejects all these forms and all these shapes of taghut and believes in Allah alone, and he is the one who succeeds. Its example is like a person who, in difficult circumstances, grasps a firm support that will never fall.

Here we find ourselves before a tangible picture of a conscious reality. To believe in Allah is in fact to have available a support that never suffers decline. It is a firm, unbreakable support, and whoever grasps this support firmly will never go astray. This support is directly connected with the One who is the master of success and failure. Faith is in fact the name of attaining that supreme reality upon which all the realities of this universe are established, namely, attaining the Divine Being. Faith is the name of attaining that great order which the Divine Being has established for the universe, and upon which this universe stands. And whoever strengthens his faith, walking on the straight path, reaches his Lord. His feet do not slip, he does not lag behind, nor does he fall into the labyrinths, nor into aimlessness, nor does he become a victim of misguidance.

"And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing..." (wallahu sami'un 'alim). He hears the speech of all languages. He knows the hidden contents of hearts. Therefore whoever believes in that Being will not be at a loss. No injustice will be done to him, and he will never fail.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 257 (part 1 of 2):

The discourse now moves forward, and a vivid, moving scene is painted. The straight path of guidance and the paths of misguidance and error stand clearly before the eyes. One sees on the screen that Allah takes the believers by the hand and brings them out of darkness into light, while the Taghut, who are the helpers of the disbelievers, take hold of the hands of the disbelievers and lead them from the light of faith into the darkness of disbelief.

This is a wondrous, vibrant, living scene. The steed of imagination gallops at one moment toward one scene and at another toward the other. It returns from here and bolts off there. Such a static and motionless style of speech, which occupies the place of discourse, cannot spur on the steed of imagination. Neither can human feeling enjoy it, nor does conscience and intuition stir. And it can address only the human intellect through words alone.

If we wish to gauge the greatness of the Word of Allah correctly, we could express this same meaning in different words, for example, by saying: Allah is the friend of the Muslims; He brings them to the path of faith, and those who adopt disbelief draw them toward the path of disbelief. "See, these words and this manner of speech lie before us lifeless. In them there is not that warmth, that movement and that inspiration which are in the Word of Allah." (For details, see the chapter "Tariqat al-Quran" in my book al-Tasvir al-Fanni fi al-Quran.)

Yet, along with this sensory and evocative depiction, observe the beauty of expression and the realistic conveyance of meaning in the Holy Quran.

Allah is the Walī of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their walis are the Taghut; they bring them out of light into darkness. "Those who believe, their helper and supporter is Allah, and He brings them out of darkness into light; and those who take the path of disbelief, their helpers and supporters are the Taghut, and they lead them away into darkness."

The truth is that faith is light. In its nature and reality, it is a unique light. And indeed disbelief is darkness, and in its nature and reality it is manifold and diverse, yet all of it is darkness. The truth is that describing faith with light and disbelief with darkness is an excellent description. It is a most realistic manner of expression.

When the spark of faith first kindles in the heart of the believer, through it the whole personality of the believer is filled with light. His soul becomes illuminated and he attains tranquility. The result is that the soul of a believer spreads light in his environment; his surroundings become bright and clear. By this light, the reality of all existent things comes to the fore; the explanation of all values is made; the true nature of all concepts of life is revealed. The heart and mind of the believer grasp all these truths clearly, without any admixture. He sees every value in its own place and gives it its proper station.

Faith is a light through which a believer comprehends the law of nature prevailing in this universe. Now this believer aligns his conduct with the law of nature prevailing in this universe, which flows and operates around him. And he advances on his path with seriousness and dignity. Since he has fully grasped his path, he neither goes astray anywhere nor becomes entangled in insignificant obstacles along his way.

This is a light which shows one single, unique path. The darknesses of disbelief are of various kinds: the darkness of lust and willfulness, the darkness of immorality and depravity, the darkness of arrogance, pride and rebelliousness, the darkness of slavery and weakness, the darkness of hypocrisy and dissimulation, the darkness of greed and profiteering, the darkness of doubt and restlessness; in short, there are countless and innumerable darknesses, all of which are darknesses of disbelief and misguidance, and their common nature is that a person enveloped in them turns away from the path of Allah. He seeks guidance from other than Allah and lives according to a non-Islamic system of life. And as soon as a person abandons this unique light of Allah, this single realistic and clear light, he becomes trapped in one of the various darknesses of disbelief. These darknesses are diverse, and all of them are darknesses of the Hippie kind. And what is the end of these darknesses? Those who live in these darknesses: "Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever." (Quran 2:257) "They are the people of the Fire, and they will remain in it forever." If these people do not strive to find guidance in the light of Islam, then they deserve to remain in the Fire forever.

The truth is that truth is one unique reality. Truths cannot be two, misguidance has many kinds and forms, and whatever lies outside truth and righteousness is all misguidance.

Before we conclude our discussion of this lesson and move on, it is appropriate that we make a principled point about the rule: "There is no compulsion in religion" (Quran 2:256). Alongside this general rule, Islam has also enjoined the obligation of jihad, and there have been occasions on which Islam took part in jihad. Yet in an earlier verse it is said: "And fight them until there is no more fitnah and the religion is for Allah" (Quran 2:193).

Some of Islam's self-interested enemies have alleged that enjoining jihad alongside the principle "There is no compulsion in religion" is a contradictory matter. In response to this question, some people, while apparently defending Islam and inwardly being hostile to Islam, have tried to remove the spirit of jihad from the consciousness of Muslims. Such people try to diminish the importance of the obligation of jihad, although the obligation of jihad has played a very important role in the establishment of Islam and its propagation. Such people, with great cunning, in a very gentle manner and in a very wise-seeming way, want to instill in the hearts of Muslims that today there is no longer any need for jihad, nor can there ever be a need for the obligation of jihad in future. Apparently these people say this in defense of Islam (see Arnold's book "The Preaching of Islam," translated by Dr. Ibrahim Hasan and Brothers).

Both kinds of these people are Orientalists who work in the same field. Both are at war against Islam. They want to distort the Islamic method. These people want to eliminate the consciousness which the system of jihad creates in the soul of a Muslim. These people fear the consciousness of jihad in Islam, because on the battlefield of jihad they were never able to confront Islam. Therefore, by erasing this consciousness, they want to create security and tranquility for themselves; and since they removed jihad from the heart of the Muslim, or confused it, they have struck decisive blows against the body of the Muslim Ummah from various directions and have defeated it on every front. These people are trying to convey to the Muslim Ummah that the war between Muslim nations and the colonial power is merely a war over economic and commercial markets. Therefore, in this war the Muslim Ummah should not bring in the spirit of jihad, which is useful only in ideological warfare. Hence, in this modern age, talk of jihad is without justification.

Islam first initiated jihad at the time when persecution was being inflicted upon Muslims, so that their lives, property and way of life could be protected; that is, jihad for the establishment of peace. We have already explained this principle in the second part of this commentary, at the occasion of the commentary on the verse: "And fitnah is worse than killing" (Quran 2:191). In accordance with this principle, Islam declared ideological oppression, and the physical torment resulting from it, and the cruelty inflicted upon the people of an ideology because of their ideology, to be worse than killing. According to this principle, the value of ideologies is greater even than human life. If a Muslim is permitted to take up arms in defense of his wealth and his life, then he is all the more permitted to take up arms in defense of his religion, creed and ideology. At that time, Muslims were being ground under the millstone of oppression solely because of their creed. They had no other option before them except to take up arms in defense of their most precious wealth, namely the wealth of faith. This oppression was being inflicted upon them solely because of their creed, and these persecutions were being carried out in various parts of the globe. The land of Andalusia has witnessed these brutal atrocities. It bears witness to the mass slaughter and plunder inflicted upon Muslims solely because of their religion and creed. Then this land also bears witness to the atrocities which the Catholic sect of Christians committed against other sects, in order to forcibly make them Catholic. Today the condition of Spain is that Muslims and other Christian sects have been wiped out from there. Then Jerusalem and the surrounding Islamic territories are well acquainted with the Crusader invasions, whose target was solely to dominate the Islamic ideology of life and the religion of Islam. The people of Islam defended against these wars also on the platform of the Islamic ideology of life, and they succeeded in this well, and saved that region from the unfortunate fate of Andalusia. Even today, in communist regions, idolatrous regions, Jewish regions and Christian regions, Muslims are being oppressed, and this is solely because they are Muslims. Therefore, if they are Muslims in the true sense, then jihad is obligatory upon them today just as it was obligatory before, so that these oppressions against Muslims may be stopped.

The second motive behind the Islamic doctrine of jihad was that, after ideological freedom, opportunities should also be created for the freedom of ideological preaching and propagation. Islam presents an excellent solution to human life and to this universe. It proposes an excellent system for the development of human life on this earth. It wishes to convey this excellent creed and complete system to all of humanity, so that they may hear and understand it; and after hearing and understanding, they are free to accept it or reject it. For Islam does not advocate any coercion or compulsion in matters of creed. But before complete ideological freedom, there is a need that there be no obstacle in the way of the Islamic message reaching all humanity, because this message has been sent by Allah for all people. Therefore, all the obstacles that stand in the way of the common people hearing this message, accepting it, and, if they wish, joining the caravan of those guided, must be removed. Among these obstacles, the greatest is the tyrannical system of life established on this earth. This system stands as a barrier between the common people and this message. And those who, somehow, hear this creed and message and embrace it, this tyrannical system begins to persecute them. Therefore, whenever Islam has waged jihad, it has eliminated such false and tyrannical systems of life, and in place of such systems it has established a just system of life in which the call of truth and the caller to truth enjoy complete freedom everywhere. This aim and objective remains in place even today. Therefore, even today jihad is obligatory upon Muslims, so that they may spread this message, provided that Muslims are truly Muslims.

Another objective for which Islam has permitted jihad is the establishment and protection of the Islamic system of life. This is the only system of life which grants a human being the freedom to reach out to his fellow human being. And in it every human being is also completely free with respect to other human beings. In this system, worship is reserved exclusively for the One God, Exalted and Supreme. And this system eliminates from the world every kind of slavery that one human being imposes upon another. In this system no individual, no class, and no nation can legislate for another human being, nor can anyone make human beings his slaves and subjects through such legislation. In this system all human beings have one Lord. He lays down laws for all humanity with perfect equality. And all human beings bow in prostration before that Lord with humility and submission; they worship only that one Lord and believe only in Him. In this system, obedience to one human being by another is practiced in only one case: when that person is the implementer of the Shariah of Allah, and the task of implementing the Shariah has been entrusted to him by the Ummah. Even the implementation of the Shariah cannot be undertaken by anyone on his own, because legislation is solely the work of Allah. In human life, the Shariah is a manifestation of the majesty of Allah. Therefore no human being is entitled to reserve for himself the task of framing the Shariah, although he is merely a servant of Allah.

This is the fundamental principle of the Islamic system of life, and as a result of this principle and constitution there grows a pure moral system of life in which all of humanity enjoys complete liberty and freedom, including those people who do not accept the Islamic creed of life at all. In this system, the honor of every person is protected, and even those who do not accept the Islamic system of life at all have their rights protected, every inhabitant who resides in an Islamic country, whatever his creed may be. In this system, no one is compelled to adopt the Islamic creed. In it, no one is compelled in matters of religion. In it, there is only freedom of preaching.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 2, verse 257 (part 2 of 2):

Islam has made jihad obligatory for the sole purpose of establishing in the world the above-mentioned exalted and perfect system of life, and of taking measures to support and protect it. It was Islam's right that, through jihad, it should eliminate false and corrupt systems of life which were founded on the principle that some human beings are the slaves of other human beings, and in which some human beings claimed the station of divinity and assumed divine functions, although this was not their right. And it is evident that when Islam rises with this objective, the false systems of life also rise up against it and become its enemies. Therefore there was no alternative but for Islam to eliminate these tyrannical systems and, in their place, to proclaim on this earth its own exalted and perfect system. Then, under the shelter of this system, it grants them freedom within their particular beliefs, and the only obligations upon them are adherence to Islam's collective civil code, Islamic ethics, and the economic policy of the state. As for religious and inner beliefs and inclinations, they are completely free in these matters. In their personal laws and transactions too, they are completely free. They may settle their affairs according to their own beliefs, but the Islamic system of life shall be established over them, which protects them. Their freedom shall be safeguarded under its shadow. They shall have complete freedom of opinion, their honour shall be protected, and they shall receive their full fundamental rights, but within the framework of this system.

This jihad remains even now, and it is obligatory upon Muslims to keep this jihad in place for the establishment of the Islamic system of life.

﴿Until there is no more fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah﴾ ... "until no fitnah remains and the religion becomes entirely Allah's." And that human divinity ends in this world, and that no worship or servitude except to Allah remains in the world. (For a fuller explanation of the question of jihad, see the book "Al-Jihad fi al-Islam" by the great Muslim Sayyid Abul A'la Mawdudi. Also my book "As-Salam al-Alami fi al-Islam" (Sayyid Qutb).)

In short, Islam did not take up the sword in order to compel people to adopt Islamic beliefs and concepts. Nor did the spread of Islam in the world occur by the force of the sword, as some enemies of Islam allege. Rather, the truth is that Islam began jihad in order to establish on this earth a peaceful system of life, under whose shade people of all beliefs and various religious conceptions could live a life of peace and harmony. Yes, they may preserve their beliefs and live freely within the political sphere of Islam, even if they do not accept Islamic beliefs.

For the existence of the Islamic system, its expansion, and the peace and security of the people of Islam, and for the peace and tranquillity of those who wished to enter this system of life, the armed power of Islam was urgently needed. Likewise, for the establishment and protection of religion, the existence of armed power was absolutely essential. The institution of Islamic jihad is not of minor importance. It is not the case that there is no need for it at present, or that there will be no need for it in the future. The worst enemy of Muslims makes them believe that jihad is no longer necessary. Yet the truth is that Islam needs a collective system, this system needs a collective strength, and this strength lies in the spirit of jihad. This is the nature of Islam, without which Islam cannot be established nor can it play its leading role.

﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ ... But alongside this, the Holy Qur'an also gives this command:

﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of power and of steeds of war, by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy and others besides them whom you do not know but Allah knows.﴾

This is the fundamental point in the view of Islam, and in its light Muslims should understand their religion, and from this perspective the people of Islam should read their history. Muslims should not adopt, regarding the Islamic theory of jihad, a stance in which they stand like an accused person trying to defend themselves. In this matter they should adopt the stance of a confident, determined and self-respecting person who is convinced that he is higher than all the concepts of this world. The Islamic system is higher than all systems, and the religion of Islam is above all religions. The people of Islam should not be deceived by those who, while apparently appearing to defend the religion of Islam, are in reality scraping and removing the concept of jihad from their hearts and minds, in order that they may protect the nations hostile to Islam. Jihad is in essence a process that shatters the supremacy of oppressive tyranny. And there is good for all humanity in jihad. The greatest enemy of humanity is the one who deprives it of jihad and erects obstacles in the path of humanity and jihad. Therefore such a person is regarded as enemy number one of humanity. And if there is any guidance and right direction in humanity, it should pursue this great enemy of humanity. Because the believers are a chosen community; they have been distinguished by the gift of faith. Therefore, both for their own souls and for the sake of all humanity, it is their duty to pursue the denier of jihad, and this is a duty for which, according to the Sharia, they will be held accountable before Allah.

Lesson 18 at a Glance

These are three verses, and their subject is one: what is the reality of life and death, and what is the secret of life after death? The belief in life after death is an important aspect of Islamic doctrine, on which the Qur'an has reasoned at length, and from the beginning of this Juz' it is discussed repeatedly. Moreover, these verses are directly connected with the attributes of God mentioned in Ayat al-Kursi. All these verses reveal the clear endeavour of the Qur'an, which it is making to create in the consciousness and perception of a Muslim a correct Islamic outlook on life. For an insightful assessment of human life, there is a need for a clear and pure concept of it in the human mind, one based on a true observation of this universe and founded on firm and heartfelt conviction. This is because if the entire system of human life, the complete conduct of man, and the rules of all his morals and manners are not deeply connected with this belief, this worldview and this complete conception of the universe, then that system of life can be neither firm and stable nor have any constant standard. This is why the Qur'an has placed great emphasis on purifying ideas and on the clarification and firming up of beliefs and concepts, and the Meccan period of the Qur'an consists mostly of this. The same pattern is also seen in the verses of the Medinan period, where detailed guidance and legislation also take place.

Among these, the first verses relate the conversation that took place between Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and the king of his time. The name of the king is not given here, because mentioning his name adds nothing to the essential matter. Here, before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslim community, this conversation is presented with astonishment, that this person debated with Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about the Lord of the universe and adopted such a foolish stance. He and the Qur'an, in their own eloquent style, have related this debate.

This person who debated with Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was not a denier of the existence of God. If he was a denier, he was a denier of Allah's Oneness and Lordship.
