He was not prepared to accept Allah as the sole Controller and sole Sustainer of this universe, just as among the misguided people of the age of ignorance (jahiliyyah) there were some who acknowledged the existence of God but associated others with Allah, and attributed certain acts and events to those partners. Likewise, these people also denied the attribute of Allah's sovereignty (hakimiyyah). According to the Islamic worldview, just as the cosmic affairs of this universe are in the hand of Allah, so too the authority for legislation and the decision of collective affairs rests with Allah, and He has no partner in this.

This denier of the truth, the king, was very obstinate, and he was a denier of the truth because Allah had given him kingship.

[Qur'anic text: "أَنْ آتَاهُ اللَّهُ الْمُلْكَ" — "because Allah had given him the kingdom."] Whereas the requirement of this cause was that, because of it, he should have become a firm believer, grateful and acknowledging of Allah's favours. But he adopted the path of disbelief and rebellion because of his power and kingship, and he showed ingratitude for this blessing of Allah, and he did not grasp the true reality and the real concept of this bounty and honour. In place of gratitude, he adopted the way of disbelief, and that which should have been the cause of their guidance became the cause of their misguidance. They are rulers because Allah has made them rulers; Allah did not make them rulers so that they might make the common people their own servants and make them follow laws made by themselves. They themselves are servants of Allah, just as other people are servants of Allah. Like them, they also receive the law from Allah. When they rebel against Allah, they neither remain rulers nor can they make any law. These rulers are caliphs (khulafa'), not the true sovereigns.

This is why, when these kings debate with the prophet of their time, Allah finds their conduct strange.

[Qur'anic text: "أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى الَّذِي حَاجَّ إِبْرَاهِيمَ فِي رَبِّهِ أَنْ آتَاهُ اللَّهُ الْمُلْكَ" — "Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship?"] "Have you not considered?" This is an expression of astonishment at a blameworthy attitude and a contemptuous manner of conduct. Denial and disdain go together because of their verbal and semantic harmony. The conduct of this king is in reality reprehensible, because if someone begins to argue and dispute on account of having been given favours, it is certainly blameworthy. It is also blameworthy that someone should appropriate to himself the attributes of the Lord of the universe, and that a ruler should rule over the common people according to his own desires and not seek guidance from Allah in the work of legislation and interpretation.

[Qur'anic text: "إِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ رَبِّيَ الَّذِي يُحْيِي وَيُمِيتُ" — "When Ibrahim said: My Lord is He who gives life and causes death."] "Life and death are events the recurrence of which takes place every moment. These realities constantly come before human perception and human intellect. But despite this repetition and frequency of occurrence, life and death are an astonishing mystery. To solve this sealed secret, human reason turns to a source that is beyond humanity, and to a point of reference and origin that has no connection with this creation. Therefore, for the correct solution of this unsolvable riddle, it is necessary for a person to turn to the Divine Being, who is capable of creating and also capable of annihilating."

"Until today we have not been able to grasp the reality of death and life. However, among the living we perceive the signs of life, and from the dead we learn the characteristics of death. Therefore we are compelled to entrust the reality of life and death to the true power that is beyond all the powers we know, namely Divine power."

This is why Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) stated one attribute of his Lord in which He has no partner, and in which no one can imagine that he could be a co-worker. When this king asked Ibrahim (peace be upon him), "Who is your Lord who makes laws for you, who holds supreme authority and who possesses full powers of legislation?", Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) answered that my Lord is He in whose hand are life and death. Therefore He alone is the Ruler and Legislator.

Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) knew well the reality of life and death, and by life and death he meant that Allah is the Creator of these realities, because he was a messenger and was granted those innate secrets and mysteries about which we discussed in the first part. The creation of life and death is an action in which none of Allah's servants share with Him. But the king who was debating with Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) thought that he was the absolute ruler of his people; all his commands are enforced upon his people; he can impose the death penalty and can also pardon. So in effect this too is a kind of lordship. Therefore he said to Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him): "I am the chief of this people. Their affairs are in my hand. Therefore I too am a kind of lord, before whom you too should bow and acknowledge my rule and supreme authority." Accordingly he said: "I give life and cause death" [Qur'anic text: "أَنَا أُحْيِي وَأُمِيتُ" — "I give life and cause death."].

On this occasion Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) did not deem it appropriate to begin a detailed discussion with him on the subject of the reality of life and death, especially with a person who was himself in doubt and wavering about the reality of life and death, which has always been a difficult question: that is, the mystery of how Allah grants life to a human being and how He brings death upon him. This is a secret which the whole of humanity has not been able to reach up to today. So at this point Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) thought it fitting to set aside that difficult cosmic reality of Allah and to take recourse to an outward sign which constantly comes before this person's observation. First he presented only the cosmic Divine practice, that Allah is He who gives life and causes death. Now he adopted an outward challenge to his opponent: "You argue about the power of Allah; then change one of Allah's laws and see." He gave this challenge in order to show that a lord is not one who rules over one department of human life or over one region; rather he exercises control over the whole universe, and the demand of his general lordship is that he should also be a legislator for all people, because He is their Lord.

So Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: [Qur'anic text: "فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْتِي بِالشَّمْسِ مِنَ الْمَشْرِقِ فَأْتِ بِهَا مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ" — "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west."] "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." This too is a continuously occurring cosmic reality. Our eyes see this sight every day, our perceptive faculty finds it every day, and never does any delay or interruption occur in this system. This universe is a witness that appeals to our nature, even though we may not fully understand the disposition and temperament of this universe, and even though we may not have acquired knowledge of the various theories about astronomy. This is because Allah has sent prophets, and they have always addressed human nature. Whatever stage human nature may be at in its intellectual and rational development, and whatever levels of progress human nature may have attained collectively, the prophets have taken hold of human nature's hand and brought it to the next levels of progress. This is why Hadrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) challenged that king, and the argument based on observation of nature was unanswerable. The result was: [Qur'anic text: "فَبُهِتَ الَّذِي كَفَرَ" — "So the one who disbelieved was confounded."] "So the denier of the truth was dumbfounded."

This challenge stood before that denier of the truth. The matter was perfectly clear; there was no room for any misunderstanding. The appropriate course would have been for him to believe straightforwardly and bow in submission, but the one who adopts a disbelieving attitude and then also becomes arrogant, these qualities prevent him from returning to the truth, and he remains perplexed, troubled and bewildered. He does not know what to do and what not to do. But Allah does not show him the path of truth because he is not one who seeks guidance at all; he has no desire to come to the path of truth. He does not take the straight way so that he may reach the destination. Therefore the result is: [Qur'anic text: "وَاللَّهُ لا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الظَّالِمِينَ" — "And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."] "But Allah does not guide the wrongdoers."

Allah presented this event before His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and his first community, the Muslim community, as an example of enmity, malice, misguidance and obstinacy. Also for those who carry out the work of Islamic call (da'wah) in the modern age. It was recorded in the Qur'an as a historical experience, showing how the people of the call should confront those who deny the truth.

The context, moving on, takes up such realities as are the constituent elements of a clear outlook together with faith and certainty: "My Lord is He in whose power are life and death," and "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east; you, then, bring it from the west." One reality is found in human souls; the other is manifest in the horizons of the universe. Both are great cosmic realities, yet alongside their greatness they are commonplace, present in daily observation, the daily abode of thought and vision, and attaining these realities requires no great scholarly capacity, nor any lengthy reflection. Allah is merciful and generous to His servants. In the matter of faith in Allah and being guided to Allah, He does not engage in the kind of scholarly and logical debate that lies beyond the reach of an ignorant person, or beyond the intellectual capacity of those who are novices in reflection. This is a living and important matter; it is indispensable for human nature. Without it human life cannot be established, nor can human society be organised. Without it, people cannot recognise the source of their collective system, their supreme authority and their etiquettes. Therefore Allah, in addressing man on the matter of faith, keeps in view those realities which are before everyone and which relate to human nature, and which are such that every sound nature acknowledges them of its own accord. The indications of these realities and observations are so firm that a person can hardly escape their grip, and to free himself from them he must resort to extreme effort, hardship, pride, arrogance and stubborn obstinacy.

Beyond beliefs and matters of faith, in those affairs of human life on which human existence wholly depends, man too follows the path of nature and remains within the sphere of nature's signs. For example, in matters such as the search for livelihood, air, water, and reproduction and multiplication, man has not been left to his own condition even in these vital matters. Until his thinking became complete and mature, and his knowledge advanced and became firm. Had he been left as he is, he would have long since been destroyed and ruined. Faith is as important and necessary for man as food, drink, and air are necessary for his life. This is why Allah, the Exalted, speaks on these subjects in accordance with the demands of the human nature, and presents such signs and evidences as are spread over the face of the universe around man.

Who was this man who passed by a town? What was that town which had fallen upon its roofs? The Qur'an is silent about this. And if it had been the will of Allah, the Qur'an would have given details about that town. If omitting these details would have made any difference to the expression and explanation of the wisdom of the Qur'an, then the Qur'an would certainly have mentioned these details. Here only a glimpse of this town has been shown, and in keeping with the method of Fi Zilal al-Quran, we too do not consider it appropriate to go beyond this glimpse into details. The glimpse of this town that has been shown is extremely clear, impactful, and is imprinted and engraved upon the mind. A clear picture of death, then decay and collapse, with all its features, becomes fixed in the mind. ﴿وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَى عُرُوشِهَا﴾ "...which lay fallen upon its roofs." This town has fallen onto its foundations and has been reduced to rubble. The person who passes by it has this thought arise in his feelings. He begins to think ﴿قَالَ أَنَّىٰ يُحْيِي هَٰذِهِ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا﴾ "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" "This settlement which has been completely destroyed, how will Allah give it life again?"

The speaker believes that Allah exists, but on seeing the present state of ruin and destruction of this town, he thinks. In his feelings this notion arises: how will Allah make it vibrant and flourishing again after this all-encompassing destruction? This expression of feelings! The feelings that can arise upon seeing a scene. The Qur'an expresses them with great tenderness and impactful expression. Thus the Qur'an imprints its own image and its expressions upon the mind of the addressee. Thus it appears that the scene is present before the reader as if seen directly. He is seeing it, and in his heart the very feelings are arising that once arose in the heart of that man.

﴿أَنَّىٰ يُحْيِي هَٰذِهِ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا﴾ "How will He give it life?" How will construction emerge from this destruction? ﴿فَأَمَاتَهُ اللَّهُ مِائَةَ عَامٍ ثُمَّ بَعَثَهُ﴾ "So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him up." Allah did not tell him in words that he would be brought to life in this way. Rather, it was shown to him in the world of events as an experience. Because impressions and awareness are sometimes so deep and subtle that they cannot be expressed through rational proofs, nor can such an impression be created through logic or intuition. Sometimes it happens that even ordinary and commonplace events cannot give rise to such an impression. This awareness and impression can only be produced through direct personal experience. After such an experience, this awareness overcomes a person's feelings. The heart becomes content with it, and then no further need for assurance remains.

﴿قَالَ كَمْ لَبِثْتَ قَالَ لَبِثْتُ يَوْمًا أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ﴾ "Allah asked him, 'How long have you remained?' He said, 'I have remained a day or part of a day.'" How could he know how long he had remained? The sense and awareness of time comes when a person is alive and his understanding is functioning. It is a reality in itself that human sense is in fact not a correct standard for perceiving reality, because the senses sometimes deceive and sometimes are deceived in perceiving reality. For example, here the sense was deceived in perceiving a long period of time, and he took it to be a day or even less. And sometimes it happens that the human sense considers a short period to be a long time.

﴿قَالَ بَلْ لَبِثْتَ مِائَةَ عَامٍ﴾ "Allah said, 'Rather, you have remained a hundred years.'" The nature of this experience required, especially since it was a sensory experience, that there should necessarily be signs indicating that a long period of a hundred years had passed. But the signs of food and drink of this man did not show such signs, because no change had occurred in his food and drink. Nor had they become spoiled and rotten.

﴿فَانْظُرْ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِكَ وَشَرَابِكَ لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ﴾ "Look at your food and your drink, it has not spoiled." And clearly, such signs could then relate only to the person himself or to his donkey.

﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلَىٰ حِمَارِكَ وَلِنَجْعَلَكَ آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ وَانْظُرْ إِلَى الْعِظَامِ كَيْفَ نُنْشِزُهَا ثُمَّ نَكْسُوهَا لَحْمًا﴾
"And look at your donkey—and We do this so that We may make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh."

Which bones? Does it mean the bones of this man? If it were so, as some commentators say, that the bones of this man had become bare of flesh and skin, then when sight was placed in his eyes and he began to understand, he would first have looked at his own condition and begun to think. And at that time his answer would not have been ﴿لَبِثْتُ يَوْمًا أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ﴾ "I have remained a day or part of a day."

Therefore the correct interpretation is that these bones refer only to the skeleton of the donkey, which had become bare of flesh and skin and separated. After this, the miracle occurred that these bones began to join together. Flesh and skin began to cover them. And then that very same intact donkey was brought back to life. And this man, who during that long period had himself remained intact in his original condition along with his food and drink, saw this miracle unfold before his very eyes. So that in one place, the stark difference in the outcome of these two material things, although the atmosphere and the seasonal influences were the same, might manifest another miracle. This miracle shows that Allah has complete power over His creation. His power and authority are unrestricted. Through this miracle it becomes evident that Allah will bring the whole universe back to life, and its condition will be somewhat like this.

Here the question arises: how did this miracle occur? It occurred in the same way that all miracles occur. In this way the miracle of bringing the first life into existence on the earth took place, which we often forget. We do not know how the beginning of life came about. How did life come? It came, and as Allah willed, He brought it, and it is what stands before us. Darwin was a high-ranking scientist among biologists. He kept advancing his theories step by step downward. He wandered far into the depths of life, and finally he was able to reach the point where its beginning is a living cell. Here he stops, and his path is closed from ahead. How did life enter this living cell? He cannot discover this secret. Yet despite this, he is not willing to accept the reality that human perception ought to accept, which human natural thought and logic compel at every moment to be accepted: that a Being be acknowledged who gave life to that cell. Darwin's refusal is not based on any scientific or logical proof, but rather on the attitude of the church toward people of knowledge and wisdom throughout its history. Because of this prejudice, Darwin says, "An explanation of the affairs of life in which the existence of a Creator is acknowledged is like adding an extraordinary element to a purely physical mechanism." The question is: what is that physical mechanism? The mechanism has no remote connection with the reality that stands before our thought and view and insistently demands that we explain its secret, namely the secret of the first life.

There comes a stage at which even Darwin himself is helpless before this natural order and logical reasoning. The reasoning which insistently demands that the Creator of the universe be acknowledged behind the first cell, he presents the first cell as the result of a first cause. And if someone asks him, what is this first cause? He has no answer from the biologist. Yet this is an important question: who is the originator of life within the first cell? Without answering this question, he begins his theory from that cell, although today this famous theory of his has also become questionable. His theory is that life in its present form is an advanced development of that cell, whereas there may be, and is, another mode of operation for the beginning of life.

Darwin could not answer the important question about the beginning of life. He took the path of escape and presented his own fabricated, bogus theory. (For details see the chapter "Freud" in the book "Al-Insan bain al-Maddiyyah wal-Islam.")

The clarification of this contradictory situation is actually made clear by the fact that the will of Allah is unrestricted. Allah's will is free even from that all-encompassing law of nature which we consider necessary and absolute and which sits in our minds; this law of nature cannot be opposed, nor can any particular be excluded from it. For us it is sufficient that the belief that no change can occur in the law of nature with regard to the will of Allah is false. And this confusion arises for us because we necessarily apply our estimations or rational judgments, and so-called scientific principles, even to the Being of Allah. This is the error of our thinking which gives birth to many other errors.

1. For example, when do we have the right to make the Absolute Powerful subject to the law that we profess, which has been derived from our limited resources and limited experiences? Then, because of our limited faculty of perception, we interpret those experiences, in which the possibility of error is always present.

2. Suppose we correctly understood one of the laws of nature, and it truly is a law of nature. But who told us that this law is the most absolute law, unconditional, and that there is no law or principle more universal, comprehensive, or inclusive than it?

3. Suppose we grant that this law is absolute, is unconditional, and under ordinary circumstances deviation from it is not possible. But this law is laid down by Allah. How did the Being of the Divine become confined within a law that He Himself made? The Being of the Divine is, after all, the Absolute Master of all.

In short, this experience proceeds in this way. It adds to the intellectual capital of modern people of the call a correct faith-based conception of life, and along with the manifestation of the reality of life and death, it adds this other reality to which we have just alluded: that Allah's will is unrestricted. The Qur'an has repeatedly stated this reality in order to firmly establish it in the conscience of the believers, so that believers establish a direct relationship with their Allah, attach no importance to apparent causes in this regard, and do not regard those intermediaries that are commonly considered binding. Allah does whatever He wills. And this is exactly what that man said, before whom this experience was repeated: ﴿فَلَمَّا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ قَالَ أَعْلَمُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ "When it became clear to him, he said, 'I know that Allah is over all things competent.'"

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 2, verse 260:

After this, a third experience of the reality of death and life is described. This experience was given to Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who is among the great prophets of the Muslim ummah.

This is a longing to reach the workings of divine power (qadr-e-Ilahiyah). The longing expressed by Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who was a most forbearing, obedient and resolute prophet (ulul-azm), shows that sometimes a desire arises even in the hearts of the chosen and closest servants of Allah to gain access to the secrets hidden behind the workings of Allah's power. The expression of this desire by a servant like Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who was content with Allah's decree, humble, submissive and devoted in worship, is in reality the result of this same kind of longing.

This longing is not connected with faith, with the perfection of faith, or with the firmness and steadfastness of faith. Through this longing, Ibrahim was not demanding a stronger proof, nor did he wish to remove a weakness in his faith and attain firmness in it. These things he already possessed. Gaining access to the secrets behind the veil is in fact a different kind of yearning. It is a kind of spiritual longing. The believing servant wishes to be connected with the secrets of Allah and wishes to see these events taking place in practice. Such zeal and longing is a natural matter in the human being. It has no connection with belief in the unseen (iman bil-ghaib). Belief in the unseen exists in its perfect degree, and yet this impulse also exists in its perfect degree. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was speaking with the Essence of the Lord, and the Generous Lord was speaking with Ibrahim (peace be upon him). What more faith or what more proof did Ibrahim (peace be upon him) need than this conversation? What he wished to see was that he might see power working in the workshop of creation, so that the longing for attaining the secrets within might find satisfaction. He wished to become a companion of these secrets and to be absorbed in them. This is a matter that has no connection with the essence of faith, because a prophet's faith does not require any other faith; it is already at the level of perfection.

When the conversation of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and this experience of his are complete, it becomes clear that from faith various kinds of emotions arise in the heart of the believer, and these longings that arise in the heart of the perfect believer compel him to try to peer into the sanctuary of power.

"And [mention] when Ibrahim said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' [Allah] said, 'Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but [I ask] that my heart may be assured.'"

"When Ibrahim said, 'Show me how you bring the dead to life?' He said, 'Do you not believe?' He replied, 'I do believe, but I desire assurance for my heart.'" Ibrahim (peace be upon him) meant that inner tranquillity would be attained when he saw the hand of power at work. And the satisfaction of the urge to uncover the secrets within the house comes when a person opens these secrets and they become manifest to him. Allah knew well that His servant and friend was a firm believer, but this question was purely for the satisfaction of desire and the declaration of zeal. This sequence of question and answer, on the part of Allah Most High, toward His obedient and forbearing servant, was a form of kindness and grace and an act of honouring him.

In short, Allah provided the means for the satisfaction of Ibrahim's (peace be upon him) longing for inquiry, and placed him on the straight path through a personal experience.

"[He] said, 'Take four birds and train them to come to you. Then place on every hill a portion of them, then call them; they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise.'"

Allah commanded Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to take four birds and make them familiar to himself, and to learn their characteristics and their signs well, so that no error would occur in recognising them. Then he was to slaughter them, cut them into pieces, and scatter their parts over the surrounding mountains. Then he was to call them, and their scattered limbs would begin to become whole again; life would return to them, and they would come running to him. And so it happened.

Ibrahim (peace be upon him) saw with his own eyes the secret of creation. It is the secret that is being repeated at every moment, but people can see only its traces after it is complete. This secret was the secret of the bestowal of life, the life that was given to this universe when nothing existed before, and which is now being repeated in the form of every living creature.

Ibrahim (peace be upon him) saw this secret with his own eyes. There were a few birds from which life had been separated; their flesh was scattered in various places. Now their parts were gathering and life was being restored to them, and they came and reached Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

How did this happen? This is precisely the secret whose comprehension lies beyond the reach of human power. At times a person sees this secret in the same way Ibrahim (peace be upon him) saw it, and he confirms it in the same way Ibrahim (peace be upon him) confirmed it. But he cannot grasp its reality. The method of its occurrence is not known to him. It is the command of Allah. People can know and attain only a limited measure of the knowledge of Allah, which He gives to whomever He wills, but He has not informed anyone about the secret of life, because it is a secret far greater than human capacity and power. He has informed no one, because it is a very great secret in comparison with human ability and power. Its nature is different from the nature of our senses and perception, and for the performance of the duty of vicegerency (khilafah) on this earth people do not possess even the power of this creative knowledge. This is a special attribute of Allah, and the knowledge of creatures is very limited in comparison with it. If a person even tries to peer into the chamber of hidden things, he will see only veils upon veils. His effort will be fruitless, and the domain of the knowledge of the unseen will remain confined to the knowledge of prophethood.

Lesson No. 19: At a Glance

Taken together, the three preceding lessons in this part dealt with some fundamental articles of faith, clarifying aspects of this worldview and seeking to strengthen its roots from various angles. This was one stage in the line of this lengthy surah along which the whole surah is moving: preparing the Ummah to discharge the duties incumbent upon the Muslim community in pursuit of the goal of leadership of humanity, as we have already explained.

From here until nearly the end of this surah, the discourse now turns to the explanation of the fundamental economic principles upon which the collective system of the Muslim Ummah is to be founded, and in accordance with which the organisation of the Muslim community was also intended. This collective system is in essence based on mutual cooperation and social solidarity (takaful), and its formation rests upon ushr, zakah, charity and alms. This economic system is entirely different from the interest-based system that prevailed in that age of jahiliyyah. That is why here the virtue and etiquette of sadaqah are described, and riba is condemned. In the lessons that follow, you will read that the fundamental principles of lending and trade are also set out, and that all these matters together form part of the economic system of Islam, and that the collective life of Islam rests upon them. The three lessons that come next are interconnected; they are in fact different aspects of one subject (economics), namely the economic system of Islam.

In this lesson, emphasis is laid upon spending in the way of Allah and upon the expenditure of wealth, and emphasis is placed on one economic aspect of Islam, namely sadaqah and the collective system of social support. It is explained that spending in the way of Allah is in reality a form of jihad, and it is clear that jihad in the way of Allah has been made obligatory upon the Muslim Ummah. This is because Allah has imposed upon the Muslim Ummah the duty to spread this call throughout the whole world, to convey this message to the entire world, to support the people of faith everywhere in the world, to eliminate from the whole world mischief, oppression and transgression, and to shatter all those forces which are dominant against the people of Islam, which spread corruption on earth, and which are obstructing the people of the world from adopting the straight path of Allah. In other words, they seek to deprive the world of that great good which is borne by the Islamic system of life. To deprive the world of that good is so grave a crime that none could be graver, and there is no greater violation against the human soul, the human body and property than this.

In this surah, the call to spend in the way of Allah is repeated again and again, but here the principles and etiquette of spending in the way of Allah are explained in somewhat more detail. Here the practice of spending is portrayed through a very beloved and familiar image. Its collective principles, its etiquette, its effects and its psychological implications are discussed at length. Those etiquettes through which the psychological reform of the one who spends himself takes place, and which, on the other hand, make it beneficial for the one who receives charity, and as a result of which a social revolution comes about such that this society collectively becomes a mutually supportive and socially secure society. Mutual love and sympathy arise among its members, and because of this humanity reaches a lofty station in which the giver and the receiver become people of exactly the same level.

Despite the reality that the guidance given in this lesson is general, is not confined by any restriction of time or place, and has the status of a permanent constitution, it must nonetheless be kept in view that at that time the Muslim community had conditions within it for the reform of which these instructions were revealed. It is also entirely possible that in later ages too, the future Islamic society might be in need of such guidance. At that time there were within the Islamic society persons in whose eyes wealth was everything, and for whose reform such strong blows were needed, and for whom such effective impact was required. They needed the realities to be brought before their observation through proverbs, so that this matter might penetrate to the depths of their hearts.

In that society of the time, if on the one hand there were people who could not conceive of giving wealth to anyone without usury, then on the other hand there were in that society also people who spent reluctantly or only for show. Some spent and then continually reminded others of their favour, and thus became a source of distress for others. Some gave worthless and useless possessions in the name of Allah. Alongside these, there were also those who sincerely spent in the way of Allah and who used to spend their best wealth, spending secretly when the occasion called for secret spending and openly when the occasion called for open spending. That expenditure was purely for Allah, entirely pure and clean.

Both kinds of persons mentioned above existed in the Muslim community. We should reflect upon this reality, and if we grasp it, it will be extremely beneficial for us.

The first benefit of grasping this reality is that we will be able to understand the true nature of this Book correctly, and its purposes will become clear to us. We will see that the Holy Qur'an is a living and dynamic reality. In the light of these events it appears to us as constantly active and moving, and this movement of the Qur'an is visible within the Muslim community. It confronts real circumstances. Sometimes it preserves certain realities and sometimes it transforms certain conditions, and thus this community advances step by step, while the Qur'an confronts those conditions. It is continually active and dynamic. Its movement has continuity and permanence. It is engaged in battle in the practical arena of life. The Holy Qur'an alone is the progressive, motivating element in that society, the element that advances in the practical field.

Today we have a great need to perceive the Qur'an in this manner, and to see that the Qur'an is a living reality, a dynamic factor that takes action to move forward. For today, the Islamic movement, the Islamic system of life and the Islamic society have long been absent. The Qur'an, as we have felt and understood it, is a book isolated from the living stream of human history. The Qur'an as we have understood it today does not present any blueprint of that system of life which this very Qur'an once brought practically into existence on this earth, and which was once a living reality in the history of the Muslim community. And we have forgotten the lesson that for the first Muslim mujahid of that time, the Qur'an was the order of the day; that is, for them the Qur'an was guidance that had to be acted upon. It was incumbent upon them to enforce in practice the daily instructions. In our understanding and perception, that practical Qur'an has, as it were, died or fallen asleep, and we do not try to understand and feel the Qur'an in the way the Muslims of the first age understood and felt it.

Our manner has become that we recite the Qur'an with fine melody and singing and sway to it, or our intuition takes from it some vague, general, incomprehensible and unexplainable impressions, or we recite it as a daily routine, from which a vague and general state of ecstasy, joy and inner tranquillity arises in the hearts of sincere believers. The reality is that all these benefits are also present in the recitation of the Qur'an, but beyond all these benefits the true objective is that the Qur'an should create understanding, insight, action and movement in the heart of the believer. It should bring it to life. The highest aim is that such a state should arise in the heart and mind of the Muslim that he continues on with the guidance of the Qur'an while carrying a living and practical life, such a life as the Qur'an wishes to establish here and for which it was sent down: a life which the believer finds in the field of this struggle and in this arena of conflict, for which a believer always keeps himself prepared, because in the life of the Muslim Ummah this conflict is an unavoidable matter. What is desired is that a Muslim turn towards the Qur'an with the intention of deriving from it a plan of action for his life, exactly as the "first Muslim" used to do, and that he seek Qur'anic guidance and indications concerning today's life, today's events and today's problems which swirl around him. He should also interpret the history of the Muslim Ummah in the light of Qur'anic guidance, regard the Qur'anic words and indications as the explanation of Islamic history, and feel that Islamic history is no separate history apart from the Qur'an. Islamic history is the history of the Qur'an. And the circumstances in which the Muslim Ummah today finds itself are also a part of Qur'anic history. Today's conditions are the logical outcome of the conditions which the predecessors of this Ummah faced. At that time too the Qur'an desired a definite change in those events and occurrences, and today too it desires exactly such changes. Therefore a believer feels that just as this Qur'an was a book of action for that Ummah, it is for me too a book of action today. Today too he wishes to turn to the Qur'an in the affairs of his days and nights and in the events that befall him. It is the fundamental principle of his thought and his outlook. Today too it is the true motive for his striving and his effort and his action. Tomorrow too it is a motive for him, and forever it is the axis of his life.

The second benefit of grasping this truth is that it gives us a clear perception of the reality and nature of human nature and human temperament. The call of Islam, and the duties and obligations it imposes, have always had to deal with human nature. In these verses, through the example of the first Islamic community, a clear picture of human nature has been drawn, and through it human nature becomes evident in its original form and reality. The Qur'an was being revealed to that first community. Its supervisor and educator was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself. There were within the ranks of that community certain weak aspects which needed reform, which needed constant attention, and which needed to be identified and taken into account. It should be remembered that the reform of the Companions (ṣaḥābah) (may Allah be pleased with them) does not contradict the fact that they were the most distinguished of all segments of the Ummah. Understanding this reality is very beneficial for us. Thus we will be able to comprehend the reality and nature of a human community and organisation without excess or deficiency, without our being wrapped in some artificial shell, and without forming any misleading notions about it. Another benefit of this is that the clouds of despair are dispelled from our minds and hearts, because when we see that the lofty station which Islam prescribes for humanity is far from us, it is sufficient for us that we keep walking on this path and continue the striving to reach that lofty station. Another benefit we gain is that we come to realise that continuous invitation is needed to bring people to lofty stations and to the higher levels of perfection. There should never be any shortfall, laxity, despair or interruption in it, even though some souls may have defects and flaws, for that is what human beings are. Through continuous invitation and reformative effort, a human being gradually walks the path of being reformed. He needs constant invitation to raise him to the lofty station of the Qur'an. He always needs to be reminded of goodness. There is always a need for goodness to be presented to him continually in its beautiful form and evil in its ugly form, and a constant aversion to weakness of character and defects should be instilled in his heart. And whenever he goes astray, his hand should be taken and he should be set back on the right path, for this journey of life is very long and arduous.

The third benefit we gain from this is that we well grasp this simple truth which we often overlook: that a human being is, after all, a human being. The Islamic call is, after all, a call to Islam, and this struggle is, after all, a struggle of human beings and human effort. This struggle is first of all against one's own weaknesses, one's personal defects, and the passions of greed and miserliness hidden within the human soul. After that, it is a struggle against falsehood, evil, oppression and misguidance in the life spread around the person. This is a kind of two-fronted war which the caller must wage, and upon the leadership of the Muslim Ummah on this earth this two-fronted war will inevitably have to be fought, just as the Qur'an had to fight this battle for the first time, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had to fight it first of all. During this continuous struggle it is inevitable that there will be some mistakes and lapses, and that in the various stages of this difficult path some shortcomings and weaknesses will appear. And through new events and new experiences these defects and lapses will be corrected, and according to the method which the Qur'an has adopted in guidance and reform, the hearts and minds of people will continue to be reformed. Here I will repeat what I have said before: that we should make the Holy Qur'an our counsellor and guide in all circumstances and in all the struggles of our life, so that it appears that in our thoughts, in our conscious awareness, in our practical life and in all our affairs, the Qur'an is flowing and pervading just as it fully flowed and pervaded the life of the first Muslim community.

Islamic way of life does not begin with obligations and duties. Islam begins its work with love, winning hearts and the call to goodness. It awakens human consciousness and creates in human life feelings that are ever-living. It presents before human beings, for their study and observation, a picture of life that sprouts, grows, and at last yields a beneficial fruit, from which man derives benefit. It presents before man the example of the crop, which is a common gift of Allah and the earth. The field takes one grain, but returns hundreds of grains; in relation to the seed and the kernel, it yields many times over. In the Qur'an this living scene is placed before those who spend their earnings in the way of Allah.

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that sprouts seven ears, and in every ear there are a hundred grains.﴾

"The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain sown, which sends out seven ears, and in each ear there are a hundred grains."

This imaginative mode of expression reaches the level of calculation. A single grain becomes seven hundred grains, but the manner in which the Qur'an presents this meaning, living and radiant, is extremely beautiful and graceful. It produces in human consciousness a kind of excitement and fervour. The human conscience awakens. The scene of a living and growing crop comes before the eyes. A living disposition becomes manifest. A green field yielding produce comes before the sight. A common and wondrous experiment of ordinary vegetation, not unfamiliar, comes before us: one stalk, seven ears, and in each ear a hundred grains.

Before this living and vivid scene, the human conscience too turns towards giving and bestowing, but in truth it does not really give; it receives. Thus this giving and generosity follows a path in which it grows manifold. In this way the human impulse of generosity becomes many times greater, and like the crop, he brings forth many times more return. And Allah multiplies for whomsoever He wills, beyond that. He gives without reckoning and gives in abundance.

He is so abundant in provision for His creation that it is boundless and beyond reckoning. His mercy is so vast that its limits are not known. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ "He is both Bountiful and All-Knowing."

He is so open-handed that there is no restriction in His giving. His giving neither ends nor does its flow diminish. He is All-Knowing; He is the Master of intentions. He rewards even intention and good deeds. Nothing is hidden from Him.

Now the question arises: what is that spending in the way of Allah which grows and is beneficial, and what is that generosity which Allah multiplies in this world and the Hereafter? (Allah multiplies) for whomever He wills. This spending is that which elevates human emotions and purifies them. That spending in the way of Allah is one which does not crush a person's nobility or self-respect. That spending which is carried out as the outcome of inner purity and cleanliness of heart. It is done solely out of the desire for the pleasure of Allah, and there is no other aim before one's eyes.

Showing off one's favour (ihsan jatana) is a despicable, disliked and base act. It is a mindset that is extremely lowly. A person's self displays such a favour only when he is afflicted with a false sense of superiority and is gripped by the disease of self-glorification (ta'alli). Or he wants to humiliate the recipient, or he harbours the desire that people should pay attention to him and look upon his act of spending with approval. In this case too, the object of his concern is people, not Allah. All these feelings are such that they can never flourish in a pure heart, nor do such feelings arise in the heart of a true believer. Therefore, showing off one's favour is simultaneously a source of torment for the giver and for the recipient. For the giver it is a torment, because pride and arrogance arise in his heart. There arises in his heart the thought and the desire that a brother should appear before him humbled and broken in condition. And in the heart of the giver himself, feelings of hypocrisy, ostentation and distance from Allah will arise. For the recipient, the torment is that he regards himself as inferior and broken in condition, and then in his heart feelings of contempt and vengeance arise.

The purpose of Islam in spending in the way of Allah is not merely that a gap be filled, that someone's need be met and a hungry stomach be filled. This purpose is by no means the only one. Through it, Islam, on the one hand, makes arrangements for the moral purification of the giver; it purifies his self, it stirs up feelings of sympathy within him, and by creating a bond between a Muslim brother and brother, it moves him, as a human being and as a Muslim, to come to the aid of a poor person solely for the pleasure of Allah. Islam reminds the giver that he has the favour of Allah upon him, and that he has also made a covenant with Allah concerning this favour. And that covenant is that he should eat from this bounty and provision, within the bounds of need and without extravagance, and also spend from it in the way of Allah. That is, without any obstruction and without showing off one's favour. On the other hand, through this Allah also provides for the comfort and contentment of the recipient, and good relations are established between one human being and another human being, and between one believer and another believer. And in an Islamic society there is also no fear that mutual cooperation and solidarity (takaful) will be absent among its members. Thus the building and unity of an Islamic society, the single-mindedness of its inclinations, and harmony in its duties and responsibilities come into being. But by showing off one's favour all these benefits are destroyed, and spending in the way of Allah becomes poison and fire. Even if no harm has reached the recipient from the giver's hand or tongue, merely showing off the favour is a very great torment. It is in itself embodied torment. Through it, spending becomes ineffective; discord arises within society, and enmities and hatreds arise among the members of society.

Experts in modern psychology have reached the conclusion that as a result of showing off a favour, or of doing a favour, in the end enmity inevitably arises at some time between the benefactor and the person to whom the favour was done. In support of this they give the argument that the recipient, in his own heart, develops a sense of inferiority and weakness of feeling before the giver, and this awareness constantly pricks his heart. And a grateful person, in order to overcome this awareness, in reaction attacks the very benefactor and conceals his enmity in his heart, because in relation to the benefactor he always considers himself inferior, and the benefactor himself also develops within himself the awareness that he is superior in comparison with that person. Thus this awareness, namely on one side a sense of superiority and on the other side a sense of inferiority, transforms into enmity toward one another.

Indeed, the experience of the psychologists sometimes proves entirely correct among jahili and non-Islamic societies. Such jahili societies are those which have neither an Islamic spirit nor the rule of Islamic thought. But the Islamic system of life has solved this problem in an entirely new manner. That is, Islam establishes in the minds and hearts of all people the reality that wealth and property are in truth the property of Allah, and that those who hold wealth and provision in their hands are its trustees and guardians. And this is a reality which not even the most ignorant person can deny, because the near and distant causes of wealth and prosperity are created by Allah. Not one of these causes lies within the scope of human power. All of it is what Allah has given. Take a single grain of wheat. Many forces of this universe participate in its production, from the sun down to the earth, and from water to the air. Not one of these forces lies within the scope of human power. Other things may be understood by analogy with a single grain of wheat, whether it is a fibre of cloth or any other thing. Thus, with this understanding, if any wealthy person spends anything, it is as though he spends something that Allah has given. Moreover, according to this understanding, if a person does a good deed and stores it up for his hereafter, it is as though he lends to Allah, and Allah will give him its reward many times over. However, this destitute person becomes a means of the otherworldly reward of that wealthy person.

Allah the Exalted has laid down, for giving and receiving, manners which we are explaining here. These manners firmly establish in the human mind and heart the notion that no giver should show self-glorification, nor should any receiver fall victim to a sense of inferiority, and that both should observe the manners and principles which Allah has prescribed for them, and fully adhere to the covenants which Allah has taken from them. He says:

﴿وَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ "There shall be no fear upon them." That is, for them there is no danger that enmity will arise with them, nor the danger that they will become poor, nor the danger that any of their reward will be lost.

﴿وَلا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ "Nor shall they grieve." That is, in this world too there will be no sorrow for them, and in the Hereafter they will not be distressed by encountering an evil end.

For further confirmation of the above-mentioned wisdom regarding spending and hypocrisy, and for further clarification of this point, the real aim of spending in the way of Allah is the refinement of the self and the purification of hearts, and the establishment of purely religious love between the giver and the receiver. In the next verse it is said:

Here it is decided that charity after which the needy person is hurt is not needed at all. A kind word and gentle speech are far better than such charity. A good word heals the wounds of hearts. It produces happiness and the seeking of pleasure, and through it wounds close. Forgiveness and overlooking faults remove the rancour from hearts, and in its place brotherhood and friendship arise. In such circumstances, sweet speech and pardon serve as the first brick on the path of friendship and brotherhood. Through them souls become pure and two hearts become united.

After stating that the giver has no superiority over the recipient, because in giving charity a person is in fact lending to Allah, it is then said: ﴿And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing﴾. He is independent of a giver's gift after which he hurts a needy person, and He is Forbearing, because He gives everything to His servants and yet they do not thank Him. But Allah does not hasten to punish them, nor does He quickly inflict harm upon them. Allah gives His servants everything, and before giving everything He grants them existence. Therefore, the servants too should learn forbearance from Allah. If they give something of what Allah has given to someone, they should not immediately turn against the one who is grateful to them, even in circumstances where something about him displeases them, or where that grateful person is thanking them.

The Qur'an repeatedly brings the attributes of Allah before people, and what is intended is that people develop those attributes within themselves as far as they are able. Among the etiquettes of Islamic life, this is an important form of conduct: a Muslim continually develops the attributes of Allah within himself and keeps traversing the various stages of this path, and he attains whatever share of those attributes belongs to him, in accordance with his temperament and the capacities of his nature.

When this intuitive impression reaches its extremes, and natural manifestations of a progressive and beneficial life are presented before those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah, and this spending is such that after it no harm arises from reproach and taunting, and after indicating that Allah has no need of such spending, charity and favours that are followed by hurt, and that Allah is the Provider and the Giver, He does not hasten in sending down His wrath and in inflicting harm. In short, when this intuitive impression reaches these heights, the address turns to those who are believers, that they should not nullify their charities and good deeds by reproaching and hurting others after giving.

Here the Qur'an depicts a strange situation before them. These are very beautiful scenes, which proceed in one place along with the earlier scene, where the first scene was of a field that is growing. In these two new scenes, however, the nature of spending in the way of Allah that is purely for Allah is described, and the reality of spending that is accompanied by demands for gratitude and by hurt is also described. These scenes are in the style the Qur'an adopts for artistic depiction, in which meaning and sense are given a concrete form, the effects of an action are shown in a dynamic form, and the depiction takes place in such a way that the whole scene stands before our imagination.

This is the first scene. It is a complete picture made of two parts, which are opposite to each other in form, arrangement and outcome. Each scene in turn has various parts that are harmonious with one another. They are also in accord and of the same colour in expression and observation, and in the meanings and emotions that this depiction was meant to create: the meanings whose expression was intended through this whole portrayal, or the awareness that was meant to be produced through these scenes.

In the first scene we are confronted with a heart that is harder than stone. ﴿Like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ ... He is not aware of the freshness and sweetness of faith, yet he covers his hardness of heart with the veil of showing off. This heart, over which lies the veil of showing off, is like a rock upon which a layer of soil has settled: a stone with no freshness on it and no softness in it. There is only a thin layer of soil on it, and that layer conceals its hardness and roughness. Exactly in the same way, a person hides, through his showing off, the state of his heart, which is empty of faith.

﴿Then a heavy rain struck it and left it bare, smooth rock﴾ ... Heavy, pouring rain removed that thin layer of soil. The rock was exposed, and what was it? A hard, firm and harsh rock, on which no vegetation was possible and from which no produce could be obtained. This is the very parable of the heart that spends its wealth merely for show. It will benefit nothing, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

This scene is set against a second one, which is its exact opposite. There is a heart filled with faith, refreshed by the freshness of belief. It spends its wealth purely seeking the pleasure of Allah. It is fully certain that it will receive a reward for whatever it spends, and it spends only as a requirement of its faith and its conviction. This conviction is deeply rooted in the depths of its heart. On one side is the hypocritical heart, which is likened to a rock covered by a thin layer of soil. On the other side is a heart full of faith, which is likened to a green garden with fertile land and deep soil, whereas the rock had only a thin covering of soil. The garden is on a high place, while the said rock is in a deep pit, so that these two scenes become proportionate and similar. Now, if heavy rain falls on this garden, its freshness does not end, just as the thin layer of soil on the rock is washed away. Rather, the rain makes this garden even greener and more flourishing. It gives it new life and it grows. ﴿Heavy rain strikes it, and it yields its produce double.﴾

This rain brings the garden to life and makes it green, just as charity purifies the heart of a believer and, because of it, the believer's relationship with Allah becomes strong. Just as the heart of the believer is purified, the wealth of the believer also becomes pure, Allah places blessing in it, and in the same way, through spending in the way of Allah, purity arises in the collective life of the Muslim community, and through it, collective ties grow. And if that heavy rain does not fall, even a light drizzle is sufficient for it, and when the soil already contains moisture, even a light shower is enough.

This is a complete picture, whose scenes stand clearly in contrast to one another, whose details are mutually proportionate, and which is presented in a miraculous mode of expression. Harmony is found in its style, and its scenes are perfectly clear as a remedy for every inner doubt and every false notion. This scene presents a clear picture before human intuition and human consciousness. It presents all the conditions and all the feelings with great distinction, which affect the human heart, and a person easily finds the path of guidance.

Since the subject of this scene was related to thought and reflection, and its real purpose was that the knowledge of Allah be attained and that, beyond this apparent world, His wonders of power be seen with one's own eyes, therefore at its end this conclusion is drawn: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ As for the second scene, it is the extreme parable of boasting about charity and causing harm. In it, the Lord explains how Allah destroys and ruins such charity and boasting, at a time when the giver of charity needs the benefit of that charity and boasting the most. He becomes weak, his physical powers are lost, yet he cannot find any remedy for this ruin. This is an extremely severe depiction of the evil end, and extremely effective and instructive. In this scene, after peace and prosperity, there is complete destruction and desolation.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 266:

Here charity is presented in a tangible form, according to its reality and its effects.

﴿A garden of date-palms and grapevines, beneath which rivers flow; in it are fruits of every kind for him...﴾ "This charity is like a garden irrigated by rivers, laden with date-palms, grapes and every kind of fruit." Its shade is dense, pleasant and fresh. In it there are abundant fruits of every kind. Just as this garden is beneficial, so charity was beneficial, useful and gladdening. This charity was beneficial to the giver, beneficial to the recipient, and beneficial to the whole society. Its spiritual benefits were countless, and it contained goodness and blessing through which the society was receiving wholesome nourishment, and which was a cause of collective growth and progress in the society.

Is there anyone so wretched as to own such a garden, possessing this kind of exalted brotherhood and goodness, and then to reduce that garden to ashes through the harms and calamities of boasting over one's charity or causing hurt after giving, just as a fiery whirlwind scorches and reduces a green and flourishing garden to ashes?

And under what circumstances does this happen? In circumstances where the owner of that garden is in need, has become physically weak, has a family to support, and needs the shade and blessings of that garden urgently. ﴿And he has become old, and he has weak offspring, then a whirlwind strikes it, in which is fire, and it is burned.﴾ "He has grown old, and his children are also incapable, and in such a state he is struck by a fierce whirlwind containing fire." Who would like such a situation? Who, if he could understand such an outcome, would not strive to avoid it?

﴿Thus does Allah make His signs clear to you, that perhaps you may reflect.﴾

Thus this vivid scene is staged. It begins with great joy, pleasantness and ease. The scene opens with freshness, abundance, delight and beauty. Then comes the scene of destruction, and it is a frightening one. A whirlwind arrives which withers its freshness. When all these scenes appear on the stage, they produce in a person an unconscious awareness, and this awareness is so impactful that a conscious person has no hesitation in adopting the right path. Before the opportunity slips from a person's hand, and before the gardens of dense shade and the trees laden with fruit wither and are scorched, a conscious person makes his decision to accept or reject.

I cannot help but say here that this beautiful and graceful style of speech, and these coherent and harmonious scenes of which each individual scene in this lesson is composed, and the excellent manner in which each individual scene is presented, this coherence and harmony is not limited only to these individual scenes, but this harmony is also found in all these scenes collectively. All these scenes are also interconnected and proportionate. Look! There is an agricultural environment. There is a seed from which seven ears grow. There is a rock upon which a thin layer of soil has settled, and upon it suddenly torrential rain falls. Then there is a garden on an elevated place, laden with every kind of fruit, and bearing double fruit. This garden consists of date-palms and grapevines. Here there is heavy rain and there is drizzle. And then there is a whirlwind which often wreaks havoc on agricultural fields. In short, all the natural elements of an agricultural environment are present here, and no element is missing that could be effective.

This is an important characteristic of the eloquent style of the Holy Qur'an: it reduces the distance between human perception and the natural environment of this earth, because the human existence is composed of the same constituent elements of this universe. Between man and the growth of vegetation in the universe there is complete harmony. Just as a whirlwind scorches the freshness of this universe, so misguidance destroys and annihilates the spiritual world of a person. This is the Holy Qur'an: a beautiful manner of speech, which is certainly from the One who is Forbearing and All-Aware.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 267:

After the explanation of the etiquette and results of spending in the way of Allah, the discourse now moves further forward on the subject of spending in the way of Allah. The reality of spending, its method and its requirements are explained.

The rules and foundations that were laid down in the earlier verses for spending in the way of Allah, and upon which the structure of this practice was ordered to be raised, require that the best of wealth be spent in the way of Allah. One should not even intend to spend in the way of Allah inferior and worthless things in which the owner himself has no interest. If such items were offered to a person in a sale or transaction, he would hardly be ready to pay even a meagre price for them. Allah is Self-Sufficient, the King; He has no need to accept such worthless things.

This call of Allah is for all Muslims, whenever they exist and wherever they may be, and this command applies to all wealth that comes into their hands: all wealth that they have earned by lawful and pure means, or wealth that has been produced for them from the earth, such as agricultural produce and minerals, for example petroleum and the like. For this reason the words of the verse are general. That is, the wealth that existed at the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and that which came into being later; the wording of the verse is general, and its application extends to wealth that comes into being afterwards. Zakat is obligatory on all of them. Yes, the nisab of zakat has been fixed by the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ. Therefore every kind of produce should be analogized to those kinds of wealth that existed at the time of the Messenger ﷺ; every new produce should be analogized to those commodities that existed at the time of the Messenger ﷺ, according to their respective nature.

In some narrations the occasion of revelation of this verse is also mentioned. I think mentioning them here would not be inappropriate, because through these narrations those circumstances in which these verses were revealed come alive again, and through them the lowly social condition that the Qur'an intended to reform, and for raising whose standard the Holy Qur'an was striving, is also brought to mind.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Hadrat Bara' ibn 'Azib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "This verse was revealed concerning the Ansar. When the time for picking dates approached, they would bring from their orchards clusters of dates whose colour had turned yellow but which were not yet ripe, and they would hang them between the pillars of the Prophet's Mosque. The poor Muhajirin would eat from them. Some people would bring inferior dates as well and hang them among them, thinking that this was permissible. Concerning those who did this, Allah revealed this verse: ﴿And do not aim at the bad [of your wealth] to spend from it, while you yourselves would not take it except with closed eyes...﴾" Al-Hakim also narrated this hadith from Bara', and said that although this hadith meets the conditions of authenticity of Bukhari and Muslim, Bukhari and Muslim did not narrate it. Ibn Abi Hatim, with his chain, narrated from Hadrat Bara' through another chain, who said: "It was revealed concerning us. We were owners of date palms, and everyone would bring whatever dates they had, and some would bring unripe ones and hang them in the mosque. The People of the Suffah had no arrangement for their food and lodging. Whoever among them became hungry would come and strike the hanging dates with his staff, and would eat whatever fell from them, both the half-ripe and the fully ripe."

Some people among them were not generous; they would bring unripe and inferior dates. Especially, they would bring a cluster that had already broken and whose grains were unripe, and hang it up. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And do not aim at the bad [of your wealth] to spend from it, while you yourselves would not take it except with closed eyes...﴾ He said: if any one of you were given such a gift, he would not accept it unless he overlooked its faults or acted with shame. So after this, every one of us would bring the best of what he had.

Both narrations are close in meaning. Both depict the actual situation that existed in Madinah. These two hadiths show, alongside a page of history, another page on which the Ansar of Madinah left indelible marks of generous giving. Moreover, these hadiths show that within a single community some individuals are of a remarkable and elevated station, while others need training and refinement, and need to be set on the path of a higher level. As happened in the case of some Ansar, it was necessary to forbid them from spending inferior wealth in the way of Allah: wealth such that, if it were presented to them, they would not accept it, except where shame prevents them from refusing, and in a transaction they would overlook defects, that is, by reducing the price. Yet the One before whom they are presenting the gift is the Lord of Being, Allah.

For this reason the verse concludes with the phrase: ﴿And know that Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.﴾ That is, He is absolutely independent of whether anyone gives in His way or not. If someone spends in His way, he does so for his own benefit. So it is fitting for him to spend the best thing and to do so willingly. Moreover, He is Hamid (Praiseworthy): He accepts pure things, praises them, rewards them, and gives a good reward. In sum, at this point, through the mention of these two attributes, human hearts are stirred in the same way as the hearts of the Ansar were stirred, concerning whom these verses were revealed: ﴿O you who believe, spend from the good things you have earned, and from what We have produced for you from the earth...﴾ Otherwise, Allah has no need of the worthless thing that you pick out and spend as charity, while Allah is the One who praises you when you spend pure things in His way, and because of that pleasure He gives you a good reward, even though this wealth was given to you by Him. The true Giver is He; He rewards you for this generosity as an honour, because what you give is what He Himself has bestowed upon you. How magnificent is this exposition! What a wonderful manner of encouragement! This is a remarkable method of training that the Holy Qur'an has adopted.

The reality was, and remains, that withholding spending in the way of Allah, or presenting worthless and useless things before the court of Allah, carries within it certain wrong notions. Such a person in fact does not have full certainty in the reward that Allah has fixed for these deeds, or he is seized by fear of poverty, which never afflicts those whose connection is with Allah, who have complete trust in Allah's Being, and who are certain that the final outcome of everything rests in the hand of Allah. In contrast to firm faith in Allah, the reality of these notions has been laid bare; it has been made manifest and clearly explained where these notions arise within the human soul, and what is the force that repeatedly awakens them in human hearts. It is then stated that this force is the satanic force.

Sayyid Qutb's commentary (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 268:

Satan frightens you with poverty and destitution. Because of this, he creates greed and miserliness within your souls. Satan commands you to indecency (fahsha'). In the Arabic language, fahsha' refers to every act of disobedience in which a person exceeds the limit, although its use is mostly confined to one particular sin. Nevertheless, the word is general. It was precisely this fear of poverty that led the Arab tribes in the days of ignorance (jahiliyyah) to bury their daughters alive, which was itself a form of indecency. Similarly, the urge to amass as much wealth as possible drove them to usury (riba), which was also a form of indecency. Moreover, the fear that spending in the way of Allah will make them poor is itself indecency.

On one hand, Satan frightens you with poverty and urges you toward indecency, while on the other hand, Allah assures you of forgiveness and promises that He will reward you for spending in the way of Allah: "وَاللَّهُ يَعِدُكُمْ مَغْفِرَةً مِنْهُ وَفَضْلاً" ﴿Allah promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty﴾ — "But Allah gives you the hope of His forgiveness and bounty."

Here the word maghfirah (forgiveness) is mentioned first, because bounty and generosity come after forgiveness. This bounty and generosity includes the means of sustenance on this earth as well; that is, as a reward for spending in the way of Allah, abundant provision will come to you even in this world. "وَاللَّهُ وَاسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ" ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ — "Allah is vast in bounty and all-knowing."

He gives out of His vastness and generosity, and He knows all the inner stirrings of the heart. He is also aware of all the inclinations and tendencies of the human conscience. Therefore He does not merely grant wealth or merely forgive; He also bestows wisdom (hikmah). Through wisdom and understanding, a person acquires balance and moderation. A person is granted an awareness of causes and purposes, and as a result, he gives every thing its proper place according to its reality. He makes all decisions after careful thought and understanding.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 269:

يُؤْتِي الْحِكْمَةَ مَنْ يَشَاءُ وَمَنْ يُؤْتَ الْحِكْمَةَ فَقَدْ أُوتِيَ خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا ................ "He grants wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is granted wisdom has indeed been given abundant good."

He is given moderation (i'tidal) and balance, so he is protected from extremism and transgression of limits. He is made to understand the causes and consequences of all things, so he does not err in determining the value of things. He is given clear insight, so he chooses what is righteous and correct from among his movements, stillness, deeds and actions. And this is a wealth that appears in many different colours.

وَمَا يَذَّكَّرُ إِلا أُولُو الألْبَابِ................ "And none will take heed except those of understanding." In short, it is only those who are insightful and intelligent who take heed. Such people remember a lesson, and they also forget; but once they are alerted, they do not fall into heedlessness again. If they take a lesson from an event, they do not fall onto the path of misguidance. All of these acts are counted among the duties of intellect. It is the proper office of intellect to find the path of guidance and its signposts, to adopt a reasonable course, and not to spend life aimlessly in play and amusement.

Allah grants this wisdom to whichever of His servants He wills. This wisdom and understanding depend upon the will of Allah. This is the fundamental principle of the Islamic conception of life: everything here ultimately returns to the free and sovereign will of Allah, glorified is He. Yet alongside this, the Qur'an has also stated another principle: whoever sincerely seeks the path of guidance and strives fully for it, Allah never deprives him of the path of guidance, but rather He gives that seeker full assistance in this matter.

وَالَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا فِينَا لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَمَعَ الْمُحْسِنِينَ................ "And those who strive in Our cause, We will surely guide them to Our paths, and indeed Allah is with the doers of good." (29:69) Therefore, everyone who wishes to adopt the path of guidance should remain fully assured that the Divine will shall surely bestow its share upon him, and that he will be granted wisdom and understanding along with guidance, and abundant good along with them.

Wait! Before we finish reflecting on this verse, it is necessary to point to another important truth. Consider: Satan frightens you with poverty and urges you towards shameful conduct, while Allah promises you His forgiveness and bounty. Allah is All-Embracing in bounty and All-Knowing. He grants wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is granted wisdom has indeed been given great wealth.

Before a human being there are only two paths; there is no third path. One is the path of Allah and the other is the path of Satan. He will either lend his ear to the promise of Allah or respond to the call of Satan. Remember that whoever is not walking on the path of Allah and is not heeding the call of Allah is walking on the path of Satan and has been led astray by his enticement. There is only one way of life, namely the path of truth: the methodology and system that Allah has laid down. Any other path is the path of Satan, and its end is Satan; it leads to Satan.

The Qur'an repeatedly states this truth and repeatedly emphasises it, so that the one who abandons the Islamic way of life and wishes to adopt a satanic system of living has no room to claim that he is in any way upon the path of guidance. There is now neither room for doubt nor any concealment in this. On one side is Allah, and on the other is Satan; on one side is the Divine way of life, and on the other is the satanic method; on one side is the path of Allah, and on the other is the path of Satan. Whoever wishes may choose whichever path he desires.

لِيَهْلِكَ مَنْ هَلَكَ عَنْ بَيِّنَةٍ وَيَحْيَا مَنْ حَيَّ عَنْ بَيِّنَةٍ................ "So that whoever perishes may perish upon clear proof, and whoever lives may live upon clear proof." (8:42) Nothing should remain hidden, and there should be no room for doubt or suspicion. Either it is misguidance or it is the straight path. This right path alone is truth and reality, and it is the only path. Every path other than this is false and a path of error.

After this important point we come to the main matter, namely charity and spending in the way of Allah. Whatever anyone spends in the way of Allah, Allah has full knowledge of it. Whether it is charity or a vow, whether it is secret or open, it is within the knowledge of Allah, and the demand of divine knowledge is that He rewards that act, and He also rewards the intention and purpose that lies behind that act.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 270:

A person's spending of whatever he expends from his wealth is covered by the term sadaqah (charity). Zakah (obligatory almsgiving), khairat (voluntary charity), sadaqat, and wealth given for jihad fi sabilillah (struggle in the way of Allah) all come under the scope of sadaqat. Nazr (a vow) is also a form of infaq fi sabilillah (spending in the way of Allah). The only difference is that the one who spends binds upon himself a specific, known thing.
