The second is partnership of capital on the basis of mudarabah, that is, one person provides capital and another conducts business with it, and both share in profit and loss. Moreover, economic development will also be possible through companies that sell their shares directly in the stock market (apart from founder's bonds, through which greater profit is drawn), and that earn profit from lawful and permissible business. Then economic development will also be possible through sums deposited in banks merely as trust, without profit, such that the banks use such sums directly in companies, industries, and commercial and business ventures, or participate in them indirectly, on the condition that they do not fix a predetermined profit for those deposits, and that the bank distributes its profit or loss under a set system among those who keep their deposits with it, while the bank is permitted to keep for itself a fixed and specified profit in return for its business activities. In short, beyond these means and resources, further means and resources for economic development can also be created, the details of which are not the place for here. If a people's faith is firm, countless such resources can be created. Moreover, let the intention become pure and a firm resolve be made that we will acquire the means of sustenance and progress from pure and clean sources, and will spurn filthy and impure sources.

Finally, the Holy Qur'an explains a particular form of the rulings concerning debts: that if the debtor is unable to pay the debt and faces difficulties, the solution is not to add to his debt through riba, but rather to grant him respite until his circumstances improve. And for the one who wishes to gather greater goodness, it is better that he forgive the debt altogether. In the view of Islam, this is the lofty rank.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 280:

This is the pleasant kindness that the Islamic system presents to humanity. It is a dense shade in which humanity, weary from the scorching heat of selfishness, greed, miserliness and self-interest, takes refuge and breathes a sigh of relief. It is a mercy for the debtor, a mercy for the creditor, and a mercy and compassion for the whole society in which both of them live.

We are certain that the modern, impoverished people who are raised under the shadow of the material jahiliyyah (ignorance) of our age will consider these words meaningless, and these words will seem unreasonable to them. The distorted taste of their mouths cannot at all perceive the sweetness of these words. Especially those savage usurers (sood-khor) who are spread across every corner of this earth, who wander about in search of their prey, who look for needy and destitute people upon whom mountains of calamities have fallen, who are in need of bread, clothing and medical treatment, so that they may exploit them. Sometimes these people do not even have enough money to bury their dead, and in this stingy and miserly world they find no one who would be a selfless helper for them. Therefore, compelled, they fall into the nets of these savage usurers. Their condition is like that of a prey which itself walks into the snare. Need and compulsion push them and drive them towards these usurers. Sometimes these usurers are organised in the form of treasuries (bayt al-mal) that provide capital, and sometimes they operate in the form of banks. All of them are equal in the view of Islam. Yes, the only difference is that behind them stands the strength of the economic theories of interest. Great academic books stand in support of their business. Large educational institutions and institutes are engaged in their support. Courts and large armies are the supporters of this system. All these institutions provide justification for the crime of usury, and their backers are busy providing a wide legal system and regulations to protect them, and they assist them. And as for those who do not pay them interest, through this legal system they begin to seize and harass them. And all this persecution is carried out in the name of justice.

We are fully certain that these words of ours do not truly enter the hearts of such people. Yet we are fully certain that what we are saying is the truth, and we also believe that the welfare of all humanity lies in this: that they should lend an ear to these words and act upon them, namely: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship, then let there be postponement until ease. And that you remit it as charity is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ................

In the Islamic system of life, the principle is that the destitute shall not be pursued. Neither shall the creditor do so, nor shall the law and the courts have the authority to pursue the destitute debtor. Rather, he shall be granted respite until his circumstances improve. Then the Islamic society does not leave the debtor to his own condition. First, the creditor is requested to forgive him, if he is able to do so. That is better for him, and it is also good for the debtor. It is also better for the society that provides mutual support (takaful) for its members, provided that both the creditor and the debtor understand that what is in Allah's knowledge is beneficial for them.

If the creditor were permitted to make the life of the debtor miserable and to pursue him, then in that case all the benefits that were intended by the prohibition of riba would be lost, because the debtor is destitute and has nothing. On the other hand, the creditor is legally empowered to harass him. Thus, here, in the form of a conditional sentence with its answer, the ruling is given that if he is destitute, then he should be granted respite until his financial circumstances improve. Along with this, in the case of destitution, the creditor is encouraged that if in such a situation he forgives some or all of it, that is very good for him.

Apart from respite, the Qur'an has elsewhere provided, from the zakat fund, a share for such destitute debtors so that they may repay their debts and the burden of their lives may be lifted. ﴿Indeed, the alms are only for the poor and the needy ........ and the debtors (al-gharimin)﴾. Al-gharimin refers to those debtors who have been buried under the weight of debts. It does not refer to those who took loans and indulged in luxury and pleasure-seeking, but rather to those who spent on permissible purposes, or who became debtors for reasonable causes, and whose circumstances deteriorated.

Now, at the end, the Qur'an gives, at the conclusion of the discourse, a very effective and profound hint, by which a believer is seized with trembling. He begins to wish that he might forgive the entire debt, and thereby attain success with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.

This is the day when all shall be returned to Allah, and every soul will be paid in full for what it earned. That day will be a very hard one. The heart of a believer is filled with great fear of that day. Deep within the conscience of the believer, there is perhaps a picture of the Resurrection and its terrors. For the very idea of standing before the Lord of the worlds is so awesome that the whole being of a person trembles at it.

This conclusion of the discourse is in harmony with the atmosphere of the matters mentioned above. This atmosphere is one of taking and giving, an atmosphere of earning and recompense. In this atmosphere the whole life of a person is being settled; it is an atmosphere of judgment upon the entire life of a human being. The believing heart is fearful of this atmosphere, and it protects itself from its terrors.

Taqwa (God-consciousness) and the fear of Allah are the watchman that sits in the depths of the human conscience. Islam sets this watchman in the depths of every believer's heart, so that there remains no way of escape for the believing heart.

This is the Islamic system, which is a firm and strong system. It is a serious and life-filled way of life, and it is a system that can actually be put into practice on this earth. For humankind it is the mercy and compassion of Allah. It is an honour for humanity. It is a good that humanity is being kept away from, and the enemies of Allah and the enemies of humanity stop people from coming to it.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 282 (part 1 of 2):

Lesson 21: A Brief Overview

The subject of the previous lesson was usury (riba) and charity. This lesson deals with the complementary rulings on loans, trade and related matters. The previous lesson prohibited usurious transactions. It forbade usurious loans, a usurious system of commerce, and usurious buying and selling. Here the discussion concerns benevolent loans (qard hasan), in which there is no suspicion of riba and on which no usurious profit is imposed. The discussion also concerns those commercial matters that are settled by hand (on the spot), and in which there is no trace of usurious gain.

A glance at this lesson leaves a person astonished. The manner of expression the Qur'an adopts for legislation is an astonishing one. The law is stated with such precision that no word in it can be replaced by another word, and no sentence can be changed or moved forward or backward. Along with this purely legal mode of expression, the Qur'an's beautiful literary style, the pleasantness, sweetness and flow of its words, does not suffer any loss. The legal purpose is expressed in the colour of religious sentiment, very subtly, with great impact and in the best of styles, and the connection of this verse is not disturbed either. The complete legal purpose is also fully stated. Within it, all the possibilities that may arise between the contracting parties, every position that may be taken, the responsibility of the scribes, the responsibility of the witnesses and so on, have all been taken into account. All factors that could improperly influence the matter have been negated, and precautionary measures have been adopted for every possible situation.

In stating a matter, when moving from one legal point to another, the Qur'an fully explains the point before proceeding and does not repeat it, unless there is a particular connection between it and the new point. In that case the previously stated legal point is linked to the new one, and a pointer is given.

Just as the Qur'an possesses inimitability in its choice of words and phrases for legislation, so too it is inimitable in the verses revealed for the guidance and direction of mankind. Indeed, its inimitability is more evident and astonishing in its legal wording than in its general verses. Here every legal purpose and principle is stated in such subtle and technical language that by replacing even a single word with another, that purpose cannot be achieved. No other word can take the place of any word. Had the Qur'an not been a miracle, it would not have been possible to speak in purely legal terms, in this manner of expression, and in a purely literary and technical style of expression, in a way that has no answer.

Along with all these excellences, this fact remains established: in civil, municipal, economic and commercial matters, the Qur'an legislated about a thousand years before the modern era. All modern legal experts accept this, and jurists and traditionists (muhaddithun) acknowledge that the Qur'an is the pioneer in this matter.

This verse establishes a general law. According to this verse, the writing of a contract is extremely necessary. If the matter concerns a loan and a term has been fixed for that loan, then it is obligatory that it be committed to writing; no one has the right not to put it in writing. The wisdom behind this is also stated at the end of the verse.

Here, the person who will prepare the document for these loans is also specified, for example a scribe (katib). This is a third person; none of the parties. The summoning of a third person by the contracting parties, apart from the parties themselves, is only for greater caution so that no doubt remains. Then the scribe is also commanded that he write with justice and equity, that he not side with either party, and that he make no addition or deletion in the wording.

This is because the command to write comes from Allah, that is, the scribe too is being commanded by Allah, so that he does not draw back, does not refuse to write, and that this task does not become a burden for him. This is now a duty enjoined by Allah, and by law it is the duty of the writer. And its reward is also upon Allah. The act of writing is, on his part, a thanksgiving for a blessing before Allah. It is Allah who, by His grace, taught him the art of writing. Therefore he should commit contracts to writing, because it is Allah who has given him this knowledge.

Up to this point the Lawgiver has removed the legal requirement of committing a term loan to writing. It has also been specified who will carry out the duty of writing. The obligation has been imposed upon him to write, and in the meantime the scribe is also reminded to give thanks for this blessing of Allah. The indication is that, being a person of skill, it is his duty to hold fast to the bond of justice and equity in writing.

After the completion of this first provision, the second provision now concerns the manner of writing.

The debtor (mudayyin), upon whom the right falls due, is entitled to have the document dictated. He acknowledges the debt, dictates the amount of the loan, fixes its conditions, has them noted down, and dictates its term. This is so that no injustice occurs to the debtor in the writing and document. For if the creditor (da'in) gets the document drawn up, he may increase the conditions or the amount of the loan, may alter the term, or may write into it some conditions for his own benefit and interest. Therefore the borrower is in a weak position. It may happen that, because of his needs, he cannot dare to oppose the creditor's dictation, since he wants the transaction in any case and is in dire need, and in that case the creditor would wrong him through the dictation. But if the debtor himself is having the document written, he will have written what he has accepted with a willing heart. In such a case his acknowledgment is stronger and firmer, because he himself dictated the writing. At the same time, the conscience of the debtor is also awakened, so that he keeps the fear of Allah before him, and does not reduce anything from the debt upon him, nor abandon any one of the essential conditions of the document.

If the debtor is foolish and cannot settle his affairs well, or is weak, that is, young in years or feeble of mind, or is unable to dictate for some other reason, that is, he is illiterate and ignorant, or there is some impediment in his speech, or some apparent or reasonable obstacle, then in that case his guardian (wali al-amr) should do this task. And it is also the duty of this guardian to deal with both parties with justice and equity. Justice is mentioned here because at times the guardian too may be negligent, since he is not personally concerned with the loan, so that he may set down in the writing all the interests and guarantees and so that this agreement is properly concluded.

Here the discussion concerning the written contract ends, and the discussion on all aspects of the written contract concerning loans is complete. Now the discussion turns to the second essential component of the contract, namely the witnesses to the documents.

For every contract, two witnesses are necessary, and they should be people whose testimony is acceptable. The phrase "tarduna" (whom you approve) has two meanings. One is that the witnesses should be just (adl) and their testimony should have acceptance in the community. The other meaning is that both parties to the contract should be content with their testimony. But at times circumstances are such that witnesses are not available, so the law here provides this facility: if there are no men, one man and two women may serve as witnesses. The task of testimony has been entrusted to men because in a healthy Islamic society it is generally men who perform this task, since in an Islamic society women generally do not have to struggle for their necessities of life. In their capacity as mothers and as the gentler sex, they carry out their duties, and their greatest duty is to undertake the upbringing and training of children, the greatest capital of humanity, who are the representatives of the future, and the worth of these children is greater than the few morsels and few coins that any woman can earn through her work. Whereas in today's misguided and deprived society, a woman is compelled to do this work along with these duties; in such circumstances, if there are not two male witnesses, then one man and two women may become witnesses. The question is: why are two women placed against one man? The Qur'an has not left this matter ambiguous, because in the field of legislation every expression must be clear, definite, and contain the actual cause of the legislation.

"That if one of them errs, the other may remind her." (Arabic: an tadilla ihdahuma fatudhakkira ihdahuma)

The question is: why does a woman err? There may be several causes. Sometimes the cause is that women generally do not have much experience in the field of contracts, so it is possible that the circumstances and conditions of a contract may not have settled fully in her mind, and at the time of litigation she may not be able to give testimony about them with complete accuracy. Therefore, for convenience, a second woman is kept alongside so that at the time of testimony she may remind her of the real matter, and they may cooperate with each other and be able to bring to mind the true circumstances of the disputed subject.

Sometimes the cause of error is that a woman is very yielding in temperament. The maternal instinct of a woman, and her physical, physiological and natural functions, also make it an important requirement that she be yielding, quick to respond, so that she can perform her natural duties well in the growth of the child. These duties are such that they cannot be separated from the personality of any woman. God Almighty has bestowed a great favour upon women, and likewise upon the child who is born there is the mercy of God. Therefore this temperament of the woman can never be separated from her personality. She has her own personality and her own temperament, provided the woman is healthy and her personality has not been corrupted. Whereas testimony in complex matters such as contracts is a duty in which it is necessary for a person to remain firm in their position and not be influenced by anything, and it is also necessary that the witness know the fact well and be steadfast. In such circumstances, the simultaneous testimony of two women is a guarantee that if one forgets, the other will remind her, since the error arises from forgetfulness and natural yielding. By this reminder she will return to the actual event.

Just as at the beginning of the verse the scribes were told not to refuse to write, now the witnesses too are told that when they are called upon to testify, they should not refuse to give testimony of the truth.

Thus, giving testimony is a duty and not merely a supererogatory or non-obligatory act, because testimony to the truth is an important means of establishing rights and upholding justice. Since God Almighty has imposed this duty, in the Islamic system of justice witnesses will come to give testimony with their heartfelt consent and conscious willingness, and they will come without any harm or hesitation. Likewise, they will not be doing any favour to either of the parties to the dispute, whether they have been summoned by one party or by both.

Here the discussion of testimony ends. The Lawgiver now gives guidance on another important matter. This is a general guidance, in which emphasis is placed on writing. Whether the matter is small or large, sometimes a person, thinking that the loan is small or that the matter is not of great importance, becomes lax in writing it down. Or at other times other circumstances arise in which a person is negligent about writing, such as shyness, laziness and ease-seeking, carelessness and indifference, and so on. Therefore in this verse God Almighty makes writing and committing matters to record obligatory on the basis of both intuitive and practical reasons.

"Do not be slack." When the human self perceives that the hardship of a task outweighs its worth, then the self, affected by this, shrinks from doing that task, and the Qur'an is well aware of this reality. "That is more just in the sight of Allah." Because in a matter, justice can be done with greater ease on the basis of documentary evidence compared to oral testimony, since oral testimony depends only upon memory. Likewise, the testimony of two men or two women is stronger than that of one man or one woman, and the possibility of falling into doubts is reduced. In this case the scope for doubt is reduced to the minimum: there should be no doubt in the statements contained in the agreement, or in your own souls, or in the minds of other people. Here doubt has been kept general, meaning that no aspect should be left in doubt.

Thus the wisdom of these measures becomes manifest, and those who enter into transactions are reassured. The legislation which Allah has ordained is most wise, its objectives are very profound and extremely practical, and the aim is that soundness, certainty, tranquillity and trust be established in dealings.

This commentary concerns the loan whose term is fixed. As for the trade that we carry on in the ordinary course of daily life, the ruling does not require that it be necessarily committed to writing in daily dealings. For such dealings, the testimony of witnesses is sufficient. The reason is that if writing and documentation were made obligatory in every transaction, it would result in obstacles being placed in the path of commercial and business activities, because daily commercial activities are carried out very quickly and in a short time. Islam legislates for the betterment of human life. It makes laws keeping in view all the circumstances of human life. It is a practical system of law in which there is no complexity, and the smooth flow of life is not disturbed by this law. Allah the Exalted says:

Apparently this verse shows that not writing down ordinary transactions is a concession. The real matter is that writing is obligatory and binding. Some narrations also mention that writing every transaction is commendable, not compulsory. But the preferred view is that writing transactions is compulsory.

Up to here was the legislation concerning the loan whose term is specified, or the trade whose connection is with daily dealings, and in both cases writing and testimony have been made necessary, either compulsorily or as a recommendation. From here onward, the rights of scribes and witnesses are now determined, and their duties are also specified. The first duty laid upon them is that truth and the rights of people be balanced, and that these people be able to fulfil their social duties with ease, without fear or apprehension. Allah says:

﴿Let no scribe or witness be harmed.﴾ Merely because he is discharging the duty imposed upon him by Allah. If you do this, it will be a rebellion from you against the law of Allah and an opposition to the Islamic way of life. Therefore the Islamic state must necessarily provide this protection, because scribes and witnesses often become the target of the anger and wrath of one of the parties to a case. Therefore they should have such safeguards and such guarantees that they may perform their duty with satisfaction, and indeed they should be encouraged so that they may discharge their duties and responsibilities well and perform their obligations with a contented heart, whatever the circumstances may be.

It is the habit of the Noble Qur'an that it constantly awakens the conscience of a human being and creates in the human heart the awareness that he is a responsible personality, so that the spirit of obedience to the law may arise from within the human self itself. Islam does not rest content merely with the pressure of legal provisions. This is why the Qur'an invites the believers to God-fearing, and this matter is mentioned almost at the end of every subject. The Noble Qur'an reminds the believers that it is Allah alone who has bestowed His grace upon you. It is He who teaches you and guides you. Through the fear of Allah the doors of the hearts open to the knowledge of the Divine, and their souls turn toward acquiring knowledge. And all this is only so that they may obey Him, rendering thanks for His grace and bounty, be pleased with Him, and place complete trust in His being.

﴿And fear Allah; and Allah teaches you; and Allah is Knower of all things.﴾

After this, the Lawgiver explains the supplementary provisions of the loan rulings. These rulings have been mentioned somewhat later because their connection is not with ordinary circumstances but with certain special situations. For example, if the parties to a contract are on a journey and they cannot find a person to write the document, Allah has permitted even an oral contract without writing, provided that the possession is handed over on the spot, that is, possession of the item which the debtor is to give to the creditor as a guarantee. Allah says:

But with this apparent guarantee, the Lawgiver, by instilling the fear of Allah within the consciences of the believers, motivates them to be trustworthy and to fulfil their responsibilities, because compared with an apparent guarantee, the fear of Allah is the final guarantee that can be effective in any transaction, the foundation upon which a law can be properly implemented, and the means by which a rightful person can receive his right properly and the rights of everyone can be safeguarded.

Trust is placed in the debtor that he will repay the debt fully, and confidence is placed in the debtor that he will return the pledged item in its original condition. Both are advised to adopt the attitude of fearing Allah and to discharge their respective obligations, because it is Allah who is the Lord of both of them. He is their Guardian, Nurturer, Sustainer, Judge and Qadi. All these concepts, dealings and the discharge of duties and responsibilities are of great importance.

Some exegetes have said that when this verse was revealed, it abrogated the verse of writing (kitabah) in respect of trustworthiness. But this view is not correct, because permission not to write down transactions exists only during travel, and this trust and the guaranteed debt also relate to the state of travel, and during travel both the creditor and the debtor deal with each other on the basis of mutual trust.

In short, while urging taqwa (God-consciousness) and purity, the discussion on testimony reaches its conclusion here. The testimony referred to here is not the testimony that is placed upon a document at the time of writing, but the testimony that is given in a court of law, because this testimony is a kind of trust (amanah) with the witness.

Here the matter is attributed to the heart of the believer, and sin is attributed to the heart of the believer. Thus, concealing testimony is in fact concealing sin in one's conscience. Both matters relate to the depths of the heart and mind. Therefore the speech is concluded with a warning phrase, drawing attention to the fact that

"And He will reward and punish for hidden acts of the heart according to His knowledge."

The further emphasis on these instructions continues in the next verse as well. Hearts are stirred with the fear of the Master of the heavens and the earth, who is the true owner of all things in this universe, who knows all the secrets of the heart and is also aware of all outward matters, and who gives punishment and reward for all deeds. It is He who decides the affairs of all His servants: upon some His mercy descends, and some are seized by His punishment. He has power over everything, and everything is subject to His will, and the will of Allah is unrestricted.

The Qur'an has a distinctive style: even at the close of verses that are purely legislative, it gives purely moral and spiritual guidance. In this way it links the regulation of worldly life to the Creator of the universe. This connection is a firm one. On one side is the awareness of fear of God, and on the other is the hope of the forgiveness and mercy of the Master of the earth and the heavens. This moral guarantee is what the Islamic legal system possesses, and it is what distinguishes and sets it apart from other legal systems. In an Islamic society, a Muslim holds Islamic law in deep reverence in his heart. This moral guarantee and legislation run in parallel within Islamic society. Islam also makes arrangements for the moral training of those for whom it legislates. Furthermore, Islam also provides moral training for the society for which it legislates. And this work is based solely on the complete and balanced strategy of Allah, the Exalted. On one side, the moral training of individuals and society is taking place, and on the other, wise legislation for them is taking place. The fear of Allah and the fear of the law go hand in hand. For a human being, the law is that which the Creator of the human has prescribed for him. Therefore, how can the laws of the people of the earth, the regulations of the people of the world, and the systems of the earth's inhabitants function in comparison to it? How can the shallow thinking of man, the limited knowledge of man, and the restricted reasoning of man confront it? Human desires change from day to day. At times, people never agree on anything. No opinion of man attains stability and permanence. His information changes from day to day. In such circumstances, the condition of humanity is that, separated from its Creator, it wanders about aimlessly. Yet Allah is the One who created man. He knows the nature of what He has created, what its benefit is, and what its changing interests and needs are, moment by moment and place by place.

Humanity should know that it is a great misfortune for it to turn away from the Shariah of Allah and the way of life of Allah. Let it be remembered that the flight from and rebellion against the divine system of life began in the West at the time when the oppressive and rebellious Church was tried to be removed from the necks of the people. In the West, people rebelled against the Church's concept of God and the concept of deity, to which the Church called people. According to that concept, it was forbidden for people to reflect and to use reason. The Church had imposed heavy taxes on the masses in the West and had imposed on them a tyrannical and despotic system, which created intense hatred among the masses. When the people sought to free themselves from this oppression and despotism, they thought that unless they declared war against the Church, they could not gain freedom from this oppression and despotism. However, in this matter, the people of the West did not remain on the path of moderation. They did not suffice with gaining freedom from the people of the Church, but along with that, they also freed themselves from God and the sovereignty of God. In this way, they wiped off the face of the earth every religion whose call is that people should live according to Allah's system of life. The result of this was that a great catastrophe descended upon all of humanity, and mountains of calamities fell upon it.

As for us, who claim to be Muslims, our circumstances deserve reflection. Our condition is that we have adopted rebellion against the Islamic system of life. We have abandoned the Shariah of Allah and Islamic law. And our present condition exists despite the reality that our straightforward and natural religion has given us only those commands which lift from us all the burdens that Christianity had imposed. It has broken all the chains with which we were unjustly bound. This religion has treated us with extremely compassionate and merciful kindness, and has provided for us guidance, ease, and steadfastness. It has set us on a path that leads on every side to progress and reform, and on which there is nothing but success.

Lesson 22: An Overview

This lesson is the concluding section of this great surah. It is the longest surah of the Qur'an, and its expressions also carry a large volume of meaning. Within this length and extent, a large part of the Islamic conception of life has been gathered. Alongside discussion of the various aspects of the Islamic worldview, the surah contains full details about the various attributes of the Islamic community, its duties, its methods, and its policies regarding various matters on this earth. What is the role of the Muslim ummah in this whole universe? What is its stance regarding the opponents, adversaries and enemies of the Islamic system of life? What is the temperament of these enemies, and what are their resources in opposing the Islamic system? Furthermore, what means and resources is the Islamic community adopting against them, and by what means is it confronting their conspiracies? Besides these matters, the surah also tells us what role has been assigned to the human being himself on this earth as a whole, what is human nature, and what shortcomings and lapses has man committed in human history. These have been clarified by presenting historical narratives. In short, these and all the other matters whose details were explained in this lengthy surah.

This lesson is the conclusion of this lengthy surah, and though it consists of only two verses, these two verses have gathered within them all the themes and ideas that were discussed in this longest surah. These verses are indeed a fine conclusion to the surah, harmonious and proportionate with the whole surah, and suited to the purposes of the surah and the atmosphere of events within it.

The surah began with these words: "Alif, Lam, Mim. This is the Book of Allah. There is no doubt in it. It is guidance for the God-fearing who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them, and who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and who have certainty in the Hereafter."

In these words there are clear indications to the fact that the believers believe in all the messengers and all the books, and make no distinction between them. Now let us reflect on the words of this conclusion: "The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and the believers too. Each one believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers. They say: 'We make no distinction between any of His messengers.'" In short, this is a conclusion in the way that the two halves of a book's cover are joined together to each other.

In this surah a large part of the duties of the Muslim ummah has been described, and details of Islamic laws in various fields of life have also been given. Alongside this, it has also been explained in detail how the Children of Israel neglected their duties and how they turned away from the divine Shariah. Thus the verses of the conclusion make clear how duties are fulfilled and obedience to the Shariah is carried out, and why people fall short of their responsibilities and commit disobedience to the Shariah. It is also said that Allah does not wish to place any hardship upon the Muslim ummah, nor does He wish to load it with a heavy burden, nor does Allah have any special friendship with the Muslim ummah, as the Jews and Christians used to think that they were among Allah's special beloved ones; nor is the situation that Allah has neglected the Muslim ummah. Rather, the reality is: "Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. For it is what it has earned of good, and against it is what it has earned of evil."

This surah also narrates the stories of the Children of Israel. It describes the circumstances in which Allah showed His grace to that people at very difficult times, and it also mentions their denial and ingratitude in response to those blessings. Then the punishments are also mentioned which Allah gave them as expiation for their ingratitude, and these punishments extended even to the death penalty. Allah says: "So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves..." Regarding such circumstances, at the end of this same surah the believers are taught a prayer, that with humility and submission they seek refuge from such conditions as befell the Children of Israel. He says: "O you who believe, pray thus: 'Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err. Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy upon us.'"

In this surah Allah made fighting in the way of Allah obligatory upon the believers, and commanded them to strive in the path of Allah and to spend their wealth in His way, so that both disbelievers and disbelief could be countered. Thus at the end of the surah, in this prayer, they seek Allah's help to discharge all these responsibilities. They seek Allah's support against the enemy: "You are our Protector, so help us against the disbelieving people."

In short, this is the conclusion of this entire surah. In it the themes of the surah are summarized through indications, which are proportionate and parallel to the principal lines of the entire surah. Then every word of this conclusion, consisting of these two verses, carries wide meanings. Each word has its own subject and its own importance, and it points to the discussions that have passed behind it. These discussions are great discussions, concerning the Islamic worldview, and the importance of the Islamic worldview in the religion of Islam, its characteristics and its various aspects. They contain the details of the nature of the believers' relationship with their Lord, their conception of Allah, and the duties and responsibilities which Allah has imposed upon them. They supplicate that Allah may place them in the shelter of His mercy, that they may be subject to the Divine will, and that Allah's help may remain with them. In short, every word of this conclusion has its own great importance in its place. And whoever has lived his life in the shade of the Qur'an, and knows what is the manner of expression of the Qur'an and what are the secrets and mysteries of each of its verses, knows that each word of these has its own splendour and each word is a marvel... It is appropriate that we discuss these verses at some length.

These verses present an excellent portrait of the believers. This is the portrait of that chosen community in whose life the reality of faith was manifest in practice, and all the communities that come until the Resurrection will have these same features, in whose lives the reality of faith takes practical form. Allah honours this community of believers by joining their mention with the Messenger ﷺ in the attribute of faith. This is a great honour and distinction, because through this association the community of believers attains the reality of prophethood, and the Muslim community also gains the awareness of what its status and position on this earth is, it comes to feel what lofty rank it has been raised to by Allah. Thus Allah joins the believers with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the attribute of faith, so that the Messenger ﷺ and the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) all believed. The same attribute, in one and the same verse, and then in the words of Allah: "The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and the believers too; each one believes in Allah..."

The faith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in what is revealed to him is direct, because he is the recipient of revelation. Lofty revelation descends upon his pure heart, and his connection with the Supreme Reality is direct and unmediated. This is a reality which takes shape in the person of the Messenger himself, by his own essence, without acquisition or striving. There is no intermediary between the Messenger and the Divine Being, and the Messenger has no designs regarding his station of prophethood. Therefore, concerning the rank of faith, only the Messenger can reflect, and only one who has attained the rank of faith exactly as the Messenger ﷺ did can describe it and explain it. Thus this direct faith in the Divine Being and the Divine Word belongs solely to the Messenger. Now Allah, by making His servants share with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the attribute of faith, bestows upon them a kind of honour and distinction. Yet the reality of the attribute of faith in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the reality, essence and condition of all believers other than him, differ as far as heaven and earth. And what is the reality of this faith, and what are its boundaries? Allah says:

"Each one believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers. We make no distinction between any of His messengers. And they say: 'We hear and we obey. Our Lord, we seek Your forgiveness, and to You is the final return.'"

This is the complete faith which the religion of Islam has presented. This is faith worthy of which this ummah, which is the heir of this religion, should firmly hold on to it. It is the one who calls to this religion, and this call must be given by it to the whole world until the Resurrection. This call has its roots spread across the long valleys of history. Its caravans continue to move. These are the caravans of prophethood, and they are spread across the long history of humanity. It is this faith that, since the beginning of humanity, has divided human beings into two fronts: one front is that of the believers, and the other front is that of the disbelievers. One front belongs to the Party of Allah, and the other to the Party of Satan. And the whole of human history bears witness that apart from these there is no third front.

"Each one believes in Allah..." Belief in Allah is the cornerstone of the Islamic conception of life. It is the foundation of the system of life which gives stability to life. It is the basis of Islamic ethics, and upon it the Islamic economic system is established. And it is the foundation of every movement which a Muslim launches here or there.

And what is the meaning of faith in Allah? It is that Allah alone is the Ilah (God). He is the Lord; He alone deserves worship. He alone has the right to rule over the human conscience, over human conduct, and over every turn of human life. Therefore, He has no partner in His divinity. He has no partner in the guardianship of this world. He has no partner in the creation of this universe. He has no partner in running this universe. No one can interfere in His work in running this universe. No one is a participant in the running of this life. He has no partner in the provision of this creation. He has no partner in the benefit or harm of this creation. In short, whether a matter of this universe is great or small, it cannot reach completion except by His will and pleasure.

In the matter of worship and servitude He has no partner, so that people might turn towards anyone else. There is no partner in the rites of worship, no partner in obedience and servitude, and no partner in the religion. Therefore worship will be for Him alone, and obedience will be for Him alone, or for the one who works for Allah and implements His Shariah, and who derives his authority and sovereignty from Allah. For the Sovereign Authority is that Being alone. Therefore intellectual dominion over the masses, or dominion over their conduct, can be exercised only by the one who derives supreme authority for himself from the religion of Islam. Hence moral principles, the principles and rules of legislation, the principles of our collective system, and our economic principles, all of them can be derived only from the commands of the Divine Being and from His Being. This is the meaning of faith and its essence; this is the Islamic conception of life, by adopting which a person can be freed from the bonds and servitudes of other than Allah. He becomes free from all limits and restrictions except the Divine Shariah. Not only is he freed, but the human being comes to prevail over all powers other than the Divine Kingdom.

wa-malā'ikatihi... "and His angels." Belief in Allah's angels is one aspect of belief in the unseen (ghayb). At the beginning of this surah, that is in the first part, we have already discussed the effects that belief in the angels has on human life and what its benefits are. This belief raises a person above the lower level, which is confined to this world and is the distinguishing mark of animals. Through this belief the source of human knowledge and recognition goes beyond the senses, and a person rises above the level of an animal. In the same way, he declares that he is a human being and that his distinctive qualities are entirely separate. It is a natural demand of the human being that he has a desire to discover the unknown realities hidden behind the veil of the unseen. Although these realities lie beyond the sphere of his senses, a person, by the demand of his nature, senses their existence. If the unseen realities that Allah has bestowed are not placed before this natural urge and need of man, then this urge of man gets lost among human and religious mythologies and satisfies that natural demand. In this way he quenches a natural thirst, and if he does not fall into these superstitions and illusions, he becomes a victim of psychological confusions and anxieties.

Believing in the angels is also a reality that human understanding and perception cannot reach by itself, that is, solely on the strength of the sensory and rational faculties given to him. But by his nature, man possesses an intense desire to reach these unseen realities. Since Allah is the Creator of man, He is well acquainted with his structure and his inclinations. He also knows the matters that are beneficial to man and through which his reform can be well achieved. Therefore Allah, out of His mercy and compassion, informed man of some unseen realities, and through similitudes He sought to bring these unseen realities closer to his understanding and perception, because without similitudes man's present means of understanding were unable to perceive them directly. Thus Allah saved man from toil and hardship in seeking to know these realities through his own struggle, because by his own powers alone it was not possible for him. In this matter he was in need of divine knowledge and recognition. If these realities had not been told to him by Allah, his heart would never have been at peace and his personality would have been deprived of tranquility and stability. Those who wage war against their own nature and deny the unseen realities by their conception of life fall into such superstitions and delusions that one cannot help but laugh at them, or else they are afflicted with mental confusion and their lives become a victim of complications and ridiculous superstitions.

Belief in the angels is belief in unseen realities which, from the standpoint of reason and wisdom, are certain realities. Furthermore, these realities come from Allah, and as a result of believing in them the human consciousness about this universe is expanded. In the imagination of a believer, this world does not appear as shrunken as it is merely to the extent that it can be grasped by his senses, because human senses can control only a very small part of this universe. A person who believes in the angels also has a consciousness that, in his company and surrounding him, there are countless unseen believers who share with him the faith in their Lord, who constantly seek forgiveness for him, and who are his helpers and supporters in every good deed, if Allah wills. In short, it is a subtle and fresh sense of companionship which a believer always enjoys. In this way he obtains divine recognition of the unseen, which is granted to those who believe in Allah and believe in the angels.

wa-kutubihi wa-rusulihi, la nufarriqu bayna ahadin min rusulihi... "and His books and His messengers. We make no distinction between any of His messengers." The concept of faith in Allah that Islam has given has the natural consequence that we believe in all the books of Allah and all His messengers, and in this matter we do not discriminate between one messenger and another. This is because the demand of belief in Allah is that a person believes in all the realities that have come from Allah, and confirms all the messengers who were ever sent by Allah. Since the source is one, from which all these messengers came, and all the books that were revealed were revealed from one and the same Being, therefore, as a result of this concept of faith, there can be no difference or distinction in the station and status of the messengers in the mind of a Muslim. Every messenger was sent by Allah, Jalla Shanuhu, and he was sent in a form that was suitable to the circumstances of the people to whom that messenger was sent. This sequence continued in this way and finally ended with Hazrat Muhammad, Khatam al-Nabiyyin (ﷺ). The mission of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) took shape in such a form that it became a final and complete system of life for all humanity until the Day of Resurrection.

As a result of this concept of faith, the Muslim community was made the inheritor of the mission of all the messengers. Now the Islamic system of life is the inheritance of the Muslim community, and on this earth a great responsibility has been placed upon its shoulders. The believers are the bearers of Allah's authority; they will raise only the banner of Allah, and on the strength of that banner they will confront on this earth all the marks and signs of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). At one time this jahiliyyah raises the banner of territorial nationalism; at another time it advances in the guise of racial nationalism; at another time it comes in the colour of class; and at another time it comes in the imperialist form under the shadow of the flags of the Zionists and the Crusaders. At times it comes in the form of atheism and irreligion. In short, its colours and modes differ with the variation of time and place; at times it comes under one name and at times under another name or sign. But its standard-bearers are the same, namely, the worshippers of jahiliyyah.

The treasure that the Muslim community is entrusted with guarding on this earth, it has received from all the messengers who were sent to this earth from the most ancient times. And this treasure is a most precious treasure for all humanity. It is the treasure of guidance and light; it is the treasure of certainty and tranquility; it is the treasure of felicity and the pleasure of Allah; it is the treasure of knowledge and recognition. Be aware! A heart that is empty of this treasure will be a victim of darkness and grief; it will be afflicted with anxiety and confusion and will be seized by doubts and suspicions; it will be overwhelmed by misfortune and distress. Its life will pass just as a person wanders aimlessly in layer upon layer of darkness, in a barren desert, unable to see where to place his foot and where not to.

The cry and lamentation of such hearts is extremely painful. They have been deprived of the provision of the journey, by whom this precious treasure has been looted, and they have been deprived of such a sympathetic travelling companion. This painful cry and lamentation has been heard in every age of history, provided the hearts are alive, that they have feeling in them, and that they possess within themselves the urge for recognition of the truth and the attainment of certainty. As for those hearts that have died, that are dull, whose intellect is thick, and whose wellsprings of thought have dried up, it is possible that in them there is no such longing for the attainment of recognition, and they are indifferent to the attainment of knowledge. But on this earth, the way of life of such people is like that of beasts: they eat and drink like cattle. Their favourite pastime is to commit oppression and tyranny on this earth, to engage in bloodshed and violence, to spread corruption in this land, and to depart from it in such a way that they are cursed by all people and receive the curse of Allah.

Those societies are extremely wretched societies that have remained deprived of this wealth, even though they are immersed up to their necks in material comforts. These fallen societies are ruined and devastated, even though their graph of material production may be very high. These societies are miserable societies, even though they enjoy complete civil liberties, life internally is peaceful, and they face no external threat. In this modern age we have many examples of such societies, and only a person who is extremely cunning and so shameless as to be able to deny plain and evident realities could deny this.

As for the people of faith, their attribute is that they believe in Allah. They believe in His books and His messengers. They come into the presence of Allah with submission, contentment, hearing and obedience. They are certain that they will ultimately return to Allah. Therefore they constantly seek forgiveness for their shortcomings: wa-qalū samiʿnā wa-aṭaʿnā ghufrānaka rabbanā wa-ilayka al-maṣīr ("They say, 'We hear and we obey. Our Lord, we seek Your forgiveness, and to You is the return.'")

From these words, the effects of belief in Allah, in the angels, in the books, and in the messengers appear like light. Their manifestation takes the form of hearing and obedience. Whatever message comes to the people of faith from Allah, they listen to it, and they act upon every command that Allah gives. That is, Allah alone becomes their leader, and they carry out every signal of their leader. This is because there is no conception of Islam in which obedience to Allah's commands is absent, and in which the implementation of the divine system throughout the whole of life is not essential. If a society reaches the state where its people, in the small and large matters of their lives, have set out to disobey Allah, such a society cannot be called a society of believers. Or where Allah's Shariah is not enforced, and whose moral conceptions, whose conduct, whose social, economic and political affairs are all derived from non-Islamic conceptions, how can such a society be called an Islamic society? Therefore the essence of faith is that it settles in the heart of the believer and is confirmed through action.

Along with hearing and obedience, a person should also have full awareness of his shortcomings and failings. He should be certain that he cannot render the due thanks for Allah's blessings, and that he cannot fully discharge his duties. Therefore he entreats Allah that He may remedy his shortcomings through His mercy and forgiveness. Ghufrānaka rabbanā ("O our Lord, we seek Your forgiveness").

It is noteworthy that the station of seeking forgiveness for one's shortcomings comes after hearing and obedience and complete submission before Allah. Before this, complete compliance without any disobedience and without any denial is necessary. Only after this can a person develop the certainty that he is to return to Allah, both in this world and in the Hereafter. In all his actions and dealings, and in every deed, he will have to answer before Allah, and Allah's judgment in that matter will then be irrevocable. Apart from Him there will be no place of refuge; there is no power that can save one against Him. Nothing except His forgiveness can save one from His decision and command; only His mercy can be of use.

wa-ilayka al-maṣīr ("And to You is the return"). In these words the belief in the Hereafter is expressed. Among the requirements of belief in Allah, one clear requirement is belief in the Hereafter; in the Islamic conception of life these are inseparable. The summary of this conception of life is that Allah created man and, under a covenant, made him His khalifah (vicegerent) on earth. This covenant, with its conditions contained within it, encompasses the whole life of man on this earth. Allah has appointed him as khalifah here for the purpose that, during the life of this world, He may test him, and after the final test He may reward or punish him in the Hereafter. Therefore, according to the Islamic conception of life, belief in the Hereafter is one of the important requirements among the essential demands of faith. Believing in it has profound effects on the thoughts of a believer and Muslim and on his conduct. In the light of this faith, the values of life of a believer in this world are formed, and its tangible results follow. He walks as an obedient servant; he walks on the path of goodness; he seeks goodness and remains steadfast upon truth, whether its outcome in this world brings him comfort or hardship, whether he gains or loses in this world, whether he is victorious or defeated, whether he is acquiring something or losing something, whether he is granted life here or is granted martyrdom. This is because his real reward will be received on the Day of Judgment, when he will be successful and triumphant in the test of this world. His resolve is so firm that from his path of obedience, the path of truth, the path of righteousness and the path of sincerity, neither the opposition of the entire world, nor the mischief-making of the entire world, nor its strife and killing can turn him back, because his affair is with Allah. He is implementing the covenant of "Alastu" with all its conditions, and he seeks his recompense in the Hereafter.

This is one great unity. Such is the temperament of the Islamic worldview, and it has been encompassed in this brief verse: belief in Allah and the angels; belief in all the books and all the messengers without distinction or discrimination; complete return to Allah with hearing and obedience; and belief in accountability on the Day of Judgment together with a constant awareness of it.

This is Islam: the creed that is the seal of all creeds, the final message. It is a creed that carries the caravan of the believers along with it from the dawn of humanity to the end of humanity. The direction of its journey through the whole of human history is set by the Messengers of Allah, under whose leadership humanity advances step by step through the stages of progress. This creed introduces man to the greatest order of this universe, to the extent of his capacity. Finally there comes the Islamic system of life, which proclaims Tawhid (the oneness of Allah), and the human intellect is left free so that it may now advance on its own in the recognition of the Lord.

This is the way of life that makes a human being aware of his humanity. It raises him above the level of inanimate matter and animals. It gives him a distinct identity even from the angels and the devils. It acknowledges man as man. It accepts his weaknesses and also takes into account his capabilities. It takes him as a creature whose body has various kinds of inclinations. He possesses an active intellect. He has a soul whose inclinations are varied. Therefore it imposes on him only those duties and obligations which this body, this human being, and his personality can bear. This creed maintains the best balance between these duties and the capacity and strength of man. It places such a burden that man does not feel exertion or fatigue. This creed fulfils the physical demands of man. It also takes care of his intellectual demands, and it populates his spiritual world as well. And all of this is done with a most natural balance; and after all these matters, it grants man the freedom to choose whatever path he adopts for himself.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 2, verse 286 (part 1 of 2):

For a Muslim, it is part of his very outlook that his Lord is Merciful, and that the duties and obligations which He imposes upon him, as the Master, are extremely just and equitable. The trials He sends are also just, and ultimately on the Day of Resurrection he will be dealt with with complete justice. And he will be fully content. Therefore, he does not feel any hardship or difficulty in the duties imposed by Allah. He does not consider them a burden. This is because he has the firm conviction that the Allah who has imposed these duties knows well that the capacity to perform them actually exists within him. Had he not had the strength, He would not have made them obligatory. This concept fills the heart of the believer with tranquillity, love and affection, and on the other hand it creates within him resolve and enthusiasm to perform these duties and obligations. He feels that since Allah the Exalted has placed these duties upon him, they are inevitably part of his responsibility. And whenever he feels weakness, sometimes exhaustion, and the duties begin to feel heavy, he regards this as his own personal weakness; the burden is not too great. Thus he renews his resolve, removes his weakness, and again firmly resolves to fulfil the duties for as long as he is able to do so. The renewing of resolve is, for the believer, a sign that if the path becomes long, he should renew his resolve. Thus the concept becomes a spur for the soul of the believer and his manly courage, and in this way his determination and his will become firm. Therefore he understands that whatever there is, it is from Allah the Exalted.

The second important part of this conception of life is: "لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا اكْتَسَبَتْ" ("For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has earned"): "Every soul earns only for itself, and it bears the burden of its own deeds."

Every individual is responsible for his own deeds. Therefore he will receive only what he himself earned. Likewise, punishment will be given to anyone only for the crime that he himself commits. Everyone will be responsible for his own deeds. Every person will come before his Lord carrying his own record of deeds, and in it will be exactly what he earned and what he committed. No one will be able to make excuses there, nor will anyone there hope for another's help or intercession. Man, as an individual, will stand before his Lord.

When this concept of individual responsibility settles in the heart of a believer, every individual becomes responsible for the rights of Allah which are attached to him. He does not give up these rights of Allah in any circumstance because of other human beings, except where giving them up is in accordance with the Shariah. Now, regarding the rights of Allah attached to the person of the believer, he stands firm against every deception, every transgression of limits, every misguidance and every corruption. This is because he is personally accountable for his own self and the rights of Allah attached to it. And the rights of Allah attached to every soul are only those which Allah has commanded or those from which He has forbidden. That is, every individual, in his conduct and in his consciousness, should worship Allah alone. If he falls short in these rights because of some human being, for example if someone misguides him, deceives him, or compels him, then the result will be that on the Day of Resurrection those people will not be able to help this believer. (However, if he commits this disobedience under compulsion while his heart remains content with the Islamic duties and rights, then he will be considered excused.) In short, such persons will neither be able to defend this believer on the Day of Resurrection, nor to intercede, nor will they be in a position to lift his burden or bear it themselves.

The result of this personal concept of responsibility is that every person, with great courage, defends himself and the rights of Allah attached to him, because the punishment for it will fall only upon him, and he himself will be responsible for his deeds. It should be remembered that the theory of individual responsibility does not mean the danger that anyone should neglect fulfilling his collective responsibilities within society. This is because the collective responsibilities too have been placed by the Shariah upon an individual as an individual. If collective responsibilities are not fulfilled in society, the individual will still be responsible, because these too have been placed upon him individually by Allah. For example, every individual is commanded by Allah to fulfil the collective obligation from his wealth and his riches. Furthermore, he has also been commanded to enjoin upon others *tawasi bil-haqq* (mutual advice to truth), to establish justice and equity in society, to strive to eradicate falsehood from his society, to strengthen truth and goodness in society, and to uproot evil and what is reprehensible from its very root. In his record of deeds, all his performances and shortcomings regarding collective affairs too will be recorded, and he will be individually responsible for, or deserving of, reward and punishment.

When the believers heard and understood the command of individual responsibility, then from their hearts came this supplication, which is very comprehensive and full of sincerity. The Qur'an describes this supplication in its own particular style of depiction. It appears as if the believers, with hands raised, stand before us. They have formed rows, and with humility and submission they are reciting this supplication. (Especially upon attaining the reality of duties and responsibilities.)

This is such a supplication which vividly depicts the believers and their relationship with their Lord. They have a deep awareness of their helplessness and weakness. They find themselves in need of their Lord's mercy and forgiveness. They seek refuge at His court. They surrender themselves to Allah alone, they attach themselves to Him and sever their ties with all besides Allah. They are ready for jihad in His path, and they seek His help alone. And their supplication is in the form of a deeply moving and mournful melody, in whose vocal rise and fall the throbbing of their hearts and the restlessness of their souls is clearly heard and clearly seen.

رَبَّنَا لا تُؤَاخِذْنَا إِنْ نَسِينَا أَوْ أَخْطَأْنَا
"Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make errors." 

If a person becomes so weak that such a lapse occurs, in which he has no hand, and such forgetfulness occasionally does happen, then such mistakes come under the ruling of error and forgetfulness. For a believer, the correct course regarding them is to seek forgiveness from Allah immediately and turn towards his Lord. Forgetfulness is that in which a person does not persist in the error, or does not deliberately disobey, or does not disobey out of arrogance and pride, or does not walk deliberately on a crooked path. In these circumstances, none of the situations is what a believer adopts before his Lord. Nor in such circumstances will he deserve pardon and forgiveness from Allah. Yes, it is another matter that he repents and turns sincerely to Allah. In short, the request for forgiveness which the believers made regarding forgetfulness has been accepted by Allah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There will be no blame upon my Ummah for error and forgetfulness, so long as they regarded such acts as wrong." (Tabarani and others)

رَبَّنَا وَلا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَا إِصْرًا كَمَا حَمَلْتَهُ عَلَى الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِنَا
"Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us."

This supplication comes upon the tongue of the believing man because of the sense of responsibility that has been placed upon the Muslim Ummah regarding the messengerhood of all the Messengers. This Ummah has come under the trust of all the messengerships. As their Lord has shown this Ummah repeatedly in this Qur'an, what treatment those nations to whom messengers were sent before them gave to their messengers, and what burdens were placed upon those nations because of their disobedience. And these burdens were placed upon them because of some of their crimes. For example, because of some evil deeds of the Children of Israel, some good, pure foods were made unlawful for them. Allah the Exalted says: "And upon those who followed Judaism We made unlawful every animal with claws, and of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat, except what is on their backs or their entrails or what is mixed with bone." (6:146) Or as in Surah al-Baqarah, when they began worshipping the calf, and Allah commanded them to kill one another, so that their wrongdoing might be expiated. Upon them trade and hunting on the Sabbath were made forbidden. For this reason, the believers are taught here a supplication, that they should raise their hands in prayer that Allah does not lay upon them the burdens that were laid upon those before them. This is because the very purpose of the advent of the Final Prophet is that through him he removes from the believers and from all humanity the burdens that were placed upon humanity, and breaks the chains with which humanity was unnecessarily bound, and as a result the Islamic way of life came as a simple and straightforward system, which is both easy and gentle.

In complete accord with human nature, it walks hand in hand with the innate disposition, and this is why Allah the Exalted said to the Messenger ﷺ: "وَنُیَسِّرُکَ لِلیُسرٰی" ("And We shall ease you towards ease") "And We will guide you with ease towards easy duties."

What is that great burden which was placed upon the earlier peoples, and was placed because they violated their covenant as vicegerents of Allah on earth and broke their pledge? And that great burden which has now been lifted from the shoulders of the Muslim Ummah: the question is, what is it and what is its nature? This great burden is the burden of the enslavement of man to man, in which one servant becomes the slave of another, in which one human being becomes the code of life for another human being. In this way one section of humanity becomes subject to the person of another, or humans become slaves to a class, or humans become slaves to a race. This is that great burden from which Allah the Exalted freed the believers. He delivered them from all these enslavements and admitted them solely into His servitude, slavery and obedience. After this liberation, the believers began to take their code of life from Allah alone. Thus, by bringing them into the servitude of the One Allah alone, their spirits, their intellects and their entire lives were freed from the servitude of other human beings.

The servitude and slavery of Allah, Glorified is His Majesty, in the sense that a person takes his values of life, the standard of good and evil, and the laws of collective life solely from Allah, is the starting point of freedom for all humanity. In this way a person is freed from the slavery and servitude of other tyrannical and domineering human beings. Likewise, he is freed from the slavery of religious priests, clerics and leaders. Moreover, a person is freed from the bonds of superstitions, myths, customs and traditions, and, most importantly, a person is freed from the bonds of the desires of the self and the physical appetites and cravings. A person is liberated from every lost slavery which is unjustly mounted upon human shoulders, and history bears witness that such slaveries had broken the backs of human beings, and because of which people's heads bowed before other tyrants in the face of Allah, the One, the Subduer.

رَبَّنَا وَلا تُحَمِّلْنَا مَا لا طَاقَةَ لَنَا بِهِ
"Our Lord, burden us not with that which we have no strength to bear."

Through this supplication there is expressed the awareness of the believers that they have now been freed from human slavery. Moreover, they are fearful that through their shortcomings they might return to slavery again, which was a most evil era.

"Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear" is a supplication through which the reality of complete submission is expressed. From the hearts of the believers the very intention and resolve to oppose the commands of God has now departed. Whatever the commands may be, they present only this petition: that they are weak. They hope that in the enforcement of commands, their condition will be taken into consideration. "Our Lord, have mercy upon us and protect us from burdens beyond our capacity, so that in fulfilling the commands there may be no incapacity or shortfall. Otherwise, they have firmly resolved to demonstrate complete submission and obedience." The sole hope of the weak servant is that the King of kingdoms will show kindness to them, and that the same treatment which He is accustomed to show His servants, of generosity, gentleness and love, will continue to be extended to us. We acknowledge our shortcomings, and those shortcomings can be forgiven and rendered ineffective only when the grace of Allah is with us.

وَاعْفُ عَنَّا وَاغْفِرْ لَنَا وَارْحَمْنَا
"Be gentle with us, forgive us, and have mercy upon us."

Because the only guarantee of success in this trial is that Allah's pleasure can be obtained only in this way: however diligently a person may be faithful, some deficiency remains in his work, and if the grace of Allah is not with him, He will deal with him through pardon, forgiveness and gentle mercy. Hadrat Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) narrates that she said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds alone." The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) asked: "O Messenger of Allah, not even you?" The Messenger ﷺ said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy."

This is the essential point in the perception of a true believer. He acts to the best of his ability, yet he is fully aware of his shortcomings. After that, he has complete hope that Allah will pardon his shortcomings, and that he will be treated with gentleness.

All at the end, the believers hold fast to the firm support of Allah: they prepare themselves for jihad fi sabilillah (struggle in the way of Allah). This is because it is Allah's will that the truth should prevail, that the religion of Islam and the Islamic system of life should dominate on this earth, and that the situation should be such that "there is no more fitnah (strife, disorder) and the religion is entirely for Allah." Now the believers take hold of the firm support of Allah. They raise the banners of Islam over their heads. They identify themselves only by these banners, whereas the symbols and banners of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) are very different. Now they seek the help of Allah the Exalted, because He alone is their Protector and their Heir. They fight the disbelievers only for the sake of Allah, those who stand outside the religion of Islam.

﴿Anta Mawlana, fansurna ala al-qawmi al-kafirin﴾ (286)

"You are our Protector; so help us against the disbelieving people."

This is the conclusion of this great surah, in which the themes of the whole surah are summarized. In this summary, the outline of the Islamic conception of life is stated, and it is explained what the relationship of a true believer with his Lord is in every circumstance.
